<header>OF THE CITY OF JAMATHAY, ALIAS JANSU 361</header>

In this city sits one of the twelve barons of the great Kaan, for it is chosen for one of the twelve sages. They are idolaters. Their money is made of paper and belongs to the great Kaan, and Messire Marco Polo himself, the one of whom this book treats, governed this city for three years. They live by merchandise and arts, for there they make armor for knights and men-at-arms in very great quantity: for I tell you truly that in this city and around its appurtenances dwell many men-at-arms. There is no other thing worth mentioning. We shall depart from here and will tell you of the two great provinces that are of Cathay itself; they are toward the West, and because there is much to tell, we will tell you about them, all their customs and their usage, and we will tell of the one that is called Nanghin." (Ed. Soc. Géog., p. 160.)

Mandeville, who follows Odoric, tells us that upon leaving the island of the Pygmies:

"One enters into the Kingdom of Janchan, which contains 12 Provinces, in which one divides the entire Empire of the Tartars; one names the Capital of this Kingdom Janchan; it is a very rich merchant city, & which pays large sums to its King: for they say themselves that they give fifty thousand <term>Cumans</term> <gloss>a unit of currency equal to 10,000 pieces</gloss> in gold florins. There is in the city of Janchan a convent of Friars Minor, & three Churches, whose revenue is 12 <term>Cumans</term>; one <term>Cuman</term> is ten thousand pieces; & the annual tribute is fifty times fifty thousand pieces: for that is precisely the sum which is contained in one <term>Cuman</term>: & five leagues from this city there is another called Méke, where from a whitish wood, they make vessels that resemble Palaces, so many are the rooms." (Bergeron, col. 17.)

"When one has passed the river Kiang, one encounters a very large lock near the Castle of Quacheu, where begins a hand-made canal, upon which one comes into this city of Yangcheu. It is very mercantile, very populous & of great approach: the Emperor has there an office of very great revenue; & although it has every sort of merchandise, yet it is that its principal 
</translation>

riches come to it from the distribution of salt; for there are many saltworks toward the East of the city, where salt is made from sea water, just as in several places in Europe. There is a great number of very rich merchants, who resell this salt in the Provinces, which are at the heart & in the middle of the Empire, & who have embellished this city with buildings very large & very superb. Freshwater canals cut & divide this city into several quarters, with twenty-four stone bridges with several arches, without speaking of others that are smaller & in greater number. To the west & outside the city there is an artificial canal that separates the city from the suburb, it was a good German league: it was entirely burned in this last war against the Tartars." (Martini, Thévenot, II, p. 129).

The Fathers Bouvet, Fontaney, Gerbillon, Le Comte, and Visdelou, going from Ningpo to Peking by the Grand Canal route, pass through Hang-tcheou and Yang-tcheou. # VOMITING

Vomiting is sometimes required by a bad mixture of humors <term>cacochymia</term> <gloss>morbid state of the fluids</gloss> collected around the stomach, pancreas, and spleen, which is more vigorous; and here the "Manna of Vomiters," liquefied salt of antimony, also corrected glass of antimony, and wormwood crocus of metals are excellent.

Take of:
Crocus of metals, four grains.
Water of blessed thistle, one ounce and a half.
Scelotyrbic syrup, half a dram.
Mix and infuse through the night,
in the morning strain through blotting paper,
and mix into the strained liquid.
Syrup of cinnamon, three drams.
Sign: Draught for vomiting.

<column-break/>

Take of:
Cream of mercury, half a scruple.
Corrected glass of antimony, two grains.
Mix with
Conserve of Spanish sorrel, two drams.
Let it be given in a small vial.
Sign: Vomiting sugar.
To be followed by warm broth.

---

# SWEATS

Through sweats, nature sometimes disperses the accumulation of humors of its own accord. This movement must be assisted and promoted, and the remains clinging in the center and periphery of the body must be dispersed through <term>adelos diapnoe</term> <gloss>imperceptible perspiration</gloss> and sweat. Mineral, antimonial, and jovial <term>bezoardic</term> <gloss>antidotal/counter-poison</gloss> agents are appropriate here. A decoction of holy wood <note>guaiacum</note>, sassafras, and sarsaparilla with specific additives is most suitable. Salt of wormwood and blessed thistle. A simple or compound antiscorbutic mixture with essences, spirits of scurvygrass, hartshorn, and holy wood, and antiscorbutic syrups is very beneficial. Sweat should be induced in bed twice every week on an empty stomach.

Take of:
Shavings of guaiacum wood, one ounce and a half.
Sarsaparilla.
Sassafras, six ounces each.
Boil with a sufficient quantity of spring water down to half.
In the morning, in six ounces of the strained liquid,
dissolve:
Salt of wormwood, one scruple.
Magistery of hartshorn, half a dram.
Syrup of blessed thistle.
Sorrel, citron, three drams each.
Spirit of liquefied salt, one dram.
Mix. Sign: Sweat-inducing draught for several doses.

<column-break/>

Take of:
Simple mixture, half a dram.
Syrup of germander, one ounce and a half.
Essence of scurvygrass.
Watercress.
Fumitory, half a scruple each.
Wine of blessed thistle, one dram and a half.
Mix. Sign: Sweat essence.
To be taken with a draught of wine.
Take of:
Diaphoretic antimony, six grains.
Coral-shaped flowers of sal ammoniac, two grains.
Oriental bezoar stone, one grain.
A little pearled sugar.
Mix. Sign: Sweating powder.

An <term>anopseis</term> <gloss>a cleaning/clearing out</gloss> is highly necessary here, and it can be accomplished through continued use

### To the same.

The nurturing <term>Themis</term> <gloss>Goddess of divine law</gloss> never watches over those with gentle eyes
    Who, having barely tasted the sweetness of wisdom,
Run through the open fields of <term>Astræa</term> <gloss>Goddess of justice</gloss>, with an immature effort
Scrutinizing what <term>Baldus</term> <gloss>medieval legal scholar</gloss> holds, or what <term>Bartolus</term> <gloss>medieval legal scholar</gloss> says; as if it were enough,

    With this perhaps sagacious spirit, my good friend Dietschi,
You will weigh matters, while you touch more closely the face
Of divine <term>Minerva</term> <gloss>Goddess of wisdom</gloss>, while you learn to compose
The customs of human associations, the best foundations of civil life.

## ANOTHER.

Therefore, diligent cultivator of the nine Sisters <note>i.e., the Muses</note>,
    Do you ask to hold a place among men?
Since you dare to contend for the highest of Goods,
    And you do not hesitate to climb the learned pulpits of the wise.
The great <term>Aristotle</term>, the wise <term>Plato</term>, <term>Epicurus</term>,
    Teach charming writings, whatever anyone may say.
Each one preferred his own opinion to the deeds of the others:
    I can recount as many views as there are days in the world!
One tends toward shining riches, another finally,
    A part rejoices in having praise and the good of luxury.
You defend in your <term>theses</term> <gloss>propositions</gloss> what the true opinion is.
    You propose your themes to be discussed.

</translation>
<translation page="23">

Thus it is fitting to reach the desired middle path,
And to reconcile a new member to <term>Themis</term>.
See how much better it is than just living, to live happily,

Proceed with your tasks, but proceed to sacrifice to the Muses,
This <term>Summum</term> <gloss>Highest Good</gloss>, Dietschi, will bring the highest rewards.
Proceed to stand as you do, most learned of the youth;
Thus your praise and your honor will endure. I PRAY.

## ANOTHER.

He who seeks the arduous monuments of the ancient Wise Men
And breathes in the secret riches therefrom:
He attempts the steep heights of virtue, and begins
To raise his head out of the vast clouds.
<term>Ethics</term>, my Dietschi, now promises you <term>λήμματα</term> <gloss>premisses/assumptions</gloss>, which open to all
The highest peaks of the highest good.
A great work, and one not of mediocre study nor of a single hour,
Which holds all the points of celebrated praise.
For the highest good (believe me) is the most welcome port
Which lifts all the tedium of exhausted evil.
It is the most welcome <term>cynosura</term> <gloss>guiding star/North Star</gloss> of our life,
Which directs the doubtful raft on the straight river of life.
Press on, Dietschi, to finish the web you have begun,
And loosen the <term>Sophism</term> <gloss>fallacious argument</gloss> with its varied twists.
A joyful fortune promises you a benign countenance
And brings bright fates to your studies.

->*Nicolaus Crappius of Eisfeld, Franconian.*<-

<translation page="12">it is the creator and governess of distinguished things, without whose usefulness there is no knowledge. And just as we desire that the keels or foundations of a ship and other things be the first and most firm, since otherwise nothing subsists solidly, and those things that have grown without foundations are prone to ruin; so too, whatever part of human action is built up without piety perishes in a moment. This is most salutary for the Republic, it is a friend to parents, pleasing to God; it conciliates the Lord and fosters close relationships. This is the cultivation of God, the reward of parents, the stipend of children. Who, by the immortal God, will give me a man more upright than this our John? For he measured everything he did by piety; with the broadest spirit and spread sails he aspired to that same <term>cynosura</term> <gloss>guiding star</gloss>, he followed it with a divine breeze, he directed his helm toward this as a goal and port in this ocean of life, he turned his prow, very well aware that if this helm of piety were retained, he would never suffer shipwreck among various and dangerous twists and turns and the cliffs of misfortune, but would reach the port with full sails. To offer sacrifice to this better, fleeing the company of the wicked, he lived his life in deserts, where he was occupied with prayers, with unfolding prophecies concerning the future Messiah, and with every office of piety. Piety urged him to prefer horrid solitudes and a very poor life to the cultivated city of Jerusalem and the banquets of the Pharisees, in which he could have held the first place everywhere. Piety applied the torch so that he would scorn the offices and honors which they were vying to confer upon him. Piety caused him to obey God rather than men; piety caused it, nor was constancy lacking; for when there were many whom—the true way having been abandoned—gifts, or a force of silver and gold, or even fear and threats, snatched into the fork of errors, he alone in public sicknesses, in the waves and darkness, while others were wavering or blinded,</translation>

<translation page="13">standing firm and pushing back, was not moved from his course by the storm of danger or by the breeze of honor, neither by hope nor fear. Furthermore, he embraced humility with both arms, as they say, of which he gave illustrious proofs. <summary>This text explores legal debates surrounding primogeniture, specifically addressing the rights of heirs when disinherited, the inheritance of kingdoms by firstborn females versus males, the validity of custom versus statute, and whether a nephew or a paternal uncle has a stronger claim to succession.</summary>

<translation page="8">If [a father] has disinherited the firstborn, the right of primogeniture will not stand, and this [leads to the] first [question]: if the son denies that the cause [for disinheritance] is true, on whom does the burden of proof lie? I answer that he can, according to Baldus in the first chapter, paragraph "Furthermore," concerning who loses a fief, and Hostiensis feels in the said chapter "Although" that it is limited according to the mind of Baldus in the said paragraph "Furthermore," provided the firstborn is older than twenty-five years, as if Baldus feels that if he is younger, the renunciation is not valid or he will have the benefit of restitution in full as one injured. pages.8:
If [a father] has disinherited the firstborn, the right of primogeniture will not stand, and this [leads to the] first [question]: if the son denies that the cause [for disinheritance] is true, on whom does the burden of proof lie? I think one should not rely on the first statement; rather, the adversary of the firstborn ought to prove that the cause is true, as is fully noted in the <term>authenticis</term> <gloss>the Novellae constitutions of Justinian</gloss> "It is not permitted" and in the <term>authenticis</term> "Concerning free [persons]," and later or he disinherits. I consider what remedy the disinherited son has in the right of primogeniture. I answer: he brings this complaint or acts for the supplement [of his portion] if any part was established for him, and that supplement will be the entire kingdom as if it were indivisible, according to Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae in the said chapter "Although," where Hostiensis notably says that the entire kingdom in the right of primogeniture is the legitimate portion of the sons, if the kingdom were of inestimable value, because the kingdom is indivisible. And if we do not attend to the entire legitimate portion in the kingdom, hence the civil law, about which [one reads] in the <term>authenticis</term> "Concerning thirds and halves," in the first column. Does the right of primogeniture in a kingdom yield to the firstborn who has become a monk? I answer no, according to Baldus in the chapter "When into him," concerning election; rather, the right of primogeniture passes to the second-born, or if the brothers of the firstborn do not exist, the magnates of the kingdom shall elect a king, who will be confirmed by the Pope or Emperor, according to this [same] Baldus in the said chapter "When too much," and it is relevant to the chapter "First," concerning soldiers and vassals who [have] war weapons from power, and the chapter "If a cleric," if there is controversy concerning fiefs. I ask whether the firstborn can renounce the right of primogeniture so that the second-born succeeds. I answer that he can, according to Baldus in the first chapter, paragraph "Furthermore," concerning who loses a fief, and Hostiensis feels in the said chapter "Although" that it is limited according to the mind of Baldus in the said paragraph "Furthermore," provided the firstborn is older than twenty-five years, as if Baldus feels that if he is younger, the renunciation is not valid or he will have the benefit of restitution in full as one injured. Limit this saying of Baldus: unless the minor of twenty-five years who has reached puberty has sworn and affirmed the renunciation [under] the <term>authentica</term> "The oaths of those at puberty," Codex "If against [a transaction]." Can the right of primogeniture be sold? I answer yes, according to the mind of Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae in the said chapter "Although." Lastly, I ask whether the firstborn is bound to assign some goods from which his other brothers can lead a life honorably. I answer yes, inspecting the quality of the persons and the quantity of the kingdom, according to Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae in the said chapter "Although," which saying I limit to be true unless said other brothers have [means] from elsewhere from which they can lead an honorable life, as in the law "If anyone from children," in the gloss on the word "of children," Digest "Concerning acknowledging children," and failing the reason, it ceases.

[And] Johannes Andreae in the said chapter "Although," we saw in the above that the firstborn daughter does not succeed in the way of primogeniture in kingdoms. But it remains harsh [the question] concerning a male son born from the said daughter, whether he succeeds in the right of primogeniture in kingdoms. I answer that he does not, by the text in the law "If alive," Codex "Concerning maternal goods," where [it says] that what is not conceded to the root, that is the mother, is not ceded to the descendants from her, and so Baldus determines in the law [in the] Digest "Concerning senators," which things they do [regarding] the question [which] flourishes between the King of France and the King of England, as Baldus says in the said first law. I ask if by statute or custom it is provided that the firstborn succeeds in feudal goods, whether it extends to non-feudal goods. I answer no, according to Baldus in the law "All peoples," in the fourth [paragraph] concerning justice and law. I ask if there is a statute in England that the firstborn succeeds, whether such a custom or statute extends to goods existing in Lombardy. Baldus in the law "All peoples," law "All" [concerning] the most holy Trinity and the Catholic faith, concluding, says: one must ask first, whether such a custom is valid. Second, supposing the validity of the custom, what [is the] law in a case where a will is made. Third, what [is the] law in an intestate case. Concerning the first, Baldus says the custom is valid provided they furnish sustenance to the other brothers, which article I spoke of fully above. Concerning the second article, let us give an example: an Englishman made a will and a statute [giving] to the firstborn [the] English goods, which is an institution there, [asking if it] draws to goods situated elsewhere, for example in Lombardy. Baldus answers that it draws to goods situated elsewhere, whether he died having made a will by all common law in the fatherland, or by the third [law], or by the singular law of the statute-maker, for example in the fatherland two [governed] by law, by fact, he posited [in] the Digest "Concerning establishing heirs," with system. Concerning the third saying, let us give an example: the law [applies] in a case of the intestate. An Englishman having goods in England and in Lombardy died leaving three sons; it is asked whether the firstborn, regarding all goods, excludes his brothers, given the custom in England that the firstborn succeeds with the brothers excluded. In this article, the doctors conclude, especially Lyra, Guilielmus, Bartolus, and Baldus in the said law "All peoples," that this custom is not extended to goods situated elsewhere after the law "Pupil," Digest "Concerning tutors and curators given by them." And thus, regarding goods existing in England, only the firstborn succeeds, but regarding goods existing in Lombardy, in which such a custom does not flourish, all sons succeed in succession, Codex "Concerning one's own [heirs] and legitimate [heirs]." But it is more beautiful to see and ask, given a custom which speaks in the person in this way: that the firstborn only succeeds, whether a foreigner dying intestate in a place in which such a custom flourishes, and having goods, whether the firstborn succeeds in whole in said goods. Bartolus answers in the said law "All peoples" that such a custom will not have place, since all sons succeed equally. The reason is that wherever a statute speaks in the person by enabling or disabling, it certainly does not bind a foreigner, law second in the end, Digest "Concerning tutors and curators given by them," with system; therefore, when he was dying there, he will not be bound by such a custom. It is otherwise if the custom spoke in the thing, for example if goods come to the firstborn, it would bind even a foreigner regarding goods which the statute could bind, [as per] the law "Rescript," final paragraph, Digest "Concerning duties and honors," law "Whether in whole," Codex "Concerning private buildings," and it is noted in Codex "If concerning custom," and in the law "Concerning which," Digest "Concerning laws," and so determines Bartolus in the said law "All peoples." From which you have that the words of the statute or custom are to be weighed diligently, whether they speak in the thing or in the person, similar in the law "Or which to another," paragraph "If," Digest "Concerning what is done by force or fear." [There is a] beautiful doubt: whether the custom of primogeniture binds a cleric. And lest the matter lack examples, let us propose a father dying, leaving a firstborn layman and a second-born cleric. It is asked whether the firstborn excludes the second-born cleric by virtue of the custom of primogeniture. Hostiensis in the chapter "Concerning many," final paragraph, where [he mentions] "according to the position" in his <term>Summa</term> <gloss>a summary or manual of canon law</gloss>, says the custom does not bind clerics. And Albericus in the law "With which," Codex "Concerning natural children," follows Hostiensis, for Hostiensis makes [the argument] that the truth or custom of laymen does not bind a cleric, chapter "Of the church of Saint Mary," concerning Hostiensis, with system. To the contrary, Johannes Andreae determines in "Mercurials without fault," concerning rules of law, book six, which [the] moderns follow, especially Angelus de Ubaldis in the chapter "That to clerics," concerning the competent forum, where they conclude that if the custom of the right of primogeniture was [in force] before the second-born became a cleric, it certainly excludes the second-born cleric from succession. And the reason is that it is equitable that what a cleric receives by himself, he ought also to receive by himself, chapter "If," concerning force and the honor of clerics, law first, Digest "What each [man's] right," according to [which] a cleric firstborn receives by himself by the said custom, excluding the second-born layman; therefore, [he ought] to receive by himself so that it is equal, so that the firstborn layman by virtue of the said custom excludes the second-born cleric. Also, it makes [the case] that even the sacrament of matrimony or baptism does not take away the right of another acquired [by] the rule "That which is ours," and it is noted in the chapter "How much," in the last gloss, concerning divorces; therefore, neither does the order of the clerics take away the right to the firstborn already acquired by the firstborn by virtue of the custom. But if the second-born [was] a cleric before the custom was introduced, then he would not be bound by such a custom, the reason ceasing, as is asked above, and so he understands the opposition of Hostiensis in the said paragraph. But Johannes Andreae in the said "Mercurial without fault," and according to Angelus de Ubaldis in the said chapter "That to clerics," who says he consulted [regarding a case] concerning [the] Achaei, when it was established that a male excludes a female, certainly a female monk would be excluded from succession while a male exists by virtue of the said statute, unless the statute was edited after she was born, because then it would bind [her] by such a statute that was established after she was born. Again, let us propose some Count had a son, then he is made king; afterwards, he being king, a son is born. It is asked now whether the first son who was born before the father was king is called the son of the king, or whether he succeeds to the kingdom. I answer, according to the gloss and Lyra in the law "Imperial," Codex "Concerning marriages," that the second-born succeeds and he will be called king, but not the firstborn at the time when the father was count; on which article [see] also Albericus in the law "Senators," Digest "Concerning senators," law "Emancipated," paragraph first, Digest of the same title, and in law third, paragraph "In sons," by Wy., Digest "Concerning curators," and it is noted in the law "Custom," Digest "Concerning punishments." I ask, given the custom of primogeniture, [if] a king or duke has a natural son [born] from [concubinage], afterwards the man from a wife received a son natural and legitimate, then he legitimated the natural son only, afterwards he died...
pages.9: ...for the king, leaving a son from a concubine legitimated after the birth of the legitimate and natural [son], leaving said legitimate and natural [son] from a wife: who is to be preferred in the right of primogeniture? Many held that the legitimated [son] born from a concubine by the subsequent [act] makes him [legitimate], namely [per the] <term>authentica</term> "By what modes natural [children] are made one's own," where he who is legitimated from the beginning of birth, leaving the right of legitimation, reads himself [as legitimate]. Second, the law "To the son" is adduced, since [it is in the] Digest "Libertus," later. Third, law 1, Book "More," book 12. Fourth, that the natural [son] from a concubine is the firstborn and legitimated, therefore he is said to be prior in time and right, law 1, "First," Digest "Concerning the signification of terms," disciples in the first part, <term>Flor</term>. This [is because] in succession we attend to primarity at the time of death, not before death, law "After," according to "Prior," Digest "Concerning one's own [heirs] and legitimate [heirs]," law "If to a son given outside," [Digest] "Concerning un-testamentary." At the time of death the natural [son] from a concubine is firstborn and legitimated, therefore he is said to be preferred to the right of primogeniture. Lastly, the law "Postliminy," concerning "Retro," Digest "Concerning captivity and postliminy." To the contrary, the truth is that the firstborn from a wife, legitimate and natural, is said to be preferred to the one legitimated after the birth of the natural and legitimate [son] by the common sentiment of the writers, such as Bartolus, in the <term>Questionibus dominicalibus</term> <gloss>Sunday Questions</gloss>, question 50, and Albericus de Rosa in the proemium [of the] Digest, Johannes Andreae concerning [things], and Baldus in [the] <term>Zabarella</term> <gloss>a surname</gloss>, in law "Which," law "Concerning vindication of things," and Johannes Andreae in "Mercurial without fault," and Angelus in law "Gallus," according to which [he writes] "If only from a book and later," and in his disputation which begins "Noble in certain genus." By which common sentiment makes the text in the <term>authentica</term> "By what modes natural [children] are made one's own," according to that in [the] 5th [law] "From this point," the gloss which says "In time," and it makes [a point] that the sons must be legitimate by the text where after the marriage is performed. To the same makes the text in the law "Chapter," [in the] <term>Libri feudorum</term> <gloss>Books of Fiefs</gloss> "If a fief was provided," and it makes [the point] and the text in the law "Chapter," if [one] for the king, others of any kind, concerning rescripts, book 6, in the chapter "If apostolic," concerning prebends of the same book. Also, it makes the reason of law "As often," law "Concerning vindication of things," [which] alleges that what is ours cannot be taken away without our act, law "If Stichus," according to the Digest "Concerning novation," and in the rule of law "That which is ours." Therefore, legitimation will not take away the right of primogeniture in whose quasi-possession was the legitimate and natural [son] from a wife before the natural [son] from a concubine was legitimated. Also, it makes [a point] more strongly, for the law [says] legitimation may draw back, however it never draws back to the prejudice of a third party, according to Bartolus, and Bartolus proves in the law said "Law Gallus," according to which "If only," and I said in the disputation of the legitimized. Therefore, this legitimation only does not draw back to the prejudice of the legitimate and natural [son]. Which does not oppose the first argument, said [in the] "Religious" [laws], to which I answer that the text there says that the legitimated [person] succeeds in the same manner as one legitimate from the beginning, not however [does it] follow: therefore he is feigned [as] legitimated from the beginning. Similarly, a subdeacon can be elected as bishop just as a deacon and priest, chapter "Many," [and] chapter "And," concerning qualities. Therefore, [that] a subdeacon is a priest is feigned. This is not a good distinction. [It] does not oppose, according to the said law "To the son," which I answer that there from the beginning the son was legitimate and natural. [It] does not oppose the said law 1, which I say or we speak of the end [of] the said law 1, according to the common sentiment understood, and then I answer that it does not speak there of succession but of fiefs, or otherwise, I answer that it prefers the first who had attained primarity because by the order of the prelacy the magistracies are deferred, law "Rescript," Digest "Concerning duties and honors." [It] does not oppose the fourth argument, the said law "First," which I say that it is a fallacy of accident, by the example of that sophist who says: I propose to you this, that this donkey which you have is a foal and is a mother, therefore your mother is a donkey; this is not a good consequence, just as in our case it is not a good consequence: "this natural [son] only is firstborn and is legitimated, therefore he is a legitimate firstborn," because quality ought to be understood with time, where or [with] the participle to which [it] adds, law "Titius," Digest "Concerning military testaments," where Bartolus decides this question concerning the legitimate against the legitimated. [It] does not oppose another argument, the said law "Here, to the son," and the said law "Retro," with [those] which follow, which I answer [that] fictions are not drawn back to the prejudice of a third party, as I said in the foundations. Conclusion: in all these things [one] excludes the natural legitimate [son] from a wife [as] the right of primogeniture is preferred to the legitimated [son] after the birth of the legitimate natural [son]. But what in [the case of a son] legitimate by subsequent marriage, where for example [a man] has a son from a concubine, then he will have received a son legitimate and natural from a wife, afterwards the wife being dead, he contracted marriage with the concubine, the mother of the natural son, only; will the legitimated [son] from the marriage be preferred to the natural and legitimate son from the wife? As at first sight one should say yes, for so much that the sons are legitimate, by the notable Johannes Andreae and Andreas de [Buccis] in the chapter "Lator," of the same title, where he concludes that the said chapter "Natural," if [concerning] fiefs, if it was proverbial, [it] does not have place in the legitimated [son] by subsequent marriage. To the contrary is the determination [of] Johannes Andreae [in] <term>Belui</term> <gloss>surname for Johannes Andreae</gloss>, in the <term>authentica</term> "By what modes natural [children] are made one's own," almost by the reasons which I said in the preceding article. Nor does the said chapter "Tanta" oppose [the view] that it makes [the point] there according to [the] text there, "after marriage is performed," nor does [it] oppose in the said chapter "Lator" [because] it does not speak in prejudice of a third party, as is in our case, since the natural and legitimate son was in quasi-possession of the right of primogeniture. But it is most beautiful that we oppose: the King [has a] son natural, afterwards he accepted a wife and from her he received a son legitimate and natural, he died; it is asked who is to be preferred in the right of primogeniture, the legitimated [one] or the legitimate and natural [one]? Certainly from the preceding we have to determine that the legitimated [one] [is not preferred], since [the other] is found here legitimate in quasi-possession [of] the right of primogeniture before the birth of the legitimated and natural [son], from the reasons ceasing in the other article and the first, and so determines Baldus in the law "Ea quae," law "Concerning fideicommissa," regarding patrimonial goods; it is otherwise however regarding the succession of kingdoms, which said Baldus will declare, and [it is] true unless he had legitimate [children] besides the legitimated [one] to the regalia, and by name he had said that he legitimated [him] also to the regalia, [as says] this Baldus in the said law "Ea quae" in the preceding question. Again [it is said] that the son of the King of Aragon has a natural son only and made him be legitimated by the Pope so that he succeeds in the kingdom, and thus in the right of primogeniture; the King of Aragon dies leaving his brother legitimate and natural and leaving a legitimated son; it is asked who is preferred. I answer the brother legitimate and natural is preferred, because the Pope without cause cannot legitimate in fiefs and dignities to the prejudice of agnates, according to Johannes Andreae in the chapter "Through the venerable," [and the chapter] "If they are," law "Rei" [dominicae], that is "Semi," in the chapter "Grandi," concerning the supplement of the negligence of prelates. Nor does the said law "Gallus" oppose [the view], according to which "If only," since it speaks [concerning] firstborns, not in dignities. It is asked whether the right of primogeniture ought to be deferred. I answer no, according to Baldus in the <term>authentica</term> "From the text," in the last column, book [of] Coll. of the same [title], [and he] limits [it] to be true unless for perpetual money he bought such a fief in which is the right of primogeniture, [even] if it is indivisible, nevertheless the price will be owed according to Angelus de [Iler.], in the chapter 1, according to "Furthermore," [concerning] duchies of [Ph.] fiefs alienated, [but] because [the] law [of] "All" alleges according to the end, [Digest] "Concerning testaments," joined to the law "That," law "Coll." [concerning] Caesar. Let us propose that it does not appear who is the firstborn, or I answer that the witnesses are dead or are absent from [the] public. It is asked whether one or the other, or neither, succeeds in the right of primogeniture? I answer that each [does], according to the mind of Baldus in the law "From this right," Digest "Concerning justice and law," [and] the said <term>authentica</term> "From the text" in the last column; similarly of the two emperors in the Clementines, "Unique," concerning the taking of an oath. A difficult article is whether in a kingdom the nephew from a deceased firstborn is preferred in the right of primogeniture to his uncle, or whether the uncle excludes the nephew. In which article we will say [that] we shall know that in the first place I will place the authorities for the nephew and afterwards, then the authorities for the uncle against the nephew. Third, I will place the laws and reasons for the nephew against the laws and reasons for the uncle. Fifth, I will say what I feel in this point, saving however better counsel. Therefore for the nephew, in the first place is the authority of Oldradus, 214, according to my order. This is the authority of <term>Alb.</term> <gloss>Albericus</gloss>, proemium, Digest "Concerning [fiefs]," the third is Johannes Andreae in the addition [there] above the rubric concerning fiefs. The fourth is a certain modern, such as Abbot Siculus in the chapter 13, concerning [tutors]. The fifth, thus pronounced King Robert with the counsel of two cardinal lords learned in law, as <term>Alb.</term> reports in the said proemium of the <term>florum</term> <gloss>a collection of legal opinions</gloss>, and thus it is frequently observed in the kings of Gaul, Castile, and Spain. To the contrary, for the uncle against the nephew are illustrious authors, in the first place Andreas de Iler. in chapter 1, "Concerning [fiefs] in the succession of fiefs," Bartolus in the <term>authentica</term> "After the brothers of brothers," [Digest] "Concerning laws," [concerning] the brief. Ricardus Malumbra, whom <term>Cynus</term> reports and follows, according to Raymundus in the law "Final," one. Law "Concerning maternal goods," and there Raymundus says the moderns have held [so]. Thus also holds Baldus in the law "Final," one, although Baldus [also holds] in the law "From this right," Digest "Concerning justice and law," and in the law "With the ancients," law "Concerning the right of deliberating," [but] he does not solve [it]; rather he says "Let Apollo solve [it]," and Baldus also in doubt nevertheless [is] for the uncle in the law "As intestate," law "Concerning one's own [heirs] and legitimate [heirs]." But Nicolaus de Matta in the law "Final," concerning the right of all right, [in the] Book, since Baldus reports [it] in the law "Liberti," law "Concerning goods of freedmen," he distinguishes: either we speak in feudal law, and then the nephew excludes the uncle, law "Libertus," according to [Et.], according to 1, Digest "Concerning goods of freedmen." May the Lord also grant him the desire of his heart,
And may He remove every evil affliction from the midst of his house,
And may a mystery of goodness accompany him from hour to hour,
And may peace, peace, rest with him in the valley of his dwelling.
Therefore, in the joy of my heart, I said in my calling:
Peace be to the scroll, the book, the letter of loves.
And if I have found favor in your eyes with my vows,
Then accept this, my song, which I have composed.
I will praise you until my soul within me honors you,
I will recount your name to give thanks among the peoples.
Live, live, so I say, and may your heart rejoice as you desire,
And may the Most High requite your rewards with good things.

soon crudities <note>indigested matter</note>. From these, these are the words of the most celebrated and most experienced Lord Waldschmid, my teacher, to be honored at the altars. See, if you please, the seventh chapter of the first book of his Institutions of Medicine:

> "As if from a fountain, there spring up various kinds of fevers, flatulence, swellings, obstructions, <term>cacochymia</term> <gloss>ill condition of the humors</gloss> of the blood, a disturbance of its mixture, depravation of the nutritive juice, scabies, diarrhea, dysentery, and so on. Drink inflicts harm when it is poured cold into the burning viscera, where the same thing happens in the viscera as is wont to happen when cold iron is immersed in a heated one; that is, an inflammatory obstruction is produced, and the ether, having been greatly agitated beforehand, now, with the obstruction supervening, disturbs everything in the vicinity and stirs it into tumult."

## TH. IX.

Through excessive sleep and a sedentary life, the ventilation of the blood and insensible perspiration are impeded, whence heterogeneous parts, which otherwise are wont to be evoked through insensible perspiration, remain mixed with the mass of the blood, whence obstructions arise, and from there the blood is not a little infected, from which afterwards an acrid intemperance arises. While motion and vigils exceed their limits, the spirits are impoverished; the more spirited parts fly away through the pores of the skin as through an open door, while only the thicker parts, which are less apt for motion, remain. While that which ought to be excreted is retained, and vice-versa, that which ought to be retained is excreted, it is an evil. However, there is more danger in the retention of things to be excreted than in the retention of things that should be retained. That the passions of the mind, when they exceed their limits, inflict various alterations upon the fluids, and that they have much efficacy in producing this effect, no one will deny. There is no need, therefore, for me to treat of them at greater length, since their manner of working and afflicting is already known to the public.

<summary>This page discusses the systemic effects of poor digestion, sedentary habits, and emotional stress on blood health, arguing that obstructions and the retention of waste products are primary causes of dysentery.</summary>
<keywords>Waldschmid, blood, obstruction, perspiration, sedentary life, spirits, humors</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="10">
## TH. X.

Having examined the causes of this affection, the procession of symptoms comes into view. I proceed, therefore, to the diagnostic signs, even if they have already become known from the definition of the disease; I shall set them forth more broadly here, intending to explain the phenomena that occur in this effect. But I seem to hear some whispering that that doctrine concerning signs lacks a foundation, and that the semiotic part is merely conjectural. I will freely concede that a physician cannot predict the outcome of diseases and define their end with, as it is said, metaphysical certainty. However, it suffices that the thing can happen as it is conceived; if it happens otherwise, I say that occurs by accident. For he who has rendered the animal economy and the nature of the fluids well understood to himself, will he not be able to give the signs of an impending storm, and likewise predict how the disease will end?

## TH. XI.

The excreted humors now come to be examined, as to what their nature may be. The lymph, which trickles from the intestinal glands into the cavity of the intestines, is excreted along with the mucus adhering to their walls. Whether such mucus exists, I no longer doubt, for I have seen the matter frequently when the most celebrated man, Lord Dorstenius, was conducting anatomical dissections. To this lymph are mixed sanguineous parts, as well as shreds of the intestines. The excretion is frequent, for that acrid salt of which I spoke above pricks the intestinal tunics so that, with the fibers swollen and constricted, it is necessary that, if there be anything that ought to be excreted, it be excreted, and that there be a desire to void, which is called <term>tenesmus</term> <gloss>painful, ineffective straining to defecate</gloss>.

<summary>The author transitions to diagnosing dysentery through symptom analysis and the examination of excreted matter, specifically identifying the role of intestinal lymph and the condition known as tenesmus.</summary>
<keywords>diagnosis, semiotics, animal economy, lymph, intestinal glands, Dorstenius, tenesmus</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="28">
The reason "mostly" is used is that there are many such things. If refuting the ten categories <note>referring to the system of categories in Vaisheshika-derived philosophies</note>, nine categories are considered truly existent, while the tenth is "non-existence" <term>abhava</term>. Because the majority are truly existent, the word "mostly" is used. Regarding "obtained through direct perception" <term>pratyaksa</term>, if refuting the six categories, according to the treatise below, five categories—such as substance—are obtained through direct perception. Only the category of "inherence" <term>samavaya</term> is not obtained through direct perception; thus, the word "mostly" is used. If refuting the ten categories, speaking generally of all categories, [such as] difference, inherence, those with ability, and those without ability, "non-existence" is said not to be obtained through direct perception, while the other five are. However, among those that are mostly truly existent, five are obtained through direct perception and four are not. Therefore, it is said that the majority are obtained through direct perception. The word "mostly" applies to both "truly existent" and "direct perception." Since maintaining the six categories is their original position, the *Shastra of One Hundred Verses* <note>original: "Bai lun"</note> and others do not refute the ten categories, and this treatise does the same. However, refuting the ten categories as well does not contradict the logic.

Their position is irrational.

This follows with the second part: a direct refutation of their errors. Within this, there are three sections. First, a general refutation. Next, the opponent responds.
</translation>

The Wolf lies in wait for the full sheepfold with dogs,
He tears, mangles, rends, and scatters, he attacks and gnaws
With a sharp tooth; thus, thus the innocent crowd
Falls into the rapid troops, a miserable thing to relate.
The affair is carried out with swords: not one was able
To lift his right hand in opposition: with hands raised
To the Stars they are cut down, the severed head is mocked, and the mouth
The rabid soldier, devoid of light, mangles:
They strew the tracts with bodies; the whole path overflows
With blood, the infant of those fleeing from the maternal
Bosom slips, and is immediately pressed, about to die, by the hoof
Of a trampling horse: then they extend the most cruel
Chains, worthy of eternal darkness, to the youth.
One labor holds them all, a clamor from every mouth
Is brought forth: rend them with quick right hands, allies:
Thus may DISCORD strike the European Nations.
The causes of war stand: if we have conquered, the fates
Of their own accord call for this: impious Mars will rage over the whole world:
Meanwhile we proceed to extend our shores.
    Here I, scarcely loosening my mouth because of tears,
I say: Calliope, you tell of an unspeakable thing: nor did she allow me
To speak further, as to what the meanings of the mind were: what do you ask,
She replies, unspeakable? I would wish my lips were mute:
A mute mouth, and deaf ears: and no vision:
But alas! Too true are the things we have spoken: everything, the Turk
Dreads, which the earth holds: the house of the Thunderer itself
</translation>

Groans over the ever-discordant shores of Europe.

<translation page="15">
### 98.
Galen himself testifies that a cough is malignant or dangerous when it arises from an <term>ulcer</term> <gloss>an open sore</gloss> or <term>empyema</term> <gloss>pus accumulation</gloss> of the respiratory organs, in his 6th book of Epidemics, section 2, text 24.

### 99.
**THE SUBJECT MATTER OF REMEDIES** is accustomed to be referred to three types: <term>surgery</term>, <term>pharmacology</term>, and <term>diet</term>.

### 100.
<term>Surgical aids</term> are bloodletting, cupping, enemas, frictions, ligatures, and cauteries, some of which are potential, such as vesicatories <gloss>blister-inducing agents</gloss>, and others actual, such as fontanels <gloss>artificial ulcers or setons for drainage</gloss>.

### 101.
<term>Bloodletting</term> is approved whenever the blood is at fault, whether it acts as a principal cause, as in inflammatory conditions of the lung, or as an auxiliary cause, existing in the remaining neighboring parts or even in the whole body.

### 102.
Furthermore, blood must be removed whenever the fault is violent, whether in form, quantity, or motion, and whenever strength permits and nothing prevents it.

### 103.
The use or administration varies according to the variety of the part either receiving or emitting the blood.

### 104.
Instead of <term>bloodletting</term>, it will be permissible to use <term>cupping</term>, especially on the lower parts, so that blood is not drawn to the parts of the chest and from there to the lungs.

### 105.
Or, for the sake of revulsion <gloss>drawing blood away from an affected part</gloss>, we can use frictions and ligatures on the extremities.

### 98.
Galen himself testifies in *Epidemics 6, section 2, text 24* that a malignant or dangerous cough is one that arises from an <term>ulcer</term> or <term>empyema</term> <gloss>an accumulation of pus</gloss> in the breathing organs.

### 99.
**THE RESOURCES FOR TREATMENT** are usually categorized into three types: <term>surgery</term>, <term>pharmacy</term> <gloss>the use of medicines</gloss>, and <term>diet</term>.

### 100.
<term>Surgical resources</term> include <term>bloodletting</term>, <term>cupping glasses</term>, <term>clysters</term> <gloss>enemas</gloss>, <term>frictions</term> <gloss>massages</gloss>, <term>ligatures</term> <gloss>bandages or tourniquets</gloss>, and <term>cauteries</term>. Some of these are potential, such as <term>vesicatories</term> <gloss>blister-inducing agents</gloss>; others are actual, such as <term>fontanelles</term> <gloss>issues used to drain bodily humors</gloss>.

<term>Bloodletting</term> is indicated whenever the blood is "at fault," whether it acts as the primary cause, as in inflammatory conditions of the lung, or as an auxiliary cause, as when it exists in other neighboring parts or even in the whole body.

Furthermore, blood is to be drawn whenever the fault is severe, whether due to its form, its quantity, or its movement, provided that the strength of the patient allows it and nothing prohibits it.

The usage or administration varies according to the variety of the part of the body that is receiving the blood or the part from which the blood is being drawn.

Instead of <term>bloodletting</term>, it is permissible to use <term>cupping glasses</term>, especially on the lower parts of the body, so that blood is not drawn to the parts of the chest and from there to the lungs.

### 105.
Alternatively, for the purpose of <term>revulsion</term> <gloss>drawing blood or humors away from an affected area</gloss>, we may use <term>frictions</term> and <term>ligatures</term> on the extremities.

it is confidence, provided one measures their own strength by a just standard, attributing to oneself only as much as suffices for an art that must be defended against contempt. <margin>Book V, Epistle III.</margin>
Pliny: *My consistency is too modest for me to consider that which is approved by me as sufficiently perfect.*

X. Indeed, the method of seeking the judgments of others is not the same for everyone. Many, while they are little consistent with themselves in opposing matters, valuing glory more than dishonor, while they solicit fame for their writings by exposing the offspring of their genius to the learned world, look out for themselves only so far that they fear to write their own name on the front of the work, or sometimes they change it. Indeed, it is clear that those who have discovered new things and are about to pass them on to others, while the palm of victory is ambiguous, following a clever plan, imitated that painter of ours, Apelles, and took for themselves a name while lurking behind the painting, ready to listen with a sufficiently secure mind to what the learned would judge. You would say that these people keep a crooked path.

<margin>See Gerhard Johannes Vossius, On the Mathematical Sciences, Chapter XXXVI, Theme XLIII.</margin>

<margin>Century II to the Belgians, Epistle XLIX. Single book On the Imitation and Recitation of the Ancients.</margin>
Justus Lipsius labored on this, and after Lipsius, Gerhard Johannes Vossius. There were Recitations, by which Poets and other Writers exposed their labors to the judgment of others, just as painters and sculptors exposed their hands. This exposure, since it was done by reciting, found its name: Recitations. A custom most useful in the opinion of the greatest men, and appearing worthy to be recalled by our wishes. Lipsius: *Certainly, if there is anything useful today in this abundance of those writing or longing to write, it would be the stopping or directing of certain talents. And how could it be otherwise? When, for the sake of amending, one brought forth one's own work to recite it, those who were learned and erudite would listen and judge.

<margin>Lipsius, Chapter 1.</margin>
XII. Such were the <term>Cynosurae</term> <gloss>guiding stars/poles</gloss>, and now there are more, now fewer, since the Recitation itself was also of different kinds: public, to which the known and unknown alike were admitted, and private, consisting almost entirely among known friends and acquaintances, which had more fruit and utility, while the former had more appearance and ambition.

<margin>Book VII, Epistle XVII.</margin>
XIII. I seem to see these steps in Pliny: *First*, he says, *I examine what I have written myself; then I read it to two or three; soon I pass it on to others to be annotated, and if I doubt their notes, I weigh them again with one or two others; finally, I recite it to many; and if you believe me, I then amend it most sharply.*

XIV. But should a place also be given here to the judgment of the common people? There were those in the past to whom this was pleasing, when the use of the vernacular and common language, in which the writings were produced, was shared on both sides. Pliny on the tragic poet Pomponius Secundus: *If*, he said, *a close friend thought something should be removed, but he himself thought it should be kept, he used to say, "I appeal to the people"; and thus, from the silence or assent of the people, he would follow either his own judgment or that of his friend. So much did he grant to the people.* But it is dangerous to listen to the common people, to whom, according to those whom the learned follow, things are generally not pleasing; just as they are not pleasing to the learned, according to whom the common people pronounce. Although Pliny did not hide what he felt about the decision of Secundus: *So much*, he says, *did he grant to the people. Whether rightly or wrongly is nothing to me, for I am not accustomed to summon the people, but certain learned men, whom I may look upon, whom I may trust, and whom, finally, I may observe as individuals, and whom, not as individuals, I may fear.* Hence there will be less room for hesitation regarding the common people of our age, who are as rude in literature as they are in the languages in which literature is taught today, as to what is to be decided. We ought to be, as it were, Antigenidases, Antimachuses, Heraclituses here, and with that one man, holding all others post-Platonic and anyone learned after them: and with this one, as if dismissing them with a plumb line, exclaim:

> I did not compose for you, but for those who understand me.
> One man for me is worth thirty thousand; the countless others
> are nothing.
<margin>Diogenes Laërtius and Illustrius on Heraclitus.</margin>
</translation>

Then Gángleri said, "You have given him very many names, and my belief is that this must be great wisdom, for he who knows the reasons and events can explain why each of these names has come about." Then Hár answers, "It is great wisdom to examine that thoroughly, but it is quickest for you to know that most names have been given because of events; for as many as there are branches of languages <note>original: "túngnanna"</note> in the world, all peoples believe they need to change his name into their own language for invocation and prayer for themselves. But some events regarding these names occurred during his travels, which are recorded in stories, and you would not be able to be called a wise man if you could not tell of those great events."

21. Then Gángleri said, "What are the names of the other Æsir? Or what do they do? Or what have they done for fame?" Hár answers, "Thor is the most famous of them, he who is called Asa-Thor or Öku-Thor <gloss>Chariot-Thor</gloss>; he is the strongest of all gods and men. He possesses the realm that is called Þrúðvángar <gloss>Strength-fields</gloss>, and his hall is called Bilskirnir: in that hall are five hundred and forty floors; that is the largest house that men have made." So it says in <term>Grímnismál</term> <gloss>Sayings of Grímnir</gloss>.

10.

It is. <note>The agent is either principal or ministerial.</note> The principal agent is **GOD**; the ministerial agent is an Angel, as in *Judges 6:21* and *13:16*. In the latter, the question can be asked whether that Angel should be understood as the uncreated Angel, a view which we adopt; for when asked about his name, he replied that it was wonderful, which is said of the Messiah in *Isaiah 9*. The moving cause is either internal or external. The internal cause is the special grace of **GOD** toward men, by which He wished to testify to His favor and gracious presence. The external causes are the prayers and vows of the Saints, whence it is said in *1 Chronicles 21* that (David) called upon the Lord, and He answered him by fire from heaven; and in *2 Chronicles 7:1*, when Solomon had finished praying, fire descended from heaven. This should incite us to pray diligently, for in this way **GOD** sends the heavenly fire, the Holy Spirit, into the sacrifices of our lips and hearts, and renders them ignited.

The final cause, or the end, is either physical or theological. The former is the consumption of the sacrifices; the latter is the excitation of faith in those who sacrifice, and the testimony of special providence and gracious presence.

### IX.

The adjuncts are: 1. *Time*, which is in a certain way extraordinary, as when fire was sent down by **GOD** at the dedication of the Levitical worship, at the confirmation of a promised deliverance, at the inauguration of Solomon’s Temple, and during the proof of true worship and the refutation of false. The time observed also appears to be in some way ordinary, when, namely, the evening time of sacrificing is read to have been determined for this act. This is certain from the Law concerning the first sacrifice of Aaron and the dedication of Solomon’s temple, and it is said in express words concerning the sacrifice of Elijah.</translation>

<translation page="11">
11.

*1 Kings 18:36*: "And it came to pass at the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice."

### X.

2. *Place*, which was not fixed but determined by the circumstances of the event, being either extraordinary and profane, or ordinary and sacred. The place where Abel sacrificed, the rock of Gideon, and the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite appear to have been extraordinary and profane. Regarding the latter place, it should be noted that, through this sacrifice, it was in a certain way sanctified and destined for the future building of the temple. The ordinary and sacred place was both the Tabernacle of the congregation and the temple itself, as in the first sacrifice of Aaron and that of King Solomon, by which those places were consecrated to divine worship.

### XI.

Cognate are the other fires that descended or were sent down from heaven, such as the fire by which Elijah was caught up into heaven, the Sinaitic fire, the federal fire of Abraham, etc.

### XII.

From these matters thus far tasted, we elicit and present this definition, or rather description, of sacrificial fire: *Sacrificial fire is a certain supernatural and typical flame, created by GOD and often sent down visibly from heaven, ignited by Him, and that for the glory of His name and the salvation of all men, especially the Jews; and also for the sudden and sole consumption of burnt offerings, and for the typical prefiguration of Christ or the entire Most Holy Trinity.*

## QUESTIONS.

1. Question: *Does the sacrifice of Abel also pertain to this?*</translation>

The internal is the special grace of **God** toward men, by which He wished to testify to His favor and gracious presence. The external are the prayers and vows of the Saints, whence it is said in *1 Chronicles 21* that David called upon the Lord, and He answered him by fire from heaven. And in *2 Chronicles 7:1*, when Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven. This should incite us to pray diligently, for thus **God** sends the heavenly fire, the Holy Spirit, into the sacrifices of our lips and hearts, and renders them ignited.

The final cause, or end, is either physical or theological. The former is the consumption of the sacrifices; the latter is the stirring of faith in those offering the sacrifice, and a testimony of special providence and gracious presence.

### IX.

The adjuncts are: 1. *Time*, which is in a certain way extraordinary, as when fire was sent down by **God** during the dedication of the Levitical worship, the confirmation of a promised liberation, the inauguration of Solomon’s Temple, and the proof of the true cult and refutation of the false. This is certain from the Law regarding the first sacrifice of Aaron and the dedication of Solomon’s temple, and it is said in express words regarding the sacrifice of Elijah.

<translation page="89">
PANARCHIAS, BOOK VI.

of their <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence</gloss>, produces the primary multitude. For everything that produces by its own being, also acts, and bestows upon that thing what belongs to its essence. For it gives what it has, not what it does not have. Now its <term>hyparxis</term> was to be the One-All. Therefore, it gave to this generation of its own what it was, namely, that it should be One and all things. But why do we call the former Father, and call the begotten the Unity? (According to the doctrine of both Proclus and Damascius the Platonists, although theologians most truly hold that all things are contained in God, and not in a Son distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit, in a most excellent way). Among Zoroaster and Hermes, indeed, that One also is called the Monad. But for us, for the sake of clearer doctrine, it has seemed better to call that One, this Unity. One, indeed, because it is only one and independent. Unity, however, both depends upon that, and looks toward multitude; in that One-All, indeed, there is multitude, but unified and most simple. In Unity, however, the multitude is already distinct and poured out into number. The One has snatched itself above every relation and transcends every respect of multitude. Unity, however, looks toward number and is referred to multitude. Therefore, this primary Unity is from the first One. But the multitude that is in this Unity comes from that, if I may say so, omnity. But for what reason did that One-All bring forth this Unity-All from itself? Why did that Father beget this Son? Was He who grants fruitfulness to all other things required to be sterile? He neither ought to have been, nor could He have been. He ought to have been, because He was and is good. He could have been, because He was and is omnipotent. Therefore, He had a necessity to produce; He made the will by producing. Will created necessity. For necessity follows the will of God, says Hermes. Therefore all things are from Him and through Him. Which he also said most correctly: 
"By His own will You created all things."
By His will He founded all things.
"And this is His work, to see the Father. His essence is to carry all things in the womb and to do."
And this is His work, to be the Father. His essence is to carry all things in the womb, and to do.
Elsewhere also he teaches thus:
"For all things that are, these are one in God, and made by God, and depending from thence."
For all things, whatsoever they are, are in God, and made by God, and dependent from thence.
Therefore, God is both the begetter and maker of all things begotten. But in what way did He beget or make them? By the power, clearly, which He had in making them. For God is the Father of beings and the begetter. But beings were made and begotten by Him. Between these two is the middle power, through which the begetter produces, and the begotten are produced. For unless He were able to produce, these things would not have been produced. Power, therefore, is a progression and a kind of ascent from the One, and an extension into the essence of beings. Thus, the transition from the One is made through power into essence. Therefore, this most primary power is supra-essential. For it is before essence, since it is intermediate between the One and essence. It precedes beings and is the first generation of the One itself. And for this reason, it is rightly celebrated by Zoroaster as the power of the Father, and by Hermes as the Son of the Father, as we shall see shortly. Let us return to the mode. If the transition into being is made from the One through the power of the One, and as if through an outpouring and progression of the One: then essence is begotten from the One by a certain motion. For it is necessary that this happens either by motion, or by rest, or in both ways, or in neither. If in neither, then not in both. If not in both, at least in one or the other. But is it by rest or by motion? Hermes says: 
"The One remains standing and is not moved."
The One, however, remains standing and is not moved. But that which remains does not progress. And conversely, that which progresses does not remain. But the One itself remains. Therefore, it does not progress. Progression is a certain motion. But motion is an action. Every action, however, is either in essence or from essence. In essence, it does not seem that the motion of progression and production happens. For beings would not exist thence through that motion. Therefore, in order for them to emerge, they required motion from essence. Or rather, from the <term>hyparxis</term> of the One. For its <term>hyparxis</term> is that which is the essence to beings. What then? By the exit of beings from the <term>hyparxis</term> of the One, is the One emptied for beings? Far from it. For it is not moved. Therefore, they proceeded by rest. But it does not rest either. For it does not have something in which to rest other than in itself. Nor is there anything toward which it might move. For it is everywhere. For Hermes says most truly:
"And nothing is outside of Him, nor is He outside of anything."
And nothing is outside of Him, and He is outside of nothing. But in what way, finally, did He produce the secondary beings? Perhaps by His own rest He draws them out from Himself? Are they indeed removed from Him, while He remains? But a drawing out is a certain action. And action is motion. Therefore, is He also moved? Does He have rest first, and motion afterwards? Does the question therefore return to the same point? Not at all. But in Him, rest moves, and motion rests. And that which moves in Him is moved stably from Him, and that which rests, rests movably. Namely, it remains itself. And it remains, drawing all things out of itself by its own fruitfulness and bringing them forth outside itself. It brings them forth from itself, remaining itself what it was before. For in what way could it become less than the One? Or how could the things which it brings forth from itself depart outside of it, when it is everywhere? And does it still contain all produced things within itself? Therefore, it is not emptied by those first things of its own, nor does it evacuate itself so that it becomes less than the One, or less than all things.
</translation>

<translation page="90">
FRANCISCUS PATRICIUS

Nor does it depart anywhere from its own One, or from the fullness of its own omnity, nor is it split into many. The light of the sun indeed emits rays from itself, yet it does not itself become a lesser light. Fire puts forth heat from itself, yet it does not retain a lesser heat than before; rather, it retains the same. Thus the First, thus the Principle, thus the One, thus the Good, thus God, produced all things without anything diminished in terms of primality, or principality, or unity, or goodness, or deity, and without any matter assisting. Rather, He drew even that out from Himself and brought it forth outside Himself. But He brought it forth because He is the One, so that from there a multitude of things might be born. He brought it forth because of goodness, so that the multitude and that number might be beings, and non-beings would not exist at all. For He retained these in Himself, so that when He willed, He might bring them forth, and when He did not will, He might not. Thus, the One, in the production of secondary things, does not progress beyond itself, nor is it moved. But while He brings them forth, and they progress from Him, He remains in Himself. They, however, proceed and emanate by an action from His <term>hyparxis</term>, not otherwise than as water emanates from its own spring, the spring itself indeed unmoved, but putting forth the water; the water, however, moved and flowing from thence. What then? If it is unmoved and remains in itself, does it not seem to produce? Production is an action, and action is motion. Is it both moved and not moved? And does it produce and not produce? And does it effect things and not effect them, in its own ways, namely, ineffable ones? It does not effect them, indeed, because since they are already existing in Him, He only discerns them from Himself. It does indeed effect them because He brings them forth from Himself, and they flow forth from Him. Does the previous question therefore seem to return? Do they proceed from the One by themselves? Or do they have another cause of their own production? Certainly, they are produced either from themselves, or from another, or from the One itself. From another, it is least to be said. For what is prior to the One, or equal to the One? Not from themselves, except insofar as they do not resist the producer and offer their assent to their own production. The One, however, brings them forth from Himself by the necessity of His own goodness toward action, at the same time making them distinct from Himself and from His own omnity, so that the cause would not be the identity of these with those, but the otherness of these from those. Which cause was no other than the progression and bringing forth of things from Him. For every bringing forth, or emanation, involves a secretion. And every secretion from the One is a cause of multitude. And when multitude begins in the One, then the bringing forth follows. But if the One is not that which makes the secretion from which multiplication happens, and from this the bringing forth, what would that be? Certainly, it is nothing other than that power of which we spoke, intermediate between the One and being. For unless this intervened, production would not happen. But who moves this power so that it might make the secretion? Perhaps nothing other than goodness. For unless this moved that, so that it might separate all things from itself, and bring all things forth from itself, so that it might communicate itself to all, it would seem to be touched by envy. But what envy is there in the Most Simple? What passion in the Most Perfect? Therefore, the Good itself, not as the One, but as the Good, is the most primary cause of the secretion of fruitful things from the One-All, from the firsts. Now, secretion is the cause of multiplication. Multiplication is the cause of progression. Let this be made manifest by an example. The center of a circle is one and indivisible. In that one, the ends of all lines proceeding from it are contained, not at all distinct from one another in it. From it, the lines proceed, countless and now distinct from one another, all the way to the circumference, which were all undifferentiated in the center. Yet, while they are secreted from the center, they are multiplied; and while they are multiplied, they proceed from the One; and proceeding, they depart from it. This departure is after the center. And its cause is not the center. But it is a certain flow from it by which the lines are both secreted from it, and multiplied, and proceed, and depart. Nor is the center itself the cause of this departure. Nor does it depart from itself, nor is it emptied so that it might multiply itself into lines. But after their departure, the center still remains. Nor is it diminished by the exit of the lines, nor does it suffer anything. Yet the lines exiting and proceeding from it are no longer what they were in it. But they are both from it and distinct from one another. They have, however, from it that which they are, and it bestows being upon them. Nor are they torn away from it, but they depend upon it. For the cause of every bringing forth remains. And that which proceeds remains in the property and terms of its cause. So that what proceeds seems both to be in the same cause in which it had been, and also to have departed from thence. In this holy way (if it be not forbidden to use this likeness), all things are secreted from the One indiscriminately, and are multiplied, proceeding as discrete things. But what, in that progression from the One, do they carry with themselves from the One? Or does it bestow something upon them? Or does it bestow them by its own goodness, and they, rejoicing in that goodness, willingly carry with them those things with which they are, as it were, gifted? But what are these things which they carry with them as gifts? Truly, a second One, given as a portion to each from the first One, through which both the individuals are one, and through which they are also many. And through which they are also beings. For beings could not be unless they were one. Nor could they be many unless they came from the One. Thus, these things secreted from the One, after the One-All, are simultaneously one and many. And they are after the principle, which had been the fourth condition of the principle. And they are from the One, and from the principle, which had been its third condition. And this is His work, to be the Father. His essence is to carry all things in the womb, and to do.

For all things, whatsoever they are, are in God, and made by God, and dependent from thence.

What then? By the exit of beings from the <term>hyparxis</term> of the One, is the One emptied for beings? Far from it. For it is not moved. Therefore, they proceeded by rest. But it does not rest either. For it does not have something in which to rest other than in itself. Nor is there anything toward which it might move. For it is everywhere. For Hermes says most truly:

And nothing is outside of Him, and He is outside of nothing. But in what way, finally, did He produce the secondary beings? Perhaps by His own rest He draws them out from Himself? Are they indeed removed from Him, while He remains? But a drawing out is a certain action. And action is motion. Therefore, is He also moved? Does He have rest first, and motion afterwards? Therefore, it is not emptied by those first things of its own, nor does it evacuate itself so that it becomes less than the One, or less than all things.

Now its <term>hyparxis</term> was to be the "One-all." Therefore, it gave to this, its offspring, its own nature, namely, that it should be both unity and all things. But why do we call that father "the One," while we call the offspring "unity"? (According to the doctrine of both the Platonists Proclus and Damascius, although theologians very truly hold that all things are contained in God, and not in a Son distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the most excellent way.) Among Zoroaster and Hermes, indeed, that One is also called the "monad." To us, however, for the sake of clearer doctrine, it has seemed better to call that One "unity."
