In unity, however, the multitude is now distinct and poured out into number. The One has snatched itself above every relation and transcends every respect of multitude. Unity, however, looks toward number and is referred to the multitude. Therefore, this primary unity is from the First One. The multitude, however, which is in this unity, comes from that, so to speak, "all-ness." But for what reason did that One-all bring forth this unity-all from itself? Why did that father beget this son? Should he who grants fertility to all other things have been sterile? He neither should have been, nor could he have been. He should have been, because he was and is good. He could have been, because he was and is omnipotent. Therefore, he had the necessity to produce; he made the will by producing. Will made necessity. For the necessity of God follows his will, says Hermes. Therefore, all things are from him, and through him. He who also said most correctly: 
<note>original: "Τῷ αὐτοῦ θελήματι πάντα δημιούργησας."</note>
By his own will, he fashioned all things. 
<note>original: "Καὶ τοῦτο αὐτῷ τὸ ἔργον ἐστὶ πατέρα ἰδεῖν. τοῦτον ἐστιν οὐσία, τὸ κύειν πάντα, καὶ ποιεῖν."</note>
And this is his work, to be the father. His essence is to carry all things in the womb, and to make them.

He also teaches thus elsewhere: 
<note>original: "Πάντα γὰρ ὅσα ἐστὶν, ταῦτα ἓν τῷ θεῷ ἐστιν, καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ γινόμενα, καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἠρτημένα."</note>
For all things, whatsoever they are, are one in God, and are made by God, and are dependent thence.

God, therefore, is both the progenitor and maker of all generated things. But in what way did he beget or make them? By the power, namely, which he had in making them. For God is the father and progenitor of beings. Now beings have been made and begotten by him. Between these two, there is a middle, which is power, through which the progenitor produces, and the generated are produced. For unless he were able to produce, these things produced would not be. There is, therefore, power, a progression, and, as it were, an ascending from the One and an extension into the essence of beings. Thus, from the One, the transition is made through power into essence. Therefore, this most primary power is supra-essential. For it is before essence, when it is between the One and essence. It precedes beings and is the first offspring of the One itself. And for that reason, it is rightly celebrated by Zoroaster as the power of the father, and by Hermes as the son of the father, as we shall see a little later. Let us return to the mode. If, through the power of the One, the transition is made from the One into being, and as if by an egress and progression of the One, then essence is begotten from the One through a certain motion. For it is necessary that this be done either through motion, or through rest, or in both ways, or in neither. If in neither, then not in both. If not in both, then at least in one or the other. But is it through rest or through motion? Hermes says: 
<note>original: "Τὸ ἓν μένον ἕστηκε, καὶ οὐ κινεῖται."</note>
The One, however, remains at rest and is not moved. But that which remains does not progress. And conversely, that which progresses does not remain. But the One itself remains. Therefore, it does not progress. Progression is a certain motion. But motion is an action. Every action, however, is either in the essence or from the essence. In the essence, indeed, the motion of progression and production does not seem to occur. For beings would not exist thence through that motion. Therefore, in order for them to exit, they required a motion from the essence, or rather from the <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence</gloss> of the One. For its <term>hyparxis</term> is to it that which essence is to beings. What then? By the exit of beings from the <term>hyparxis</term> of the One, is the One exhausted for the beings? Far from it. For it is not moved. Therefore, they proceeded by rest. But it does not rest either. For it has nothing in which it might rest other than in itself. Nor anything to which it might be moved. For it is everywhere. For Hermes says most truly: 
<note>original: "Καὶ οὗ δ' αὐτοῦ οὐ δέν ἐκτὸς, οὐδ' αὐτὸς οὐδενός."</note>
And there is nothing outside of him, nor is he outside of anything. But in what way, finally, did he produce the second beings? Perhaps by his own rest, he extracts them from himself. Are they, however, moved away from him, while he remains? But extraction is a certain action. Action, however, is motion. Therefore, is he also moved? Does he have rest first, and motion afterwards? Does the question therefore return to the same point? Not at all. But in it, rest is moved, and motion rests. And that which is moved in him is moved stably from him, and that which rests rests movably. Namely, it remains itself. And it remains, extracting all things from itself by its own fecundity and bringing them forth outside of itself; it brings them forth from itself, remaining itself what it was before. For in what way could it become less than one? Or in what way could the things which it brings forth from itself depart outside of it, when it is everywhere? And it still contains all the produced things within itself. Therefore, it is not exhausted by those first things of its own, nor does it empty itself so that it becomes less than one, or less than all.

of their <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence</gloss>, it produces the primary multitude. For everything that it produces with its own being, it also acts, and it attributes to that thing its own essence. For it gives what it has, but not what it does not have. Now its <term>hyparxis</term> was to be the "One-all." Therefore, it gave to this, its offspring, its own nature, namely, that it should be both unity and all things. But why do we call that father "the One," while we call the offspring "unity"? (According to the doctrine of both the Platonists Proclus and Damascius, although theologians very truly hold that all things are contained in God, and not in a Son distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the most excellent way.) Among Zoroaster and Hermes, indeed, that One is also called the "monad." To us, however, for the sake of clearer doctrine, it has seemed better to call that One "unity." It is "the One," because it is only one and independent. "Unity," however, both depends upon it and looks toward the multitude; in the "One-all," the multitude is indeed unified and most simple. In unity, however, the multitude is now distinct and poured out into number. The One has snatched itself above every relation and transcends every respect of multitude. Unity, however, looks toward number and is referred to the multitude. Therefore, this primary unity is from the First One. The multitude, however, which is in this unity, comes from that, so to speak, "all-ness." But for what reason did that One-all bring forth this unity-all from itself? Why did that father beget this son? Should he who grants fertility to all other things have been sterile? He neither should have been, nor could he have been. He should have been, because he was and is good. He could have been, because he was and is omnipotent. Therefore, he had the necessity to produce; he made the will by producing. Will made necessity. For the necessity of God follows his will, says Hermes. Therefore, all things are from him, and through him. He who also said most correctly: 
<note>original: "Τῷ αὐτοῦ θελήματι πάντα δημιούργησας."</note>
By his own will, he fashioned all things. 
<note>original: "Καὶ τοῦτο αὐτῷ τὸ ἔργον ἐστὶ πατέρα ἰδεῖν. τοῦτον ἐστιν οὐσία, τὸ κύειν πάντα, καὶ ποιεῖν."</note>
And this is his work, to be the father. His essence is to carry all things in the womb, and to make them.

He also teaches thus elsewhere: 
<note>original: "Πάντα γὰρ ὅσα ἐστὶν, ταῦτα ἓν τῷ θεῷ ἐστιν, καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ γινόμενα, καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἠρτημένα."</note>
For all things, whatsoever they are, are one in God, and are made by God, and are dependent thence.

God, therefore, is both the progenitor and maker of all generated things. But in what way did he beget or make them? By the power, namely, which he had in making them. For God is the father and progenitor of beings. Now beings have been made and begotten by him. Between these two, there is a middle, which is power, through which the progenitor produces, and the generated are produced. For unless he were able to produce, these things produced would not be. There is, therefore, power, a progression, and, as it were, an ascending from the One and an extension into the essence of beings. Thus, from the One, the transition is made through power into essence. Therefore, this most primary power is supra-essential. For it is before essence, when it is between the One and essence. It precedes beings and is the first offspring of the One itself. And for that reason, it is rightly celebrated by Zoroaster as the power of the father, and by Hermes as the son of the father, as we shall see a little later. Let us return to the mode. If, through the power of the One, the transition is made from the One into being, and as if by an egress and progression of the One, then essence is begotten from the One through a certain motion. For it is necessary that this be done either through motion, or through rest, or in both ways, or in neither. If in neither, then not in both. If not in both, then at least in one or the other. But is it through rest or through motion? Hermes says: 
<note>original: "Τὸ ἓν μένον ἕστηκε, καὶ οὐ κινεῖται."</note>
The One, however, remains at rest and is not moved. But that which remains does not progress. And conversely, that which progresses does not remain. But the One itself remains. Therefore, it does not progress. Progression is a certain motion. But motion is an action. Every action, however, is either in the essence or from the essence. In the essence, indeed, the motion of progression and production does not seem to occur. For beings would not exist thence through that motion. Therefore, in order for them to exit, they required a motion from the essence, or rather from the <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence</gloss> of the One. For its <term>hyparxis</term> is to it that which essence is to beings. What then? By the exit of beings from the <term>hyparxis</term> of the One, is the One exhausted for the beings? Far from it. For it is not moved. Therefore, they proceeded by rest. But it does not rest either. For it has nothing in which it might rest other than in itself. Nor anything to which it might be moved. For it is everywhere. For Hermes says most truly: 
<note>original: "Καὶ οὗ δ' αὐτοῦ οὐ δέν ἐκτὸς, οὐδ' αὐτὸς οὐδενός."</note>
And there is nothing outside of him, nor is he outside of anything. But in what way, finally, did he produce the second beings? Perhaps by his own rest, he extracts them from himself. Are they, however, moved away from him, while he remains? But extraction is a certain action. Action, however, is motion. Therefore, is he also moved? Does he have rest first, and motion afterwards? Does the question therefore return to the same point? Not at all. But in it, rest is moved, and motion rests. And that which is moved in him is moved stably from him, and that which rests rests movably. Namely, it remains itself. And it remains, extracting all things from itself by its own fecundity and bringing them forth outside of itself; it brings them forth from itself, remaining itself what it was before. For in what way could it become less than one? Or in what way could the things which it brings forth from itself depart outside of it, when it is everywhere? And it still contains all the produced things within itself. Therefore, it is not exhausted by those first things of its own, nor does it empty itself so that it becomes less than one, or less than all.
pages.90: Nor does it depart anywhere from itself as One, or from the plenitude of its own all-ness, nor is it split into many. The light of the sun, indeed, emits rays from itself; yet the light itself does not turn out to be less. Fire brings forth heat from itself, yet not less than before; indeed, it retains the same for itself. So the First, so the Principle, so the One, so the Good, so God, has produced all things without any diminution of his own primacy, or principality, or unity, or goodness, or deity, and without any helping matter. Indeed, he extracted them from himself and brought them forth outside himself. He brought them forth, however, because he is one, so that from this a multitude of things might be born. He brought them forth because of his goodness, so that that multitude and number might be beings, and that they might by no means be "non-beings." For he retained these within himself, so that when he wishes, he brings them forth, and when he does not wish, he does not. Thus, the One, in the production of secondary things, does not progress itself, nor is it moved. But while he brings them forth, and they progress from him, he remains in himself. They, however, proceed and emanate by an action from his <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence</gloss>, no differently than water emanates from its fountain, with the fountain itself indeed remaining unmoved, but bringing forth water; the water, however, is moved and flows forth from there. What then? If it is unmoved and remains in itself, does it not seem to produce? Production is an action, and action is motion. Or is it both moved and not moved? And does it both produce and not produce? And does it effect things and not effect them, in its own ways, namely, ineffable ones? It does not effect them, indeed, because since they are already existing in him, he only discerns them from himself. It does indeed effect them, because he brings them forth from himself, and they flow from him. Does the previous question therefore seem to return? Do they proceed from the One by themselves? Or do they have another cause for their procession? Certainly, they are produced either by themselves, or by another, or by the One itself. By another, indeed, it is least to be said. For what is prior to the One, or equal to the One? Not by themselves, except insofar as they do not resist the producer and open their assent to their own production. The One, however, brings them forth from itself by the necessity of its own goodness to act, simultaneously making them other than himself and other than his own all-ness, so that the cause might be not the identity of these with those, but the otherness of these from those. Which cause was nothing other than the very progression and procession of things from him. For every procession, or emanation, occurs with a secretion. Every secretion from the One, however, is a cause of multitude. And when a multitude begins in the One, then a procession succeeds. But if the One is not that which makes the secretion from which the multiplication is made, and from this the procession, what then would that be? Certainly, nothing other than that power of which we spoke, which is the middle between the One and being. For unless this intervened, the production would not happen. But who moves this power, so that it might make the secretion? Perhaps nothing other than goodness. For unless this moved that, so that it might separate all things from itself and bring forth all things from itself, so that it might communicate itself to all, it would seem to be touched by envy. But what envy is there in the most simple? What passion in the most perfect? Therefore, the Good itself, not as One but as Good, is the most primary cause of the secretion of fertile things from the "One-all," from the firsts. Now, secretion is the cause of multiplication. Multiplication is the cause of progression. Let this be made manifest by an example. The center of a circle is one and indivisible. In that One are the ends of all the lines proceeding from it, not in the least distinct among themselves in it. From it, lines proceed that are innumerable, now distinct among themselves, all the way to the circumference, which were all indifferent in the center. While, however, they are secreted from the center, they are multiplied; and while they are multiplied, they proceed from the One; as they proceed, they depart from it. This departure is after the center. And the center is not its cause. But there is a certain flux from it, by which the lines are both secreted from it, and multiplied, and proceed, and depart. Nor is it itself the cause of this departure. Nor does it depart from itself, nor is it exhausted so that it might multiply itself into lines. But after their departure, the center still remains. Nor is it diminished or does it suffer anything because of the exit of the lines. The lines, however, exiting and proceeding from it, are no longer what they were in it. But they are both from it and distinct among themselves. Yet they have from it that which they are, and it attributes being to them. Nor are they torn away from it, but depend upon it. For the cause of every procession remains. And that which proceeds remains in the property and terms of its cause. So that that which proceeds is seen both to be in the same cause in which it had been, and also to have departed thence. In this holy way (if it is not sacrilege to use this human similitude), all things are secreted from the One indistinctly, and they proceed as all things multiplied and distinct. What, however, in that progression from the One, do they themselves carry with them from the One? Or does it bestow something upon them? Or rather, does it bestow them by its own goodness, and they, enjoying that goodness, willingly carry with them those things with which they have been, as it were, endowed? But what are those things which they carry with them as a gift? Surely the second One, given as a portion to each from the first One, through which both the individuals are one, and through which they are also many. And through which they are also beings. For beings could not be unless they were one. Nor could they be many unless they came from the One. These, therefore, secreted from the One, after the "One-all," are simultaneously one and many. And they are after the principle, which had been the fourth condition of the principle. And they are from the One, and from the principle, which had been its third condition. For in what way could it become less than the One? Or how could the things which it brings forth from itself go outside it, when it is everywhere? And does it still contain all the products within itself? <translation page="90">
Nor does it depart anywhere from its own One, or from the fullness of its own "all-ness," nor is it split into many. The light of the sun indeed emits rays from itself, yet the light itself does not become less. Fire throws heat from itself, yet it does not retain any less than before; rather, it retains the same for itself. Thus the First, thus the Principle, thus the One, thus the Good, thus God, produced all things without anything being diminished in its priority, or in its principality, or in its unity, or in its goodness, or in its deity, with no matter aiding. Indeed, it even brought forth the matter itself from itself and outside itself. It brought it forth, however, because it is one, so that from thence a multitude of things might be begotten. It brought it forth on account of goodness, so that the multitude and that number might be beings, and that non-beings might by no means exist. For it retained these in itself, so that when it wishes, it may bring them forth, and when it does not wish, it may not bring them forth. Thus, the One, in the production of secondary things, does not progress from itself, nor is it moved. But while it brings them forth, and they progress from it, it remains in itself. They, however, proceed and emanate from the action out of its subsistence, not otherwise than as water emanates from its own spring, the spring indeed being unmoved, but bringing forth the water; the water, however, is moved and gushes forth from thence. What then? If it is unmoved and remains in itself, does it not seem to produce? Production is an action, and action is a motion. Or is it both moved and not moved? And does it produce and not produce? And does it effect things, and not effect them, in its own ways, namely, ineffable ones? It does not effect them, indeed, because since they are already existing in it, it only distinguishes them from itself. It does effect them, however, because it brings them forth from itself, and they flow from it. Does the prior question therefore seem to return? Do they proceed from the One by themselves? Or do they have another cause for their procession? Certainly, they are produced either by themselves, or by another, or by the One itself. By another, indeed, it must least of all be said. For what is prior to the One, or equal to the One? Not by themselves, except insofar as they do not resist the producer and offer assent to their own production. The One, however, brings them forth from itself, by the necessity of its own goodness toward action, at the same time making them distinct from itself and from its own "all-ness," so that it might become the cause, not of the identity of these with those, but of the otherness of these from those. Which cause was nothing other than the very progression and procession of things from it. For every procession, or emanation, involves a secretion. But every secretion from the One is a cause of multitude. And when a multitude begins in the One, then a procession ensues. But if the One is not that which causes the secretion, from which multiplication occurs, and from this, what is the procession? Certainly it is nothing other than that power of which we spoke, which is intermediate between the One and being. For unless this intervened, production would not occur. But who moves this power so that it might cause a secretion? Perhaps nothing other than goodness. For unless this moved that, so that it might separate all things from itself and bring them forth from itself, in order to communicate itself to all things, it would seem to be touched by envy. But what envy is there in the most simple? What passion in the most perfect? Therefore, the Good itself, not as the One, but as the Good, is the most primary cause of the secretion of fertile things from the "One-all," from the first things. Secretion, however, is the cause of multiplication. Multiplication is the cause of progression. Let this be made manifest by an example. The center of a circle is one and indivisible. In that One are the ends of all the lines proceeding from it, not in the least distinct from each other within it. From it, the lines proceed, innumerable and already distinct from each other, as far as the circumference, which were all indifferent in the center. While, however, they are secreted from the center, they are multiplied; and while they are multiplied, they proceed from the One; and proceeding, they depart from it. This departure is after the center. And the cause of it is not the center. But it is a certain flow from it, by which the lines are both secreted from it, and multiplied, and proceed, and depart. Nor is the center itself the cause of this departure. Nor does it depart from itself, nor is it emptied so that it might multiply itself into lines. But after their departure, the center still remains. Nor is it diminished or harmed by the departure of the lines. The lines, however, going out and proceeding from it, are no longer what they were in it. But they are both from it and distinct among themselves. Yet they have from it that which they are, and it bestows being upon them. Nor are they torn away from it; but they depend upon it. For the cause of every procession remains. And what proceeds remains in the property and boundaries of its cause. So that what proceeds may seem both to be in the same cause in which it had been, and also to have departed from thence. In this sacred way (if it be not forbidden to use this analogy), all things are secreted from the One indiscriminately, and they proceed as all things multiplied and distinct. What, however, in that progression from the One, do they carry with them from the One? Or does it bestow anything upon them? Or does it bestow them by its own goodness, and do they, enjoying that goodness, carry them with them willingly, things with which they have been, as it were, gifted? But what are those things which they carry with them as gifts? Truly, the second One, given to each as a portion from the first One, through which individual things are one, and through which they are also many. And through which they are also beings. For they could not be beings unless they were one. Nor could they be many unless they came from the One. These, therefore, secreted from the One, after the "One-all," are both one and many at the same time. And they are after the principle, which had been the fourth condition of the principle. And they are from the One and from the principle, which had been its third condition. For these are neither before the One, nor with the One, but from the One. <summary>Patrizi explores the process of emanation from the absolute One, using the analogy of a center and its radii to explain how the One produces multiplicity without being diminished or moved.</summary>

In essence, indeed, there does not seem to be a motion of progression and production. For beings would not exist from thence through that motion. Therefore, in order to exit, they required a motion from the essence, or rather from the subsistence of the One. For its subsistence is that which is essence to beings. What then? By the exit of beings from the subsistence of the One, is the One emptied for the beings? Far from it. For it is not moved. Therefore, they proceeded by rest. But it does not rest either. For it has nothing in which to rest other than itself. Nor is there anything into which it might be moved. For it is everywhere. For Hermes says most truly:
> <term>Καὶ οὗ δ' αὐτοῦ οὐ δέν ἐκτὸς, οὐδ' αὐτὸς οὐδενός</term> <gloss>And nothing is outside of him, nor is he outside of anything.</gloss>
And nothing outside of him, nor is he outside of anything. But in what way, finally, did it produce secondary beings? Perhaps it draws them forth from itself by its own rest. But are those things separated from it, while it remains itself? But a drawing forth is a certain action. An action, however, is a motion. Therefore, is it also moved? Does it have motion and rest in itself? Rest first? Motion afterwards? Does the question therefore return to the same? Not at all. But in it, rest moves and motion rests. And what moves in it moves stably from it, and what rests, rests movably. Indeed, it itself remains. And remaining, it draws all things from itself by its own fertility and brings them forth outside itself; it brings them forth from itself, remaining what it was before. For in what way could it become less than the One? Or how could the things which it brings forth from itself go outside it, when it is everywhere? And does it still contain all the products within itself? Therefore, it is not emptied by those first things of its own, nor does it evacuate itself so as to become less than the One, or less than all things.
pages.90: Nor does it depart anywhere from its own One, or from the fullness of its own "all-ness," nor is it split into many. The light of the sun indeed emits rays from itself, yet the light itself does not become less. Fire throws heat from itself, yet it does not retain any less than before; rather, it retains the same for itself. Thus the First, thus the Principle, thus the One, thus the Good, thus God, produced all things without anything being diminished in its priority, or in its principality, or in its unity, or in its goodness, or in its deity, with no matter aiding. Indeed, it even brought forth the matter itself from itself and outside itself. It brought it forth, however, because it is one, so that from thence a multitude of things might be begotten. It brought it forth on account of goodness, so that the multitude and that number might be beings, and that non-beings might by no means exist. For it retained these in itself, so that when it wishes, it may bring them forth, and when it does not wish, it may not bring them forth. Thus, the One, in the production of secondary things, does not progress from itself, nor is it moved. But while it brings them forth, and they progress from it, it remains in itself. They, however, proceed and emanate from the action out of its subsistence, not otherwise than as water emanates from its own spring, the spring indeed being unmoved, but bringing forth the water; the water, however, is moved and gushes forth from thence. What then? If it is unmoved and remains in itself, does it not seem to produce? Production is an action, and action is a motion. Or is it both moved and not moved? And does it produce and not produce? And does it effect things, and not effect them, in its own ways, namely, ineffable ones? It does not effect them, indeed, because since they are already existing in it, it only distinguishes them from itself. It does effect them, however, because it brings them forth from itself, and they flow from it. Does the prior question therefore seem to return? Do they proceed from the One by themselves? Or do they have another cause for their procession? Certainly, they are produced either by themselves, or by another, or by the One itself. By another, indeed, it must least of all be said. For what is prior to the One, or equal to the One? Not by themselves, except insofar as they do not resist the producer and offer assent to their own production. The One, however, brings them forth from itself, by the necessity of its own goodness toward action, at the same time making them distinct from itself and from its own "all-ness," so that it might become the cause, not of the identity of these with those, but of the otherness of these from those. Which cause was nothing other than the very progression and procession of things from it. For every procession, or emanation, involves a secretion. But every secretion from the One is a cause of multitude. And when a multitude begins in the One, then a procession ensues. But if the One is not that which causes the secretion, from which multiplication occurs, and from this, what is the procession? Certainly it is nothing other than that power of which we spoke, which is intermediate between the One and being. For unless this intervened, production would not occur. But who moves this power so that it might cause a secretion? Perhaps nothing other than goodness. For unless this moved that, so that it might separate all things from itself and bring them forth from itself, in order to communicate itself to all things, it would seem to be touched by envy. But what envy is there in the most simple? What passion in the most perfect? Therefore, the Good itself, not as the One, but as the Good, is the most primary cause of the secretion of fertile things from the "One-all," from the first things. Secretion, however, is the cause of multiplication. Multiplication is the cause of progression. Let this be made manifest by an example. The center of a circle is one and indivisible. In that One are the ends of all the lines proceeding from it, not in the least distinct from each other within it. From it, the lines proceed, innumerable and already distinct from each other, as far as the circumference, which were all indifferent in the center. While, however, they are secreted from the center, they are multiplied; and while they are multiplied, they proceed from the One; and proceeding, they depart from it. This departure is after the center. And the cause of it is not the center. But it is a certain flow from it, by which the lines are both secreted from it, and multiplied, and proceed, and depart. Nor is the center itself the cause of this departure. Nor does it depart from itself, nor is it emptied so that it might multiply itself into lines. But after their departure, the center still remains. Nor is it diminished or harmed by the departure of the lines. The lines, however, going out and proceeding from it, are no longer what they were in it. But they are both from it and distinct among themselves. Yet they have from it that which they are, and it bestows being upon them. Nor are they torn away from it; but they depend upon it. For the cause of every procession remains. And what proceeds remains in the property and boundaries of its cause. So that what proceeds may seem both to be in the same cause in which it had been, and also to have departed from thence. In this sacred way (if it be not forbidden to use this analogy), all things are secreted from the One indiscriminately, and they proceed as all things multiplied and distinct. What, however, in that progression from the One, do they carry with them from the One? Or does it bestow anything upon them? Or does it bestow them by its own goodness, and do they, enjoying that goodness, carry them with them willingly, things with which they have been, as it were, gifted? But what are those things which they carry with them as gifts? Truly, the second One, given to each as a portion from the first One, through which individual things are one, and through which they are also many. And through which they are also beings. For they could not be beings unless they were one. Nor could they be many unless they came from the One. These, therefore, secreted from the One, after the "One-all," are both one and many at the same time. And they are after the principle, which had been the fourth condition of the principle. And they are from the One and from the principle, which had been its third condition. For these are neither before the One, nor with the One, but from the One. ### III.

Hence, if we ask about the person who has completed usucapion, we say that whatever legal right other owners possess in their own property, the same right is held by him who has completed usucapion in the property so acquired.

### IV.

For every individual owner has one right over his own property, and that the highest, which is called *Ownership*.

### V.

We wish for this to be understood generally here, not restricting it to one or the other of its species.

### VI.

Accepted thus in an absolute sense, it is considered neither direct ownership nor beneficial ownership, unless the subject matter at hand suggests otherwise.

### VII.

Or the person of him who allowed himself to be prescribed against; or the quality of the thing whose ownership is acquired through usucapion.

### VIII.

For this acquisition adds to him who has completed usucapion only as much right as he had from whom the thing was transferred. Or, as the scholars say, prescription does not extend beyond the right that was prescribed.

### IX.

Therefore, the new owner shall have the right of holding and possessing the thing; or he shall be able to obtain it by his own right, so that he may hold and possess the item acquired through usucapion.
</translation>

### XXXVIII.

A demonstration of the *propter quid* <gloss>the reason why</gloss> can proceed from every kind of cause; principally, however, from the formal cause; and hence, that which is accustomed to be said by some, that the middle term of demonstration is most especially the definition of the subject itself, is to be understood as the formal definition.

### XXXIX.

Nor do I think it should be denied that it can be proven, and that demonstratively, that such a formal definition agrees with its subject; but not as its definition; nor even through a formal cause; but either from the material, or the end, or from the efficient cause itself; for of a formal definition, there is no other definition given in the same genus.

### XL.

But when a proper attribute is demonstrated of its subject through the formal cause of that attribute itself, then there is nothing to prevent the formal definition from also being proven demonstratively through the formal cause, that is, the definition of the subject.

### XLI.

Concluding therefore, we rightly establish as the most excellent middle term of demonstration neither the definition of the subject alone, nor the definition of the attribute alone, but both combined together, inasmuch as it contains in itself all the causes of the conclusion.

### XXXVIII.

A demonstration of the *propter quid* <gloss>that which is on account of which</gloss> can proceed from every kind of cause; primarily, however, from the formal cause; and hence, what is commonly said by some, that the medium of demonstration is most especially the definition of the subject itself, should be understood as the formal definition.

### XXXIX.

Nor do I think it should be denied that it can be proven, and that demonstratively, that such a formal definition agrees with its subject; but not as its own definition; nor even through a formal cause; but rather from the matter, or from the end, or from its efficient cause; for of a formal definition, there is not given another definition in the same genus.

### XL.

But when a proper property is demonstrated of its subject through the formal cause of that property itself, then there is nothing that prohibits the formal definition from being proven by a demonstration in the same way through a formal cause, that is, the definition of the subject.

### XLI.

Concluding therefore, we justly establish as the most excellent medium of demonstration neither the definition of the subject alone, nor the definition of the property, but both joined together, as that which contains in itself all the causes of the conclusion.

<translation page="11">Aristotle labors in vain. Fourth, in the beginning of *On the Heavens* he says, "For these also are bodies and magnitudes. This however will be a body and magnitude. These however are defects in themselves," and everyone explains this: and simply in the same place that bodies having body and magnitude are mixed, which have elements. Not only are qualities in the mixture, but elements. Fifth, principally, if this position holds, then the complexion <note>the balanced state of qualities in a mixture</note> would be by mixture, which is against them. And it is proven: for "by" <note>per</note> is a quality insofar as it is a quality, which is insofar as it is an instrument of substance; for to be an instrument is an accident to a quality insofar as it is a quality, and an accident is posterior to that to which it happens. Therefore, the connection from qualities insofar as they are qualities is through a connection from <note>them</note> insofar as they are instruments, and thus the complexion will be by mixture. Sixth, an instrument ought to be more so: but the primary qualities are instruments of the forms of the elements. Therefore, the forms and qualities ought to be simultaneous, and thus all will be in act in the mixture. Seventh, one simple form cannot be an instrument for two forms entirely in species, but each part of the mixture is an instrument of the form of the mixture. Therefore, not of the elementary forms. Eighth, Aristotle shows in the second book of *On Generation* that there are four bodies in the world, because there are four combinations of the poles. Then I argue: in the mixture there are four pole-conjugations. Therefore, the four elements are there in act; otherwise, the reasoning of Aristotle is null, and especially since Aristotle there says that water is the coagulation of cold and moist, and fire is the burning of hot and dry. But in the mixture are the goods of this; therefore, they are finite. Plato also says that man is a <term>microcosmon</term> <gloss>little world</gloss>, that in him four elements are observed, and four qualities, which Plotinus also affirms. From these, we conclude that qualities cannot be in the mixture unless the elementary forms are there.

### Chapter VIII.

<note>A woodcut depicts an ornamental initial D.</note>
They said that the elements do not contribute to the being of the mixture, nor to the substantial forms, nor to the qualities, but rather that the mixture can exercise their works, and thus be saved according to their powers. But let us show that this is impossible. For either the elements are in the mixture, because the forms and qualities of the mixture can exercise the effect, and then <note>they are</note> theirs; or because there are in the mixture, not indeed qualities of the same species as the qualities of the elements, but because of powers of another kind, distinct from the forms and qualities of the mixture. First, let us destroy the first part, and we will refute the second. If therefore it is (as he says nearby), then the heaven would be a mixture of primary qualities and of the forms of the four bodies, which Aristotle proves to be false in the book *On the Heavens*. And he brings an enthymeme: for the light of the sun can exercise all the works of the elements, as Averroes demonstrates in the second book of *On the Heavens*, second part, 42. It exercises, moreover, dryness in autumn, coldness in winter, moisture in spring, heat in summer. Therefore, the four qualities are contained in the light by power. Therefore, light would be the complexion of the sun, just as the quality of the mixture is the complexion of the mixture. Furthermore, the sun produces fire by its presence, water by its absence, and the intermediate elements by its intermediate disposition. Therefore, the sun contains the four elements, both because of a similar action and because of its nobility. Therefore, because of its substance, it will contain elementary forms, and because of its light, qualities. Therefore, it is a tempered mixture, just as a generable mixture. Again, then gold would be mixed from metals; for gold, because of its nobility and because of convenience in working, contains all metals, as the alchemists say. Therefore, there will not be only four simple bodies. Moreover, then the rational soul would be a mixture of the forms of the four elements and the natural soul, both because it can use their works and because it is nobler. These things, however, we have not yet seen in any of the books of Aristotle. Now let us argue against the second member. First, because if they are alone in the mixture, then they are not qualities, nor forms; then they will not be able to come into operative act from their own sort. Moreover, as a thing relates to being, so it relates to working; but a being in power is not a perfect being. Therefore, it cannot act. Again, the moving species always estimates, as he hands down in the ninth book of philosophy and the third of physical listening; since therefore the elements are not there in act, nor can they act, unless we recur to the form of the mixture, and thus it will be the first member. But because this position (however one understands it) is against Aristotle, I argue with his words. He himself says at the end of the first book of *On Generation*, concluding <column-break/> what mixture is: "mixture is the union of things mixed, which have been altered." Nor does it avail to say (as some assert), "The Philosopher of altered things" or "have been altered," assuming it is past tense. For that word "of mixed things" says what is actual: that there is a mixture of those things that have altered themselves, as the text says. But neither powers nor the ability have altered, because it is not a mixture. Furthermore, he says in the same place: "When a drop of wine is not mixed in a thousand thousand amphorae of water, it is dissolved; for the species is transmuted into the whole water." Therefore, that which is mixable must remain somewhat in act. Again, he shows which are easy by division, of which the humid are examples. If, therefore, the mixables were only in the mixture by power or potentiality, why would he labor so much in showing what is easy and difficult to mix? If one truly considers all the words of the book *On Generation*, one will find almost everything against this sect, although they greatly glory in the words of Aristotle. They also act against these words of Aristotle brought forward in the next chapter and others, and we will induce many other things afterward in the opinion of Averroes, and we will erect his reasons. These things said about the position of the Latins are sufficient.

->The position and words of Averroes. Chapter IX.<-

<note>A woodcut depicts an ornamental initial M.</note>
Averroes moves this question in the third book of *On the Heavens and the World*, commentary 47, up to the words: "And it must be asked why the forms of the elements do not remain in act regarding the powers, namely in mixtures, carrying other forms, namely of the mixtures, which they receive." Therefore, it is their question why elementary forms, received under perfect being, are not dispositions of matter to receive other forms of mixtures, and he argues that it ought to be. It is said, when you have already posited that they are not of matter for some forms except for their own forms, that if it is argued thus: the forms by which matters are properly made proper matters for mixtures are dispositions, by the mediation of which they receive in matter the forms of mixtures. But elementary forms are those by which matter is properly made proper for the mixture. Therefore, by the mediation of elementary forms, they receive the forms of the mixtures. And thus, elementary forms will be in act in all mixtures. Then he solves the question, and first he proves that elementary forms under perfect being do not receive <note>forms</note> in matter, so that by their mediation they receive the forms of the mixtures, and he says: "Let us say therefore that if it were as we said, that namely they received under perfect being, it would be necessary that no being be generated from them; that is, that no being would receive in matter by their mediation that would be different in substantial forms, but yet it would be an accident." This is said: if elementary forms were first received in prime matter, then everything coming to matter and received in it by their mediation would be an accident. He does not deduce the enthymeme here, but in many places of *Physics* and *First Philosophy* and in the booklet *On the Substance of the World* he has deduced it. For everything coming to a being in perfect act and specific act is an accident. This is the difference between accidental and substantial forms, as he declared the same in the second book of *On the Soul*. Second, principally, he proves that elementary forms are corrupted, that is, remitted. To this end, so that matter by their mediation might receive the forms of mixtures, and he says: "And therefore it is necessary, when one form is generated from them, that their forms be corrupted according to mediation, that is, according to part." This is said: that if matter by their mediation ought to receive the form of the mixture, they are remitted according to their substances somewhat in part. Then third, he proves that they are not corrupted from every part, so that naked matter receives the forms of mixtures, and he says: "Since if they were corrupted according to the whole, then prime matter would receive all forms essentially by itself."

Second, it would follow that it would not receive the forms of mixtures by the mediation of these bodies. From these it can be grasped that elementary forms are not received under intense being, but remitted in part, not in whole; but how this reasoning is valid, we will say in the difficulties. Averroes immediately moves a question against himself and says: "If therefore anyone should say it follows from this that the substantial forms of the elements receive more and less, which is false." For this disposition is of accidents, not of substantial forms. And he argues, because everything is in many places, as in the *Categories*: that substantial forms do not receive more and less. From these two, that statement appears false. He answers and says, first, that the substantial forms of the elements are diminutive with respect to perfect substantial forms. Second, he says that their being is a medium between substantial forms and accidents. From these he infers third.

<summary>This page discusses the debate over whether elementary forms exist in act within a mixture, arguing against the view that they are merely potential and supporting Averroes' position that they exist in a remitted or diminished state.</summary>

Through these words he denotes that the form of the mixture is a connection of four forms, just as an intermediate color is a connection of refracted extremes. Whether it is so, we will say later. Then he removes the error of Avicenna, and first he narrates it and says first that this determination eluded Avicenna. This, however, is false, because then the mixture would not be one; either because of one form, and this is not so, because four perfect ones are present; or because of contact, in which way continuous or contiguous things are one; and this is not so, because then the mixture would be one by contact and not by true union. Second, the mixture is one per se, either because of one substantial form or because of one accidental form; not because of an accident, because then it would not be one per se. If it is one because of a substantial form, therefore there are not four perfect forms in one mixture. Third, he argues because then each would be distinct, that is, in another part of matter from the other. For for one point of matter to have two perfect forms is impossible, and thus not every part of the mixture is mixed. Fourth, he argues: if elementary forms remain in the mixture under perfect being, either the qualities also remain under perfect being, or only the qualities are remitted. If the former, then in the mixture there will be four perfect elements, like fire; for fire is nothing but a composition of hot and dry. If, however, the forms remain and the qualities are remitted, then it would be possible for the whole form to be without its whole quality; for the whole quality and the part are of one reason. But if a form can be without a part, it will also be able to be without the whole. But let these be so. It still remains to inquire into this man's doctrine. First, what is the form of mixture? Second <column-break/> what is mixture? Third, what is complexion? Fourth, how is mixture through complexion, and whether mixture and complexion are posterior to the ultimate form of mixture, or another form through them? Fifth, how do mixture and complexion relate to each other, and how do they relate to the form? Sixth, what was the necessity of mixture in a composite, and why were qualities alone not sufficient? From another place, the contrary appears; for through the form of the mixture, the mixture is placed in a species. Now, through that aggregate, the mixture does not seem to be placed in a species. It seems to me, saving a better judgment, that the form of the mixture is twofold: disposing matter to a further form, and perfecting matter and constituting the composite in a certain species. The form of the mixture that is disposing is a certain medium of forms, which is that aggregate disposing to the ultimate form, as he says. They said that the elements do not contribute to the being of the mixture, nor to the substantial forms, nor to the qualities, but rather that the mixture can exercise their works, and thus be saved according to their powers. But let us show that this is impossible. For either the elements are in the mixture, because the forms and qualities of the mixture can exercise the effect, and then <note>they are</note> theirs; or because there are in the mixture, not indeed qualities of the same species as the qualities of the elements, but because of powers of another kind, distinct from the forms and qualities of the mixture. First, let us destroy the first part, and we will refute the second. If therefore it is (as he says nearby), then the heaven would be a mixture of primary qualities and of the forms of the four bodies, which Aristotle proves to be false in the book *On the Heavens*. And he brings an enthymeme: for the light of the sun can exercise all the works of the elements, as Averroes demonstrates in the second book of *On the Heavens*, second part, 42. It exercises, moreover, dryness in autumn, coldness in winter, moisture in spring, heat in summer. Therefore, the four qualities are contained in the light by power. Therefore, light would be the complexion of the sun, just as the quality of the mixture is the complexion of the mixture. Furthermore, the sun produces fire by its presence, water by its absence, and the intermediate elements by its intermediate disposition. Therefore, the sun contains the four elements, both because of a similar action and because of its nobility. Therefore, because of its substance, it will contain elementary forms, and because of its light, qualities. Therefore, it is a tempered mixture, just as a generable mixture. Again, then gold would be mixed from metals; for gold, because of its nobility and because of convenience in working, contains all metals, as the alchemists say. Therefore, there will not be only four simple bodies. Moreover, then the rational soul would be a mixture of the forms of the four elements and the natural soul, both because it can use their works and because it is nobler. Again, the moving species always estimates, as he hands down in the ninth book of philosophy and the third of physical listening; since therefore the elements are not there in act, nor can they act, unless we recur to the form of the mixture, and thus it will be the first member. But because this position (however one understands it) is against Aristotle, I argue with his words. He himself says at the end of the first book of *On Generation*, concluding <column-break/> what mixture is: "mixture is the union of things mixed, which have been altered." Nor does it avail to say (as some assert), "The Philosopher of altered things" or "have been altered," assuming it is past tense. For that word "of mixed things" says what is actual: that there is a mixture of those things that have altered themselves, as the text says. Furthermore, he says in the same place: "When a drop of wine is not mixed in a thousand thousand amphorae of water, it is dissolved; for the species is transmuted into the whole water." Averroes moves this question in the third book of *On the Heavens and the World*, commentary 47, up to the words: "And it must be asked why the forms of the elements do not remain in act regarding the powers, namely in mixtures, carrying other forms, namely of the mixtures, which they receive." Therefore, it is their question why elementary forms, received under perfect being, are not dispositions of matter to receive other forms of mixtures, and he argues that it ought to be. It is said, when you have already posited that they are not of matter for some forms except for their own forms, that if it is argued thus: the forms by which matters are properly made proper matters for mixtures are dispositions, by the mediation of which they receive in matter the forms of mixtures. But elementary forms are those by which matter is properly made proper for the mixture. Therefore, by the mediation of elementary forms, they receive the forms of the mixtures. And thus, elementary forms will be in act in all mixtures. Then he solves the question, and first he proves that elementary forms under perfect being do not receive <note>forms</note> in matter, so that by their mediation they receive the forms of the mixtures, and he says: "Let us say therefore that if it were as we said, that namely they received under perfect being, it would be necessary that no being be generated from them; that is, that no being would receive in matter by their mediation that would be different in substantial forms, but yet it would be an accident." This is said: if elementary forms were first received in prime matter, then everything coming to matter and received in it by their mediation would be an accident. He does not deduce the enthymeme here, but in many places of *Physics* and *First Philosophy* and in the booklet *On the Substance of the World* he has deduced it. For everything coming to a being in perfect act and specific act is an accident. This is the difference between accidental and substantial forms, as he declared the same in the second book of *On the Soul*. To this end, so that matter by their mediation might receive the forms of mixtures, and he says: "And therefore it is necessary, when one form is generated from them, that their forms be corrupted according to mediation, that is, according to part." This is said: that if matter by their mediation ought to receive the form of the mixture, they are remitted according to their substances somewhat in part. Then third, he proves that they are not corrupted from every part, so that naked matter receives the forms of mixtures, and he says: "Since if they were corrupted according to the whole, then prime matter would receive all forms essentially by itself."

Second, it would follow that it would not receive the forms of mixtures by the mediation of these bodies. Averroes raises this question in the third [book of] *On the Heavens and the World*, commentary 47, up to the words: "And it must be asked why the forms of the elements do not remain in act regarding powers." Namely, in mixtures carrying other forms, namely of mixtures, which they receive. Therefore, the question of theirs is: why are the elementary forms, having been accepted under perfect being, not dispositions of matter to receive the other forms of mixtures? And he argues that it ought to be. It is said, since you have already posited that they are not [dispositions] of matter for certain forms except because of their own forms, for if so, I argue: the forms by which matter is properly made [into] proper matter for mixtures are dispositions, mediating through which they receive the forms of mixtures in matter. But the elementary forms are those by which matter is properly made [into] proper matter for a mixture. Therefore, mediating through the elementary forms, they receive the forms of the mixtures. And thus the elementary forms will be in act in all mixtures. Then he solves the question; and first he proves that the elementary forms under perfect being do not receive [the forms] in matter, in such a way that they receive the forms of mixtures through them as mediators, and he says: "Let us say therefore that if it were as we have said, that they were received under perfect being, it would be necessary that no being would generate from them; that is, that no being would receive in matter, through them as mediators, what would be different in substantial forms, but nevertheless it would be an accident." He says that if the elementary forms were primarily received in primary matter, then everything arriving at the matter and received in it through them as mediators would be an accident. He does not deduce the enthymeme here, but he deduced it in many places of *Physical Auscultation* and [the first book of] *First Philosophy*, and in the booklet *On the Substance of the World*. For everything arriving at a being in perfect and specific act is an accident. This is the difference between accidental and substantial forms, as he declared the same in the second [book of] *On the Soul*. Second, he principally proves that the elementary forms are corrupted, that is, remitted. To this [end], that matter may receive the forms of mixtures through them as mediators, he says: "And therefore it is necessary, when one form is generated from them, that they corrupt their forms according to a midway point; that is, according to a part." This is what is said: that if matter is to receive the form of a mixture through them as mediators, they are remitted according to their substances in some part. Then third, he proves that they are not corrupted in every part, in such a way that naked matter would receive the forms of mixtures; and he says: "Since if they were corrupted according to the whole, then primary matter would receive all forms by itself essentially."

Second, it would follow that it would not receive the forms of mixtures through these bodies as mediators. From these, it can be grasped that the elementary forms are not received under intense being, but remitted in part, not in whole. But how this reasoning holds, we will say in the difficulties. Averroes immediately raises a question against himself and says: "If therefore anyone says it follows from this that the substantial forms of the elements receive 'more and less,' which is false. For this disposition is of accidents, not of substantial forms." And he argues: because every [substantial form] is in many places, as in the *Categories*, that substantial forms do not receive "more and less." From these two, that statement appears false. He answers and says: first, that the substantial [forms] of the elements are diminutive with respect to perfect substantial forms; second, he says that their being is a middle between substantial forms and accidents. From these he infers third...</translation>

<translation page="12">because these are imperfect and middle between substances and accidents, therefore it was not impossible that the substantial forms of the elements might be mixed, in such a way that from their collection there arrives a certain other form, which is called mixture, just as when whiteness and blackness are mixed, many intermediate colors arrive from them. By these words, he denotes the form of the mixture to be a nexus of four forms, just as an intermediate color is a nexus of refracted extremes; whether this is so, we will say later. Then he removes the error of Avicenna, and first he narrates it and says first that this determination eluded Avicenna. He says second that he conceded that substantial forms do not receive "more and less," and therefore concluded that the elements are not mixed except according to qualities and not according to substances, since mixture is a union of refractors. Now only qualities are refracted; therefore, the mixture will be only of them. He argues against this: first, because then the mixture would have many perfect and actual forms of elements. This, however, is false; because then the mixture would not be one, because either [it is one] because of one form, and this is not [the case] because four perfect ones are present, or because of contact, in which way continuous or contiguous things are one; and this is not at all, because then the mixture would be one by contact and not by true union. Second, the mixture is one by itself, either because of one substantial form or because of one accidental form; [it is] not [one] because of an accident, because then it would not be one by itself. If it is one because of a substantial form, therefore there are not four perfect forms in one mixture in this way. Third, he argues: because then each would be distinct, that is, in another part of matter from the other. For for one point of matter to have two perfect forms is impossible, and thus not every part of the mixture is mixed. Fourth, he argues: if the elementary forms remain in the mixture under perfect being, either the qualities also remain under perfect being, or only the qualities are remitted. If the first, then there will be four perfect elements in the mixture, such as fire, for fire is nothing but a composition of hot and dry. If, however, the forms remain and the qualities are remitted, then it would be possible for the whole form to be without its whole quality. For the whole quality and the part are of the same kind. But if a form can be without a part, it will also be able to be without the whole. Then he writes thus about Avicenna: "The paucity of this man's exercise in natural sciences and his good confidence in his own ingenuity led him to these errors." But against Averroes, one might argue that then the figures of the elements receive "more and less." Second, that the recipient ought to be denuded of the nature of the received. That matter standing under the form of an element would not be able to receive the form of a mixture, because they are of the same genus. To the first, he answers that the figure takes on the conditions of a perfect form as far as receiving "more and less" is concerned. These are elementary forms among themselves, not in comparison to the mixture. This is, in a crude way, the position of Averroes. This is regarding his position.

### Declaration of the position of Averroes. Chapter X.

But let these things be so. It still remains to inquire into this man's doctrine. First, what is the form of the mixture? Second,

<column-break/>

what is mixture? Third, what is <term>complexio</term> <gloss>complexion</gloss>? Fourth, how is mixture through <term>complexio</term>, and whether mixture and <term>complexio</term> are posterior to the ultimate form of the mixture, or another form through them? Fifth, how do mixture and <term>complexio</term> relate among themselves, and how to the form? Sixth, what was the necessity of mixture in a composite, and why were qualities alone not sufficient? For he himself did not sufficiently express these things. Regarding the first, Averroes seems, from the words accepted here, to want the form of the mixture to be an aggregate of four substantial forms, just as an intermediate color, according to him, is an aggregate of refracted extremes. From another place, the contrary appears. For through the form of the mixture, the mixture is placed in a species; now, through that aggregate, the mixture does not seem to be placed in a species. It seems to me, saving a better judgment, that the form of the mixture is twofold: disposing the matter to a further form, and perfecting the matter and constituting the composite in a certain species. The disposing form of the mixture is a certain middle of forms, which is that aggregate disposing to the ultimate form, as he says. The perfecting form of the mixture is the ultimate form constituting the whole in a certain species. For the rational soul in man, according to Averroes, is one in the end: it is the form of the mixture and the rational [form], although under another reason. For insofar as it places man in a genus and follows the mixture, it is called the form of the mixture. Insofar as it gives being to man, it is called specific and rational; thus his words can be glossed. Regarding the second, it must be said that mixture is a union of elementary forms. But since in every union there is need for something as act and something as potency, there is need in mixture for some form to be as act, and some as potency. The form, however, which is as act is the one dominating and overcoming; the form as potency is the one vanquished and overcome. From these, one mixture is constituted, and Averroes declared this in many places. Further, what is <term>complexio</term>? Let us say that it is a union of qualities again, with some overcoming and others vanquished. From these it follows that mixture is a nature through <term>complexio</term>. For just as forms are posterior to qualities, so is mixture [posterior] through <term>complexio</term>. For if both are in the same instant, nevertheless one is posterior according to reason and nature. Further, it must be said that <term>complexio</term> and mixture, as indeterminate and in potency, precede the form; as determinate and in act, they follow it. For as indeterminate, they are dispositions reducible to the genus of the material cause; as determinate, they are disposed through the form. And since the posterior of nature is the posterior of cause, as Averroes says in the book *On the Substance of the World*, therefore mixture is through <term>complexio</term> by the priority of matter to form, and mixture and <term>complexio</term> are posterior to the form by the priority of matter to form; and conversely, the form is posterior by the posteriority of form to matter. Then it remains to declare whence the elementary forms were necessary. And it seems that they were necessary first because of the natural order; for they are middles between primary matter and the ultimate form. Second, that instruments cannot be without principal causes, and because qualities are instruments, and forms are principal causes, therefore it was necessary for the forms to be present first. Third, because of the nature of the mixture; for otherwise the mixture would not be a mixture, for <term>complexio</term> arises only from qualities. These, therefore, were to be declared.

They said that the elements do not belong to the existence of the mixture, nor to the substantial forms, nor to the qualities. But let these things be so. It still remains to inquire into the doctrine of this man. First, what is the form of mixture. Second...

<column-break/>

what is mixture. Third, what is complexion. Fourth, how is mixture through complexion, and whether mixture and complexion are posterior to the final form of the mixture, or whether another form is through them. Fifth, how do mixture and complexion relate to each other, and how to the form. Sixth, what was the necessity of mixture in the composite, and why did qualities alone not suffice. For he did not express these things enough himself. As to the first, Averroes seems, from the words accepted here, to want the form of the mixture to be a gathering of the four substantial forms, just as an intermediate color is with him a gathering of refracted extremes. From another place, the contrary seems [to be the case], for through the form of the mixture the mixture is placed in its species. Now through that gathering, the mixture does not seem to be placed in its species. It seems to me, saving better judgment, that the form of the mixture is twofold: one disposing matter to a further form, and one perfecting matter and constituting the composite in a certain species. The form of the mixture that disposes is a certain mean of forms, which is that gathering disposing to the final form, as he says. The perfecting form of the mixture is the final form constituting the whole in a certain species. For the rational soul in man, according to Averroes, is one final thing [that] is the form of the mixture and the rational [form], although under another reason. For insofar as it places man in the genus and follows the mixture, it is called the form of the mixture. But insofar as it gives being to man, it is called specific and rational; thus his words can be glossed. As to the second, it must be said that mixture is the union of elementary forms. But since in every union there is a need for something as act, and something as potentiality, there is a need in mixture for some form to be as act, and some as potentiality. The form, however, which is as act, is the one dominating and overcoming. The form as potentiality is the one conquered and surpassed. From these, one mixture is constituted, and Averroes declared this in many places. Further, what is complexion? Let us say that it is the union of qualities, again with some overcoming and others conquered. From these it follows that mixture is nature through complexion. For just as forms are posterior to qualities, so is mixture through complexion. For if both are in the same instant, nevertheless one is posterior according to reason and nature. Further, it must be said that complexion and mixture, as indeterminate and in potentiality, precede the form; as determinate and in act, they follow it. For as indeterminate, they are dispositions reducible to the genus of the material cause; as determinate, they are disposed through the form. And since that which is posterior in nature is posterior in cause, as Averroes says in the book *On the Substance of the World*, therefore mixture is through complexion by priority of matter to form, and mixture and complexion are posterior to the form by priority of matter to form, and conversely the form is posterior by posteriority of form to matter. Third, because of the nature of the mixture. For otherwise the mixture would not be a mixture; for from qualities, there is only a complexion. These, therefore, were to be declared.

That matter standing under the form of an element would not be able to receive the form of the mixture, because they are of the same genus. To the first, he answers that the figure acquires the conditions of a perfect form as to receiving more and less. To the second, however, that the receiver must be denuded of the species of the received, not of the whole genus. And if you say against it, because thus matter existing under the form of water could receive the form of fire, he answers at the end of the comment that all elementary forms are of the same order in substantiality; but they are not thus elementary forms with the forms of mixtures. The major must therefore be understood as follows: that the receiver must be denuded of every form of the same order in order to receive any of them; thus there is no need for it to be denuded of every form of another order. Whence he says that it is not necessary for the receiver to be denuded of its whole genus which it ought to receive, but only of those which are of the same proximate genus, not the remote one. And therefore, matter cannot, while the form of one element remains and then any [part] is remitted, receive another elementary form, because then it would not be mixture. He wants, therefore, that matter must be denuded of every form of the same proximate genus and of the same order, if it ought to receive any of them. Here are the elementary forms among themselves, not in comparison to the mixture. This is, in a crude way, the position of Averroes. This about his position.

### Declaration of the position of Averroes. Chapter X.

<note>A woodcut depicts a historiated initial 'S'.</note>

But let these things be so. It still remains to inquire into the doctrine of this man. First, what is the form of mixture. Second...

<column-break/>

what is mixture. Third, what is complexion. Fourth, how is mixture through complexion, and whether mixture and complexion are posterior to the final form of the mixture, or whether another form is through them. Fifth, how do mixture and complexion relate to each other, and how to the form. Sixth, what was the necessity of mixture in the composite, and why did qualities alone not suffice. For he did not express these things enough himself. As to the first, Averroes seems, from the words accepted here, to want the form of the mixture to be a gathering of the four substantial forms, just as an intermediate color is with him a gathering of refracted extremes. From another place, the contrary seems [to be the case], for through the form of the mixture the mixture is placed in its species. Now through that gathering, the mixture does not seem to be placed in its species. It seems to me, saving better judgment, that the form of the mixture is twofold: one disposing matter to a further form, and one perfecting matter and constituting the composite in a certain species. The form of the mixture that disposes is a certain mean of forms, which is that gathering disposing to the final form, as he says. The perfecting form of the mixture is the final form constituting the whole in a certain species. For the rational soul in man, according to Averroes, is one final thing [that] is the form of the mixture and the rational [form], although under another reason. For insofar as it places man in the genus and follows the mixture, it is called the form of the mixture. But insofar as it gives being to man, it is called specific and rational; thus his words can be glossed. As to the second, it must be said that mixture is the union of elementary forms. But since in every union there is a need for something as act, and something as potentiality, there is a need in mixture for some form to be as act, and some as potentiality. The form, however, which is as act, is the one dominating and overcoming. The form as potentiality is the one conquered and surpassed. From these, one mixture is constituted, and Averroes declared this in many places. Further, what is complexion? Let us say that it is the union of qualities, again with some overcoming and others conquered. From these it follows that mixture is nature through complexion. For just as forms are posterior to qualities, so is mixture through complexion. For if both are in the same instant, nevertheless one is posterior according to reason and nature. Further, it must be said that complexion and mixture, as indeterminate and in potentiality, precede the form; as determinate and in act, they follow it. For as indeterminate, they are dispositions reducible to the genus of the material cause; as determinate, they are disposed through the form. And since that which is posterior in nature is posterior in cause, as Averroes says in the book *On the Substance of the World*, therefore mixture is through complexion by priority of matter to form, and mixture and complexion are posterior to the form by priority of matter to form, and conversely the form is posterior by posteriority of form to matter. Then it remains to declare whence the elementary forms were necessary, and it seems that they were first necessary because of the natural order. For they are a mean between first matter and the final form. Second, because instruments cannot be without principal causes, and because qualities are instruments, and forms are the principal causes, therefore it was necessary for the forms to exist beforehand. Third, because of the nature of the mixture. For otherwise the mixture would not be a mixture; for from qualities, there is only a complexion. These, therefore, were to be declared.
