Furthermore, he without doubt will be punished more severely who commits a double offense than one who commits a certain simple sin. Thus, for example, a robber seems to be met with a more severe penalty than a thief, for the former has sinned doubly, both through the murder itself and the resulting theft, and therefore he is worthy of a double punishment and must be castigated much more harshly than the thief, insofar as the one who is free from murder is found guilty only of simple theft. In the same way, adultery itself is punished more severely than fornication, since the former comes under the name of a double offense, whereas the latter only a simple one, and so on. A double offense, therefore, is justly repressed by a double and consequently more severe punishment than a simple offense. But now, he who sins while drunk sins likewise in a double way; in the beginning, indeed, because of the drunkenness itself, which has been declared more than enough in the preceding paragraph to be a foul sin and vice, and then because of the guilt admitted, for example, injuries inflicted upon a neighbor, or murder, or anything else of this kind. Hence, he who sins through drunkenness must also be punished doubly. Pittacus of Mytilene, one of the seven sages of Greece, famous in the 44th Olympiad, seems to have observed this—a man who, according to Plutarch in his book <term>On Tranquillity of Mind</term>, page 471 of my edition, Volume 2 of his works, was *rich, wise, and just*—and who wished for drunkards to be punished with a double penalty, as Diogenes Laërtius testifies in Book 1, in his life, page 19 of the London edition by Menagius; Aristotle also mentions him frequently, such as: in Book 3 of the <term>Ethics</term>, chapter 7; in Book 2 of the <term>Politics</term>, chapter 12; and elsewhere. And truly, how severely drunkenness was castigated in many well-ordered ancient republics is abundantly attested to by the older monuments of historians. Concerning the Athenians, the matter is certain, for they, since they disapproved of the vice of drunkenness in all people, according to the institution of Solon, punished the drunkard, especially if he were a leader, with death, according to Diogenes Laërtius in Book 1, in the life of Solon, page 14 of the London edition.</translation>

Thus, the vice of drunkenness was considered horrible by pagan writers, as it inflames and exposes every other vice, as Seneca asserts in Epistle 83. Ovid offers no different testimony concerning drunkenness in Book 1 of the <term>Amores</term> <gloss>Loves</gloss>, Elegy 6, where he says:

> Night, love, and wine persuade one to nothing moderate,
> This one is free from shame, Bacchus and love from fear.

To this is worthily joined Plautus in <term>Pseudolus</term>, Act V, line 1263. Propertius in Book 2, the penultimate Elegy to Cynthia. Quintus Horatius Flaccus, in Book 2 of his <term>Satires</term>, Satire 2, and others. But Pliny, in particular, has outlined the inconveniences and foulness of this vice in Book 14 of his <term>Natural History</term>, chapter 22, page 656 of my edition: Hence, he says, come pallor and drooping cheeks, ulcers of the eyes, trembling hands spilling full vessels, furial dreams and nightly restlessness, and the highest prize of drunkenness, lust and pleasant sin. On the following day, breath from the mouth smells of the cask, and there is almost a total oblivion of all things, a death of memory. Hence also Plato warned in the <term>Minos</term>, or Dialogue on Law, page 568. He says: <term>μὴ συμπίνειν ἀλλήλοις εἰς μέθην</term> <gloss>do not drink with one another to the point of drunkenness</gloss>. And Isocrates in his <term>Paraenesis</term> <gloss>Exhortation</gloss> to Demonicus: <term>ἄν ᾗ ποτέ σοι συμπέσῃ καιρὸς, ἐξανίστασο πρὸ μέθης</term> <gloss>if it ever happens that you fall into a drinking party, rise before you become drunk</gloss>. If, therefore, drunkards commit offenses through such a foul and detestable vice, for which sober people cannot be accused, their crimes must also be punished more severely. That the vice of drunkenness aggravates a crime is taught by many: Johannes Azorius in Part 2 of his <term>Moral Institutions</term>, Book 2, chapters 13 and 14. Hieronymus Treutlerus, the jurist, in his <term>Selected Disputations</term>, Part I, Disputation 6, Thesis 5, and others.

Furthermore, that person will undoubtedly be punished more severely who commits a double offense than one who commits a simple sin. For example, a robber seems to deserve a harsher punishment than a thief, for the former has sinned doubly, both by the act of murder itself and by the consequent theft, and is therefore worthy of a double punishment; he must be chastised much more sharply than a thief who, being free of murder, is found guilty only of simple theft. In the same way, adultery itself is punished more severely than fornication, since the former falls under the name of a double crime, whereas the latter under a simple one, and so on. A double crime, therefore, is deservedly restrained by a double and thus more severe punishment than a simple one. Now, however, one who sins while drunk also sins doubly: firstly on account of the drunkenness itself, which is a sin and vice as foul as was declared more than sufficiently in the previous section, and then on account of the committed fault, such as injuries inflicted upon a neighbor, or murder, or something else of this kind. Hence, he who sins through drunkenness must also be chastised doubly. Pittacus of Mitylene, one of the seven Sages of Greece, famous in the 44th Olympiad—a man, according to Plutarch in his book <term>On the Tranquillity of the Mind</term>, page <unclear>471</unclear>, Volume 2 of his works, *wealthy, wise, and just*—seems to have observed this, for he willed that drunkards be punished with a double penalty, as Diogenes Laërtius testifies in Book 1, in his life, page 19 of the London edition by Menage; Aristotle also mentions this frequently, such as: in Book 3 of the <term>Ethics</term>, chapter 7, in Book 2 of the <term>Politics</term>, chapter 12, and elsewhere. And indeed, how severely drunkenness was chastised in many well-ordered ancient republics, the older historical monuments abundantly testify. Regarding the Athenians, the matter is certain, for they, since they disapproved of the vice of drunkenness in all people, according to the institution of Solon, punished the drunkard, especially if he were a leader, with death, as Diogenes Laërtius testifies in Book 1, in the life of Solon, page 14 of the London edition.

### ASTRONOMICAL THESES.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicts a scholar seated at a desk within a landscape setting.</note>

By the common suffrage of the learned, it emerges from the mode of consideration that the subject of a science is rendered adequate, and one science is distinguished from others; however, sciences that receive a common denomination must also have a common mode of consideration.

1° Since Astronomy, by the calculation of all who think correctly, is called Mathematical, being subalternated to Geometry, it cannot have any mode of consideration other than mathematical, just as it cannot have any subject other than the one considered.

2 Therefore, we maintain that motion around the center as such must be excluded from proper Astronomical contemplation; and we affirm that whatever is said about it by the Astronomer is entirely borrowed from the Physicist.

3 Therefore, in our judgment, nothing can be said more thoughtlessly than to assert that a celestial body moving around the center as such, or motion as it is measurable, or finally magnitude as it is movable around the center, is the subject of Astronomy; since those who speak thus commit a manifest error either in the thing considered, or in the mode of consideration, or in both.

4 Furthermore, looking more deeply into the condition and nature of a subalternated science, let us say that the subject of Astronomy is magnitude movable around the center, as it is magnitude.

5 Therefore, motion will be considered only as a sensible accident added to the thing considered; meanwhile, we think the entire proper consideration of Astronomy refers to the knowledge of quantity alone.

6 The Astronomer will therefore consider motion, magnitude, and figure, which are affections and boundaries of natural bodies, but only as certain mathematical ratios (such as the ratio of greater to lesser, equal to unequal, distant to near, proportionality, and the like) are found in them; whereas the Physicist refers everything to the nature from which they are understood to flow.

7 So it is not a wonder that, because of this diversity, the Philosopher sometimes (as in 2 Physics, ch. 2) said that Astrology abstracts from motion, but sometimes (1 Metaphysics, text 19) that it considers with motion, or indeed even considers the motion itself.

2 Water by its own nature flows to lower places. Aristotle, 2 On the Heavens.

## ASTRONOMICAL THESES.

1 From this, it is brought about that its shape is round.
2 It is also brought about that any liquid contained in a vessel has a swelling and a circumference, whose center is the same as the center of the world.
3 From this, it is clearer than light that the closer the surface of the water is to the center, the smaller the sphere it makes, and the smaller the diameter it has; but the more remote it is, the larger.
4 Since one and the same straight line takes a larger portion from a smaller circle, and a smaller one from a larger circle, it follows that the same vessel receives a greater quantity of water in a lower place than in a higher one. Although this difference is scarcely felt due to the small interval, such as, for instance, from the root of a mountain to its summit, with respect to the radius of the earth, if access were open to the center, we would perceive a great diversity.
3 Heavy things dropped from any place toward the earth or water constitute similar and equal angles on the surface of both.
1 It is therefore necessary that it be carried to the center of magnitude, which is the same as the center of gravity.
2 Water, therefore, possesses the same center of both magnitude and gravity as the earth.
3 These two elements are concentric and constitute one globe.
4 Since it is demonstrated from geometric principles that of two concentric circles, the larger includes the smaller, we affirm that the mass of water is smaller than the earth.
5 Thus, it is not true that elements, as they exist, are larger the higher they are.
6 And therefore we willingly admit their opinion, as it conforms best with orthodox truth, who believe that the earth in the beginning was round without cavities, and entirely surrounded by waters: but indeed, after God said, "let the waters be gathered into one place," cavities were made in the earth on every side, and into them all the force of the waters converged as into their own gathering places. Others also add that the waters in the beginning were rarer, but were afterwards condensed, so that they could more easily be contained in these cavities.

1 By the common constitution, the year is greater than the true solar year by 10 minutes and 44 seconds.
2 Therefore, it is necessary for the equinoxes and solstices to change their seats toward the beginning of the months, by 10 minutes and 44 seconds of one hour each year.
3 What is small in one year can grow into a large quantity in the succession of many: to such an extent that from the time of Julius Caesar to us, about 12 days have been anticipated; indeed, if the world could last that long, the day of the vernal equinox would fall on the day of the autumnal one, and vice versa.
4 Therefore, either the measurement of the year must be established differently, or that of Julius Caesar must be corrected slightly, so that such a great error is avoided and no anticipation of solstices and equinoxes occurs.
5 We say, therefore, if the vernal equinox were fixed on March 11th, so that every 136 years have passed, no intercalary day is added to February, or that which ought to be a leap year runs as a common and civil one; provided that in the fourth year after that, namely the 140th, an intercalary day is again counted, and so on successively to

All of which will be conspicuous if a comparison is made with the vision of colors in the dark; from whose eyes light is emitted into the object, and in the same eyes, the judgment of the object's reception occurs.

### ASTRONOMICAL THESES.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicts a scholar seated at a desk within a landscape setting.</note>

By the common agreement of the learned, it is accepted from the mode of considering that the subject of a science is made adequate, and one science is distinguished from others: but sciences that receive a common denomination must also have a common mode of considering.

1° Since Astronomy, by the calculation of all who think correctly, is called Mathematical, as being subalternated to Geometry, it cannot have any mode of consideration other than the Mathematical, just as it cannot have any subject other than the considered thing.

2 Therefore, we maintain that motion around the center, as such, should be excluded from proper Astronomical contemplation: and we affirm that what is said about it by the Astronomer is all borrowed from the Physicist.

3 Nothing, therefore, in our judgment can be said more inconsiderately than to assert that a celestial body moving around the center as such, or motion as it is measurable, or finally magnitude as it is mobile around the center, is the subject of Astronomy; since those who say this commit a manifest error, either in the thing considered, or in the mode of considering, or in both.

4 Furthermore, looking more deeply into the condition and nature of a subalternated science, let us say that the subject of Astronomy is magnitude moving around the center, as it is magnitude.

5 Therefore, motion will be considered only as a sensible accident added to the thing considered; meanwhile, we think the entire proper consideration of Astronomy refers to the cognition of quantity alone.

6 The Astronomer will therefore consider motion, magnitude, and figure, which are the affections and limits of natural bodies, but only as certain mathematical ratios (such as the ratio of greater to smaller, equal to unequal, distant to near, proportionality, and the like) are found in them; whereas the Physicist refers everything to the nature from which they are understood to flow.

7 So it is not a wonder, given this diversity, that sometimes (as in 2 Physics, ch. 2) the Philosopher said Astrology abstracts from motion, but sometimes (1 Metaphysics, text 19) he says it considers with motion, and indeed even the motion itself.

2 Water by its own nature flows to lower places. Arist. 2 On the Heavens.

## ASTRONOMICAL THESES.

1 Hence it is brought about that its figure is round.
2 It is also brought about that any liquid contained in a vessel has a swelling and a circumference, whose center is the same as the center of the world.
3 Hence it is clearer than light that the surface of water, the nearer it is to the center, makes a smaller sphere and has a smaller Diameter: but the farther away, the larger.
4 Since one and the same straight line takes away a larger portion from a smaller circle, and a smaller portion from a larger one; it follows that the same vessel receives a greater quantity of water in a lower place than in a higher one. Although this difference is hardly felt because of the small interval, as for example from the root of a mountain to its peak, with respect to the Earth's semidiameter: if, however, there were access to the center, we would perceive a great diversity.
3 Heavy things dropped from any place into the earth or water constitute similar and equal angles on the surface of both.
1 It is therefore necessary that they are carried to the center of magnitude, which is the same as the center of gravity.
2 Water, therefore, possesses the same center of magnitude and gravity as the earth.
3 These two elements are concentric, and constitute one globe.
4 Since it is demonstrated from Geometric principles that of two concentric circles the larger includes the smaller, we affirm that the mass of water is smaller than the earth.
5 So it is not true that elements, as they subsist <note>in their natural state</note>, are larger if they are the superior ones.
6 And therefore we willingly admit the opinion of those, as it agrees best with orthodox truth, who believe that the earth in the beginning was round without cavities, and entirely surrounded by waters: but truly, after God said "let the waters be gathered into one place," cavities were made in the earth on every side, and all the force of the waters converged into them as if into their own gathering places. Others also add that the waters in the beginning were rarer, but were afterwards condensed, so that they could more easily be contained in these cavities.
4 From the calculation first made by Julius Caesar, and now commonly received, the solar year contains 365 days and 6 hours. However, according to the more accurate calculation of astronomers, it contains 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, and 16 seconds.
1 According to the common constitution, the year is greater than the true solar year by 10 minutes and 44 seconds.
2 Therefore, it is necessary for the equinoxes and solstices to change their seats toward the beginning of the months, by 10 minutes and 44 seconds of an hour each year.
3 What is little in one year can grow into a large quantity in the succession of many: so much so that from the time of Julius Caesar to our own, the days have anticipated by about 12. Indeed, if the world could last that long, the day of the vernal equinox would fall on the day of the autumnal one, and vice versa.
4 Therefore, either the measure of the year must be established differently, or that of Julius Caesar must be corrected a little, so that such a great error is avoided and no anticipation of solstices and equinoxes occurs.
5 We say, therefore, if the vernal equinox were established on March 11, so that always after 136 years have elapsed, no intercalary day is added to February—or rather, what should have been a leap year runs as a common and civil year—yet so that in the fourth year after that, namely the 140th, an intercalary day is again counted, and so successively until

Just as Christians were accustomed to gather in cemeteries for the preaching of the Divine Word and the celebration of the Holy Eucharist (see Magdeburg History, Century XII, c. 5, arg. 4, col. 840; Hunn, Vol. I, Latin Works, col. 1549-1551; Gerhard, Common Places, Vol. VIII, Loc. XXIX, On Death, §. 268, p. 482-489; and in Catholic Confession, Book II, P. II, art. 9, arg. 13, p. 511-514; Chamier, Vol. III, Catholic Panstratia, Book XXVI, c. 19, p. 594-596; Glassius, Book III, Philologia Sacra, Tr. VI, Can. 14, m. 2, n. 1, p. 559), so we are completely persuaded that they also administered Baptism in public meetings held over cemeteries. Eusebius Pamphili reports (Ecclesiastical History, Book IV, c. 15, fol. 86, Latin Edition, Basil. 1544) that the Christians of Smyrna formerly held solemn and celebrated gatherings at the place where the burnt bones of the martyr Polycarp had been buried. Since these gatherings were destined for no other purpose than the exercise of Divine Worship, they undoubtedly administered Baptism, as part of Divine Worship, solemnly over Polycarp’s tomb. Although in this last case, it must be noted that this administration of Baptism was not undertaken with the same intention as it was in the Corinthian Church, namely to prove the resurrection of the dead. For the writers of sacred history would by no means have passed over that in silence. Indeed, it suffices for us that the Rite of Administering Baptism Over the Dead has become known from the Apostolic account alone. And let this be the end! We pay immortal thanks to God, the Greatest and Best, for the granted assistance of His Spirit, and we commend our studies, now to be continued elsewhere, most humbly and devoutly to Him.

## PHILOLOGICAL EXERCISE.

<note>A horizontal row of seven small asterisks.</note>

Just as the great Offspring of God, having overcome Death, broke the sealed Tomb,
And lifted His invincible Head above the Stygian enemies:
So once the crowd of the Pious shall come forth from the graves
To the repeated breezes of Light,
And the Christians shall joyfully take trophies from the Enemy.
Impious rabble, why do you now deny that new times of Life
Survive after death, and a just Tribunal?
The bodies you see brought to the tombs are not
Dead, but rest buried in peaceful beds;
The times will soon come when, with Jehovah calling out,
We shall lift these eyes again from long Sleep,
And one day raise our reawakened limbs from the couches.
Whence the converted Corinth, testifying to its Faith,
Performed Baptism at the tombs of the departed,
Whose holy fame it was delightful to remember,
Because the honors of the revived Flesh surely remain.
While you, Rehberg, strive to defend this Rite,
I congratulate you, and I pray that the pious Divinities
May favor your pious undertakings. Thus live for God, your Studies, and your own.

->REHBERG,<-
->as a symbol of sincere affection,<-
->this votive poem<-
->is consecrated<-
->by the<-
->Dissertation PRESIDENT,<-
->Master Daniel Graden, of Danzig.<-

## IX.

The liberal man should also strive to observe the mean in receiving. Therefore, he should not receive from those from whom he ought not, nor where it is least appropriate to receive. He should not be importunate or troublesome to others in asking and receiving, lest he be called <term>αἰτητικός</term> <gloss>a mendicant or beggar</gloss> by others. We have already established, not without foundation, that the liberal man ought to be more occupied with giving than with receiving. Furthermore, he who is about to perform a benefit should do so from his own resources, not diverting the fountains of others toward himself to pour forth the liquid of liberality. *For indeed, as Seneca says in his first book on Clemency, he is not liberal who is liberal with what belongs to another, but he who subtracts from himself what he gives to another.* Meanwhile, the liberal person should not neglect his own family affairs, but should strive to promote them by honest and lawful means, if only to the end that he might possess his own goods with which he can both provide sustenance for his own and, when necessity presses, assist the indigence of others. For we are able to benefit ourselves when we are liberal to others. See the Axiom 2, Table 8 of the Moral Course by the Lord President.

## X.

As regards the extremes of liberality, it has Prodigality as its opposite in excess, and Avarice in defect. The former, named for spending, is a vice by which we exceed the limit in giving and diminish the limit in receiving, having no regard for the circumstances which have been suggested in the immediately preceding theses. Prodigality is usually established as twofold: *Simple* and *Mixed*. The former rashly pours out resources on any matter whatsoever, with all hope of receiving omitted. This especially befalls the youthful age. The *Mixed* is entangled with many other vices; it bestows upon some, but unjustly takes from others, whence such a prodigal is both unjust and stained with other vices.
</translation>

## XI.

**Avarice** (so called from <term>aveo</term> <gloss>to crave</gloss>, because the avaricious man is greedy for money) is, conversely, a vice by which we exceed the limit in excessively receiving and retaining, with no regard for justice or honesty, or (as the *Philosopher* <note>referring to Aristotle</note> intends) it is an incurable evil and an inextinguishable thirst for money. For by theft, robbery, usury, fraud, perjury, lying, and six hundred other unjust methods, he snatches and scrapes together whatever he can. Wherefore, just as there is scarcely any vice worse than avarice, so there is nothing more wicked than an avaricious man. But this, too, is accustomed to be distinguished by some ethicists into *simple* and *composite*. *Simple* is that which fails in giving, without <term>αὐξήσει</term> <gloss>excess</gloss>, or which exceeds in receiving without <term>δόσει</term> <gloss>a deficiency [in giving]</gloss>. *Composite* is that which both fails in giving and exceeds the limit in receiving. This is heard to be the worst of all. Excessively stingy <term>φειδωλία</term> <gloss>parsimony</gloss> is said to pertain to the former; the art of stealing, pimping, usury, gambling, and all that which takes from others in an undue manner pertains to the latter. *See Adrianus Heereboord, Ethical College, page 94.*

## XII.

Furthermore, authors prove from the various arguments of the philosophers that **Prodigality** is less vicious and less opposed to liberality than avarice. Our century is indeed full of avaricious men who would not contribute even a tiny coin, even if they could thereby liberate a brother captured in Turkey. Nor are there a lack of prodigals who would pour out even Persian mountains, which are entirely of gold, to satisfy their lusts. None of these deserves praise, for whether the one or the other happens, one departs from the straight path of virtue, and the mediocrity, which was mentioned in the definition, is violated. Yet, upon a comparison instituted between the prodigal and the miser, it will appear manifestly that the latter is worse than the prodigal. For [the miser is] more tenacious
</translation>

## IX.

The liberal man should strive to observe the mean in receiving no less than in giving. Therefore, let him not receive from those from whom he ought not, nor where he ought not to receive at all. As regards the extremes of liberality, it has Prodigality as its opposite in excess, and Avarice in defect. This kind falls especially upon the youthful age. *Mixed* prodigality is implicated with many other vices; it bestows upon some, while taking away from others through injury, whence such a prodigal is also unjust and stained with other vices.

We have already established, not without foundation, that the liberal person ought to be more occupied with giving than with receiving. Likewise, let him who intends to do good confer benefits from his own property, and not pour out the liquor of liberality by diverting the sources of others to himself. *For indeed, as Seneca says in his first book on Clemency, he is not a liberal person who is liberal with what belongs to another, but he who, in what he gives to another, subtracts from himself.* Meanwhile, the liberal person should not neglect his own household affairs, but should strive to promote them by honest and lawful means, at least to the end that he may possess his own goods, with which he may both suffice for his own sustenance and, in an urgent necessity, be able to assist the indigence of others. For by prospering ourselves, we are liberal to others. See the Axiom 2, Table 8 of the Course of Ethics by the Honorable President.

## X.

Regarding the extremes of liberality, it has Prodigality as its opposite in excess, and Avarice in defect. The former, so called from "squandering" <note>Latin: *prodigendo*</note>, is a vice by which we exceed the measure in giving and diminish the measure in receiving, with no regard for the circumstances that were suggested in the immediately preceding theses. Prodigality is usually divided into two types: *Simple and mixed.* The former squanders resources rashly on any object whatsoever, with all hope of receiving back abandoned. This vice principally falls upon the age of youth. *Mixed* prodigality is implicated with many other vices; it bestows upon some, but takes away from others through injury, whence such a prodigal person is also unjust and stained with other vices.

## XI.

**Avarice** (so called from <term>aveo</term> <gloss>to crave</gloss>, because the avaricious person is greedy for money) is a vice to the contrary, by which we exceed the measure in receiving and retaining too much, with no regard for justice or honesty, or (as the *Philosopher* <note>Aristotle</note> maintains) it is an incurable evil and an inextinguishable thirst for money. For through theft, rapine, usury, fraud, perjury, lying, and six hundred other unjust means, he seizes and scrapes together whatever he can possibly seize and scrape together. Wherefore, as there is scarcely any vice worse than avarice, so there is nothing more wicked than the avaricious man. But this also is usually distinguished by some ethicists into *simple* and *composite*. *Simple* avarice is that which fails in giving without an excess in <term>accumulation</term> <gloss>original: "αὐξήσει"</gloss>, or which exceeds in receiving without a defect in <term>giving</term> <gloss>original: "δόσει"</gloss>. *Composite* is that which both fails in giving and exceeds the measure in receiving. This is reputed to be the worst of all. Furthermore, authors prove from various arguments of the philosophers that **Prodigality** is less vicious and more opposed to liberality than avarice. of the Religious Peace <note>original: Pacis Religiosae</note>, and the subscription of the Protestants does not import a total consensus, but is limited by those words: "as much as concerns or may concern each individual, as stands everywhere." *Magnificent Lord President in the aforementioned treatise on Assemblies, chapter 4, number 109; Cranius on the Religious Peace, part 1, Problems 10; Limnaeus, volume 1 of Public Law, book 1, chapter 13, number 34 and following; Dissertation of Syringio on the Religious Peace, thesis 37.*

### III.

Imperial Cities <note>original: Civitates Imperiales</note> enjoy the rights of territorial superiority <note>original: superioritas territorialis</note>. For they are indeed immediate <note>subject directly to the Emperor</note>, and are states of the Empire to whom territorial superiority cannot be denied (§ "wie wol auch in der Regierungshandlung," Recessus of Augsburg of the year 1548), and in their territories they enjoy the rights of Princes, and can do the same as the Emperor does in the whole Empire. *Reinking on Secular Government, book 1, Class 5, chapter 5; Limnaeus, volume 3 of Public Law, book 7, chapter 1, number 49; Rumelinus on the Golden Bull, part 1, Dissertation 1, question 11; Wurmser's Exercises in Public Law 3, question 17, where more doctors are alleged.* Hence it is clear that this superiority in the cities is not incorrectly called the "territorial authority of the land" <note>original: die Landfürstliche Obrigkeit</note>, because the principal right here is said not to come from a Prince as a Monarch, but from the right of the Prince, as Limnaeus notes from Besoldus in the aforementioned chapter 1, number 50, at the end. And by the generic definition of Princes, Imperial cities are most properly contained, as Reinking notes from Gail in the aforementioned chapter 5, number 18.

<translation page="10">are seen: others are imperfect, which consist of only one or another humor being withdrawn beyond the due quantity: and of this or that species; in the order which we stated above.

45. III. By reason of the mode; some occurs through vomiting, although more rarely, see Mesue in the *Canon*, Intention 1, chapter 2; Hippocrates pursued this alone regarding human nature, because perhaps the use of hellebore is more frequent in these times: others through the bowel; examples of which occur in Forestus and the illustrious Plater in the cited place.

46. IV. By reason of the cause, as many differences can be posited as there are diversities of them; concerning which we have already acted. Among them, however, that which occurs on account of the abundance of humors contained in the vessels before the cathartic was administered, and which invite nature to expulsion, is to be noted above the rest; which is as it were a certain critical <term>hyperkatharsis</term> <gloss>excessive purgation</gloss>, concerning which [we shall speak] next in the treatment: but all the rest are morbid and pernicious.

47. V. By reason of the affected location; the evil either occupies the veins more proximal to the intestines, especially the superior and inferior mesenteric ones; or more remote ones, as happens when the evil increases.

48. VI. The difference is to be derived from the symptoms which will be able to be diagnosed from the signs.

49. Wherefore, before we approach the treatment of this most calamitous evil, we shall premise a few things concerning the signs, both diagnostic and prognostic.

<margin>Diagnostic signs.</margin>
50. In general, indeed, the affection is manifest enough in itself: and the diversity of them, which are discerned meanwhile, is subjected to the eyes: just as vomiting and rejection through the bowel. Nor are the differences sought from the form known with greater trouble. For that the body is being purged more than is right, the quantity and quality of the rejected matters, the patient's <term>dysphoria</term> <gloss>distress/unease</gloss>, and the worsening of symptoms indicate; as can be gathered from Hippocrates, *Aphorisms 1, 2* and commentary 2 on the *Prognostics*, text 14.

<margin>Symptoms.</margin>
51. But the symptoms often indicated, besides those already mentioned—which clearly not only accompany the purgation itself, but also partly accompany and partly follow any other laborious purgations—such as nausea, vomiting, fainting, and the rest which Mesue recounts in the *Canon*, Intention 2, *Summa* 2, chapter 3, relate either to the natural, the vital, or the animal faculty.

52. We, however, for the sake of clarity, neglecting this order and following Mesue in the *Canon*, Intention 4, shall consider them according to the parts which are especially afflicted in this case. Wherefore, in the stomach there first presents itself the weakness of the same; then pain, thirst, and hiccup; but in the intestines, an ulcer, bloody excretion, and tenesmus; in the head, pain, vertigo, weakness of sight; but in the whole body here and there, convulsion; then in general, fever, weakness, and lassitude. We shall delineate in few words the generation of all these, whether they be symptoms or symptomatic diseases, from hyperkatharsis.

53. Therefore, I. Weakness is induced in the stomach 1. by the medicine, which, by infesting it with manifest and occult qualities, dissolves its strength: since all medicines that purge harm the stomach, if we believe Galen in the book *On Those Who Ought to be Purged*. Also *On the Faculties of Purgative Medicines*, chapter 1, and *On Acute Diseases*, commentary 1, texts 11 and 12. 2. From humors carried upward. 3. From the immoderate evacuation itself: whence the body of the stomach is colliquated, thinned, relaxed, and with the heat dissolved, coldness is introduced. 4. By error in the use of non-natural things; especially through drink assumed intemperately for the sake of quenching thirst, which accompanies immoderate purgations.</translation>

<translation page="11">54. II. They bring on pain, again the medicine itself; concerning which there exists an example in Hippocrates in *Theophorbus’ Son, book 5 of the Epidemics*; likewise sharp, salty, bilious humors and flatulence [bring pain] by inflaming, eroding, ulcerating, and distending the stomach.

55. III. Thirst, although otherwise according to *Hippocrates, Aphorism 4, 19* it may be a sign of perfect purgation—clearly with viscous and cold humors stagnating in the stomach and quenching natural thirst being evacuated—nevertheless, as often as it arises either from a medicine that is hot and sharp (whether by nature or by preparation, such as extracts made chemically with spirits of wine) or on account of the excessive deprivation of moisture (as much excrementitious as natural) and the drying, thinning, and wasting away of the stomach, it is deservedly called morbid and hectic due to exhaustion: *see also Galen’s commentary on the said Aphorism.*

56. IV. Hiccups are stirred up by humors, flatulence, and bilious, sharp, malignant, and viscous medicines that stubbornly adhere to and are impacted upon the substance of the stomach.

57. V. An ulcer of the intestines in this case occurs 1. from an eroding, sharp, malignant medicine; such as *Colocynth, Squirting Cucumber, Elaterium, Scammony*, and all those which purge both above and below, *Hippocrates, book 4 On Diseases*. An example is read in the same author, *5 of the Epidemics*. 2. On account of the continuous influx of salty, bilious, and burnt humors.

58. VI. The causes of tenesmus are the same.

59. VII. The reason for bloody flux is clear from what was said above; it is a most terrifying and formidable evil in this case.

60. VIII. Effluvia and vapors, stirred up on account of the excessive agitation of the humors, produce headaches primarily by heating, biting, eroding, and distending.

61. IX. The causes of vertigo are the same, although the account is different.

62. X. Weakness of sight happens here because the humors and spirits dedicated to vision are mixed with elevated vapors; then [also] from desiccation on account of excessive evacuation.

63. XI. Convulsion, quite familiar to this evil but to be feared most of all others, arises here partly on account of the poisonous quality of the purgative; partly because of the twitching of the nervous and muscular kind, caused by sharp, corrupt, malignant humors resolved by agitation into vapor and flatulence.

64. XII. Fever is kindled both by reason of the inflaming medicine and by the separation of cold humors; then also on account of continuous vigils, mental distress, pains, and other things supervening upon this evil.

65. XIII. Finally, weakness and lassitude of the whole body follow the excessive profusion of useful humors and the resolution of spirits and strengths.

66. Common to all these evils are errors of non-natural things committed during the time of purgation, concerning which *Mesue [writes] in the cited book.*

67. To recount all the signs of the causes in the order in which we treated the causes themselves would be superfluous and odious on account of tautology; since in general they can all be reduced to the rationale of the purgative itself, the singular disposition of the body, and the condition of the humors: the first two are revealed indeed by the report of the patient and the physician (if he is willing to confess the error); but humors, when they are excreted, betray themselves by odor, color, substance, biting, heating, etc., at their exit.

68. The vices of the generating and sending part are known by their own proper signs.</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the various morbid symptoms and diagnostic signs resulting from excessive purgation (hyperkatharsis), including physical ailments like stomach weakness, ulcers, and systemic reactions such as fever and convulsions.</summary>
<keywords>Hyperkatharsis, excessive purgation, iatrogenic illness, humoral pathology, Mesue, Hippocrates, Galen, clinical diagnosis, medical symptoms</keywords>

54. II. They bring on pain, again the medicine itself; concerning which there exists an example in Hippocrates in *Theophorbus’ Son, book 5 of the Epidemics*; likewise sharp, salty, bilious humors and flatulence [bring pain] by inflaming, eroding, ulcerating, and distending the stomach.

Thirst, although otherwise according to *Hippocrates, Aphorism 4, 19* it may be a sign of perfect purgation—clearly with viscous and cold humors stagnating in the stomach and quenching natural thirst being evacuated—nevertheless, as often as it arises either from a medicine that is hot and sharp (whether by nature or by preparation, such as extracts made chemically with spirits of wine) or on account of the excessive deprivation of moisture (as much excrementitious as natural) and the drying, thinning, and wasting away of the stomach, it is deservedly called morbid and hectic due to exhaustion: *see also Galen’s commentary on the said Aphorism.*

56. IV. Hiccups are stirred up by humors, flatulence, and bilious, sharp, malignant, and viscous medicines that stubbornly adhere to and are impacted upon the substance of the stomach.

57. V. An ulcer of the intestines in this case occurs 1. from an eroding, sharp, malignant medicine; such as *Colocynth, Squirting Cucumber, Elaterium, Scammony*, and all those which purge both above and below, *Hippocrates, book 4 On Diseases*. 59. VII. The reason for bloody flux is clear from what was said above; it is a most terrifying and formidable evil in this case.

60. VIII. Effluvia and vapors, stirred up on account of the excessive agitation of the humors, produce headaches primarily by heating, biting, eroding, and distending.

61. IX. The causes of vertigo are the same, although the account is different.

62. X. Weakness of sight happens here because the humors and spirits dedicated to vision are mixed with elevated vapors; then [also] from desiccation on account of excessive evacuation.

63. XI. Convulsion, quite familiar to this evil but to be feared most of all others, arises here partly on account of the poisonous quality of the purgative; partly because of the twitching of the nervous and muscular kind, caused by sharp, corrupt, malignant humors resolved by agitation into vapor and flatulence.

64. XII. Fever is kindled both by reason of the inflaming medicine and by the separation of cold humors; then also on account of continuous vigils, mental distress, pains, and other things supervening upon this evil.

65. XIII. Finally, weakness and lassitude of the whole body follow the excessive profusion of useful humors and the resolution of spirits and strengths.

66. Common to all these evils are errors of non-natural things committed during the time of purgation, concerning which *Mesue [writes] in the cited book.*

68. The vices of the generating and sending part are known by their own proper signs.

Thirst, although it is otherwise according to *Hippocrates, Aphorism 4.19* a sign of perfect purgation—clearly with the viscous and cold humors stagnating in the stomach, which extinguish natural thirst, being evacuated—nevertheless, whenever it arises either from a medicine that is hot and acrid, whether by nature or by preparation (such as extracts chemically made with spirit of wine), or due to an excessive deprivation of moisture, both excrementitious and natural, and from the drying, thinning, and wasting away of the stomach, it is deservedly called morbid and hectic, resulting from exhaustion: *see also Galen's commentary on the said Aphorism.*

56. IV. Hiccups are stirred up by humors, flatulence, and bilious, acrid, malignant, and viscous medicines, which obstinately adhere to and are impacted in the substance of the stomach.

57. V. An ulcer of the intestines in this case occurs 1. from an eroding, acrid, malignant medicine; such as *Colocynth, wild cucumber, elaterium, scammony*, and all those which purge both above and below, *Hippocrates, book 4 On Diseases*. An example is read in the same author, *book 5 of the Epidemics*. 2. On account of the continuous influx of salty, bilious, and burnt humors.

58. VI. The causes of tenesmus are the same.

59. VII. The rationale for bloody flow is clear from the above; in this case, it is a most terrifying and formidable evil.

60. VIII. Effluvia and vapors, stirred up on account of the excessive agitation of the humors, produce headaches primarily by heating, biting, eroding, and distending.

61. IX. The causes of vertigo are the same, although the rationale is different.

62. X. Weakness of sight occurs here when the humors and spirits dedicated to vision are mixed with elevated vapors: then by drying out due to excessive evacuation.

63. XI. Convulsion, sufficiently familiar to this evil, but most to be feared above all the rest, arises here partly because of the poisonous quality of the purgative; partly on account of the twitching of the nervous and muscular kind, caused by acrid, corrupt, malignant humors, resolved by agitation into vapor and flatulence.

64. XII. Fever is ignited partly by reason of the inflaming medicine, partly by the separation of cold humors; then also on account of continuous wakefulness, afflictions of the mind, pains, and the rest that supervene upon this evil.

65. XIII. Finally, weakness and lassitude of the whole body follow the excessive profusion of useful humors and the resolution of the spirits and strengths.

66. Common to all these evils are errors in the non-naturals committed during the time of purgation, of which *Mesue writes in the cited book*.

67. To recount all the signs of the causes in the same order in which we have treated the causes themselves would be superfluous and, on account of tautology, hateful; since in general all can be reduced to the very method of the purgative, the singular disposition of the body, and the condition of the humors: the first two are indeed revealed by the report of the patient and the physician (if he is willing to confess the error); but humors, when they are excreted, betray themselves by odor, color, substance, biting, heating, etc., at their exit.

68. The vices of the generating and sending part are known by their own signs.

<translation page="10">
So too, those powerful ones who rule widely in the world,
    Whose royal majesty holds weight,
Will speak nothing against him acting in such a way,
    Daring not to have opposed themselves to God.
But rather, with the gravity of their proud brows set aside,
    They will submit their proud hearts to my servant.
And they will recognize CHRIST coming with a humble breast,
    Offering faith with a heart that does not pretend.
But not only the people surviving from the lineage of Judea
    Will worship with such holy piety.
Indeed, even the nations that cultivate foreign realms
    Will bring his divine powers in praise, adoring him.
And before him, under whatever axis of the sky, he was less
    Known, or the worship of his word was less loved.
He will be affected there by the honor of solid piety.
    Who he is, and from the word he shall be clearly seen.
For nothing of such things comes to the ears of those,
    To whom some messenger has not carried these things.
My servant, powerful in virtue, favors all things,
    By the excellent dexterity of his counsel.
Let them receive it with cheerful spirits, and they will see with joy
    How great the future glory of my servant shall be.
But who will there be, who offers us easy ears,
    And desires to have the known strength of GOD?
Among whom could a gathering ever have earned,
    I ask, a faith equal to such great matters?
</translation>

<translation page="11">
> A greater number will be the crowd falling back into impiety,
>     Than those for whom true salvation is a concern.
> Few will receive Christ, for whom the rest of the common people,
>     The greatest part, will allow no place.
> And in that state, under the guise of such servile condition,
>     The wise will not know God, but the pious crowd will.
> But he, in the manner of a pleasant plant, will grow up,
>     As a shoot greens in silent soil.
> For just as seeds of cultivated earth die,
>     Which nevertheless bear grain in the summer season:
> So Christ will suffer death through his own wounds,
>     So that wretched man may be restored to safety.
> Who, persuaded by the cunning of the crafty demon,
>     Transgressed the commands of God that were not to be violated.
> In the same way that a new plant [grows], so finally will Christ
>     Become greatest before the eternal Father.
> He who neglects all things in this world, before him,
>     And the form of his kingdom has no beauty.
> No thing is more contemptible than his ministry,
>     And nothing is believed to be more empty than his word.
> Thus the glory of Christ escapes human senses,
>     It is higher than what anyone sees by reason.
> He will rule over his enemies by the word,
>     Nor does he hold decaying scepters with an external hand.
> In Christ there is no grace of a beautiful form,
>     Or outward charm that could have pleased a human.
</translation>

<summary>These pages continue the exegesis of the prophetic figure of Christ, contrasting his humble appearance and rejection by the masses with his ultimate spiritual authority and the salvation he brings to both Jews and Gentiles.</summary>
<keywords>Christ, Salvation, Ministry, Piety, Gentiles, Judea, Glory, Prophecy</keywords>

### To Master CASPAR and Master ANDREAS, brothers of the Bayer family, most esteemed citizens of Pano-Anklam and Albi-Hamburg, mourning the passing of Master PAUL BAYER of blessed memory, Ducal Treasurer of Pano-Stolpe.

->*Greetings and Consolation.*<-

Why, you two brothers, along with the remaining brothers,
Are you both mourning the blessed tomb of your pious brother?
Do you not know with how much grief Pomerania lies?
How pain and trembling stream into public losses?
With what eyes will the countryside of Stolpe be able to look?
Alas! Upon the ashes of the beautiful monastery to be scattered!
Now he says: "Farewell, ashes of Stolpe and Pan,
I now inhabit the citadels, the camps, and the homes of the heavens.
I now dwell in the winding royal palaces of the sky,
Which no fierce soldier can burn with fire.
Here I act with the applause of joy, and I celebrate the LORD;
This high house is prepared for all the pious."
</translation>

<note>A large decorative initial letter D stands at the start of the poem.</note>

While fierce Bellona <note>the Roman goddess of war</note> in uncertain battle retards
The fates of peace, happy for the upright, envious for the wicked,
We are always groaning and we all demand back peace,
A good than which nothing better is given to exist.
Do we now consider our sighs useless and vain?
Why, then, does it help to pour out prayers in vain?
Far from it; let distrustful impatience depart far away,
Those vows before GOD are established, provided they are in the right manner.
For the peace which Mars <note>the Roman god of war</note> disturbs for us on earth,
Constantly stirring up dreadful battles in the present;
GOD knows how to confer this in the future life,
Calling us to Himself by a peaceful death thereafter.
O thrice happy, and thrice and four times blessed!
They who shall be partakers of this peace.
There will be no noise of war, nor the neighing of the horse,
Nor the sound of the bombard <note>an early cannon</note>, nor any sword,
Drums will cease, and the harsh clanging of trumpets
Which stimulate timid men to horrible arms,
But singing melodic songs with lutes and the cithara,
They will enjoy eternity in eternal peace.
</translation>

<translation page="15">For the painting reports that he conducted this with a joyful triumph,
Fighting great wars for the powerful Caesar with his mighty hand.
Thus he struck down the fleeing enemies with firm strength,
Just as a wolf kills soft lambs with its mouth.
They breathe out their souls with their blood poured forth by him,
A hundred are pierced through: the earth is soaked in gore.
Therefore, Caesar also rendered such great honors to him,
That the Margrave is an Elector, bearing the scepters.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' begins the stanza.</note>

YOU SEE Albert, shining in helmet and iron,
As he fights in the middle of the whirlwind, setting wars in motion.
His feather stands out above others on his nodding helmet,
As the Martial star <note>Mars</note> surpasses the other stars in the sky.
When fierce Mars saw him waging battles,
He said, he will be worthy of the name of the descendant of Aeacus <note>Achilles</note>.
Hence he is also deservedly called the Teutonic Achilles,
Because his glorious deeds earned him honor.
But I would sooner recount the deeds of noble Hercules,
Than I could number the slaughters of Albert.
O how often is the brave man carried into the midst of enemies,
How often did he bear weapons against his chest:
And as a rock on the sea stands unmoved against the waves,
He sustains the heavy onsets.
You may see the threads of the Nymphs, where he has forced a thousand
Defeated in battle to suffer hard chains.
The Pole, terrified by this sight alone, turns his back,
Forgetting his weapons, pale in the face, he trembles.
Others come and pray for tranquil peace,
They offer their hands, broken by the victor, to him.
Titan <note>The sun</note> will sooner lack his own splendor,
Than the virtue of such a man could lie hidden.
And the setting of the sun shall sooner be turned into its rising,
Than the fame of this leader shall lie buried.</translation>

<translation page="16"><note>An ornamental decorative initial 'A' starts the first poem section.</note>

ADDED to these is Johann, celebrated for the virtue of famous war,
Possessing the strength of Hector in his great body.
He drove the enemies from his fatherland in his youthful years,
Whose slaughter our towns still know.
Behold, he drags with him a thousand bound captives,
Who did not provide for themselves by swift flight.
He established a thousand funerals of heroes in these lands,
Who fell by the hand of a demigod armed for war.
The Viadrus <note>The Oder River</note> still remains a witness, which here, bloody with slaughter,
Had flowed, soaking everything with hostile blood.
When he had stripped arms from the people of Lusatia,
While the Prince was protecting the Marchian wealth.
He whom victory follows, joyful in a great triumph,
To where the Oder rolls its yellow waters.
After time had now made this man strong,
He was always a lover of tranquil peace.
Everything was safe under this illustrious Prince,
All that the March has flourished.
Hence you may see citizens in our regions,
Who count many talents of gold at their tables.
Thus he increased his fatherland with wealth and virtues at the same time,
While he was studious of noble peace.

<note>An ornamental decorative initial 'H' starts the second poem section.</note>

TO THESE you are joined, O Joachim, hero similar to a god,
Who draws the forests and hard rocks with you.
For the gifts of your tongue are so very famous,
That Tully <note>Cicero, the Roman orator</note> himself yields to you in eloquence.
Your grandfather deserved the surname of Achilles, the descendant of Aeacus,
Because he waged hard battles with a strong hand.
But because you excel all others, Duke, with an eloquent mouth,
You will be, by true name, Nestor <note>A wise Greek king known for his oratorical skills</note>.
The Greeks marvel at the words of the big-talking Ulysses,
But the nine-fold crowd <note>The Muses</note> is stunned by you, the eloquent one.
So great is your voice, Prince, and your powers of speaking,</translation>

<translation page="18">And if by chance you refuse, at least you will please by having read,
And having refused with a brow without a cloud, and with reason.
They say that Amphion surrounded Aonian Thebes <note>The city of Thebes in Boeotia</note> with walls,
And enlivened the hard stones,
And drew the rocks, which followed without any wagons,
No machine was placed under the weight to bear it,
The frequent stones came together into walls of their own accord,
The lyre is nothing other than that which is more powerful than arms,
Kindness alone breaks reluctant spirits,
A good and prudent man, with the sweet weight of words,
Will entice the people, to whatever uses he may call them,
Whom he previously accustomed to treat with serene command,
And he will lead them wherever he wishes, without force, without the lash.
No less does a courageous spirit in any crisis possess
Praise, but see that it serves justice,
Nor let Mars <note>the god of war</note> please you, unless when it is necessary to take up arms,
Or if force alone rejects what is just and what is right for you,
And you have never taken up just anger against anyone.
That most sad virtue, which is produced by the evils of others,
Mourning, and the fire that rises from ignited cities,
And pitiable famine, and armed death follow.
A golden moderation, and pleasing modesty of character,
Let it curb both luxury and too loose a rein,
All rivers flow gently, as each is greatest:
Torrents roar immensely, and having threatened much
In vain, they often subside into themselves without damage.
Live happily, and surpass the prayers of those who pray,
You and your nobles, and store in a mindful heart
What you have sworn at the sacred altars (if anything is holy),
And you first, by whose just rule is held
An island rich in fields, and wealth, and arms, and men,</translation>

<translation page="19">And to whom, since the public burden of affairs now weighs upon you,
You divide the immense cares for yourself, most beautiful one,
What you owe to the people, what you have long since, with altars as witnesses,
Promised solemnly, let no age erase for you,
Nor let sudden storms snatch away what has been sworn,
Nor seek to transcend the laws which the page of the divine word
Has prescribed to man, the greatest of things,
And deservedly, piety is the safest virtue for man,
Since the fear of the Lord, joined with the love of the people,
Establishes the empire, like an anchor with a double fluke,
It secures the ships left in a station in doubtful times.

Nor may you, O chosen nobles and highest powers
Of the council, be unmindful, lest a future age refute you,
Sworn faith stands, marked in eternal adamant
In heaven; it is not safe to abuse the divine power.
No joys will stand for long when Heaven has been deceived,
Thus that good progenitor of gods decreed from on high,
Vengeance agitates him, ever mindful of evils,
And let not the wrath of the injured Thunderer <note>Jupiter/God</note>, which he bears with him,
Be mentioned of you in any age hereafter,
The anger of the Ruler of Olympus is indeed slow, yet grave.

But you, highest of Gods, who have so often from on high
Had pity on the nations stained with blood,
May you wish this day to be happy for centuries
For the Saxons and the Scots, and may our descendants remember this day,
Which was able to end the madness of both peoples,
The immortal hatred, and the never-healable wound:
And that which was previously a scattered and discordant mass of things,
Shall be said to have come together into a new face and body,
And may the people be happy under a new president of affairs,
But far happier shall he be in the obedience of the people,</translation>

<summary>The text addresses a ruler, emphasizing the power of clemency over force, the necessity of justice, and the importance of adhering to divine law and sworn oaths for the stability of a unified realm.</summary>
<keywords>clemency, justice, piety, fear of God, unity, Saxons, Scots, royal duty</keywords>

raw:
<translation page="15">In this matter, I care nothing for the sneers of the Longolian followers of Tully <note>referring to those who obsessively imitate Cicero's style</note>. Yet, for the time being, I will grant Amsdorf <note>Nikolaus von Amsdorf, a prominent Lutheran reformer</note> that you do not lie when you say I draw from the storehouse of a wealthy master, Erasmus. From whom, I ask, do you steal your own works? I prefer not to say, since others have already spoken. Who are these elegant men who deliberately stammer out the hunchback of Plato and the stuttering of Aristotle? O, you excellent imitators, you servile herd. Who does not know that you are imitators—I will not say thieves—not of Paul, not of John, not of Hilary, not of Erasmus, but of Luther? And of only one man, contrary to the precept of Fabius <note>Quintilian, who advised against imitating only one model</note>? And I wish that you would abandon that father of yours for a while and find pleasure in reading and imitating others, not so much for your own sake as for the sake of our common salvation. I pledge to you that the Prophets, the Apostles, and the remaining writers of our Church would suffer your thefts, let alone your imitation, without revulsion. You would be loved by Christ himself as such thieves, and for your hanging <note>a metaphorical reference to the "gallows" of spiritual sacrifice</note>, you would receive the heavenly hall. By us you would be cherished if only, setting aside shame, you would candidly confess the progress of your honest imitation. If I warn you again in vain, you will admit, Amsdorf, that I have warned you. Regarding Erasmus, who is being pelted in such miserable ways, there is no reason for me to write to you, Haner, at present. One thing causes pain: that a man of my reputation must be lacerated by such importunity. But this is again a relief to me, that in Luther, black hatred has long been gestating, which, now hunting for an occasion from every quarter, has brought forth fruit unhappily. The glory of the Rotterdamer’s name burns the man, and the breadth of this polymath <note>Erasmus</note> exhausts him. Whoever does not scent this has no nose at all. He feels that Erasmus is lifting his sunken head. He feels that he and his faction are gradually</translation>

<translation page="16">being cast out. Hence those tears; it is decreed by the son-in-law to drive the father-in-law from the kingdom; you cannot share the world, you must possess it alone. You might say that Lucan touched the matter with the point of a needle, even though he knew neither man. We await the *Apologeticon* <note>defense/apology</note> of Erasmus, a man who is indeed old, yet neither toothless nor bleary-eyed. He does not need my defense; he whom even silence sufficiently defends against the blasphemies brought against him, partly by triumphant and august truth, and partly by the backfiring envy of his adversary. The belching arch-evangelist <note>a mocking reference to Luther</note> has spit nothing against the man that is not highly refutable, and of which a good portion does not fall back upon the one spitting. Erasmus has earned, forsooth, that Wittenberg should hold him in such honor. Socrates received almost the same gratitude from the Athenians. This is truly the act of not sacrificing an ox with Pyrrhia for a well-deserved service, but of killing the one who deserved well. The truly good man extended weapons to his enemies with which he might be finished off. I have written at greater length than I thought, while I incite you to the struggle and, having seized the handle, defend myself briefly. Greet our friends, Christoph Fuerer and Albert Ledser, in the Lord. Farewell. Be comforted and be robust. Set your face like flint. Farewell again and a third time.

->Eisleben, on the Vigil of Palm Sunday, in the year<-
->1534.<-

->**Georg Witzel**<-

I respond by denying the antecedent. For it cannot justly seem controversial to anyone that an Angel should endure in this way for eternity, and consequently that the eternal duration of an Angel is future. Likewise, if God were to preserve the world for eternity, some possible men would be future, namely those whose individual existences would be in this or that difference of time. Others would not be future, namely those whom God would never create. Just as, therefore, the proposition "Every man is an animal" is valid because this predicate applies to all possible individual men, and thus infinitely in a <term>syncategorematic</term> <gloss>potentially, or successively infinite</gloss> sense, and on the other hand does not apply to certain other things, such as wood or stone, so by the same law will the proposition that is made about future years or men be valid, because it applies to individuals and does not apply to certain other things. Otherwise, almost all scientific propositions, which always apply collectively or distributively to infinite possible individuals contained in this or that species, would have to be condemned. Moreover, an equivocation is contained in the objection. For some things are future with the simultaneity of their parts, such as a man and a horse, and these must sometime exist in the same difference of time according to all their parts. Others, however, are future successively, such that one part exists before another, as happens in motion or in time, or in other collections of things that are produced through various times. And in these, it is sufficient that their individual parts be future in some difference of time, but it is not required that the parts themselves all coexist at any one time. This response is confirmed and explained. Even men who are future until the Day of Judgment will never actually be together. Likewise, the hours of tomorrow will not all be together at any distance of time; yet who would deny that it can be affirmed simply of all of these, and of the whole of tomorrow, that they are future?

You will urge: That can be called future which, in its entirety, will be past. But eternal duration <note>from the side of the future</note>, and the individuals that are produced successively in that duration, will not be adequately past at any distance of time. Therefore, they cannot be called simply future. I respond: It is no less part of the nature of the future to be sometimes present than to be sometimes past. Indeed, Aristotle, as is clear from logic, says that "past" and "future" are cases of the present tense in verbs, and both he and other philosophers explain the matter through the future and the past in relation to the present as to the primary <term>analogatum</term> <gloss>the primary thing to which a name refers</gloss>. And yet, for something to be called future, it is sufficient if any part of it, taken separately, is at some time present. Therefore, it also suffices if any part of it, considered separately, is at some time past, although in its entirety it is never adequately past.

I respond secondly. To say that infinite duration is not future because it will never be past is a <term>petitio principii</term> <gloss>begging the question</gloss>. For "past" <note>Latin: "præter-itum"</note> means the same as "passed-by" or "gone-by." But "past" signifies the term and end of a thing, that which is gone by. And thus, in other words, that which is in question is assumed as the reason.

### THEOREM IV.
#### On the extrinsic term of the infinite.

<note>An ornamental drop cap 'E' marks the beginning of the text.</note>
We have examined the principal properties of that infinite consisting in quantity or number, which that very sharp recent investigator of the infinite examined in the entire first question in eleven articles. For this reason, we have indicated only in passing what he discovered more fully. But because we are not content only with those things that serve our purpose, let us distinguish with fuller words the twofold term of the infinite: one intrinsic, the other extrinsic.

Conclusion 1. An intrinsic term is one that pertains to the very constitution of the infinite, such that with any term removed, the infinite itself would not remain. Such an intrinsic term, on either side, is repugnant to the infinite because of the absurd consequences it carries with it.

Conclusion 2. An extrinsic term is one whereby, and even if any term is removed, the infinite would still remain. A term of this kind is, for example, the beatific vision. Since there are possible more and more creatures without end, that cognition will be more perfect which represents more or fewer creatures. Therefore, there are possible more and more perfect cognitions which are concerned with more creatures, yet none of these cognitions will equal the perfection of the beatific vision. Therefore, in that collection of infinite and more perfect cognitions, the beatific vision will be an extrinsic term, for with it subtracted, that collection still retains its infinity. And similarly, with all other terms subtracted from that side—if, for instance, you wish to be able to assign, after the beatific vision, another cognition immediately most perfect among the rest, and so on—even with all these terms removed, that infinite collection remains, which includes only cognitions tending toward more and more finite individual creatures without limit. Among these cognitions, there is no highest or last one. Therefore, it is always possible to find some infinity for whose completion all those terms from the upper side are not necessary. And thus they can be called extrinsic, and not intrinsic, terms in the constitution of the Infinite, as it is Infinite. Hence, the argument of those is solved, by which they thought they could prove with Durandus the repugnance of species of more and more perfect creatures to infinity. For there is not (as they suppose) a last or penultimate one among those species, and the rest; it would indeed have an extrinsic term, namely God, but not an intrinsic term in the sense explained above.

This theorem regarding the infinite being capable of an extrinsic term, but not an intrinsic one, is not to be noted only in passing, since the entire question of quantity depends on it, and many things are more clearly explained and more easily perceived from it. For from this is solved the argument, otherwise difficult, which is usually made against the infinite—whether actual or objective in the mind of God—given the infinite divisibility of quantity itself, and it is of this kind.

### §. The difficult argument of the adversaries is answered.

If an hour is divisible to infinity, it has infinite proportional parts distinct from one another, namely a half and the half of another half, and so on to infinity, as almost all Peripatetics, along with Aristotle, teach. Let God, therefore, determine to create in individual proportional parts of an hour individual collections of Angels in proportional increases, so that, for example, in the first half-hour He would create two, in the other half of the following half-hour He would create four, and so on. In that case, God would not see in any part of the half-hour...

### THEOREMA IV. <note>Theorem IV</note>
#### Concerning the extrinsic limit of the infinite.

<note>An ornamental drop cap 'E' marks the beginning of the text.</note>
We have weighed the principal properties of that infinite consisting in quantity or in number, all of which that most acute and recent investigator of the Infinite examined in the first question in eleven articles: wherefore we have only indicated in passing what he previously discovered more extensively; but because we are not content only with those things that pertain to his own interest, let us distinguish with broader words the double limit of the infinite, one intrinsic, the other extrinsic.

Conclusion 1. The intrinsic limit is that which pertains to the very constitution of the infinite, such that with any limit removed, the infinite itself would not remain; but such an intrinsic limit is repugnant to the infinite from both sides because of the absurd consequences it draws with it.

Conclusion 2. The extrinsic limit is that by which, and with any limit removed, the infinite would still remain: such a limit is, for example, the beatific vision, for since there are possible more and more creatures without end, that knowledge will be more perfect which will represent more or fewer creatures, therefore there are possible more and more perfect knowledges which are concerned with more creatures, yet none of these knowledges will equal the perfection of the beatific vision; therefore in that collection of infinite knowledges that are more and more perfect, the beatific vision will be an extrinsic limit, for with that subtracted, that collection still retains its infinity. And similarly with all other limits subtracted from that side, for if you wish to assign after the beatific vision another most perfect knowledge of the rest, and so on, with all these limits still removed, there remains that infinite collection which comprises only those knowledges tending toward the individual finite creatures more and more without limit, for among these

others interspersed between one centennial year and the following, which certainly no one will deny is admirable and exceeds human grasp.

knowledges there is no supreme and ultimate one, therefore it is always possible to find some infinity, for the completion of which all those limits from the higher side are not necessary. And thus they can be called extrinsic limits, and not intrinsic in the constitution of the Infinite, as it is Infinite. Hence the argument of those is solved, by which, with Durandus, they thought they could prove the repugnance of species of creatures that are more and more perfect to infinity. For there would not (as they themselves suppose) be an ultimate, penultimate, etc., among those species; it would indeed have an extrinsic limit, namely God, but not an intrinsic limit in the sense explained above.

This Theorem concerning the infinite being capable of an extrinsic limit, but not an intrinsic one, must not be noted only in passing, since the whole question concerning quantity depends on it, and many things are explained more clearly and perceived more easily from it. For from this is solved the argument, otherwise difficult, which is usually made against the infinite, whether actual or objective in the mind of God, assuming the infinite divisibility of quantity itself, and it is of this kind.

If an hour is divisible to infinity, it has infinite proportional parts distinct from one another, namely a half and the half of another half, and so on to infinity; as almost all Peripatetics with Aristotle teach. Let God therefore decide to create in each proportional part of the hour individual collections of Angels through proportional increases: So that, for example, in the first half-hour He would create two, in the other half of the following half-hour He would create four, and so on.
