<translation page="82">
<header>C H A P T E R V.</header>

we have spoken of the office of the Angels in defending the pious.

2. When. Clearly that same night: for only one night intervenes between the imprisonment and the gathering of the council. They are therefore liberated on this very night, and they rest here most safely, with great security, soon to return to their duty, as the persona of the Angel serves for consolation, and so too does the brevity of time. Adversities do not last long. Therefore, they must be endured with a brave heart.

<margin>Liberation increases the constancy of the Apostles in teaching.</margin> 3. Why are they liberated? The speech of the Angel declares it: Go and stand and speak to the people in the temple, all the words of this life. The sentiment of the Angel is that they must teach the Gospel more spiritedly from then on, because it is like the end or purpose of their liberation, as if he were saying, You were not to be liberated unless you were to teach from then on, even more constantly against the Pharisees. There are arguments for diligence: because they must go, as if he were saying, from the prison to the temple, from chains to doctrine. Then, because he commands them to do it standing, that is, fearlessly and spiritedly. Third, because in the temple, not privately. Nor does the contamination of the temple stand in the way of their being sent there.

<margin>A paraphrase of the Gospel.</margin> Fourth, because to the people, that is, publicly, to all who gather for sacred rites. Fifth, what will they teach? <greek>πάντα τὰ ῥήματα τῆς ζωῆς ταύτης</greek> <gloss>all the words of this life</gloss>. It is a brief paraphrase of the Gospel, according to that in John 6: "You have the words of eternal life," and in the same place, "The words that I speak, they are life." It is called life because it contains the method for obtaining eternal life. Nor does it only contain the method, but it provides the power to attain it. Hence that in Romans 1: "It is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." Those are the words of this life. Nor is any <term>hypallage</term> <gloss>a figure of speech in which cases are exchanged</gloss> needed here, because the relation <greek>ταύτης</greek> <gloss>this</gloss> points to the present life, concerning which the question was for them with the Pharisees. But that was not this external life, but that eternal one, and the whole sum of evangelical doctrine.

4. The obedience of the Apostles follows, who enter the temple, and that at the break of dawn, so that you may know that the temple was sought out again soon after the prison, and in the morning, because they gathered for sacred rites in that temple even before sunrise.

They teach, therefore, in a suitable place and time. Let us learn what becomes those who have been liberated from dangers, namely, to devote themselves to piety with greater diligence.

III. The attempt of the enemies follows, the matter not yet being revealed to them. First, they convene the council. <margin>What the High Priest does with his minions, the Apostles having been liberated.</margin> Its author is the High Priest and a certain few, that is, the Sadducees. Hence the Sanhedrin and <greek>γερουσία</greek> <gloss>senate/council of elders</gloss> of the sons of Israel, that is, the fullest assembly, a perfect Senate as if in a grave matter. This senate was not accustomed to be gathered in light cases.

2. The inquiry into the matter, and the truth discovered: they send ministers to the prison, who bring the captives. Having returned, what do they report? We found the prison fortified, the guards standing outside, but upon entering, we found no one. You see an unusual change of events.

Here, above all, weigh why this miracle is not explained as such by the Angel or by the Apostles, but rather its narration is attributed to the ministers of the enemies. It is done for the greater emphasis of the matter, so that you may see that neither the guards sensed such a thing, nor did others suspect it, but it is an unforeseen and stupendous miracle.

Then, why should this lie hidden from such great men? Certainly, the novelty of the matter should have struck them; and it would be more valid among them, as they ought to have learned it from no others than their own ministers.

But they are not moved even by this. Learn, therefore, at least this effect: that it might be established how God eludes the counsels of his enemies. They think the prey is in their hands, but what? They are eluded like gaping crows. Thus we previously saw Sapphira, who for three hours remained ignorant of her husband's fortune.

3. As to how they are affected: it is stupor; <greek>διηπόρουν</greek>, that is, they are of an ambiguous mind; they do not know what they are doing, and this is also what is to be gathered by them from this, so confused are they. It is certain, however, that they were obstinate, because they think only of the outcome, nothing of repentance, as if to say, the power of the miracle did not escape them, but blind with envy, they resist, greedy also for the outcome.

4. A fuller knowledge of the matter. While they stand astonished and stupified, another messenger is present who explains the matter more fully. What sort of messenger this was matters little; it is possible he was a simple and good man; however, it is more probable that he was some flatterer who wished to hunt for some favor with the High Priests. As happens, it seems to them that he is present by chance, when they neither sent for him nor expected him by plan. But as far as God is concerned, he is present, sent by certain plan and providence. Thus, many things happen to us by chance and accidentally in our actions, which, however, as far as God is concerned, come about by plan and the reason of providence.

<margin>The Jews are hardened to the wonder of the liberation.</margin> IIII. One could have expected from good natures some indication of their amendment here, but he proceeds to recount that the matter always turns for the worse among the High Priests.

For first, they are captured again, and that by the captain of the temple, so that you may know that this is a decree of the council, for he has a legal interest here. This is their amendment. But malice is provident: they do not inflict force as before, but rather they invite them in a friendly manner to the meeting, as if to be heard freely.

This is the custom of hypocrites; they are accustomed to ensnare blandly those whom they dare not openly overwhelm. And what is the reason for this action? Do they begin to grow wise? III. There follows the attempt of the enemies while the matter was not yet revealed to them. First, they convene the council. <margin>What the High Priest does with his cohorts when the Apostles are liberated.</margin> The author of this is the High Priest and a few others, that is, the Sadducees. Hence the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>sanhedrin/council</gloss> and the γερουσία [senate/council of elders] of the sons of Israel, that is, the fullest gathering, the perfect Senate as in a grave matter. This senate was not accustomed to be gathered in trivial causes.

2. The investigation of the matter, and the truth discovered: they send ministers to the prison, who bring the captives. Returning, what do they report? We found the prison secured: the guards even standing outside: but upon entering we found no one. You see an unusual change of events.

Here, first of all, weigh why this miracle is not explained as such by the Angel or by the Apostles: but rather its narration is attributed to the enemies' ministers here. This is done for the greater emphasis of the matter, so that you may see that neither the guards perceived such a thing, nor did others suspect it: but the miracle was unforeseen and astonishing.

Then, why does this escape such great men? Surely the novelty of the matter should have struck them: and it would be more valid among them, as they should have learned it from no others than their own ministers.

But they are not moved by this. Learn, therefore, at least this, that the effect was that it might be evident how God eludes the counsels of His enemies: they think the prey is in their hands: but what? They are eluded, like gaping crows. Thus we previously saw Sapphira, who for three hours remained ignorant of her husband's fortune.

3. As to how they were affected, it is astonishment: διηπόρουν [they were perplexed], that is, they are of an ambiguous mind: they do not know what to do; this becomes also what is to be gathered by them from this, so they are confused. That they were obstinate, however, is certain, because they think only of the outcome, nothing of repentance, as to where it would end, as if to say, the power of the miracle did not escape them: but blinded by envy, they resist, greedy even for the outcome.

4. A fuller knowledge of the matter. While they stand astonished, another messenger arrives, who recounts the matter more fully. What kind of messenger this was matters little: it is possible that he was a simple and good man: more probably, however, some flatterer who wanted to hunt for some favor with the High Priests from this. As it happens, it seems to them that he is present by chance: when they had neither sent for him nor expected him by counsel. As for God, however, he is present, sent by certain counsel and providence. Thus many things happen to us by chance and accidentally in our actions: which, however, as far as God is concerned, happen by the counsel and reason of providence.

<margin>The Jews are hardened to the wonder of the liberation.</margin> IIII. One could have expected here from good minds some sign of their amendment: but he proceeds to recount how the matter always turns for the worse among the High Priests.

For first they are captured again, and that by the prefect of the temple, so that you may know that this was a decree of the council: for he is here by right. This is their amendment. But malice is provident: they do not inflict force, as before, but rather they invite them in a friendly manner to the assembly, as if to be heard freely.

This is the custom of hypocrites: they are accustomed to ensnare smoothly those whom they dare not openly overwhelm. And what is the reason for this act? Are they beginning to become wise? Not at all: but they fear stoning: Behold the fear and the cause of fear. You have the same in the cause of Christ in Matthew 21 and Luke 20. It is a chorus of evil men, yet an impotent attempt, and full of danger.

2. They set them again before the council. You may see spirits exasperated. They do not want to appear to have gathered in vain.

pages.83:
<header>COMMENT. ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES</header>

And while they do not find them in the prisons, they bring them from the temple, so that they might vomit out their bile in some way: and since they were overcome by the previous act, now they may at least seem superior to the Apostles by this one.

<margin>The authority of councils was always great.</margin>
3. A grave reprimand is described. First, they charge them with contempt for their decrees. Did we not command you again and again? i.e., You do not care for our decrees. We despise this senate. You may see here that the authority of <term>ousias</term> <gloss>assemblies/bodies</gloss> was always great, and there is nothing else that imposes itself even on learned men more than the authority of Councils and elders. You will discover this if you read the skirmish of Erasmus with Luther concerning free will, and in other questions. The second crime is the novelty of the doctrine: By your doctrine, they say, you have filled Jerusalem, i.e., with your new dogma. They do not say doctrine in general, but that of the Apostles, i.e., private doctrine, which has nothing in common with Moses and the Fathers. Indeed it is new, because it disagrees with the doctrine then received. The Pharisees do not teach thus, and for a long age, with few exceptions, no one taught thus. By itself, however, it is most ancient, deriving its origin from Adam, this doctrine was explained by the Prophets, at last restored by Christ: now it is defended by the Apostles, by voice and by miracles.

The third crime is, You wish to bring the blood of this man upon us, as if to say, The matter looks toward sedition. You adapt your doctrine to the envy of our person. Erasmus assiduously charged this same thing to Luther and Zwingli.

He called the death of Christ blood; they speak of "this man" with great contempt, as if to say, You make him the Son of God and the Messiah: we call him nothing more than a naked and seditious man: and as if it were permitted safely, we say he was killed by right. You make us the authors of this. They were in truth the authors of Christ's death, as is evident from Matthew chapter 27. "His blood be upon us and upon our children." But because the matter is greater than their shoulders, and the matter looks toward great envy, they do not want this to be said publicly. i.e., our order, our persons, the public peace, and tranquility should have been spared.

Verse 29. "But Peter and the Apostles answering said, We must obey God rather than men."

In this second persecution we have arrived at the defense of the cause; that is, Saint Luke has taught by whom it was excited, by whom they were liberated, and finally, how they were drawn to the defense of the cause, not indeed by force, but by smooth and friendly words. Now, therefore, the defense of the cause must be heard.

<margin>The divine apology of Peter against the accusations of the High Priest.</margin>
As on other occasions, so here too the divine Peter pleads the common cause: that the decrees of the Elders are justly neglected by the Apostles: but as far as the remaining chapters of doctrine are concerned, nothing is taught here by them which they do not dare to openly confess. The elders hear this freedom of action with great indignation, so much so that they turn themselves to capital punishment, had not Gamaliel impeded them in the heat of the moment with singular prudence. He teaches by many arguments that nothing should be decided precipitately here, especially in a matter so grave, and finally, his opinion was followed by all by common consent.

There are three parts. The first includes the defense of Peter. The second contains the affection of the enemies and the attempt to kill. The third has the defense of Gamaliel.

1. Peter speaks in the common name, and therefore the remaining Apostles are joined to him. The cause is common, the danger is common, the liberation is common: the defense, therefore, is justly also common.

<margin>God must be obeyed rather than men.</margin>
2. But what does he answer? There were three objections: the first that he despises the decrees of the council. To this he answers thus, "We must obey God rather than men." You have a similar response above in chapter 4. The same Peter and John answer, "Whether it be just in the sight of God to obey you rather than God, judge ye." The sentiment is the same in both places: namely, that the authority of God ought to prevail more than that of men. Therefore, both are to be obeyed: as long, that is, as the magistrate, as an inferior lord, does not oppose his edicts to the superior Lord, God. All the obedience due to the Magistrate looks toward this. In Romans 13, one must obey even the impious, and in serving for fortune. For the magistrate is in his own way the lord of the body and of fortunes. But if they begin to disagree, and the magistrate wishes to take to himself the right over souls, to judge the Spirit, to impede the word of God: here then holds the rule of Peter, "We must obey God rather than men."

<margin>How far the magistrate must be obeyed.</margin>
By which sentiment he does not remove the authority of the magistrate, except in a certain case, where, namely, he opposes himself to God and wishes to bind souls. For as our fortune and body ought to serve the magistrate: so our soul and spirit is free from the lord of princes: it acknowledges only God as judge: then with what observance is he to be cultivated by us, and that in the place of God: finally, when is it free for us to depart from him, or to oppose ourselves to him: when he opposes the knowledge of God, when he also does not perform his duty politically, and not only does not punish crimes, but perpetrates them, so that he is not a magistrate but a Tyrant. Such examples are indeed rare, yet some exist. When Schedasus begged for the Spartan magistrate in vain, he implored the aid of God, whence the republic paid the penalty because it did not punish the lustful youths. Thus, with God so instigating, Switzerland cast off an impious magistrate. Vicenza also came into the power of the Venetians because the Republic did not act against fornicators. In Rome, the Kings were ejected on this occasion and the Republic was changed into a free state. I said those examples were rare, and not easily imitated, unless God is instigating. For experience has taught how badly the matter turned out for the settlers and farmers throughout Germany.

The Junoesque peacock unfurls its praised wings:
    And covers its body and head with feathers.
In the new spring, the lively stag changes its antlers:
    And restores the long seasons of its old age.
He who wishes to enjoy perennial praise on earth
    Must extend his virtue through excellent deeds.
Whoever desires to outlive the ages of the long-lived stag
    Often has need to cast off his bad habits.
Until, free from hardships and every crime,
    He may bear the long joys of eternal life.
Truly, your ancestors and great-grandfathers, the Barons,
    Earned their name and these shields by these means.
If you follow the praiseworthy examples of those men:
    You shall soon surpass the long ages of the aged stag.

->Jeremias Reusner<-
->Leorinus.<-

<note>Printed by Leonhard Reinmichel, Palatine Printer.</note>

<summary>This poem uses the symbolism of the peacock and the stag to encourage Erasmus of Landau to seek virtue and reject vice in order to secure both earthly fame and eternal life, mirroring the legacy of his noble ancestors.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, legacy, stag symbolism, peacock symbolism, nobility, moral improvement, Jeremias Reusner</keywords>
</translation>

# Meanings of the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas

Because of these four great elements and false forms, the original wisdom-light is transformed into false perceptions. By taking these false forms as the object of perception, and through long-held false views, one grasps a small portion of the four great elements to be a "self," and the false perception relies on these four great elements to be a "body." Thus, the four great elements are originally without knowledge, but because of the clinging of false perception, they appear to have knowledge. The true mind is infinite, but now it is sealed and solidified by ignorance, submerged into the four great elements to function as a mind. This is what is called the body formed by the intermingling of forms and false thoughts. Therefore, it is said that "knowledge and perception are sentient beings," which refers to the sentient beings of the five aggregates. Therefore, the inner five roots and outer six dusts all belong to the "object-aspect" of the eight consciousnesses. Consequently, in the practice of Zen, one must first strip away the body and mind internally and abandon the world externally; the goal is to extinguish these two aspects of subject and object, and to investigate the fundamental substance of the eight consciousnesses and ignorance. If the body, mind, and world are not extinguished, they are always barriers to life and death. Regarding what is called the two执 <term>drsti</term> <gloss>attachments/views</gloss> of self and dharma: clinging to the body as "self" is the attachment to self, and clinging to the roots and dusts is the attachment to dharma. Practitioners of the Two Vehicles <note>the Hearer and Solitary Realizer vehicles</note> only break the view of self to exit the life and death of sections <note>ordinary transmigratory life</note>. The attachment to dharma, starting from the initial faith through the three stages of the virtuous to the first stage of the bodhisattva, is only then broken. This is not easily done.

The twenty-four types of "non-associated" <term>citta-viprayukta-samskara</term> <gloss>dharmas not associated with the mind</gloss> are divisions of form and mind. They are established nominally based on the previous three categories of dharmas, such as "acquisition." They are distinguished as being different from the mind, mental factors, and forms, and thus are called "non-associated." Because they do not associate with the mind-king and cannot perform good or evil, they are not mental factors; they are merely differences in the divisions of positions accounted for by consciousness-only. Because they are the dharmas to which my attachment clings, they are also listed among the conditioned dharmas. There are many interpretations, but this is not urgent and therefore not discussed in detail, lest it hinder the main practice.

---

The ninety-four types of dharmas above are called "conditioned dharmas" because they are the dharmas of sentient beings' life and death, and are constructed by false consciousness. Thus, they are called conditioned and worldly dharmas. The sixteen unconditioned dharmas have six types: space unconditioned, cessation through selection unconditioned, cessation not through selection unconditioned, immobility unconditioned, cessation of thought and feeling unconditioned, and suchness unconditioned. These six types are established as "unconditioned" to distinguish them from the conditioned. Although they are called supramundane dharmas, they actually extend to the Two Vehicles. "Immobility" refers to the third fruit, the Anagamin, and "cessation of thought and feeling" refers to the extinction concentration. "Space unconditioned" derives its name from a metaphor, meaning the substance of the unconditioned dharma is like empty space, without any construction or creation. The following five unconditioned dharmas are explained using this metaphor. However, this metaphor of space has different degrees of magnitude. As the *Flower Ornament Sutra* says, "If a person wishes to know the Buddha-realm, they must purify their mind like space, far removed from false thoughts and all attachments, making the mind's direction unobstructed." It also says, "The pure dharma-body is like space." This points directly to the emptiness of the nature of the dharma-realm. This is the true emptiness of the great vehicle's dharma-nature, which is the absolute purity of the one mind, and thus is like space. The meaning of space here applies to both the great and small vehicles, but primarily takes the meaning of being empty and unobstructed, without construction, as a metaphor for the following five unconditioned dharmas. "Cessation through selection" means selection, which is to choose and cut off. It is the truth manifested by the wisdom that is free of outflows, which cuts through all obstacles and stains; hence it is given this name. This refers to the realization of the emptiness of Nirvana by bodhisattvas in expedient teachings and the Two Vehicles, which strictly belongs to cessation; hence it is called "realization-cessation." The high realization of the unconditioned is specifically for the Two Vehicles and is not...
</translation>

<translation page="50">
# Meanings of the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas

...Cessation through selection is that which is manifested when the conditions are absent without relying on the power of selection. This is how the bodhisattvas of the true teaching view the nature of all dharmas as originally tranquil and extinguished. The "immobility unconditioned" refers to the fourth dhyana, where one is apart from the previous three concentrations, the three disasters do not reach, and there is no stirring of joy or pleasure in body or mind; thus it is named immobility. It is the concentration of the five Anagamins. "Cessation of thought and feeling unconditioned" refers to the state where the thoughts and feelings of the "sphere of nothingness" do not function; this is called the concentration of the cessation of thought and feeling. Both this and the immobility belong to the Two Vehicles. "Suchness unconditioned" means that the principle is not inverted or false; it does not change or shift, and is therefore called suchness. Because it is far removed from the dependent and the falsely imagined, this is precisely what is realized by consciousness-only. The ten kinds of suchness, if based on the *Awakening of Faith*, refer to original enlightenment within the substance of the eight consciousnesses and the suchness gate; this is the suchness that contrasts with birth and death. Because the one mind is not yet exhausted, this is the limit of the characteristics school. The hundred dharmas above answer in summary "What are all dharmas?" Below, it answers "What is non-self?"

Regarding "non-self," there are briefly two kinds: first, the non-self of persons <term>pudgala</term> <gloss>the individual/the person</gloss>, and second, the non-self of dharmas. These two types of non-self point directly to the source of the one mind. The two attachments of self and dharma have coarse and fine aspects. The coarse ones are called "attachment to self and dharma through discrimination," and the fine ones are called "attachment to self and dharma through innate tendency." These two types of attachments, beginning from ordinary people, externalists, and the Two Vehicles, passing through the three stages of the virtuous and the ten stages of the saints, are only completely broken at the stage of "equal enlightenment," at which point these two attachments are exhausted and the one mind is called "Buddha." Now, these two non-selves encompass both the coarse and the fine. The term *pudgala* means "number-taker-destination," meaning that sentient beings repeatedly stir up confusion and create karma, which is the "taking," and the future five paths are the "taken." This refers to the false self of the five aggregates, which is grasped by ordinary people through discrimination, and the "divine self" grasped by externalists, who take on the suffering of life and death in sections. In reality, the five aggregates grasped by the Two Vehicles, the "self apart from the aggregates," and the "Nirvana-self" of the bodhisattvas on the stages—none of whom have yet broken the storehouse consciousness—before the seventh stage, have not yet departed from the innate attachment to self, and thus take on the subtle suffering of the life and death of transformation. The treatise here only speaks of the self discriminated by ordinary people and does not yet reach the saints; this is because it follows the consciousness-only school for the moment. In truth, the Buddha's intent, using the standards of sacred teaching, is to break all of these to reach the ultimate meaning of the Great Vehicle. "Non-self of dharmas" refers to the dharmas that I grasp. The body, mind, world, and six dusts grasped by ordinary people; the false thoughts and Nirvana grasped by externalists; the partial-emptiness Nirvana grasped by the Two Vehicles; and the suchness grasped by bodhisattvas. The text says: "The objects set up before one are merely the nature of consciousness, because there is an 'attainment,' it is not true dwelling in consciousness-only. Because there is a 'realization,' this is the subtle attachment to dharma." That is, having greed and attachment is called subtle attachment to dharma. If this attachment is not emptied, the maturing of results is not exhausted. If it belongs to cause and effect, until after the Vajra-path, when the maturing is emptied, one enters the ocean of fruits. Thus the *Awakening of Faith* says: "When the bodhisattva stages are exhausted and the enlightened mind first arises, the mind has no initial sign, and one is far removed from subtle thoughts; thus one sees the nature of the mind in its completeness." This means that based on these hundred dharmas, the previous ninety-four are the two selves of person and dharma grasped by ordinary people; the six types of unconditioned are the two selves of person and dharma grasped by the Two Vehicles and bodhisattvas. Although they have realized suchness, it still belongs to the opposition of confusion and enlightenment, and totally belongs to the side of birth and death. Now, when the feeling of birth and death is forgotten, saint and ordinary are not established, one reaches the source of the one mind.
</translation>

<summary>These pages explain the classification of the one hundred dharmas into conditioned and unconditioned categories, specifically detailing the nature of the six types of unconditioned dharmas and the progressive path of breaking attachments to self and dharma to achieve the ultimate nature of the one mind.</summary>
<keywords>Hundred Dharmas, Consciousness-Only, conditioned dharmas, unconditioned dharmas, non-self of persons, non-self of dharmas, suchness, innate attachment, discrimination attachment</keywords>

# Meanings of the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas

...Cessation through selection is that which is manifested when the conditions are absent without relying on the power of selection. This is how the bodhisattvas of the true teaching view the nature of all dharmas as originally tranquil and extinguished. The "immobility unconditioned" refers to the fourth dhyana, where one is apart from the previous three concentrations, the three disasters do not reach, and there is no stirring of joy or pleasure in body or mind; thus it is named immobility. It is the concentration of the five Anagamins. "Cessation of thought and feeling unconditioned" refers to the state where the thoughts and feelings of the "sphere of nothingness" do not function; this is called the concentration of the cessation of thought and feeling. Both this and the immobility belong to the Two Vehicles. "Suchness unconditioned" means that the principle is not inverted or false; it does not change or shift, and is therefore called suchness. Because it is far removed from the dependent and the falsely imagined, this is precisely what is realized by consciousness-only. The ten kinds of suchness, if based on the *Awakening of Faith*, refer to original enlightenment within the substance of the eight consciousnesses and the suchness gate; this is the suchness that contrasts with birth and death. Because the one mind is not yet exhausted, this is the limit of the characteristics school. The hundred dharmas above answer in summary "What are all dharmas?" Below, it answers "What is non-self?"

Regarding "non-self," there are briefly two kinds: first, the non-self of persons <term>pudgala</term> <gloss>the individual/the person</gloss>, and second, the non-self of dharmas. These two types of non-self point directly to the source of the one mind. The two attachments of self and dharma have coarse and fine aspects. The coarse ones are called "attachment to self and dharma through discrimination," and the fine ones are called "attachment to self and dharma through innate tendency." These two types of attachments, beginning from ordinary people, externalists, and the Two Vehicles, passing through the three stages of the virtuous and the ten stages of the saints, are only completely broken at the stage of "equal enlightenment," at which point these two attachments are exhausted and the one mind is called "Buddha." Now, these two non-selves encompass both the coarse and the fine. The term *pudgala* means "number-taker-destination," meaning that sentient beings repeatedly stir up confusion and create karma, which is the "taking," and the future five paths are the "taken." This refers to the false self of the five aggregates, which is grasped by ordinary people through discrimination, and the "divine self" grasped by externalists, who take on the suffering of life and death in sections. In reality, the five aggregates grasped by the Two Vehicles, the "self apart from the aggregates," and the "Nirvana-self" of the bodhisattvas on the stages—none of whom have yet broken the storehouse consciousness—before the seventh stage, have not yet departed from the innate attachment to self, and thus take on the subtle suffering of the life and death of transformation. The treatise here only speaks of the self discriminated by ordinary people and does not yet reach the saints; this is because it follows the consciousness-only school for the moment. In truth, the Buddha's intent, using the standards of sacred teaching, is to break all of these to reach the ultimate meaning of the Great Vehicle. "Non-self of dharmas" refers to the dharmas that I grasp. The body, mind, world, and six dusts grasped by ordinary people; the false thoughts and Nirvana grasped by externalists; the partial-emptiness Nirvana grasped by the Two Vehicles; and the suchness grasped by bodhisattvas. The text says: "The objects set up before one are merely the nature of consciousness, because there is an 'attainment,' it is not true dwelling in consciousness-only. Because there is a 'realization,' this is the subtle attachment to dharma." That is, having greed and attachment is called subtle attachment to dharma. If this attachment is not emptied, the maturing of results is not exhausted. If it belongs to cause and effect, until after the Vajra-path, when the maturing is emptied, one enters the ocean of fruits. Thus the *Awakening of Faith* says: "When the bodhisattva stages are exhausted and the enlightened mind first arises, the mind has no initial sign, and one is far removed from subtle thoughts; thus one sees the nature of the mind in its completeness." This means that based on these hundred dharmas, the previous ninety-four are the two selves of person and dharma grasped by ordinary people; the six types of unconditioned are the two selves of person and dharma grasped by the Two Vehicles and bodhisattvas. Although they have realized suchness, it still belongs to the opposition of confusion and enlightenment, and totally belongs to the side of birth and death. Now, when the feeling of birth and death is forgotten, saint and ordinary are not established, one reaches the source of the one mind.

<header>Treatise on the Meaning of the Hundred Dharmas</header>

Because of the four great elements and false form, the light of wisdom, which is originally present, is transformed into false perception. Taking these false forms as the object of perception, and having perceived falsely for a long time, one clings to parts of the four great elements as "self." Thus, false perception relies upon these four elements to form a "body." Therefore, the four great elements are originally devoid of consciousness; it is only because of the attachment of false perception that they seem to have consciousness. The true mind is limitless, but now it is sealed and constrained by ignorance, slipping into the four great elements to function as a mind. This is what is called "mixing forms with false thoughts to form a body," which is why it is said, "Perception is sentient beings." This constitutes the sentient beings of the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss>. Therefore, the inner five roots and the outer six dusts all belong to the "object aspect" of the eight consciousnesses. Consequently, those who practice Chan must first detach from the body and mind internally and abandon the world externally; this is precisely to extinguish these two aspects—the object and the perceiving mind—in order to investigate the root essence of the eight consciousnesses' ignorance. This is why the world of body and mind must be dissolved, as it is always an obstacle to life and death. The "two attachments" of self and phenomena mentioned refer to clinging to the body as "self" and clinging to the roots and dusts as "phenomena." For the practitioners of the two vehicles, breaking the view of self is enough to escape the cycle of fractional birth and death. However, breaking the attachment to phenomena—which one begins to overcome only from the first stage of the path after passing through the three stages of virtue—is not an easy task.

The twenty-four types of non-associated dharmas represent the modes of form and mind. They are established nominally based on the previous three categories of dharmas, such as "acquisition" and the like. They are distinguished from mind, mental factors, and form, which is why they are called "non-associated." Because they do not associate with the mind-king, and because they cannot perform good or evil, they are not mental factors. They are merely distinctions within the phases established by <term>vijnapti-matra</term> <gloss>consciousness-only</gloss>. Because they are dharmas that the "self" attaches to, they are listed among the conditioned dharmas. There are many interpretations, but they are not the primary focus, so it is unnecessary to elaborate, lest it hinder the main practice.

---

The ninety-four types mentioned above are called conditioned dharmas. Because they are the dharmas of sentient beings' life and death, they are calculated by false consciousness and involve activity, hence they are called "conditioned" and "worldly dharmas." The sixteen unconditioned dharmas have six types: space unconditioned, cessation through discernment, cessation not through discernment, the unconditioned of immobility, the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling, and the unconditioned of thusness. These six types are established as "unconditioned" to distinguish them from the conditioned. Although they are called "supramundane," they actually include the small vehicle; the "immobility" refers to the third fruit, <term>anagamin</term> <gloss>non-returning</gloss>, and the "cessation of perception and feeling" refers to the samadhi of total extinction. "Space unconditioned" derives its name from a metaphor, meaning the nature of the unconditioned dharma is like space, having no activity. The following five unconditioned dharmas are all understood through this metaphor. However, this metaphor of space has different levels of magnitude. For instance, the *Avatamsaka Sutra* says: "If one wishes to understand the Buddha's realm, one should purify the mind, making it like space, distancing oneself from false thoughts and all attachments, so that wherever the mind is directed, there is no obstruction." It also says: "The pure dharma-body is like space." This points directly to the emptiness of the nature of the dharma-realm; this is the great vehicle's true emptiness of dharma-nature, which is the absolute rejection of false pollution within the one mind. It is like space because it is empty. The meaning of "space" here spans both large and small vehicles, but it is specifically used as a metaphor for the vastness and lack of activity of the five subsequent unconditioned dharmas. "Cessation through discernment" refers to using analytical discernment to sever and extinguish; it is the realization of the truth revealed by the wisdom of the undefiled, which is why it is given this name. This belongs to the partial realization of the practitioners of provisional teaching and the Nirvana-emptiness realized by the two vehicles; it is properly attributed to cessation, so it is called "realization of cessation." High-level realization of the unconditioned truly lies with the two vehicles, and not...
</translation>

<translation page="50">
...cessation through discernment refers to what is manifested when the conditions are absent without the use of discerning force. The practitioners of the real teaching, the bodhisattvas, view the nature of all dharmas as originally and inherently tranquil, hence this name is established. "The unconditioned of immobility" refers to the fourth dhyana, which leaves behind the first three, where the three disasters do not reach, and where there is no agitation of body or mind from joy or sorrow; this is the fifth anagamin samadhi. "The unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling" is the samadhi where neither perception nor feeling arises in the sphere of nothingness. Both this and the immovable state belong to the two vehicles. "The unconditioned of thusness" refers to a principle that is not inverted, false, deceptive, or changing; it is called thusness because it is far removed from dependence on others and erroneous attachment. This is exactly the ten types of thusness realized by the consciousness-only school. If one follows the *Awakening of Faith*, it is the original enlightenment within the body of the eight consciousnesses and the gate of thusness; it is the thusness that corresponds to birth and death, which has not yet exhausted the one mind. Therefore, this is the ultimate of the <term>xiangzong</term> <gloss>school of characteristics</gloss>. The hundred dharmas above are a summary answer to "what are all the dharmas?" The following answers "what is no-self?"

The phrase "no-self" has two types: first, the no-self of <term>pudgala</term> <gloss>person</gloss>, and second, the no-self of phenomena. These two types of no-self reveal the source of the one mind directly. The two attachments of self and phenomena have coarse and fine aspects. The coarse ones are called the attachment of self and phenomena arising from discrimination; the fine ones are called the innate attachment of self and phenomena. These two types of attachments, from the common person, the outsider, and the two vehicles, through the three stages of virtue and the ten stages of sages, are only completely broken upon reaching the stage of equal enlightenment. These two attachments are what make the one mind appear as a sentient being, and their absence is what makes the one mind a Buddha. Here, both coarse and fine attachments are included. <term>Pudgala</term> means "transmigrator of the numbers," referring to how sentient beings repeatedly generate delusions and create karma, taking on future births in the five realms. This is discussed in the context of the false self of the five <term>skandhas</term> discriminated by commoners and the "spirit self" clung to by outsiders, who take on the sufferings of fractional birth and death. In truth, the self clung to by the two vehicles as distinct from the <term>skandhas</term>, and the Nirvana-self, as well as the innate attachment of self not yet broken by bodhisattvas on the grounds before the seventh stage—all involve the subtle suffering of transformation birth and death. The present treatise only discusses the discriminated self of commoners, not reaching that of the saints. In truth, according to the school of characteristics, the teachings of the sages break through all of this, reaching the depth of the great vehicle's meaning. The "no-self of phenomena" refers to the dharmas one attaches to. Commoners are attached to the body, mind, world, and the six dusts. Outsiders are attached to false thoughts and Nirvana. The two vehicles are attached to partial-emptiness Nirvana. Bodhisattvas are attached to thusness. The treatise says that when objects are established before one's eyes as "consciousness-only," because there is something attained, it is not truly dwelling in consciousness-only. Because there is a realization attained, this is a subtle attachment to phenomena; what is called "arising greed and attachment" is this subtle attachment. Because this attachment has not yet been emptied, one has not yet exhausted the maturation of consciousness. If this relates to cause and effect, until after the diamond-path, when the maturation of consciousness is empty, one enters the sea of fruition. Just as the *Awakening of Faith* says: "When the bodhisattva stages are exhausted and the awakened mind first arises, the mind has no initial state, distancing itself from subtle thoughts, therefore one sees the mind-nature in its finality." Thus, according to these hundred dharmas, the previous ninety-four are the two types of self and phenomena clung to by commoners; the six types of unconditioned are the two types of self and phenomena clung to by the two vehicles and bodhisattvas. Even if they have realized thusness, it still belongs to the duality of confusion and enlightenment, ultimately belonging to the side of birth and death. Now, by forgetting the states of birth and death, and by not establishing distinctions between sages and commoners, one arrives at the source of the one mind.
</translation>

It clarifies that both commoners and sages have specific attachments that must be overcome to realize the one mind.</summary>

<translation page="49">
# Commentary on the Meaning of the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas

Because the four great elements <note>earth, water, fire, wind</note> are illusory forms, the originally present wisdom-light turns into deluded perception. By taking these illusory forms as the realm of what is perceived, deluded perception persists for a long time. It then seizes small parts of the four great elements to serve as a "self," and deluded perception relies upon these four elements to act as a "body." Thus, the four great elements are originally devoid of awareness; it is only because of the attachment of deluded perception that they appear to have awareness. The true mind is boundless, but now it is sealed and solidified by ignorance, infiltrating the four great elements to act as the mind. This is what is called "the combination of form and deluded thoughts acting as the body." Therefore, it is said: "Knowledge and perception are sentient beings." This refers to sentient beings of the five aggregates. Therefore, the inner five roots and outer six dusts all belong to the "object part" of the eight consciousnesses. Consequently, when practicing Zen, one must first internally discard body and mind, and externally renounce the world. This is precisely to erase these two parts—the "object part" and the "perceiving part"—in order to solely investigate the original substance of the ignorance of the eight consciousnesses. If body, mind, and world do not disappear, they are always obstacles to life and death. Regarding what are called the two attachments to self and dharmas, attachment to the body as "self" is the attachment to self, and attachment to the roots and dusts is the attachment to dharmas. When those of the two vehicles <note>Sravakas and Pratyekabuddhas</note> practice, they only break the view of self, thereby exiting fractional life and death. The attachment to dharmas, however, only begins to be broken from the initial stage of faith, through the three virtuous stages, and all the way until the first stage of a Bodhisattva. How could this be easy?

The twenty-four kinds of non-associated [dharmas] represent the positions or states of form and mind. They are established nominally based on the previous three categories of dharmas, such as acquisition. They are distinguished from mind-kings, mental factors, and forms, and are therefore called "non-associated." Because they do not associate with the mind-king, and because they cannot perform good or evil, they are not mental factors. They are merely distinctions of positions counted by the consciousness-only [school]. Because they are dharmas of attachment belonging to the self, they are listed among the conditioned dharmas. There are many interpretations of their significance, but they are not the urgent priority, so there is no need to hinder the correct practice.

---

The above ninety-four kinds are named "conditioned dharmas" because they are the dharmas of the life and death of sentient beings, and being calculated by deluded consciousness, they involve creation and action. Thus, they are called "conditioned" and "worldly dharmas." Regarding the sixteen unconditioned dharmas, there are six types: the unconditioned of space, the unconditioned of analytical extinction, the unconditioned of non-analytical extinction, the unconditioned of immovability, the unconditioned of the extinction of perception and feeling, and the unconditioned of thusness. These six types of dharmas are established as "unconditioned" to distinguish them from the conditioned. Although they are called "supramundane dharmas," they actually extend to the two vehicles; the "immovable" is the third fruit, the Anagamin, and the "extinction of perception and feeling" is the samadhi of extinction. The "unconditioned of space" takes its name from a metaphor, meaning that the substance of the unconditioned dharma is like empty space, without any creation or action. The following five unconditioned dharmas generally use this metaphor. However, this metaphor of empty space varies in magnitude. As the *Avatamsaka Sutra* says: "If one wishes to know the Buddha-realm, one should purify one's intent like empty space, distancing oneself from deluded thoughts and all grasping, so that wherever the mind is directed, there is no obstruction." It also says: "The pure Dharma-body is like empty space." This directly points to the emptiness of the nature of the dharma-realm. This is the great vehicle's true emptiness of dharma-nature, which is the absolute purity from defilement in the one mind, and is thus like empty space. The meaning of empty space here extends through both great and small vehicles, but primarily takes the emptiness and lack of creation as a metaphor for the following five unconditioned dharmas and the ultimate truth. The "unconditioned of analytical extinction" means to distinguish; it means to cut off and extinguish. It is the true principle revealed by using non-lethal wisdom to cut off all defilements and obstacles, hence this name is established. This concerns the partial severing and partial realization of Bodhisattvas in provisional teachings, and the Nirvana-emptiness realized by the two vehicles. Because it correctly belongs to extinction, it is called "realized extinction." High realization of the unconditioned is not truly for the two vehicles.

It clarifies that the nine-four conditioned dharmas are objects of deluded consciousness and introduces the six unconditioned dharmas as metaphors for the unconditioned nature of reality.</summary>

<translation page="50">
"Analytical extinction" means that which is revealed when conditions are lacking without the power of analysis. This is the name established by Bodhisattvas of the true teaching who observe the nature of all dharmas as originally and inherently extinguished through "true-as-it-is" observation. The "unconditioned of immovability" refers to the fourth dhyana, where one leaves the first three dhyanas, the three disasters do not reach, and there is no movement or agitation of body and mind from joy or pleasure; hence, it is named "immovable," which is the samadhi of the Anagamin. The "unconditioned of the extinction of perception and feeling" refers to the samadhi where neither perception nor feeling arises in the realm of nothingness. This, along with the immovable, belongs to the two vehicles. The "unconditioned of thusness" refers to the principle which is neither inverted nor deluded; it does not err and does not change, hence it is named "thusness." Because it is distant from the [dependent] and the [imaginary], this is exactly the ten kinds of thusness realized by consciousness-only. If one follows the *Awakening of Faith*, it is precisely the original enlightenment within the substance of the eight consciousnesses and the gate of thusness; it is the thusness of birth and death that has not yet exhausted the one mind. Therefore, it is the highest point of the Characteristic School. The hundred dharmas above are a summary answer to "what are all dharmas?" The following answers "what is no-self?"

The statement "no-self" has two types: first, no-self of the person, and second, no-self of dharmas. These two types of no-self directly reveal the source of the one mind. The two attachments—to self and to dharmas—have coarse and subtle forms. The coarse ones are called "discriminative attachments to self and dharmas," and the subtle ones are called "innate attachments to self and dharmas." These two types of attachments persist from ordinary people, externalists, and the two vehicles, passing through the three virtuous stages and ten holy stages, until the stage of equal enlightenment, when they are finally broken. Once these two attachments are gone, the one mind is called Buddha. Now, these two types of no-self encompass both the coarse and subtle. "Person" is translated as *pudgala* <gloss>a counting-up being</gloss>, meaning that sentient beings repeatedly stir up delusions and create karma, making them capable of "taking" future five-paths <gloss>the five realms of rebirth</gloss>. This refers to the false "self" of the five aggregates, as calculated by ordinary people through discrimination, and the "spiritual self" grasped by externalists, who thereby take on the suffering of fractional life and death. In reality, the five aggregates grasped by the two vehicles are "away from self," and the Nirvana-self [grasped] by the Bodhisattvas on the stages—before breaking the storehouse consciousness and before the seventh stage—have not yet left the innate "self," thereby taking on the subtle suffering of transmuted life and death. Now, this treatise only discusses the discriminative "self" of ordinary people, not reaching that of the sages. This is just an initial discussion from the perspective of the Characteristic School. In reality, the Buddha’s intent, when measured against sacred teaching, is to break all of these to reach the ultimate meaning of the Great Vehicle. "No-self of dharmas" refers to the dharmas grasped as "my own." Ordinary people grasp body, mind, world, and the six dusts. Externalists grasp deluded thoughts and Nirvana. Those of the two vehicles grasp a partial, empty Nirvana. Bodhisattvas grasp "thusness." The treatise says: "Presently establishing objects, one says they are the nature of consciousness-only, but because there is something 'attained,' one is not truly residing in consciousness-only. Because there is 'realization and attainment,' this is a subtle attachment to dharmas." This is what is called "arising greed and attachment toward the direction [of the goal]," which is a subtle attachment to dharmas. Because this attachment is not yet empty, the ripening [of karma] is not yet exhausted. If it still belongs to cause and effect, one continues until after the Vajra path, when the ripening is emptied and one enters the ocean of fruit. This is what the *Awakening of Faith* means by: "When the Bodhisattva stages are exhausted and the awakened mind first arises, the mind has no initial mark, and being distant from subtle thoughts, one is able to see the mind-nature in its entirety." Thus, according to this, the first ninety-four of the hundred dharmas are the human and dharma no-self grasped by ordinary people, and the six unconditioned [dharmas] are the human and dharma no-self grasped by the two vehicles and Bodhisattvas. Although one may realize thusness, it still belongs to the opposition of confusion and awakening; it is totally on the side of birth and death. Now, by forgetting the sentiment of birth and death, and by not establishing [the duality of] saint and ordinary, one reaches the source of the one mind.

<summary>This page defines no-self of the person and no-self of dharmas, explaining how both coarse and subtle attachments must be transcended to achieve Buddhahood and reach the source of the one mind.</summary>
<keywords>No-self, Pudgala, Discriminative Attachment, Innate Attachment, Thusness, Consciousness-only</keywords>

# Commentary on the Meaning of the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas

Because the four great elements <note>earth, water, fire, wind</note> are illusory forms, the originally present wisdom-light turns into deluded perception. By taking these illusory forms as the realm of what is perceived, deluded perception persists for a long time. It then seizes small parts of the four great elements to serve as a "self," and deluded perception relies upon these four elements to act as a "body." Thus, the four great elements are originally devoid of awareness; it is only because of the attachment of deluded perception that they appear to have awareness. The true mind is boundless, but now it is sealed and solidified by ignorance, infiltrating the four great elements to act as the mind. This is what is called "the combination of form and deluded thoughts acting as the body." Therefore, it is said: "Knowledge and perception are sentient beings." This refers to sentient beings of the five aggregates. Therefore, the inner five roots and outer six dusts all belong to the "object part" of the eight consciousnesses. Consequently, when practicing Zen, one must first internally discard body and mind, and externally renounce the world. This is precisely to erase these two parts—the "object part" and the "perceiving part"—in order to solely investigate the original substance of the ignorance of the eight consciousnesses. If body, mind, and world do not disappear, they are always obstacles to life and death. Regarding what are called the two attachments to self and dharmas, attachment to the body as "self" is the attachment to self, and attachment to the roots and dusts is the attachment to dharmas. When those of the two vehicles <note>Sravakas and Pratyekabuddhas</note> practice, they only break the view of self, thereby exiting fractional life and death. The attachment to dharmas, however, only begins to be broken from the initial stage of faith, through the three virtuous stages, and all the way until the first stage of a Bodhisattva. How could this be easy?

The twenty-four kinds of non-associated [dharmas] represent the positions or states of form and mind. They are established nominally based on the previous three categories of dharmas, such as acquisition. They are distinguished from mind-kings, mental factors, and forms, and are therefore called "non-associated." Because they do not associate with the mind-king, and because they cannot perform good or evil, they are not mental factors. They are merely distinctions of positions counted by the consciousness-only [school]. Because they are dharmas of attachment belonging to the self, they are listed among the conditioned dharmas. There are many interpretations of their significance, but they are not the urgent priority, so there is no need to hinder the correct practice.

---

The above ninety-four kinds are named "conditioned dharmas" because they are the dharmas of the life and death of sentient beings, and being calculated by deluded consciousness, they involve creation and action. Thus, they are called "conditioned" and "worldly dharmas." Regarding the sixteen unconditioned dharmas, there are six types: the unconditioned of space, the unconditioned of analytical extinction, the unconditioned of non-analytical extinction, the unconditioned of immovability, the unconditioned of the extinction of perception and feeling, and the unconditioned of thusness. These six types of dharmas are established as "unconditioned" to distinguish them from the conditioned. Although they are called "supramundane dharmas," they actually extend to the two vehicles; the "immovable" is the third fruit, the Anagamin, and the "extinction of perception and feeling" is the samadhi of extinction. The "unconditioned of space" takes its name from a metaphor, meaning that the substance of the unconditioned dharma is like empty space, without any creation or action. The following five unconditioned dharmas generally use this metaphor. However, this metaphor of empty space varies in magnitude. As the *Avatamsaka Sutra* says: "If one wishes to know the Buddha-realm, one should purify one's intent like empty space, distancing oneself from deluded thoughts and all grasping, so that wherever the mind is directed, there is no obstruction." It also says: "The pure Dharma-body is like empty space." This directly points to the emptiness of the nature of the dharma-realm. This is the great vehicle's true emptiness of dharma-nature, which is the absolute purity from defilement in the one mind, and is thus like empty space. The meaning of empty space here extends through both great and small vehicles, but primarily takes the emptiness and lack of creation as a metaphor for the following five unconditioned dharmas and the ultimate truth. The "unconditioned of analytical extinction" means to distinguish; it means to cut off and extinguish. It is the true principle revealed by using non-lethal wisdom to cut off all defilements and obstacles, hence this name is established. This concerns the partial severing and partial realization of Bodhisattvas in provisional teachings, and the Nirvana-emptiness realized by the two vehicles. Because it correctly belongs to extinction, it is called "realized extinction." High realization of the unconditioned is not truly for the two vehicles.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the four great elements as illusory forms and the origin of the false self. It clarifies that the nine-four conditioned dharmas are objects of deluded consciousness and introduces the six unconditioned dharmas as metaphors for the unconditioned nature of reality.</summary>
<keywords>Four Great Elements, Consciousness-only, Conditioned Dharmas, Unconditioned Dharmas, Self-attachment, Dharma-attachment</keywords>

228
C ii

<note>An ornamental red initial letter E begins the poem.</note>

Behold, Christ, having triumphed over Hell, sends the grand fathers <note>referring to the patriarchs of the Old Testament</note> to the splendid stars, victorious. 
Behold, the gate of Heaven is finally opened to the pious, 
And the sad realms of the Tartarean dog <note>Cerberus</note> are closed. 
Let the world shine brighter than its accustomed light, 
Let the wave of the swelling sea be milder for sailors. 
Let the gusts of wind be gentle, let the air be purer, 
And let every river flow with harmless water. 
Let no clouds sadden the starry Heaven, 
Let no shadow cover the serene day. 
Let not sterile oats grow among the crops, 
Let not the rich earth bear harmful grasses. 
Behold, Christ, having triumphed over Hell, sends the grand fathers to the splendid stars, victorious. 
And He shows us the path, if no crime 
Has stained our breasts with foul wickedness. 
Let the mountains rise with a joyful peak of ether, 
Let the green forest receive its leafy locks. 
Let the earth bear fruits by itself, let the plow rest, 
And let not the strong oxen put their necks under the yoke. 
Let the oaks bear honey, let the rivers run with milk, 
Let sweet must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> flow of its own accord into the full lake, 
Let the fleece become dyed with Tyrian purple by itself, 
Let the flock be dyed by itself with various colors. 
And let balsams sweat everywhere from the slender wood, 
And let a drop fall from any log of frankincense.
</translation>

<translation page="20">
<note>The initial letter of each line in the first section is printed in red ink.</note>

Behold, Christ, having triumphed over Hell, sends the grand fathers to the splendid stars, victorious. 
A revered crowd of holy fathers follows Him, 
As He conquers the terrible realms of the savage Tyrant. 
Now let new joys stir mortal minds, 
Let sad clouds fall from a joyful brow. 
Now let golden Phoebus <note>the sun</note> exult with his rays, and let Cynthia <note>the moon</note> herself 
Exult, carried on dark chariots. 
Let the splendid air rejoice, with the clouds expelled, 
And let the blue wave of the loud-roaring sea rejoice. 
Let the earth rejoice, surrounded by unusual grass, 
And let the white poplar rejoice with joyful locks. 
Behold, Christ, having triumphed over Hell, sends the grand fathers to the splendid stars, victorious. 
With this leader, Caesar will seek Latium with a Mars-born army, 
And he will strike down the opposing leaders in fierce wars. 
And the splendor of the Eagles will terrify the Ethiopians and the Indians, 
And nothing shall be greater than the unconquered Caesar.

### ON HUMAN WEAKNESS. AND
### HE SEEKS FORGIVENESS FROM CHRIST.

<note>A large blue decorative initial 'E' features white floral scrollwork.</note>

And Christ will have descended to us from great Olympus: 
And having been made a man in a human body: 
And He will have endured cruel death through wild wounds: 
And He will have broken the sad caves of the Jupiter of the underworld <note>Pluto</note>: 
And He will have wiped away our filth with His own blood: 
He will have shown the blessed realms of the shining Heaven:
</translation>

<summary>These pages contain Latin verses celebrating the Resurrection of Christ, the opening of Heaven to the patriarchs, and the resulting renewal of the natural world, followed by a transition to a poem concerning human frailty and the need for divine mercy.</summary>
<keywords>Resurrection, Christ, Hell, Heaven, Caesar, Nature, Human weakness, Mercy</keywords>

# Commendation.

It is guarded by the divine power, thus the happy hill with its joyful grass is not troubled by harsh rain from the sky. 
If indeed you look at this mountain at the time when the farmer gathers the harvest, and the sun shines upon it with its light, 
you could look out by day from the hill at the ripe grapes, glowing with the great gift of Phoebus <note>the sun</note>. 
This hill, nearest to the gods and shining with such great gifts, sends forth wine more precious than any wine of Italy, better even than Falernian wine. 
And sweet streams glide down from the peak along the ridge. 
With an irrigating sound, they nourish all the green gardens, 
as well as the neighboring fields and the fruit-bearing vines from thence. All things rejoice in the pleasing gift of the gods.

You, O you shepherds, who seek sweet breezes, 
inhabit this place. For there, the meadows near the streams 
are green on every side, and healthy winds blow. 
This place will be suitable, where one might compose songs for the peaceful Muses, 
or where someone might set sweet-speaking verses to the reed pipe. 
It will be worthy for one to celebrate sacred fires there 
with Nabataean incense <note>a reference to precious frankincense</note>, and to offer them to the foster-children of Helicon <note>the Muses</note>. 
Augusta, powerful in war and impregnable to any, 
fixed her seat there, having ruled for long years. 
This happens because of the immense mountains by which she is surrounded, 
and the excessively narrow mountain passes for martial battles, 
exposed to enemies, whom she beats back according to her desires, 
sprinkling her own threshold with the blood that brings destruction. 
From here, wealthy Italy takes her beginning, and thus to us Italy is considered to have had its origin.

<summary>This passage describes the geographical and agricultural virtues of the hill of Augusta, praising its wine, waters, and defensive position, while framing the city as the birthplace of Italy.</summary>
<keywords>Augusta, Phoebus, viticulture, defensibility, origin of Italy</keywords>

# COMMENTARIES ON ALCHEMY
## OF ANDREAS LIBAVIUS, M. D.
### Part II.
#### TREATISE THREE.
#### OF THE AZOTH OF THE PHILOSOPHERS, AND OF THE PERMANENT WATER.

# Of Azoth and permanent water.

Chemists do not ignore this, who therefore have called it volatile and spiritual, and even a spirit, and because of its non-fixed presence, have established that metals are to some extent fleeting. If cold could also squeeze out a portion of air, heat could do so much more. Now, however, from Lullius and other Philosophers, and also from Paracelsus as referenced by Quercetanus and Dornæus, we know that the word Lily is used to designate the arcane matter of the philosophers, from which the tincture is subsequently prepared. It makes no difference, therefore, whether we name it Azoth (by others Azoc), or Afad, or lily, provided that no other meanings stand in the way. As much as I have been versed in the writings of the philosophers, and also read in the ravings of Paracelsus, the name Azoth is applied most especially to five things. For Paracelsus, it is a certain medicine to be opposed to magical incantations and even to the Devil himself, because it is so strong that we can trust in it to repel him, whereas Saint Paul shows a far different armor against that spirit, and the usual impieties and lies of Paracelsus are not to be cared for. In another book which he inscribed "Azoth," or "Of the Tree of Life," he seems to designate the entire creation, fall, and restoration of man. But neither does this merit any authority, since that book is as impious toward God as it is most pestilent, and full of horrible lies and profanations of divine works, so much so that if Galen is to be condemned for an impious word about God, Paracelsus, guilty of a far graver crime and blasphemy, should be absolved by no calculation. There is hardly anything sound in Paracelsus, which he himself brought forth from his own, except for certain medical preparations and compositions. Leaving him aside, therefore, let us listen to the few things of the Philosophers. Among them, in the beginning, it differs nothing from the mercury of the philosophers and the primary matter. Then it produces sound things, and also signifies something perfected, which follows the constitution of the animated Elixir in the second perfection. Thirdly, it is a certain exaltation of mercury through a sevenfold sublimation, to which your preparation seems to me to respond. There are also other names for the first Azoth. Therefore, it must be extracted by art and brought to the degree of its perfection. That it exists in perfect bodies, and is to be elicited from there by art, this axiom indicates: Philosophy has three parts, namely Sol <gloss>Gold</gloss>, Luna <gloss>Silver</gloss>, and Mercury, from which joined together the father HERMES knew how to prepare the tincture. And: The true Mercury is extracted from two bodies, and is well washed and digested: and I swear by God that there is no other mercury in the universal way than the one now declared, on which the whole of philosophy depends. He who says otherwise speaks falsely. Again: The matter of the philosophical stone is water: and it is understood of the water of those three, Sol, Luna, and Mercury, and there ought to be neither more nor fewer. Sol is the male: Luna is the female, Mercury is the sperm. Another: Bodies submerged in Mercury return through suitable putrefaction into quicksilver, which they were before. I have brought other things elsewhere: And the Rosary of the Philosophers openly says: Our stone is named Mercury by all Philosophers, which is not born, as many think, but extracted from the body. The philosophers' stone is from three, namely Sol, Luna, and Mercury, that is, make Mercury from Sol and Luna in its being without common mercury, but by the philosophical way. These things are there. Where it is to be noted that a hiding place is encompassed by the last words. It is not made by common quicksilver; and yet it is made by quicksilver actually existing. For what is in potentiality does not come to act of its own accord; but through a similar act; and other philosophers often say it cannot be extracted by any other means; just as in the same Rosary it is denied that the quintessence can be extracted without water, which elsewhere he calls spirit and mercury, because it differs from common mercury only by preparation. ### Part II.

#### OF THE AZOTH OF THE PHILOSOPHERS AND THE PERMANENT WATER.

TO THE ONCE MOST CELEBRATED PHYSICIAN, PHILOSOPHER, AND CHEMIST, D. Johann Rungius, of pious memory, of Stettin in Pomerania, when he had sent a certain dry, shimmering mercurial powder, with the consistency of asbestos reduced to a feathery softness, under the name of Azoth and the permanent water.

<margin>4. Metaphysics, 8.</margin>
Since you seemed to have held a knowledge of natural things explored for yourself, and therefore Aristotle attempted to include everything under universal precepts, you know, distinguished man, what he pronounces in his Meteorology <note>original: "περὶ пηκτῶν καὶ ἀπήκτῶν" meaning "concerning things that congeal and do not congeal"</note>, namely: "Some things are congealed by heat, others by cold: and those things are congealable which do not have watery moisture, and are not of water, but are more of hot earth, such as honey and must; and those which have some water, but are more of blood, such as oil and molten silver," etc. It was easy for him, conversely, to say that <term>apēkta</term> <gloss>things that do not congeal</gloss>, that is, concrete-like, or as the chemical philosophers say, the incoagulable, are those which suffer no concretion from heat or cold; but when the disposition and nature of matter is to be laid down, he preferred to touch upon this, and in it to designate the cause of not congealing, since the actions of agents are of those things which suffer, nor can the <term>to energētikon</term> <gloss>the active principle</gloss> do anything unless the patient assents to it. He therefore denies that oil, quicksilver, honey, pitch, etc., congeal by heat or cold, because of the said indisposition of the matter. But, although I do not now superstitiously examine whether heat and cold are to be accepted in isolation, <term>kath' hauto</term> <gloss>per se</gloss>, and not some other formal principle, and by some property of nature, procuring concretion like the gaze of Medusa, just as Zuingerus says of the Orionian or Gorgonian salt; you, however, not long ago regarding Mercury brought to the sublime, he indeed by reason of oil, you of quicksilver, you report: yet that pronouncement seems wonderful, since it is certain that both oil and hydrargyrum, with the others he proposed, sustain concretion, even by cold alone. <margin>Year 1596.</margin>
