Since you, an outstanding man, have seemed to have possessed knowledge of natural things through your exploration, and have known that Aristotle tried to include everything within universal precepts, you know what he proclaims in his Meteorology regarding <term>peri peKton kai apekton</term> <gloss>things congealable and non-congealable</gloss>, namely: "Some things are congealed by heat, others by cold; and those things are congealable which do not have watery moisture, nor are they of water, but are more of hot earth, such as honey and must; and those which have water, but are more of blood, just as oil and molten silver," etc. It was easy for him, uncontradicted, to say that <term>apekta</term> <gloss>non-congealable things</gloss>, that is, concrete things, or as the chemical philosophers speak, those that are incoagulable, are those which suffer no concretion from heat or cold. But when the disposition and nature of matter must be placed beneath, he preferred to touch upon this rather than to designate the cause of non-concretion in it, since the acts of the agents are those of the patients, and <term>to energetikon</term> <gloss>the active principle</gloss> can do nothing unless the patient consents to it. He denies, therefore, that oil, quicksilver, honey, pitch, etc., congeal by heat or cold, because of the stated indisposition of the matter. But, although I do not now superstitiously examine whether heat and cold must be taken in isolation, <term>kath' hauto</term> <gloss>in itself</gloss>, and not some other formal principle, and by a certain property of nature, procuring concretion as if by the gaze of Medusa, just as Zuingerus writes concerning Orionic or Gorgonic salt; you, however, not long ago wrote about Mercury driven into the sublime, he indeed in regard to oil, you in regard to quicksilver: yet it seems a wonderful pronouncement, since it is certain that both oil and mercury, with the rest that he proposed, undergo concretion, even from cold alone. We experience this, of course, in olive oil during winter frosts. The experience regarding mercury is not as common. Yet I have seen—even in moderate cold (for these days, when I am writing this, the air has been softer than usual, to the extent that in the middle of December we have not yet seen proper snow)—the Mercury of the Philosophers, which I had in a glass geranium <note>likely referring to a specific type of glass vessel</note>, compacted into a solid tablet by cold alone, and I observed this also several times the previous year; when brought into a heated room, it immediately returned to its former liquid state. Indeed, it has also been observed that in the middle of mercurial waves there exist rays, like pyramidal crystals, which are those true crystals, and when resolved by heat alone, that perennial phosphoric water is produced; shining with a silver appearance without transparency, just as they excellently teach that there is in them that <term>dynamin</term> <gloss>power</gloss> of coagulating which the philosophers have so anxiously sought. If, therefore, such mercury congeals by cold alone, just as the Philosopher had differed on the generation of metals; and is resolved by heat; how does he write that it is non-congealable? He does not, however, use a light argument. He says that air excels in it, and that this is true, say the chemical philosophers.

<margin>Year 1596.</margin>
pages.43:
# Concerning the Azoth and Permanent Water.

Chemists are not ignorant of this, who therefore called it volatile and spiritual, and even spirit, and because of the presence of its non-fixed part, they determined that metals are to some extent fleeting. But it is not forced by heat or cold: which the serenity of winter, however cold, testifies, just as the most sweltering summer in the parts of Libya, Egypt, and similar regions does. Nor can it be said that air is pressed out of it by the force of cold. For it would not return to its former state if it should flee in fire. If cold could also express a portion of air, heat would do so much more. I will await your opinion on this question, and in the meantime, I shall converse with you about that kind of Mercury which the Arabs and Chaldeans, as they wish, call by the name Azoth, a sample of which, coagulated, you sent me as a gift last summer, and also about the permanent water; from which we will together bring back this fruit, that we may arrive at the true knowledge of philosophical Mercury.

The name Azoth is said to be Chaldean, and Arabic [it is said to be called <term>Azogue</term> <gloss>quicksilver</gloss> by the Spanish, perhaps with the word accepted from the Saracens as it is for <term>azog</term>] to signify the same thing that for Latin chemists is mercury, or quicksilver. Whether it is its own <unclear>annula</unclear>, or modified, I leave to be discussed by those who know those languages. Bellunensis, interpreting the word <term>Afad</term>, says it is a certain kind of lily. Now, however, from Lullius and other philosophers, and also Paracelsus, referring to Quercetanus and Dornæus, we know that the word <term>lily</term> is used to designate the arcane matter of the philosophers, from which the tincture is subsequently made. It is therefore the same thing now, whether we name it Azoth (others, Azoc), or Afad, or lily, provided that no other meaning stands in the way. As much as I have been versed in the writings of the philosophers, and also read in the ravings of Paracelsus, the name Azoth is applied most strongly to five things. For Paracelsus, it is a medicine to be opposed to magical incantations, and even to the Devil himself, because it is so strong that we can trust in it to repel him, whereas St. Paul shows a far different armor against that spirit, and the usual impieties and lies of Paracelsus are not to be cared for. In another book, which he titled <term>Azoth</term>, or *Concerning the Tree of Life*, he seems to designate the entire creation, fall, and restoration of man. But neither does this merit any authority, since that book is as impious toward God as it is most pestilential, and full of horrible lies and profanations of divine works, to such an extent that if Galen is to be condemned because of an impious word about God, Paracelsus is guilty of a far graver crime and blasphemy, and should be absolved by no calculation. There is hardly anything sound in Paracelsus, which he himself brought forth from his own mind, except for certain medical preparations and compositions. Leaving him aside, therefore, let us listen to a few things from the philosophers. Among them, in the beginning, it differs in no way from the mercury of the philosophers, and the first matter. Next, it brings forth things that are sound, and it signifies something even more absolute, which follows in the second perfection of the constitution of the animated Elixir. Third, it is a certain exaltation of mercury through a sevenfold sublimation, to which your preparation seems to me to respond. There are also other names for the first Azoth. They call it the mercury of the philosophers, the first matter, the Green Lion, the permanent water, the Dragon, the water of life, the philosophical water, the vessel of Hermes, etc. That it is the Mercury of the Philosophers is argued by the same matter, and the same apparatus, and the same properties and attributes.

<margin>What the ancients call orpiment. Whence the lily-water of Archelaus is made from orpiment. Dornæus makes it from tin, etc. The fivefold Azoth. The ravings of Paracelsus.</margin>

The Mercury of the Philosophers is that (says a certain Philosopher) which nature has worked upon a little, and fashioned into the form of metal, but left imperfect: which is to say, in perfect bodies, nature has finished that mercury, but has not yet led it to the tincture. Therefore, it must be extracted by art and brought to the degree of its perfection: that it exists in perfect bodies, and must be elicited thence by art, this axiom indicates: Philosophy has three parts, namely Sun, Moon, and Mercury, from which, joined together, the father HERMES knew how to make the tincture. And: The true Mercury is extracted from two bodies, and is well washed and digested: and I swear by God that there is no other mercury in the universal way than that already declared, upon which the whole philosophy hangs. He who says otherwise speaks falsely. Again: The matter of the philosophical stone is water: and it is understood as the water of those three, Sun, Moon, and Mercury, nor must there be more, nor fewer. The Sun is the male: the Moon is the female, Mercury is the sperm. Another: Bodies submerged in Mercury through convenient putrefaction are returned into the quicksilver which they were before. I have cited other things elsewhere: And the *Rosary of the Philosophers* openly says: Our Stone is named Mercury by all Philosophers, which is not born, as many think, but extracted from the body. The philosopher's stone is from three, namely Sun, Moon, and Mercury, that is, make Mercury from Sun and Moon in its being without the mercury of the vulgar, but by the philosophical way. These things are there. Where it is to be noted that a hiding-place is enclosed in the final words. It is not done through common quicksilver; and yet it is done through quicksilver existing in act. For that which is in potentiality does not come to act of its own accord; but through a similar act; and other philosophers often say it cannot be extracted by any other means; just as in the same *Rosary* it is denied that the quintessence can be extracted without water, which elsewhere he calls spirit and mercury, because it differs from the mercury of the vulgar only by preparation. And these things are manifest: If by the help of quicksilver, cold and raw, by its benefit the warm, dry, and clean sulphureity is extracted, etc., the pure mercury remains, etc. Again: Make mercury by mercury, etc. What indeed is the philosophical way by which it is extracted from the perfect is often said in the manner of resolving to the first matter through putrefaction in the dung of the philosophers, that is, Mercury. That this is this very mercury, both the permanent water and the Azoth, their description shows. For thus it is in the *Rosary*: Quicksilver extracted from bodies from the beginning is the permanent water of the philosophers, which is made after putrefaction and the separation of the elements. Also: The permanent or perennial water, or burning wine, is called the water of the body, that is, when the body has been reduced into mercury: which words can be taken about nothing else than the philosophical mercury. It is called permanent, moreover, because it remains constantly, not only in the homogeneous union of parts, to such an extent that it can by no art be divided into constituent portions; but it also consists of two waters, never to be separated by any ingenuity, just as water mixed with water cannot again be separated from it: Furthermore, because when it is perfect, and has become a tincture, it adheres most constantly to bodies by dyeing, made one nature with them. No other things are written elsewhere concerning Azoth. For that saying, that Azoth and fire are sufficient: you yourself confessed this to me. The *Minor Rosary* says: If you know the regimen of fire, mercury is sufficient.

<margin>Who is the Mercury of the Philosophers. Of what the Mercury of the Philosophers is made. Note: that perfect bodies direct what mercury: but the first day, extracted elsewhere or by art from quicksilver, or from immature metal in which you can see with little effort all the elegant colors. It is a vile thing, it is found in every complete pharmacy. Note: Without vulgar mercury. Which is the permanent water.</margin>

# Imperial Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, Volume 66
## First Year of Duke Yin
In the Spring and Autumn period, the noble Gongzi Yishi passed away.

Hu Yuan <note>a scholar of the Northern Song period</note> stated: The ruler’s high ministers and assistants are referred to as his limbs. Therefore, when they are ill, one must visit them; when they die, one must attend the funeral and provide generous gifts for their burial. This is the guiding principle behind the *Spring and Autumn Annals* recording the deaths of high officials.

The noble Zhong Sui died at Chui. On the day of Renwu, they continued the <term>yi</term> <gloss>post-sacrifice musical dance ritual</gloss>, but the flutes were removed. <note>From the eighth year of Duke Xuan</note>

Hu Anguo’s commentary states: According to the rites, if a high official dies, one should not report it to the ancestral temple until the rituals are concluded. If one hears of it, one should not continue the <term>yi</term> ritual. Not reporting it reflects the utmost respect and sincerity toward the ancestral temple. Stopping the <term>yi</term> ritual preserves the grace shown to a minister from beginning to end. Now, Zhong Sui was a high official of the state; for them to continue the <term>yi</term> after his death indicates a failure in the rites of treating high officials with due honor. Although the *Spring and Autumn Annals* emphasize the authority of the ruler over the minister, when the ruler shows extra courtesy and consideration, the distance and dignity of the court are only further upheld.

<summary>This page discusses the proper ritual conduct of a ruler toward the death of his high ministers, citing the Spring and Autumn Annals and scholars Hu Yuan and Hu Anguo to argue that respectful funeral rites are essential to the sovereign-minister relationship.</summary>
<keywords>Zhong Sui, Hu Yuan, Hu Anguo, Spring and Autumn Annals, funeral rites, sovereign-minister relationship</keywords>
</translation>

# Imperial Commissioned Explanation of the Classic of Filial Piety
Five

And the integrity of the minister is sharpened. The method of writing used by the Sage serves to preserve the principle of the sovereign-minister relationship.

Hu Ning <note>a Southern Song Confucian scholar</note> stated: When Emperor Renzong’s minister Fu Bi was in mourning for his mother, the Emperor cancelled the spring banquet. When Han Weigong passed away, Emperor Shenzong expressed his grief with extraordinary honors. These instances all accord with the methods of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.

In the second month, on the day of Guiyou, there were ceremonies at the Wu Temple. The flutes were brought in. Shu Gong passed away; the music was removed and the ceremony was concluded. <margin>Fifteenth year of Duke Zhao</margin>

Hu Anguo’s commentary states: If a high minister passes away while attending a ceremony at the ancestral temple, how should one respond? Although the rites may not have a specific precedent for this, one can establish a course of action based on righteousness. Reflecting on the heart of the ancestors, seeing the death of a high minister, one would certainly find it inappropriate to hear music. Reflecting on the heart of a filial son, one cannot bear to simply clear away the sacrificial offerings that have already been set out. Therefore, removing the music and concluding the ceremony is acceptable.

<summary>This page continues the discussion on ritual propriety regarding the death of ministers during state ceremonies, providing historical examples and concluding that adjustments to ritual are permissible based on the principles of filial piety and righteousness.</summary>
<keywords>Emperor Renzong, Fu Bi, Han Weigong, Emperor Shenzong, ritual, ancestral temple, Shu Gong</keywords>
</translation>

<page-num>First Year of Duke Yin</page-num>

In the Spring and Autumn period, Gongzi Yishi died.

Hu Yuan <note>a scholar of the Northern Song period</note> said: The ruler's ministers and assistants are called his arms and legs. Therefore, inquiring about their illnesses, mourning their deaths, and providing funeral gifts must be done with generous attention to the kindness of seeing them to their final rest. This is the intent behind the *Spring and Autumn Annals* recording the deaths of grandees.

Zhong Sui died at Chui. On the day *renwu*, the *yi* <note>a post-sacrifice ritual</note> was still performed, and the *yue* <note>a type of flute used in music</note> was removed during the *wan* dance. <note>Year 8 of Duke Xuan</note>

Hu Anguo’s commentary says: According to the rites, when a grandee dies, if there is a sacrifice, one should not announce it until the funeral rites are finished. If one hears of the death, the *yi* ritual should not be performed. The reason one does not announce it is to show the utmost sincerity and respect toward the ancestral temple. The reason one does not perform the *yi* ritual is to fulfill the kindness between ruler and subject from beginning to end. Now, Zhong Sui was a high minister of the state; if the *yi* was still performed upon his death, then the rites for honoring a high minister were lost. Although the *Spring and Autumn Annals* elevates the ruler and suppresses the minister, if the decorum and appearance of respect are increased, then the distinction between high and low becomes even more revered.

<summary>This page discusses the ethical requirements for mourning high-ranking ministers as prescribed in the Spring and Autumn Annals, emphasizing the balance of rituals between rulers and subjects.</summary>

<header>Imperially Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, Volume 66</header>
<page-num>First Year of Duke Yin</page-num>

In the Spring and Autumn period, the son of the lord, Yishi, died.

Hu Yuan <note>a prominent Northern Song Confucian scholar</note> said: The sovereign's ministers and assistants are called his thighs and arms <note>a metaphor for essential, trusted subordinates</note>. Therefore, when inquiring about their illnesses, offering condolences at their funerals, and sending burial gifts, one must be generous in the kindness shown at the end of their lives. This is the intent behind the *Spring and Autumn Annals* recording the death of an official.

Zhong Sui died at Chui; on the day *Renwu*, they still performed the *Yi* sacrifice <note>a post-ceremonial sacrifice performed after the main ancestral rites</note>, and the flutes were removed. <note>From the entry for the eighth year of Duke Xuan</note>

Hu Anguo’s <note>a Song dynasty scholar and commentator on the Spring and Autumn Annals</note> commentary states: According to ritual, when an official dies, one should not report the completion of events to the ancestral temple if a sacrifice is ongoing. If news of the death is received, the *Yi* sacrifice should not be performed. The lack of a report is to fulfill the sincerity of solemn respect toward the ancestral temple. The cessation of the *Yi* sacrifice is to fulfill the kindness that extends from the beginning to the end of a minister’s service. Now, Zhong Sui was a high minister of the state; yet, at his death, the *Yi* sacrifice was still performed. This signifies a failure in the ritual of honoring and treating high ministers with proper decorum. Although the *Spring and Autumn Annals* upholds the supremacy of the sovereign while placing subordinates in a lower position, when the outward manifestations of respect are increased, the boundaries between high and low become all the more dignified.

<summary>This page discusses the Confucian ritual standards for mourning high officials, emphasizing that the sovereign must show great generosity and respect at their deaths to maintain the integrity of the ruler-minister relationship.</summary>
<keywords>Zhong Sui, Hu Yuan, Hu Anguo, Spring and Autumn Annals, mourning rites, ancestral temple, minister-sovereign relationship</keywords>
</translation>

<margin>Acts 1:21</margin>
<margin>Matt. 10:1</margin>

These things signify the gravity of the ministry. For they are called onto the mountain, so that they may keep watch on the mountain of the Lord: they will also dwell on the mountain, which means that they cannot remain hidden, just like towers in more elevated places. They will also be exposed to greater storms, like the high peaks of mountains, which are struck more often and more severely than lower places. The highest peaks are swept by the winds. <margin>Whose election it is.</margin>
Next, who chose them? The Son of God, Christ Jesus himself. Hence the Apostles frequently call themselves servants of Jesus Christ. He himself commends the dignity of the ecclesiastical office. And although that election was most holy, because it was performed immediately by the Son of God himself, as in times past the election of the Prophets was by God himself: yet the calling of pious ministers today, which occurs mediately through the ordinary magistrate, ought to be considered no less valuable. For it is just: since that is the duty to which good princes and magistrates are deservedly subject, so that the Church may always have its own ministers, and those pious and learned ones.

These things teach us that the right of election belonged to Christ's free will, and he held full authority to establish the ministry. But I think one must be on guard here against **Cujacius** and **Robertus**, just as one guards against unskilled physicians. For the one applies medicine to a part where the place is not affected. The other does not even see that it is affected.

->XXXIII.<-

And to these two examples must also be numbered those: **REASON** dictates that I seek an inheritance from two [persons], but the opinion of **Pegasus** is **MORE USEFUL**. **REASON** dictates that he is bound to two, but it is **UNJUST** that he be bound. The opinion of **Labeo** has **REASON**, but we follow **THIS LAW**. By subtle **REASON** it will not be done, yet it will be said **MORE KINDLY**. By strict **REASON** they are not liberated, but it is **MORE USEFUL**; and three hundred other things of that kind. And that (as I think) is the true opinion of the law *On not all things* in the Digest *On Laws*.

->XXXIV.<-

Regarding what learned men have otherwise discoursed concerning the meaning of the law *On not all things*, it is not very clear to me whether we ought to approve it. For, to pass over certain opinions of the glossators, which have withered away by the very duration of time, the common persuasion is (whether **Zasius** first brought it, as it seems to him, or, as **Menochio** [thinks], **Lacellotus Politus**), that there are indeed reasons for all laws. And that even **Julian** does not deny this. But that they cannot be rendered immediately by all, or some, interpreters. Although this [opinion] has grown and prevailed remarkably, it does not seem correct to us, if only because it is in many ways alien to the mind of **Julian** and the reasoning of **Neratius**.

->XXXV.<-

Indeed, I will not add that it is less honorable for those who profess knowledge of the law. Whether they believe an asylum has been erected here for their own ignorance, or for that of the laws. For what need is there of arguments? **Duarenus** himself, and **Albericus Gentilis**, no light assertors of that opinion, offer us a certain **Toulouse** professor to be mocked, because, when asked for his opinion on a matter</translation>

<translation page="13">not sufficiently clear, he sought a refuge for his own ignorance, and that of the laws (as he supposed), in the law *On not all things*. **Jason** also stings **Bartolus** for the same reason, and writes that it is **MISERABLE** to say that in purely positive [laws], the will suffices in place of reason. But it is **STILL MORE MISERABLE** that the reason cannot be rendered for all things that are in the law, just as **Bartolus** said regarding the law *On not all things*. Furthermore, **Matthaeus Gribaldus** does not fear to call those men of the most miserable intellect who have been accustomed to refer the reason to ignorance regarding the law *On not all things*. And **Christophorus Ehemius** calls the law *On not all things*, when understood in that way, the firmest **SAFEGUARD OF IGNORANCE.**

### XXXVI.

Now, there is also no less error in explaining the meaning of law 21 *On Laws*. For as for what **Neratius** says, that the reasons for things which are established in such a way ought not to be inquired into, some followers of that opinion interpret it thus: namely, too sagaciously; too curiously. So much so that, with **Vigelius**, this matter has passed into a rule. Others again write that he thought only of obscure matters. And others again [say] he had an eye to the evil intention of those inquiring. But we, on the contrary, believe that none of these things occurred to **Neratius**, and that by that law, it was not the investigation of reasons itself (as being highly necessary) that was prohibited, but rather the rendering of those that have been investigated. In which **Baldus** also agrees with us. To whom, besides **Paulus Castrensis**, **Udalricus Zasius** has assented.

### XXXVII.

Therefore, these things having been deduced, it is clear that the wonderful [opinion] (which **Jason** will call [an opinion])—which he looked into in the law *On what is foreseen* § 2—that the hand of those by whom and for whom it was brought to illuminate that meaning of the law *On not all things* was not applied very appositely, although it is very true that its true reason is known and perceived by very few. But, so that the matter may be better understood, it is worth the effort</translation>

<summary>Hortleder critiques existing legal interpretations of the Roman law "On not all things," arguing against the notion that legal reasoning is inaccessible or that ignorance is a valid refuge in jurisprudence.</summary>
<keywords>Roman law, legal interpretation, Digest, Neratius, Bartolus, jurisprudence, legal reason</keywords>

I believe this fully satisfies the inquiry. However, that the Sacred Code prohibits *green grapes* <note>original: "ענבים לחים"</note> in addition to *raisins*, a reason for this is given in the *Yalkut*, folio 209, column 3: *green grapes* <note>original: "לחים להביא את הבוסר"</note>: they are named *green grapes*, so that even *sour grapes* <note>original: "omphaces"</note> or *unripe grapes* are included in this precept. When, however, among the Jews—as Hottinger reports in *Ennead. Dissertatione Philosophico-Theologica*, page 214—it is held in a lower place that if a Nazirite were intoxicated, it is as if he had eaten grapes, that must undoubtedly be attributed to their own vain and idle ingenuity. Let the rest pass.

§. 6. Finally, in the cited verse, whatever things are indeed doubtful, these are added: whatever is from the *vine of wine*, *from the kernels to the skin* <note>original: "מחרצנים ועד זג"</note>, which are usually translated as: *from the seeds to the skin*. What <term>ḥartsan</term> <gloss>kernel/seed</gloss> and what <term>zag</term> <gloss>skin/husk</gloss> might signify, scholars contend, and the dispute is still under judgment. For since, as Aben Ezra affirms at this place, *the kernels have no parallel, and likewise the skin* <note>original: "החרצנים אין לו ריע וכן זג"</note>, and since neither the word <term>ḥartsan</term> nor the word <term>zag</term> occur any longer in the Scriptures, do not wonder that scholars are split into diverse parties and opinions in explaining these words. It would be prolix to recount them; see some brought forward by Matthew Poole in his *Synopsis Criticorum* and by Bonfrerius in this place. It may suffice now, with rude Minerva <note>a modest expression meaning "with my limited talent"</note>, to have brought forward a few things concerning the words themselves. Some wish for <term>ḥartsanim</term> to denote the exterior, or the outer skin or rind of the grapes, and for <term>zag</term> the interior, the very grains within the grapes; others prefer the contrary. Rabbi Judah wishes for the former, Rabbi Jose for the latter, as their words brought forward in the *Yalkut*, folio 209, column 4, teach: *The kernels <note>original: "החרצנים"</note> are the outer ones and the skins <note>original: "והזגין"</note> are the inner ones; these are the words of Rabbi Judah. Rabbi Jose says, so that you do not err: as in the bell <note>original: "זוג"</note> of cattle, the outer part is called <term>zug</term> <gloss>bell/outer part</gloss>; the interior, however, is the <term>anbal</term> <gloss>clapper/tongue</gloss>*. His opinion is explained more clearly in the *Sepher Mitz-gad*, folio 73, column 4, where it is thus: *Rabbi Jose says the kernels <note>original: "החרצנים"</note> are the inner ones, which are usually sown; but the <term>zag</term> <gloss>skin</gloss> is the outer rind, etc.* Rabbi Solomon Jarchi agrees (which is also
</translation>

the opinion of Rabbi David Kimchi in the *Book of Roots*), who in the Basle Hebrew, Chaldean, and Rabbinical Bibles, folio 155, column 2, has it thus: *The <term>ḥartsanim</term> are the grains or seeds, and the <term>zag</term> are the rinds from the outside, in which the <term>ḥartsanim</term> are contained like a clapper in a bell.* He wants <term>zag</term> to be the exterior of a bell, from which he gathers that <term>zag</term> is also the exterior of the grape. But to others (like the illustrious Dieu in this place), <term>zag</term> is not the external surface, but the body of the bell itself, within whose cavity the <term>anbal</term> <gloss>clapper</gloss> hangs. Add also Rabbi Maimonides, Chapter V, in the cited location, §. 2, folio 40, and the Targum of Onkelos, who renders it in this way: *Of everything that is made from the vine of wine, from the kernels or seeds to the skins, he shall not eat.* And thus for <term>ḥartsanim</term> he has <term>partsanin</term>, from which word some think the Greek <term>pyren</term> <gloss>fruit stone/pit</gloss> is derived, with one letter <term>nun</term> ejected, which, besides other things that Scapula brings forward in his *Lexicon*, page 1407, denotes a grape seed. From that Hebrew word <term>ḥartsan</term>, by the worn-down letter <term>ḥet</term>, they derive the Latin word <term>acinus</term> <gloss>grape/berry seed</gloss>. See Edmund Castell’s *Lexicon Heptaglotton* under the word <term>ḥartsan</term>, which is asserted there to be the inner part of some thing, folio 1416. The same author, on page 195, asserts that <term>zag</term> denotes the follicle, the pellicle, or the outer rind of grapes, which is removed and cast away, and that it has a relationship to <term>azal</term> <gloss>to recede/be removed</gloss>. Finally, in the cited verse, the following items, which are indeed doubtful, are added: whatever is from the *vine of wine* <term>מחרצנים ועד זג</term>, which are usually translated: *from the kernels even to the skin*. What <term>חרצן</term> and <term>זג</term> signify, the learned contend, and the dispute is still before the judge. For since Aben Ezra affirms at this passage: <term>החרצנים אין לו ריע וכן זג</term> <gloss>the kernel has no companion, and likewise the skin</gloss>; and both the word <term>חרצן</term> and the word <term>זג</term> do not appear elsewhere in the Scriptures, you should not wonder that the learned are split into different camps and opinions in explaining these words. It would be prolix to report them; see some of them brought forward by Matthew Poole in the *Synopsis Critica* and by Bonfrerius in this place. Let it suffice now, with modest <note>original: "rudi Minervâ," literally "with crude Minerva"</note> understanding, to have brought forth a few things regarding the words themselves. Volume Eight

A monk asked, "What is returning to the root to attain the essence?" The master said, "Rabbit horns grow." The monk asked, "What is following the light and losing the source?" The master said, "Turtle hair falls." A monk asked, "When the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water, what is it?" The master said, "Who does not know?" The monk asked, "What is it after emerging from the water?" The master said, "The fragrance strikes the eye." A monk asked, "When the bright moon shines in the empty sky, what is it?" The master said, "It is precisely the division of the scene; why is there a need to point to the Jade Tower?" <note>The "Jade Tower" is a metaphor for a high, unreachable state; the master suggests the reality is already present without needing to point elsewhere.</note>

On the day Zen Master Qiefu of Yanzong Monastery in Fuzhou ascended the hall, a monk asked, "The master has ascended the jeweled throne; what should be discussed?" The master said, "Open your ear canals and put it in." The monk asked, "Why did the ancients say that it is a place where neither ears nor eyes can reach?" The master said, "Golden cherry trees do not grow pears." The monk asked, "For the places where both past and present cannot reach, please, Master, tell me." The master said, "How would you ask it?" The monk asked, "Among the crowd panning for gold, who is the one who obtains it?" The master said, "Raise your hand and be separated by a thousand miles." <note>The phrase "separated by a thousand miles" refers to a subtle gap or misapprehension in the monk's question.</note>

<summary>Zen Master Zhongji Mingzhen discusses the nature of realization and emptiness, while Zen Master Qiefu uses paradoxical imagery to redirect monks away from intellectualizing the Dharma.</summary>
<keywords>Zen, realization, emptiness, Dharma, Qiefu, Yanzong Monastery</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="41">
Compendium of the Five Lamps
Sigil: Thousand

To contemplate freely is the merit of the thousand-mile journey. A monk asked, "What is the matter before the Immortal Realm terrace, where the flowers grow lushly by the flying peaks?" The master said, "It appears within the light of the priceless great treasure, yet the ignorant guest remains in darkness, what can be done?" The monk asked, "When the <term>Udumbara</term> <gloss>a legendary flower that blooms rarely</gloss> is plucked, everyone looks on. What is the intent of the ultimate school tradition?" The master said, "If you, Master, ask about the intent of the school tradition, it is better to be in a quiet place and say 'svaha'." <note>A Sanskrit term often used as a concluding exclamation in mantras, here used to imply that the truth cannot be reached through questions.</note> A monk asked, "What is the boundary of all the Buddhas within the barrier?" The master said, "Creation is ultimately difficult to fathom; the spring breeze blows in vain and light." A monk asked, "What is the treasure within the Way?" The master said, "The tears of the descendants also fall." A monk asked, "After all the sages gather their light and return to the source, what is it?" The master said, "Three cries of the gibbon sever the spirit repeatedly; the traveler across ten thousand miles listens to his own sorrow." The monk asked, "I do not understand how people of the present time can match the mechanics of the ancients." The master said, "With a good heart I tell you, beware of the time before you were born."

<summary>The text presents a series of dialogues concerning the nature of the Buddha-realm, the ultimate transmission of the school, and the difficulty of aligning contemporary practice with ancient wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Compendium of the Five Lamps, Buddha-realm, school tradition, transmission, Udumbara</keywords>
</translation>

The Master said, "Pick open your ear holes and listen." The monk asked, "Why did the ancients say that it is a place where neither ears nor eyes can reach?" The Master said, "Pears do not grow on a golden cherry tree." The monk asked, "Regarding the place where the past and present cannot reach, please, Master, speak." The Master said, "How do you ask?" To the crowd filtering gold, he was asked who attained it, and the Master said, "Raise your hand and keep a distance."

The monk asked, "When the flowers are beautiful beside the cliffs of the flying peaks, what is the matter before the Immortal Realm terrace?" The Master said, "The priceless treasure manifests within the light. How can the dark guest, dim and confused, help it?" The monk asked, "When the <term>udumbara</term> <gloss>a legendary flower that blooms rarely</gloss> is plucked, everyone admires it. What is the meaning of the highest lineage?" The Master said, "If you, <term>acharya</term> <gloss>teacher</gloss>, ask about the meaning of the lineage, it is better to be in a quiet place and say, 'Svaha'." 

A monk asked, "What is the realm of all Buddhas within the enclosure?" The Master said, "Creation is ultimately difficult to fathom. The spring breeze sighs in vain." A monk asked, "What is the treasure within the Way?" The Master said, "The descendant's tears also fall." A monk asked, "After all the sages withdraw their light and return to the source, what then?" The Master said, "The three cries of the gibbon are broken repeatedly, and the traveler's sorrow is heard for ten thousand miles." The monk asked, "I do not know how people of the present time can match the subtlety of the ancients." The Master said, "I have good intentions in speaking to you, but be very careful of the time before you were born."

If, however, the latter is taken in the breadth with which Aristotle described it to us above—namely, that it is everything from which a thing is, is made, or is known—it is manifest from the thing itself that those two cannot at all be reversed. Thus, a <term>privatio</term> <gloss>privation/lack</gloss> is a principle from which a thing is made, but it is not a cause, since every cause influences reality (the matter is obscure only regarding the end/purpose, where the Doctors depart into diverse opinions), which cannot be attributed to a privation, as has already been intimated above. We are, of course, not ignorant that a privation is somewhere called a cause by Aristotle himself, but common interpretation holds that this is done less philosophically and according to the opinion of the masses.

XXIV. Furthermore, that we may more rightly investigate and assign the genuine distinction between a cause and a principle, some definition of a cause must be brought forward. By its own merit, we bring forward that which is commonly accepted today in the schools, being considered the most accurate, and it stands as follows: *A cause is a principle that of itself influences being into another*. The design of our undertaking does not require that we weigh every individual part of this definition here; only the final part must be considered somewhat more accurately here, namely, when a cause is called a principle influencing being into another. By this final particle, it is denoted that a cause influences or communicates Being distinct from its own Being. Thus, Philip of Macedon gave Being to Alexander the Great—not his own, but another, a human essence distinct in number. It is also notedly said "into another" (<term>in aliud</term>), not "into another person" (<term>in alium</term>); and thus, the objection that might be sought from the divine persons is avoided. He judged that there were two paths and two courses for souls departing from the body. <translation page="19">
<header>AGAINST ARNOLD.</header>

...which was propagated more widely later and most swiftly pervaded the region of Bashan, then the neighboring Nabataea and Arabia: from which that unhappy shoot was carried into Asia Minor, which infected and corrupted many with its poisonous juice. Finally, it reached and tempted Rome itself. It persisted, however, in Armenia for a longer time, etc. Now, if the Ebionites believed that Christ came only for the sake of the Jews, they certainly would not have betaken themselves to places for the sake of propagating their heresy, unless those places were where very many Jews were found. Nor would Rome have tolerated them, especially at that time, when the Jews, after the destruction of Jerusalem, were being excluded from the city. And what need is there for more words? Yet Symmachus and Theodotion, interpreters of Scripture—the former a Samaritan by origin, the latter an Ephesian—were received by the Ebionites into their religious fellowship: they would necessarily have excluded them if they had thought that Christ pertained to no one except those born of Jewish blood.

XV. The third piece of evidence we have observed in Arnold provides no obscure indication of his talent and intention. He had perhaps read the following in Sandius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, as it is titled—though it would more rightly be called by the name of husks <note>The author uses a play on words here, comparing the title *Nucleus* (Kernel) to *Putamina* (Husks or shells) to suggest the work is worthless.</note>—(p. 64):

> *Clement of Rome, in Constitutions, Book 6, chapter 6, lists the Ebionites among the heretics of the Jews.*

Arnold turns this to his own purpose, undoubtedly with the goal of prostituting the credibility of all historians who have written about heretics and counted the Ebionites among the heretics of the Christians, just as he is accustomed to do. Indeed, the so-called Apostolic Constitutions are not of such moment that we should, on their account, remove the Ebionites from the catalogue of heretics who have arisen among Christians. For there is no one who is unaware that these same Constitutions are refuted by most people, unless they are entirely dull of wit <note>A Latin idiom for someone lacking discernment.</note>; for example, by the Trullan Council and, among the more recent scholars of our own, by Chemnitz, Gerhard, etc.; among the Reformed, by Rivet, Cocceius, etc.; and even by the Papists themselves, by Bellarmine, Baronius, etc. So we may well marvel that the Jesuit Franciscus Turrianus took up the defense of these same [Constitutions] and, furthermore, could hope that, through the laborious commentaries he added to the book, he would achieve anything against the adversaries whom—according to the custom accepted among his own—he calls heretics.</translation>

<translation page="20">
<header>CONCERNING THE EBIONITES</header>

...undertook their defense, and furthermore, that he could hope that through the laborious commentaries he added to the book, he would achieve anything against the adversaries whom—according to the custom accepted among his own—he calls heretics. But in order that we may briefly set forth our own opinion on the present question: to the question of whether a heresy pertains to the Jews or to the Christians, it can scarcely be answered conveniently unless it is first established whether the judgment should be formed from the subject or from the object. The subject is the heretic; the object is the dogmas around which the heresy revolves. Thus, therefore, with respect to the subject, we hold the Ebionites to be heretics of the Christians—because they touted themselves as Christians and did not wish to be considered Jews any longer—in opposition to the heretics of the Jews, who proclaimed themselves Jews; not otherwise than the Socinians, the Quakers today in Europe, and the Johannites (according to Tavernier’s *Itinerary*, Part 1, Book 2, chapter 8, and Part 2, Book 1, chapter 16) in Asia are referred to as heretics of the Christians, even though, regarding their dogmas, little remains among them worthy of the Christian name. Indeed, the Ebionites expressly reckoned themselves among the Christians and separated themselves from the Jews, according to Epiphanius in number 1, where it is reported of them that they strive to usurp the title of Christians. Likewise, in number 18, we read:

> *If you object to the Ebionites concerning the eating of living creatures: "Why did Abraham offer a calf with milk to the angels (Genesis 18:7-8)? Or why did Noah eat them and receive an answer from God: 'Kill and eat'?" And furthermore, since Isaac, Jacob, and Moses similarly sacrificed in the wilderness: The Ebionite denies that he believes them, and they say, "What does it matter to me, once the Gospel has been brought, to unfold what is contained in the Law?" Whence then do you hold what pertains to Moses and Abraham? For I know that those just men are preached by you, and you boast in those parents. To this they answer thus: "That was revealed to us by Christ."*

Therefore, they insultingly traduce a good part of the Law. Hence also Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book 7, before the middle, my page 316.</translation>

<summary>Schelwig disputes Arnold's claim that Ebionites were primarily Jewish heretics, arguing instead that their expansion into non-Jewish regions and their acceptance of non-Jewish members (like Symmachus) identify them as Christian heretics. The author further critiques the use of the Apostolic Constitutions as an authoritative historical source.</summary>
<keywords>Ebionites, Arnold, heresy, Christianity, Judaism, Apostolic Constitutions, Church History</keywords>

### X.

By the words: *money or other beneficial property bequeathed and designated*, the matter of Stipends is indicated. Regarding the very name of money, which our ancestors derived from *pecus* <gloss>cattle/livestock</gloss>, that which pleases the Prince of the Peripatetics, Aristotle, and the jurisconsults of Roman Law must be mentioned beforehand: that the term money here is to be understood as embracing everything that is valued in coin. (31) Whence I recall to the matter of Stipends not only money itself, but also established wealth, estates, tithes, Prebends, Canonries, legacies, certain houses assigned to public persons, exemption from duties and burdens, annual rents, and Ecclesiastical goods; as well as sustenance, clothing, books, and other necessary forms of support of this kind. (32)

### XI.

I come now to the Subject to whom Stipends are usually granted, which in the Definition are *Doctors, and above all the poor, and most worthy students of learning.* They deserve such Stipends by reason of their respective Faculties, Arts, and Disciplines, which they profess, or as each has pledged their service to the Republic. Among these, the holy order stands out. For I read in Eusebius (33) that Constantine ordered, through letters sent to Ursus, the prefect of Africa, a large sum of money to be distributed to the ministers of the Churches, so that I might pass over in silence other benefits bestowed upon them by him with deliberate effort. The Emperor Alexius Comnenus decreed a Stipend of three hundred and three pounds and fifty bushels of grain to the <term>didaskalois</term> <gloss>teachers</gloss>, the Doctors of the Church (of whom there were four by this name). every Cathedral Church a fourth part of the Canonries and Prebends should be reserved for Doctors of Theology, because they have consumed their own patrimonies and the incomes of their kin in their studies. (35) Among whose number it is also fitting to include Envoys, and likewise Assistants in public affairs. Thus, Cunaeus (36) in the last years of his life was adorned with an ample Stipend by the States of Holland, the Fathers of the fatherland, so that he might lend and perpetually dedicate his service to them in doubtful and controversial maritime affairs. Nor shall I be able to pass by here, with what they call a dry foot, the Physicians, to whom the highest honor has also been accorded by Emperors. In such a way, Louis XI, King of the Gauls, sinned with great security and huge rewards in the case of one Physician, whom he flattered greatly out of a desire for life. Regarding whom, Becmann (37) speaks these words:

> He gave him a monthly Stipend of ten thousand gold pieces, and not only that, but he also bestowed the Bishopric of Amiens upon his nephew, and gave many public offices to his relatives and friends. And yet, the Physician was so harsh and hard in his words toward him that nothing could exceed it; therefore, the King feared him greatly, and often complained to his intimates about his excessive harshness, yet he did not dare to dismiss him from his service. For the Physician, as was his custom, once interjecting more severely: "I do not doubt," he said, "that you will cast me out as well, just like all the others; but I confirm to you by a most sacred oath that after my departure from you, you will not live beyond the eighth day." Terrified by this utterance, the King flattered him in every way and bestowed most ample gifts.

### XII.
The subject of educative action is that very thing which gives being to the effect in the genus of the material cause, and supports the effect in this way; it matters little whether you call it the subject of education, of support, or of inhesion, except that education and support seem to imply only the causality of the material cause, whereas inhesion seems to imply even the very union of the form to the subject. From this union, the educative action itself also really differs, as a mode differs from a mode, although by natural necessity an educative action must have the union connected to the absolute form, and the educative action itself, insofar as it requires having it conjoined, can be said to be a union, <note>though</note> radically, not formally or entitatively. The subject of adherence for creative action is the created terminus itself, which cannot be the subject of inhesion or support, because creative action is not support or inhesion; for that creative action is not something by means of which something else, distinct from the created terminus to which it gives being as that by which it is, is caused or supported. However, an educative action is support and inhesion, because it is that by means of which something distinct from the subject is caused and supported or inheres. Wherefore, just as the created terminus does not cause itself or anything else through creative action, so neither can that action received in it be said to be the causality of that terminus as a subject. On the contrary, however, just as something distinct from the subject in which it is received, and to which that action itself does not give being, is caused and supported by educative action, so also that action can be said to be the causality of its subject toward an effect distinct from the subject. But when the created terminus is called the subject of adherence, it is not signified by this that the terminus is only extrinsically affected by the action (since it is truly affected by it intrinsically, no less than the subject of support is by educative action), but only that it is not intrinsically affected by it as an intrinsic cause is affected by causality, just as matter is intrinsically affected by the educative action by means of which the effect is generated.

### XIII.
Actions are diversified in species according to the specific diversity of both termini and principles, so that an action is not of the same species if it does not depend on principles and termini of the same species, although it is not denied by this that an essential distinction can also be introduced into action from elsewhere, and that a terminus of the same species can be produced by the same principle entirely through an action of a different species. Just as the union between subject and form might perhaps exist not only as distinct in number but also as different in species, and not only the same in number; unless, however, a sufficient reason for a specific or numerical distinction appears from elsewhere, the union between the same form and matter in number, or the action of the same adequate agent in number toward the same terminus, will not be said to differ in number or species without cause. Moreover, both action and union differ only in number whenever one or both of the extremes of the former, or the active or passive principle (if it is an educative action) or the terminus or both of the latter, differ only in number. But it seems necessary to admit in these things that one differs more or less in number from another than from a different one, or that they have more or fewer principles from which numerical distinction is taken. A numerically identical effect can be produced of itself by actions of different species, and a cause can produce effects of different species through actions of different species, for the reason that the same cause looks toward many effects of different species producible by it, and the effect is producible by different causes. And neither the effect nor the cause becomes essentially the actual exercise of the other, as this action is essentially the actual exercise of this cause into this effect in number. It does not seem to imply a contradiction that several really distinct inadequate termini are produced by one and the same action in number simultaneously, or that one terminus is produced by several partial agents at the same time. In that case, however, essentially</translation>

<translation page="10">
such action would depend on those several termini or agents; so that with any one of them removed, that very action itself would be removed.

XIV. One efficient cause is primary and most universal, such as God; another is secondary, such as created agents, which produce an effect either of the same nature as themselves, by a univocal action, or of a different nature, by an equivocal action. The primary cause, subordinate to none and independent of every other, concurs with the secondary efficient cause in all effects whatsoever, which it does not produce by itself alone, when viewed in the physical genus, in such a way indeed that no secondary cause appears possible that is independent in its acting from the immediate influx of God. This is because every action, which is the causality and influx of the secondary efficient cause, is participated from the first Being, and thus the primary Cause flows into the same effect by the same action by which the secondary cause flows into it, which it also preserves either by the action alone being distinct, or together with the created cause, according to the varying demand and nature of things. For no creature can properly be the preservative cause of itself or the primary producer. In the genus of material cause, the primary Cause does not concur with the material cause because, even if passion itself, as not being distinct from action, is a being participated from God, it is nevertheless not received intrinsically in God; and thus it does not befit God to cause in the genus of material cause, which mode of causing involves some imperfection that is removed by the very action received intrinsically. In order for a created cause to act, there is no need for a prior impulse of God or a determination made through some impressed motive quality; rather, it suffices that there is the will of God to act simultaneously with the secondary cause and the positing of the action, as depending both on God as the primary cause and on the creature as the secondary cause.

XV. Not only the primary Cause but also creatures as secondary causes are truly active and effective. Just as they have being participated and limited from God, the first Being, so too do they have the power to act. And it is not only accidents that participate in this, but also substances, which are immediately effective of both accidents and substances, and they produce effects of both kinds in the genus of the subordinate principal cause to the Primary Cause. It is more probable, however, that accidents are not productive of any substance as principal causes, and they do not reach them even as instrumental causes immediately, but are rightly called only instruments of the substance, insofar as they dispose and determine the subject in order to produce a substantial form, and the contact required for acting between the passive and the active is had through their mediation. Furthermore, all substances are caused immediately by other substances in the genus of principal cause, with the Primary Cause, or Author of nature, succeeding in the failure of the secondary cause; yet it does not seem to prevent this—where, namely, these are not present, since the dispositions placed in the subject demand another substantial form—that it be said that <note>the Primary Cause</note> uses accidents as an instrument to produce that substance, by elevating them. Accidents, however, in the genus of principal cause, cause nothing but other accidents, and indeed in an external subject, and not in equal but lesser extension; but substances cause both other substances and accidents—insofar as they exceed the powers of the agent accident—in an external subject, and in their own subject, they cause their own proper accidents, which they either find not yet introduced or repair when destroyed. We call a principal cause that which is either of equal or greater perfection as regards entity with the effect, and has by its nature a proportion to it, and thus does not act as if elevated; or at least is connaturally sought by the effect itself if it acts as if elevated. We call an instrumental cause, however, that which acts as if elevated and is not connaturally demanded by the effect.

The total is that which in its own genus is complete and sufficient for the production of the effect, and acts as such in the second act; but a partial cause is that which concurs with another co-cause in the same genus and order toward the effect. Actions are diversified in species by the specific diversity of both the termini and the principles, so that an action that does not depend on principles and termini of the same species is not of the same species. Although by this, it is not denied that an essential distinction can also be introduced from elsewhere, and that the same specific terminus can be produced by the same principle through an action of a different species. Just as the union between subject and form can perhaps be given not only as distinct in number but also as different in species; yet unless a sufficient reason for a specific or numerical distinction appears from elsewhere, the union between the same form in number and matter, or the action of the same adequate agent in number into the same terminus, will be said to differ only in number or species. However, both action and union differ only in number whenever the one or the other or both extremes of the former, and the active or passive principle (if it is an eductive action) or terminus or both of the latter, differ only in number. But it seems necessary to admit in these cases that one differs more or less in number from another than from a third, or that they have more or fewer principles from which a numerical distinction is taken. However, an effect the same in number can be produced by itself from actions of different species, and a cause can produce effects different in species through actions different in species, because the same cause regards multiple effects of different species producible by it, and an effect is producible by different causes. And neither the effect nor the cause becomes essentially the actual exercise of the other, just as this action in number is essentially the actual exercise of this cause into this effect. It does not seem to imply a contradiction that through one action the same in number, multiple really distinct inadequate termini are produced simultaneously, or the same is produced by multiple partial agents at the same time. In that case, however, essentially

such an action would depend on those many termini or agents, in such a way that with any one of them removed, that very action would be removed.

XIV. An Efficient cause is in one way primary and most universal, like God; in another way it is secondary, like created agents, which produce an effect either of the same nature as themselves, by a univocal action, or different, by an equivocal action. The primary cause, subordinate to none and independent of every other, concurs with the secondary efficient cause for absolutely all effects that it does not produce by itself alone, viewed in the physical genus, in such a way that no secondary cause appears possible that is independent in acting from the immediate influx of God. By this very fact, because every action which is the causality and influx of a secondary efficient cause is participated from the first being, and thus by the same action by which the secondary cause flows into the effect, the Primary Cause also flows into the same, which it also preserves either by a distinct action alone, or together with the created cause, according to the different requirement and nature of things. For no creature can properly be the preservative cause of itself or the primary producer of itself. In the genus of Material cause, the Primary Cause does not concur with the Material cause, because, even though passion itself, as not distinct from action, is a being participated from God, it is not received intrinsically in God, and thus it does not befit God to cause in the genus of material cause, which mode of causing involves some imperfection that is removed by the action itself received intrinsically. In order for a created cause to act, there is no need for a prior impulse of God or a determination made through some impressed motive quality, but the will of God to act together with the secondary cause and the positing of the action both from God as from a primary cause and from the creature as dependent on a secondary cause is sufficient.

XV. Not only the Primary Cause but also creatures as secondary causes are truly active and effective; these, just as they have existence participated and limited from God the First Being, so also do they have the power of acting, and not only accidents participate in this, but also substances. These substances are immediately effective of both accidents and substances, and they produce effects of both kinds in the genus of principal cause subordinate to the First Cause. Accidents, however, are more probably productive of no substance as principal causes, and they do not even touch them immediately as instrumental; but they are rightly called instruments of substance only in so far as they dispose and determine the subject in order to produce a substantial form, and the contact required for acting between the passive and the active is had through their mediation. Furthermore, all substances are caused immediately by other substances in the genus of principal cause, with the Primary Cause or Author of nature succeeding in the defect of a secondary cause. Yet there seems to be no obstacle to saying that this one, supplying the defect of secondary causes where they are not present—when, for example, the dispositions placed in the subject demand another substantial form—elevates them to use them as an instrument for producing that substance. Accidents, however, in the genus of principal cause cause nothing but other accidents, and indeed in an external subject, and not in an equal but in a smaller extension; substances, however, cause both other substances and accidents (as regards an intension exceeding the powers of the agent accident) in an external subject, but in their own subject they cause their own proper accidents, which they either find not yet introduced or repair when destroyed. We call a principal cause that which is either of equal or greater perfection regarding entity compared to the effect, and has a proportion to it by its nature, and therefore does not act as if elevated; or at least is connaturaly sought by the effect itself if it acts as if elevated. An instrumental cause, however, is that which acts as if elevated and is not connaturally required by the effect.

XVI. An Efficient cause is in one way total, in another partial. A total cause is that which in its own genus is complete and sufficient for the production of the effect and acts as such in second act; a partial cause, however, is one that concurs together with another con-cause in the same genus and order toward the effect. Sometimes total cause is also taken for the whole collection of causes in the fourfold classification of causes.

11.
<sig>B 2</sig>

They are fervent in the Jesuit camps, the members of which especially incite this sweat: If GOD is infinite, there is no evil, no degree of goodness. For the infinity of one destroys every opposite and every inequality of distances from Divine perfection. Likewise, the freedom of the philosophers opposes this most significant argument to Divine Necessity: Whatever intrinsically acquires something, is intrinsically changed. GOD does so. Therefore. Moreover, it presses even against simplicity: Wherever there is union, there is composition. Union of persons and natures exists in GOD. Therefore. These things, however, are more showy than solid. I answer: It rests immediately upon a slippery, in part false, support: For I am not bound to grant any aseity <term>aseitatem</term> <gloss>state of being from oneself</gloss> of possibility from the fact that a possible thing always presupposes something else, namely potency, from which it might be produced and in which it might be sheltered. Nor does a Chimera <term>Chimæram</term> <gloss>a groundless fantasy</gloss> have a contradiction from itself but from GOD, not indeed from His impotence, of which there is none in Him, but from His supreme perfection, by which He feels nausea at confusing essences, and rather, by distributing them individually, denies compossibility to them. The weapon of the host can be averted with an equally easy fan: Whatever the Blessed see intuitively through a real comprehensive species, that is finite; thus he denies the Minor premise. Through an intentional apprehensive [species]. He denies the connection of the Major premise. Finally, to the Jesuitical arguments themselves, I oppose the response of the Mainz Scholastic: *If GOD is infinite, there is no evil, no degree of Goodness.* Namely, in GOD, he grants it; outside, he denies it. I expunge the scruple cast against Necessity, omitting the responses of G. Vasquez, A. Calov, and others, in this way: Whatever else intrinsically acquires something by way of a subject which it did not have before. Thus he denies the Minor premise. By way of a term. He denies the consequence. I annihilate the argumentation closing the file in the place of a colophon in this way: where there is a strict, subjective, entitative union, there is composition. And he denies the Minor premise.

### VII. GOD is a being intrinsically immense and eternal.

I say intrinsically, since for GOD, whose absolute Infinity eternally gathers every perfection within itself, immensity and eternity pertain independently of the coexistence of creatures and also of the successive turns of extrinsic time; and thus, intrinsically, immensity is equivalent to the perfection of permanent extension, and eternity to successive [extension]. Since every point of immensity encompasses space, and the one and indivisible "now" of eternity, just as the largest Sphere closes in the smaller concentric ones, encloses all time. Indeed, the indivisible immensity of GOD

<summary>This page addresses theological objections regarding the nature of God's infinity, simplicity, and immensity, specifically countering Jesuit and Scholastic arguments by distinguishing between real and intentional apprehension.</summary>

</translation>

<translation page="12">
cannot be circumscribed by the boundaries of the World to such a degree that it fills imaginary spaces, unless you think that with the world moved, GOD is also moved, or if you prefer to deny omnipresence diffused through an intermediate vacuum, or to cut it, if two non-contiguous worlds were posited. Then, having condemned the feverish [arguments] of others, as well as those of Thomas, I conclude thus: Whatever entails the infinity of essence and duration, that being is intrinsically immense and eternal. GOD is this. Therefore. There are some imaginary things which the followers of Scotus, F. Oviedo, Comp. Carleton, and the Philosopher of Mount Carmel oppose to this opinion. 1. Whatever is nothing, GOD cannot be in it. Imaginary spaces are nothing. Therefore. 2. Whatever is whole somewhere, is not outside it, and thus not everywhere. 3. And the impiety, or perhaps crudity, of C. Vorstius struggles to stall the indivisible eternity of GOD, pretending these arguments primarily:

> If eternity coexists with all the differences of time, and those coexist, which is repugnant.

But I respond to the first point, indirectly and by instance: The world is somewhere, which, however, is not a real space, but an imaginary one. 2. GOD is not in nothing locally; I deny this in a conceivable space, with Arr. Lessius and Moncel. For there is no conceivable <term>πῶς</term> <gloss>how/way</gloss> in which GOD is not, as He is intrinsically present and really in Himself, just as He was before the cradles of the world; indeed, without a doubt, He existed before time in the same "where" in which this entire universe now hangs, unless you wish to have created a new prison for Him. But that Doctor from Louvain injects:

> In an imaginary space, something cannot be except imaginarily, which does not fall upon GOD.

But he concludes wrongly from imaginary space to being inside imaginarily. For although *spaces*, these are the words of Sleevogt, *imaginary spaces before and outside the world were not or are not a real thing, yet GOD is actually and really present in them also, by that intrinsic and absolute presence by which He really exists in Himself.* For *space*, as A. Heereboord explains, *is called imaginary in that we feign and imagine it by way of a positive being in order to explain it; for it is as if it were a vacuum apt to be filled by a body.* Meanwhile, with respect to GOD, there is no vacuum, and GOD is truly in it and not imaginarily. To the second point, I respond through that <term>poluthruletòn</term> <gloss>much-discussed</gloss> instance concerning the rational soul, which is so wholly in the whole body that at the same time it is indivisibly whole in every part of the body, whole in the heart, whole in the brain, however much the heart and brain

<translation page="14">as the Emperor uses in the entire Empire, not because they are made equal to the Emperor, but because, with reference to the subjects of their own province, they are seen to possess the same or similar jurisdiction that the Emperor has over all people. For in the granting of a fief, loyalty and superiority are always reserved <note>end of the paragraph "In what causes a fief is lost" in the *Usus Feudorum* <gloss>Customs of Fiefs</gloss></note>. And to request investiture is a sign of reverence, devotion, and recognition <note>Chassaneus, *Customs of Burgundy*, Rubric on Fiefs, paragraph 1, on the word "Don. a la personne de son," etc.; Borcholt, chapter 7, number 3; Hartmann Hartmanni, *Practical Observations*, Book 2, chapter 11, title 4</note>; whence the granting of a fief is not properly an alienation <note>chapter 1, paragraph 1, "By whom investiture may be made"</note>. Bodin disagrees here, without cause—just as Jacques Cujas, a Gaul, calls his fellow-countryman Bodin by anagram, in Book 18 of his *Observations*, chapter 39—in Book 2 of the *Republic*, chapter 6, and Book 1, chapter 10. In order to relate the Roman Republic to an aristocratic state more conveniently, he writes that the Emperor, by these concessions, made his own colleagues in the Empire and his subjects his equals, not attending to the fact that those to whom such regalia <gloss>royal rights</gloss> have been granted by territorial right are no less distant from the majesty of the Caesar than vassals are from their Lord; moreover, one will call a vassal a colleague or an equal subject of his direct Lord only very absurdly, since the perpetual nature of the fief requires that the former be lesser than the latter; see Hartmann Pistoris, *Juridical Questions*, Book 2, page 4; Menochius, *Consultation* 37, number 3.

### XI.

*Princes exercise royal rights in their territories by the same right of superiority: Hence they grant moratory respites to debtors.*

Whoever has the rights of superiority is generally also the master of the royal rights; hence, by the custom of Germany, we see these sometimes conflated, although they differ if one speaks properly. For he who has royal rights does not continuously possess the same right of superiority, as Borcholt testifies in the only chapter on "What are Royal Rights," saying that the rights of superiority or supreme jurisdictions are not prescribed by the aforementioned royal rights. but in such a way that the workmanship of the conception was not of a husband, but of the Holy Spirit, who, in an ineffable manner, performed the formation of this unheard-of fetus from the substance of an untouched virgin, as if in a temple sacred to the heavenly deity. <margin>Curious question</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 2; Titus 3</margin>
¶ FAR be it, therefore, far be it, Fathers and Brothers, that we should henceforth inquire too curiously how God is in the flesh, and in what kind of flesh, and whether the man assumed was perfect or imperfect; for the Apostle himself warns us away from such questions, which are truly not so profitable as they are frivolous, saying: "Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate strife, as they are useless and vain." He said this, and (as with all things) truly. Since it is certain that we love each other less because of these new questions at great cost to our concord, while we strive more than enough to understand things that we would much more rightly commit to God, who prefers that unknowable things be adored with piety rather than that inscrutable things be debated. For with what, I ask, shall we more healthily praise what is correctly handed down and heard? That great Apostle himself did not hesitate to act in this manner, however much he was instructed in the third heaven to which he was caught up.

<margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin>
<margin>Romans 11</margin>
"O the depth," he says, "of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!" it will be gathered that Roman citizens were indiscriminately, and all of them, burdened either by a census of heads or by a head tax, of which we shall speak shortly. Therefore, it was superfluous for Constantine to exempt Roman citizens generally from capitation and render them immune.

But according to this census of things and goods, instituted by Tullius, burdens and tributes were distributed; a notable passage among others is that of Livy, Decad 3, book 4: <note>original: "Cum deessent Nautæ Coss. ex Senatûs consulto edixerunt..."</note> "When rowers were lacking, the Consuls decreed by a decree of the Senate that anyone who had been assessed by the Censors Lucius Aemilius and Gaius Flaminius up to 100,000 copper coins, whether the person himself or his father, or for whom such an amount had subsequently been amassed, should provide one rower with six months' pay; those with over 100,000 up to 300,000, three rowers with a year's pay; those with over 300,000 up to one million copper coins, five rowers; those with over one million, seven rowers; and the Senators (these were of the greater census) were to provide eight rowers with a year's pay." The same author repeats a similar thing in Decad 3, book 6: <note>original: "Deremigum supplemento agi coeptum..."</note> "It began to be dealt with for a supplement of rowers, for which purpose, since there were neither enough men, nor were they receiving pay from which they could be provided, and there was no money in the public treasury at that time, the Consuls decreed that rowers should be provided by private individuals according to their census and rank, as before, along with their pay and food for thirty days." Indeed, these burdens on goods and census were so increased that by the time of Augustus they reached as high as one-twentieth; regarding which matter, Dio speaks excellently in Book 56 of his History: <note>original: "cumque vigesima omnes gravari intellexisset."</note> "And when he understood that all were burdened by the one-twentieth." <translation page="63">...the truth, exhausting the subtle emotions. How profound! How profound! This book spans three thousand years across generations. Although it briefly appeared during the Han dynasty, it was soon neglected and forgotten. The names and locations of its mountains and rivers became full of errors, differing from those of the present day. Without teachers to pass down the knowledge, it faded into obscurity. Where the Way resides, the common customs often lose it. How sad. I have felt deep apprehension regarding this, and thus have initiated this commentary to clear the blockages and prune the overgrowth. I have grasped its singular qualities and highlighted its profound reach, hoping that the lost texts do not vanish from the world, and that the marvelous accounts do not cease for those living today. So that the traces of the Great Yu might not be erased in the future, and the affairs of the eight desolate regions might be heard by descendants—is this not a worthy pursuit? Without the swirling flight of the three-legged bird, one cannot understand the heavens. Without the traversing of deep waters and shallow pools, one cannot know the soaring of the crimson dragon. The courts of the heavenly music are not places that mere performers can tread. The fords without ships are not places that the azure rhinoceros can cross. If one does not possess the utmost understanding of the world, it is difficult to discuss the meaning of the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*. Alas, may the learned readers with broad perspectives take heed of this.

<summary>This page concludes the preface, emphasizing the importance of preserving the *Classic of Mountains and Seas* as a vital historical and cosmological record that has been neglected over the millennia.</summary>

<translation page="64">The bibliography of the Chen family states regarding the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*: "During the Han dynasty, the Imperial Librarian and Chief Commandant of Carriages, Liu Xiu—who is Liu Xin—collated the secret archives." The Jin dynasty scholar Guo Pu provided the commentary. According to the Tang dynasty records, it consists of twenty-three scrolls, with two scrolls of pronunciation guides. The current version was edited and corrected by You Mao of Xishan. It is transmitted to the world as being authored by Yu and Yi. This account appears in the *Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue*, which states: "When Yu toured the east and ascended the Southern Peak, he obtained a golden slip with jade characters that explained the laws of water. He then regulated the four great rivers, and together with Yi, he mapped the places he had visited. Yi recorded them, naming the work *Classic of Mountains and Seas*." This theory is vast and fantastical, lacking strict orthodoxy. Sima Qian said: "The accounts of the mountains and rivers of the Nine Provinces in the *Classic of History* are close to the truth. As for the monstrous creatures described in the *Basic Annals of Yu* and the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*, I dare not speak of them." These can be called famous words. Who would say he was overly cautious? Therefore, You Mao’s postscript clarifies that it was not written by Yu or Bo Yi, yet it is undoubtedly an ancient book from before the Qin dynasty, though no one can determine its true author.
