§ 8. *Observations*, in Greek <term>τηρήσεις</term> <gloss>observations</gloss>, are called those statements whose truth and certainty are obtained through experience, and can be explored especially by certain and suitable instruments. Since those disciplines whose subject matter is immersed in material things rejoice in such principles, therefore very many of them also occur in our Geography.

§ 9. *Postulates*, in Greek <term>αιτήσεις</term> <gloss>demands</gloss> and <term>αιτήματα</term> <gloss>requests</gloss>, are finished off by axioms, in which something is conceded to be possible to be done. By others, they are called *petitions*, not indeed in the sense as if they had to be obtained precariously from the listener, so that he might give his assent and hold them for true, but rather from the customary courtesy of mathematicians, lest the student or listener seem to have done absolutely nothing in the difficult business of demonstration.

§ 10. *Propositions*, in Greek <term>προτάσεις</term> <gloss>propositions</gloss>, are complex, true, and necessary entities that depend upon other complex ones as if from causes. They are called by another name, *Conclusions*, insofar as they result from a premise of demonstration. In mathematics, they are nothing other than the *subject* which comes to be demonstrated. Concerning this, it is particularly to be noted among other things that in mathematics it is not necessary that its parts, or extremes, namely the predicate and the subject, be real entities, or actually present in the nature of things. Rather, in mathematics it suffices if they, being joined to one another, have a true connection between themselves, or if the affection truly resides in the subject itself. However, there are three things especially to be considered concerning Propositions: namely 1. *their species*, 2. *the demonstration*, and 3. *the practice of demonstrating*.

§ 11. Two species are counted: namely, contemplative ones, or *Theorems*, and effective ones, or *Problems*. In Theorems, something is purely proposed for contemplation, and their subject is called <term>ἡγούμενον</term> <gloss>leading/antecedent</gloss>, or the antecedent; the predicate, however, is <term>ἑπόμενον</term> <gloss>following/consequent</gloss>, or the consequent. Problems present something to be effected, whose subject is called <term>διδόμενον</term> <gloss>given</gloss>; the predicate, however, is <term>ζητούμενον</term> <gloss>sought</gloss>. And since in theorems one uses only the intellect, whereas in</translation>

<translation page="10">problems, one also needs various instruments; it is evident that the former contain more subtlety, while the latter require more labor and industry.

§ 12. The demonstration of Propositions is the necessary deduction of them through principles, or a continuous syllogization, by means of which the intellect acquires for itself the knowledge of the proposed thing, and not a superficial or probable one, but one quite accurate and evident, to such an extent indeed that the mind is rendered absolutely unmoved, fixed, and certain, and can rest most placidly in the acquired knowledge. There is, however, another type of demonstration: the direct or *ostensive*, which shows that the thing is so through media or supporting principles; and another indirect or *reductio ad absurdum* <note>original: "per impossibile"</note>, which proves that the thing cannot be otherwise by means of media that overturn the contrary.

§ 13. The mathematical practice of demonstrating, which is commonly called method by synecdoche, is either *Synthetic* or compositive, or *Analytic* or resolutive. The Synthetic proceeds from the simpler to the more composite—that is, from the end or the principles—down to the subject (the proposition to be demonstrated, so to speak) by way of media, meaning the propositions placed between the subject and the principles. The Analytic proceeds from the composite to the simpler, and thus conversely from the subject, or the proposition to be demonstrated, through the media—that is, the propositions placed between the subject and the principles—to the end, which is the principles. The former is very suitable and convenient for teaching entire disciplines, and indeed it almost uniquely has a place in them. However, the latter, although it may be easier regarding invention and apprehension than the Synthetic, nevertheless, as even a glancing inspection of the *Euclidean elements* testifies and proves, it does not have the same place in sciences that are treated mathematically.

§ 14. In both practices, or said methods, it is customary among mathematicians that certain preludes precede the demonstration; just as certain statements not infrequently *follow* it. Of the former type are 1. <term>Ἔκθεσις</term> <gloss>exposition</gloss>, which is the special and determined exposure of the subject of the proposition by a certain example. 2. <term>Διορισμὸς</term> <gloss>determination</gloss>, or the application of the predicate to the subject, already declared by signs. 3. <term>Κατασκευὴ</term> <gloss>construction</gloss>, which is the preparation of the things necessary for the demonstration.</translation>

<summary>This passage details the technical vocabulary of mathematical geography, distinguishing between observations, postulates, and propositions, and explains the methods of demonstration, specifically differentiating between synthetic and analytic approaches.</summary>
<keywords>mathematical geography, observations, postulates, propositions, theorems, problems, synthetic method, analytic method, demonstration</keywords>

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED
## LORD RESPONDENT,
->My friend.<-

CHARLES, so it is right, and the order of studies demands,
->*That true honor be contributed to Logic.*<-
While you do not refuse this, who would deny that you should be supported?
->*Why should honor not be contributed to you in return?*<-
I hope, indeed, that those whom the class held with you
->*Will continue the work that has begun well.*<-

->M. Johannes Paulus Crusius,<-
->Preceptor of the First Class.<-

### Another.

Some seek out thorns, and handle thorny
->*Themes, in which they think they can greatly please:*<-
But unless they can perceive the fruits
->*Of their thorny labors, the glory they bring is meager.*<-
*But while you gather violets, and beautiful hyacinths,*
->*You will bring fragrant roses and pleasing balsams.*<-

->For the sake of friendship<-
->wrote<-

->**Johannes Reinhardus Storck**<-
->**of Strasbourg.**<-

->T H E  E N D.<-

And Solomon and the twelve tribes, and all the souls of the six hundred thousand of Israel, and all those above and below, *Not one is missing* <note>Numbers 31:49</note>—not one is lacking from the count, just like the host of heaven. Furthermore: *Of the greatness of His strength, not one is lacking* <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>. He is clothed in strength and created the world through the power of "These" <note>Hebrew: "הא" (Ha)</note>. And he, the "Who" <note>Hebrew: "מי" (Mi)</note>, is a mighty warrior, firm in power. *Not one is missing*—this refers to Jacob, of whom it is said: *And Jacob was a perfect man* <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. What is said regarding these three <note>referring to the Patriarchs</note> is said regarding the three above, and it is said regarding the three below.

## Correction Fifty

*In the beginning God created*—Rabbi Shimon opened and said: "Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these" <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>. Three prayers are mentioned here: *El* <note>God</note>, *Elohim* <note>God</note>, *Po'el* <note>Worker/Creator</note>. *El* represents the three faces with which the world was created. Because they are the chariot of the Patriarchs. And regarding them it is written: *These are the generations of the heaven and the earth when they were created* <note>Genesis 2:4</note>. "These" <note>EleH</note> are the first ones. But this is the sign, as it is written: "These" <note>EleH</note> are Aaron and Raphael, the heads of their generations.

<note>A decorative floral ornament is printed here.</note>
</translation>

<translation page="259">
<note>A decorative headpiece ornament is printed at the top of the page.</note>

# Correction Fifty-One

The generations of the *Tohu* <note>Chaos</note>, which is hinted at in the beginning of the verses, and the birth of the heaven and the earth, the *Tohu*, are those five, as it was said, as it is stated in the beginning of the verses, as it is stated regarding the giants who engaged in sorcery. And for this reason it was said regarding them that the world turned on their account, for in them He created them, to supply the **Shekhinah** <note>Divine Presence</note>. And it was said to her: "You created *Tohu* to improve the world on their account, to create a settlement from them for the Sabbath." And for this reason, the five *Elohim*—which are the three Patriarchs—are called three prayers to join the Holy One, blessed be He, through them, to supply the **Shekhinah** through them. She is the small "He" <note>Hebrew letter Hei</note> of the middle pillar. She is the body, and her two arms are the right and the left, through which a person and the body are held. And regarding this body it is said that she has a number, in the count of the Hosts, and all of Israel, who are the great host, are included in the host above. *To them all He calls by name*—they are all called by the name of the host above. *Not one is missing* from the account.

The **Shekhinah** is in exile because her husband is far from her. At times she is sustained by an emissary, at times by Abraham, at times by the Mother <note>Binah</note>, at times by the sons, and at times by the **Tzaddik** <note>Righteous One/Foundation</note>. Everything is given to her, for at times he is the son of the Father and Mother, and he receives sustenance through the Father and Mother. And just as there are four firmaments in them, sustenance descends to her through two firmaments. And when it descends into the body, which is Jacob, sustenance descends to her through him. And when it descends into the two legs, which are the legs that stand, which have four firmaments, sustenance descends to her through them. And when it descends into the **Tzaddik**, sustenance descends to her through him. And when it descends into the "He," and they are joined together, she does not need to have sustenance descend through a mere emissary, but through Him. And when she goes out with Him, she ascends to the *Ein Sof* <note>The Infinite</note>, which is her sustenance and her focus. It is not through one single merit, and it does not require the Father and Mother, and it does not require will, but the matter depends on this. And when she descends from her place, and the Holy One, blessed be He, descends to dwell with her, it is said of her and of the son: He is between Israel and the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the Father and Mother. He blesses and is sustained through Him, for He is the "World," and the "Heel" <note>A play on Jacob's name</note> is His. And at that time she is sustained through her ministers. All of this is according to the deeds of Israel; thus she is sustained. Happy is he who elevates her to her place, and the Holy One, blessed be He, to His place, of which it is said: *Behold, the Lord rides upon a swift cloud* <note>Isaiah 19:1</note>. All this is according to the deeds of Israel, as it is said: "If they are... I will prevail until I find a place for the Lord." And so, come and see: at that time when a person returns to his place, what is written of him? *From His place, may He look with mercy upon His people* <note>From the daily liturgy</note>. And with what do they return Him to His place? Only with the perfection of the *Tikkun* <note>Correction/Alignment</note> that they performed in prayer and crying out.

<column-break/>

# Correction Fifty-One

*In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth*—What is this? The ancients established that all the "Et" <note>The particle 'Et' in Hebrew, indicating the inclusion of the Sefirot</note> are for the exaltation. This is the aroma of the incense, the testimony that Abraham stood by. The name that is called *The Heaven*—the Heaven is the Holy One, blessed be He, and the nine heavens are those that He built with Him. And "Et"—the **Tzaddik** and the daughter, who is the Earth—the vessel that includes everything to bring forth seeds and fruits. And this is that which is said: *And every shrub of the field before it was on the earth* <note>Genesis 2:5</note>. He said this is all established in the secret of "Here" <note>Hebrew: "הכא" (Haka)</note>, even though everything is joined and established in His name. Why? Because Adam is the one who is the "He" and the "He" <note>referring to the divine name structure</note> to come to the earth. Rabbi Elazar said to him: "Father, what is the name that is 'He', which is the **Tzaddik**?" He said to him: "The Holy One, blessed be He, is the Sabbath, the 'He' is the twelve—they are included in the three—the root of the tree, and the eight worlds, which are the 'Et' in His host, the Hosts <note>Tzeva'ot</note>." And everything is with them, included in the three levels, against the three wings, and the three Patriarchs are them. But the wings of the tree, and under it the roots of the tree, and this and that—every name is the **Tzaddik**. And all this is according to the deeds of Israel. 
</translation>

<summary>These pages continue the exploration of the Kabbalistic structure of Creation, focusing on the mystical significance of the Hebrew particle "Et" and the divine names. The text emphasizes the interdependence between human action (prayer/Tikkun) and the sustainment of the Shekhinah, explaining how the Tzaddik and the Patriarchs act as conduits for divine flow.</summary>

And the Shekhinah is in exile, because she is distanced from her husband, the All. Sometimes she is provided for through a messenger, sometimes through Abraham, sometimes through the Mother <note>Binah</note>, sometimes through the children, and sometimes through the Tzaddik <note>the Righteous One/Foundation</note>. And everything is given to her. When he is between the Father and the Mother, he receives sustenance through the Father and the Mother. And when there are four firmaments in them, nourishment descends to her through two firmaments. And when he descends into the body, which is Jacob, nourishment descends to her through him. And when he descends into the two legs—those legs that stand, the six <note>referring to the Sefirot of the body</note>—and there are four firmaments in them, nourishment descends to her through them. And when he descends into the Tzaddik, nourishment descends to her through him. And when he descends into the *He* <note>the Shekhinah</note> and they are joined, it is not necessary for nourishment to descend to her through a mere messenger, but through Him directly. And when he emerges within her, he ascends to the Infinite, which is his nourishment. His intention is not through one merit alone, nor does it require the Father and Mother, nor does it require desire, but the matter depends on the Word.

And when she descends from her place, and the Holy One, blessed be He, descends to dwell with her, it is said regarding her and her son: "Is he not between Israel?" Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the Father and Mother, and He blesses and is provided for through them, and He is the maker of the world, His heel <note>a play on the name Jacob</note>. And at that time, she is provided for through His ministers. All of this is according to the deeds of Israel; thus she is provided for. Blessed is he who raises her to her place, and the Holy One, blessed be He, to His place, as it is said of Him: *Behold, the Lord rides upon a swift cloud* <note>Isaiah 19:1</note>—behold, the Lord, a small place, etc. All of this is according to the deeds of Israel. As it is said: "If they are a time of trouble, they will prevail until I find a place for Him." And so, come and see: at that time when a person returns to his place, what is written of him? *From his place, may He look with mercy upon His people.* And with what do they return Him to His place? Only with the perfection of the correction that they corrected in prayer and the cry, as it is said: "From His place, may He look with mercy upon His people." The pious ones say there is a name, morning and evening, continually every day they say it twice, and they are the *He*s that need to be returned to the *He* which is the place above, and to return the *He* to the *He* that came. And the mystery of "Lo, the Lord rides, etc." <note>Isaiah 19:1</note>—and this has already been established.

<column-break/>

## Correction Fifty-One

*In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.* What is this? The ancients have established that all the *Et* <gloss>particle indicating the direct object</gloss> references are for the sages. This is the path of the world and the congregation of Israel, which Abraham knew. The name that is called *Et the heavens*—the heavens, this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is *Et*, and *Et* are the nine heavens <note>referring to the Sefirot</note>. This is *Et* who builds with Him. And *Et* is the Tzaddik, and the daughter is the Earth, the vessel that contains all to bring forth from it seeds and fruits. And this is that which was established: *And every shrub of the field was not yet in the earth* <note>Genesis 2:5</note>. He said this is all established in the mystery of what is here, even though everything is joined and established in His name. This is *Et* the Name, the dweller of the whole, the name of the middle. And why? Because man is the one who is the *He* and the *Aleph* <note>letters of the name</note> for the earth. Rabbi Elazar said to him: "Father, what is *Et*?" He said to him: "The Holy One, blessed be He, the Sabbath, the *He* is the twelve, and they are included in the three needed by the branch and the root of the tree, and these are the eight worlds that are the sign in His host, the Hosts <note>Sabaot</note>." And every letter with them includes three ranks corresponding to the three wings, and these are the three fathers. But the roots of the tree are beneath it, and the roots of the tree are hidden, and all this name is the Tzaddik. And all this is according to the deeds of Israel. 
</translation>

<summary>This page discusses the mystical significance of the creation narrative and the divine Names, focusing on the relationship between the Holy One, the Shekhinah, and the patriarchs. It explains how human prayer and virtuous action sustain the divine emanations and restore the connection between the earthly and celestial realms, specifically through the "Correction" or "Tikkun" of the Sabbath and the divine names.</summary>
<keywords>Zohar, Tikunei HaZohar, Kabbalah, Shekhinah, Sefirot, Creation, Heaven and Earth, Rabbi Elazar, prayer, divine names, Tzaddik</keywords>

He said to him: "The Holy One, blessed be He, the Sabbath, the *He* is the twelve, and they are included in the three needed by the branch and the root of the tree, and these are the eight worlds that are the sign in His host, the Hosts <note>Sabaot</note>." And every letter with them includes three ranks corresponding to the three wings, and these are the three fathers. But the roots of the tree are beneath it, and the roots of the tree are hidden, and all this name is the Tzaddik. And all this is according to the deeds of Israel.

For this is the mark, as it is written: *These are Aaron and Raphael*, the heads of their generations.

<translation page="259">

## Correction Fifty-One

The generations of *Tohu* <note>chaos</note>, which are hinted at in the initial letters, and the birth of the heavens and the earth—*Tohu* <note>chaos</note>. And those five <term>mashi</term> <gloss>forces/traits</gloss> that were mentioned are those that were said in the initial letters, regarding which it was said they are the *Nephilim* <note>the fallen ones</note> who are the <term>refaim</term> <gloss>giants/shades</gloss>. Because of this, it was said regarding them that the world was turned back because of them, and because in them He created them, to provide for the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>. It was said to her: "You created *Tohu* <note>chaos</note> for the sake of goodness; because of them, the Sabbath was formed to create a settlement from them."

And because of this, the five *Elohim* <note>the five manifestations of the Divine Name</note>, which are the three Fathers—and they call them the three prayers—to provide for the Holy One, blessed be He, to provide for the Shekhinah through them, for she is the small *He* <note>the final letter of the Tetragrammaton</note> of the middle pillar. She is the body, and her two arms are the right and the left, by which a person is held, and the body. And regarding this body it is said that it is the one that has five in the count of the hosts, and all of Israel, who are the great hosts, are attributed to the host above. *He calls them all by name*—all of them are called by the name of the host above. *Not one is missing* from the count.

And the Shekhinah is in exile, because she is distanced from her husband. Sometimes she is sustained by a messenger, sometimes by Abraham, sometimes by the Mother, sometimes by the sons, sometimes by the <term>Tzaddik</term> <gloss>Righteous One</gloss>. And everything is given to her. When she is between the Father and the Mother, she receives sustenance through the Father and the Mother. When she has the four heavens, she receives sustenance through two heavens. And when she descends into the body, which is Jacob, she receives food through him. And when she descends into the two legs—these two legs that stand, which have four heavens—she receives food through them. And when she descends into the Tzaddik, she receives food through him. And when she descends into the *He* <note>the letter indicating the Shekhinah</note> to which they are connected, she does not need to receive food through a mere messenger, but through Him. And when she goes out with Him, she ascends to the *Ein Sof* <note>the Infinite</note>, which is her food, and her intent is not through a single merit, nor does she need the Father and Mother, nor does she need requests—rather, the matter depends on the thing itself.

And when she descends from her place, and the Holy One, blessed be He, descends to dwell with her, it is said of her and the son that she is among Israel. But the Holy One, blessed be He, who is Father and Mother, He is blessed and sustained by her, and He made the world, the end of which is His. And at that time, she is sustained by His ministers. And all of this is according to the deeds of Israel; thus is she sustained. Blessed is he who raises her to her place and the Holy One, blessed be He, to His place, as it is said of Him: *Behold, the Lord rides on a swift cloud* <note>Isaiah 19:1</note>. And all of this is according to the deeds of Israel, as it is said: If they are worthy, it will triumph until the place is found for Him. Thus, come and see: at that time that a person returns Him to His place, what is written of Him? *From the place He will look in His mercy upon His people*. And with what do they return Him to His place? Through the perfection of the correction they performed in prayer and the cry, as it is said: *From His place, He will look in His mercy upon His people*. The pious ones said: There is a name for evening and morning, constantly, every day, they say it twice. And they are the *He* <note>the letter indicating the divine place</note> that must be returned to the *He* <note>the higher place</note>, which is the place above, and to return the *He* <note>the lower divine manifestation</note> to the *He* <note>the higher divine manifestation</note> that came. And this is the mystery of: *Behold, the Lord rides on a swift cloud* <note>Isaiah 19:1</note>, and you have already established this.

<column-break/>

## Correction Fifty-One

*In the beginning Elohim created the heavens and the earth* <note>Genesis 1:1</note>. What is this? The ancients have established that all the *et* <note>the untranslatable particle in Hebrew</note> are for the expansion. This is the air of the world and the testimony regarding which Abraham testified. The name that is called *HaShamayim* <note>The Heavens</note>—*Shamayim* <note>Heavens</note> is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is *et*, and *et* is the nine heavens <note>1 Kings 8:27</note>, for *et* is His builder with Him. And *et* is the Tzaddik, and the daughter is the Earth, the vessel that includes everything to bring forth seeds and fruits. And this is what is written: *And every shrub of the field before it was in the earth* <note>Genesis 2:5</note>. It is said this is all established in the mystery of the one who is here, even though everything is connected and established in His name, which is the Name of the Perfect One, of everything—that is the name of the middle one. And why? Because Adam is the one who has the *He* <note>the letter</note> and the *He* <note>the letter</note>, the *alef* <note>letter</note> to the *adama* <note>earth</note>. Rabbi Elazar said to him: "Father, what is the meaning of *He*?" He said to him: "It is the Tzaddik." He said to him: "Blessed is the Sabbath, *He* is the twelve, they are the vessel including the three, the root of the tree, and the eight worlds, which is the letter in His host, *Tzeva'ot* <note>Hosts</note>. And every [letter] that is with them includes three levels corresponding to the three wings of the head, and these are the three Fathers. But the wing of the tree [is] below the roots of the tree, and this is the Tzaddik." 
</translation>

It further elaborates on the symbolism of the "Heavens and Earth" in Genesis, linking them to the Tzaddik and the interplay of divine names.</summary>
<keywords>Tikkunei HaZohar, Shekhinah, Tzaddik, sustenance, prayer, heavens and earth, Genesis 1:1, Rabbi Elazar, divine names</keywords>

<translation page="10">Maranta, part 6, on appeals, number 26 and following, lists as causes for such suspicion: consanguinity, affinity, friendship, Law 5, in the beginning, Digest, On Injuries, chapter "Insinuante" <note>original: "capitulo insinuante"</note>, 25, on the office of the delegate, enmity, the chapter "Quod suspecti" <note>original: "capitulo quod suspecti"</note> and the chapter "Accusatores" <note>original: "capitulo accusatores"</note>, Question 3, 5, chapter 41, § 1, Decretals, on appeals, benefit and detriment <note>original: "commodum et incommodum"</note>. Maranta, part 6, number 65, ownership, servitude, the chapter "Accedens" <note>original: "capitulo accedens"</note>, 4, on the advocacy of a judge before the litigation is contested, whose office he performed in the same matter, the final chapter, 36, on appeals, the final law at the end, Code, on assessors.

## VIII.

There follow the litigating persons, **Plaintiff** and **Defendant**. The **Plaintiff** is he who intends an action, and through it pursues his own in court. (a) The **Defendant** is he who is convened in court, and from whom something is sought. (b) All who are of their own right and have free administration of their goods can sustain these roles of litigants: hence, a minor without a tutor or curator can neither sue nor be sued. (c) A madman, a prodigal, (d) a slave, (e) a magistrate, (f) a son under family power without the consent of the parent, (g) an excommunicated person, (h) a person under a ban, (i) although they are prohibited from suing, they are rightly sued.

(a) See the beginning of the Institutes, on actions. The Anabaptists exhaust themselves here in vain in the controversy: whether it is permitted for a Christian to pursue his own right in court and to institute actions? For with the foundations of holy Scripture unmoved, they are convinced that this opinion of theirs is erroneous and false; Deuteronomy, chapter 17, verse 8 and following; Chronicles, chapter 19, verse 6; Exodus 18, verse 21; Proverbs 8, verse 16. (b) Law 3, Digest, on proofs; Law 5 and 6, Code, on being summoned. Although in a general appellation, the defendant and sometimes the plaintiff are contained, as is evident from the whole title of the Institutes on two defendants. Whence Cicero, book 2, On the Orator: "I call defendants," he says, "not only those who are accused, but all those concerning whose matter it is being disputed." And Gallus Aelius in Festus: "A defendant," he says, "is one who has a contested lawsuit with another, whether he sued or it was sued against him; however, in law, if it is in doubt who is the plaintiff and who the defendant, for example, if both provoke, the matter must be decided by lot," Law 14, of this title. (c) Law 1, Law "Final", on who has legitimate standing, Law 51, Digest, on procurators. (d) The whole title on curators of a madman or prodigal, Law 3, Code, on restoration to the former state, Law 12, § final, Digest, on tutors and curators. (e) Law 13, Digest, if anyone under caution, Law 6 and following, Code, of this title, Law 3, § 8, Digest, on the <term>peculium</term> <gloss>private property/estate</gloss>. Even if he conducts himself as a free man, the doctors of laws rule by Law 5, Code, on laws (which, however, is otherwise in the case of a serv</translation>

<translation page="11">ant judge, who by common opinion was held to be free, Law 3, Digest, on the office of the Praetor; Law 2, Code, on sentence and interlocutory order) which also has a place even if the slave appeared after the litigation was contested, for even then the debtor is absolved, Law 44, paragraph 1, of this title. (f) Law 48, of this title. (g) Law "Final" in the end of the beginning, Code, on goods which to children. Exception: 1. an accusation of adultery, Law 6, paragraph 2; Law 37, on adultery. 2. If it is a matter of things of the <term>peculium castrense</term> <gloss>military private property</gloss> or similar, Law 4, of this title, for in this case a lawsuit can be moved even between the father himself and the son, the cited Law 4; see Law 2, on the Macedonian Senate-Consult. 3. If a son-under-power is sued by an action on a judgment, Law 3, paragraph 4, on minors. 4. If he wishes a testament to be accused as false, Law 5, paragraph 5, on those things which as unworthy. For in these cases, even against the will and without the consent of the father, the son-under-power will be able to stand in court. But if the son dies after the judgment is seized, the judgment is transferred to the father regarding the <term>peculium</term> and what has been turned to his account, Law 57 of this title. Also, the same must be said if he performed the office of procurator, for the action is transferred to the principal defendant, the cited Law 57, at the end of this title. (h) Chapter 40 and there Cujas, on the sentence of excommunication; chapter 2, chapter 5, where Cujas is, on exceptions. (i) Regarding the outlawry and ban of the Holy Roman Empire, on which see Geil, on public peace, book 2, chapter 12, numbers 1, 2, and 19.

## IX.

With the persons pertaining to the judgment known, there follows the matter, which comprises as well civil cases as criminal ones. (a) Cases, however, about which it has already been acted upon once, cannot be brought into court any longer. (b)

(a) Law 1, paragraph penultimate, Digest, on calumny, and above, thesis 2, letter b; even for the smallest things, paragraph 16, Institutes, on the division of things; Law 22, in the end of the beginning, Digest, on threatened damage; Law 1, paragraph 10, Digest, on conjunctions with emancipated children. Understand this, however, in such a way that it is permitted to institute civil actions concerning the smallest things, but not criminal or infamous ones, Law 6, where the Doctors are, Digest, on accusations; chapter penultimate and final, Cause 14, Question 14. Likewise, Callistratus divides the matter of judgments into four kinds in Law 5, Digest, on extraordinary cognition. "For," he says, "either it is agitated about honors or burdens being performed, or it is disputed about a pecuniary matter, or it is cognized about the reputation of someone, or it is inquired about a capital crime." (b) The whole title on the exception of a matter judged. Thus, neither future things come into court, Law 35, of this title, for what accrues after the judgment is begun (extrinsically, of course, and not cohering to the thing sought, Law 11, paragraph 4; Law 14, paragraph final; Law 25, in the beginning, Digest, on the exception of a matter judged).</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the legal roles of plaintiffs and defendants, the various conditions affecting their standing in court (such as age, status, and excommunication), and the nature of civil and criminal subject matter in legal disputes.</summary>
<keywords>litigants, plaintiff, defendant, judge, <term>peculium</term>, <term>peculium castrense</term>, civil law, criminal law, judicial office</keywords>

I am able, I create, I proclaim, I salute, and I wish for you to be considered as such by others, and to be greeted by this public and solemn proclamation. I give, concede, and attribute to you all those rights and comforts which have been attributed by our ancestors to the Masters of the Liberal Arts or of Philosophy, whether by laws or by honorable and praised custom. But so that everyone may know for certain that you have been lawfully and solemnly created, proclaimed, and saluted by me as Masters of the Liberal Arts or of Philosophy, and that the free power of speaking, debating, and teaching in public has been given, conceded, and attributed to you by me, I now order you to ascend into this public chair of Academic Doctors, sacred to Phoebus and the Muses.

<note>A horizontal decorative divider band consisting of repeating geometric and floral patterns with small circles.</note>

Now (most distinguished listeners), it remains for me to carry out certain solemn rites and ceremonies, which our ancestors wisely devised to more augustly adorn the creation of Philosophical Masters, and which they desired to be diligently observed by their descendants.

### Therefore,

1. I place the cap upon your heads (most distinguished Lord Masters), the sign of liberal freedom.
2. I place upon your fingers a gold ring, the proof of true nobility.
3. Furthermore, I present open books to you, so that you may know that you must read and learn assiduously what you yourselves feel is still lacking in you. I place them before you closed as well, so that you may understand that one should not always cling to books and written pages, but that the memory should be exercised in such a way that, if the situation and necessity require it, you may speak about the proposed subjects from memory, and from the dignity of your Mastership, without hesitation.</translation>

<translation page="20">
4. I also add a kiss and an embrace, which signify paternal love, by the impulse of which we kiss and embrace you as our sweetest children. We hope that (as much as it is within you), being reminded by the perpetual monuments of these solemn rites and ceremonies, you will never say or do anything that is unworthy of liberal, noble, and wise men, or of the honor you have attained, or of the Philosophical order.

Since, by the singular favor of the divine power, I have now duly and happily performed what seemed necessary to be carried out according to the custom of our ancestors in this solemn promotion of Philosophical Masters, only this one thing remains (most distinguished Lord Masters): that one of you, in your name and in ours, should return due thanks with a grateful heart to God, the Best and Greatest, for the happy success of these matters which He has granted us. Likewise, you should offer thanks to the Most Serene Prince and our Most Clement Lord for so many and such great benefits with which he heroically adorns this, his Academy; and furthermore, to this most honorable and noble crown of listeners, who have not been burdened to honor our scholastic act with their most pleasant presence.

most excellent in both birth and piety, crowns the eleven thousand virgins in a dense column. There you will see URSULA, surrounded by a phalanx of the innocent, revealing the secrets of her soul to her companions, inflaming the minds of all with the fire of divine charity, exhorting them to defend the garland of white virginity, to endure the weariness of pilgrimage, to bear the vicissitudes of an inconstant life, and to meet death bravely for the defense of the faith. You will hear there the entire host applauding the plans of their leader with joyous murmurs; you will see them, as they say, with sails and oars following URSULA’s judgment, and animated by a new Spirit, all with one heart and the same will, dedicating their lives and blood to Christ the Spouse. You will watch them at the nod and command of their most prudent Captain as their ships recede far from the shore, rowing with a favorable wind for the space of a single day and night, first to be borne into Germany, then, by the warning of an Angel, to hasten to Rome to visit the thresholds of the Apostles, and finally, having fulfilled their duties of piety, to flow down again into Alemannia along the inclined bed of the Rhine, and to fix their happy station at Cologne, to attain the end of their vows and to amplify the glory and sanctity of that German city. You could by no means have expected lesser deeds or slower movements from this Virgin fleet, Academic Scholars, since its *Soul* is the extraordinary entire cohort, and its leader is *URSULA*, who achieved such great things.

But while the Virgins appear to be holding the harbor after overcoming the waves of the Rhine, they are seen to have entered another, more tempestuous sea of cruelty. At that time, a vast army of barbarians was encircling and besieging the walls of Cologne with tight blockade, threatening the city and its inhabitants with all extremes. After the provinces of Gaul and Germany had been overturned, after the temples of the eternal Divinity had been pillaged, after the altars of the heavenly ones had been stripped of gold and silver, after the sacrosanct mysteries of Religion had been profaned by sacrilegious hands, after the images and statues of the Divine had been trampled by impious feet, after the ashes of the Saints had been recklessly scattered into the waters and the air, after the ministers of GOD had been tortured with monstrous torments, the wicked cruelty of the Gentiles prepared, with the same momentum and the same fury, to destroy the most ancient sanctity of the city of Cologne, to demolish the sacred trophies of faith, to exterminate the citizens with their walls, the faithful with their Temples, and the altars with their Priests. And as this cruelty plotted such nefarious crimes, the Christian army of most innocent Virgins, having disembarked from their ships, suddenly fell into their hands. What were your thoughts then, Cologne, spectator at this encounter between the Virgin and barbarian phalanxes; what were your feelings, what movements of your</translation>

<translation page="11">
spirits? Did you not fear that the weaker sex would succumb to the most ferocious race, that feminine frailty would yield to masculine strength, and Virgin gentleness to martial fury? Did you not fear the ruin of innocence, the destruction of Religion, a stain on modesty, the weakness of constancy, and the sacrilege of sworn Faith at the hands of impious and perverse Idolaters? And you, <term>Academic Scholars</term>, did you not suspect that the tender hearts of the Virgins were being softened by the blandishments of words for the desire of panders, or being tamed by the most dire bitterness of torments for the rage of executioners? Do you imagine that those unwarlike souls, brought into the open danger of life and caught in the midst of the attacks of a raging paganism, would retreat from their purpose, and that their hands, conquered by such cruelty, would be surrendered, and their bodies and minds enslaved to the greed of the enemy? Truly, that fear would have entered my mind together with yours, had not the virtue and fortitude of the leader URSULA, favored by the divine Spirit, animated the entire cohort of virgins. Fraudulent love had indeed deployed the serene graces of the brow, it had feigned pity, it had praised the beauty of the countenance, it had exaggerated the flower of youth, the most noble marriages, the most ample riches, the enticements of pleasure, the obedience of peoples, the embraces of Caesars, and the favors of immortal GODS: But in vain; they were not softened by blandishments, those who had been hardened by the sacred warnings of URSULA. Then, indeed, the truculent Fury gathered all his furies into his soul; he grew pale in countenance, he seethed in his veins, he foamed at the mouth, he gnashed his teeth, he threatened lightning with his eyes, thunder with his voice, and death with his hand: But to no avail; the fear of torments could not break what the unconquered magnanimity of URSULA had solidified. For what (the most valiant leader of the Virgin army asked) would either blandishments allure you, or torments terrify you? The former are honey, but mixed with gall; a sweet drink, but smeared with the poison of *Circe*; a serene little flame, but shimmering with a false fire. But these latter are thorns, but ones that will blossom into roses; they are tempests, but ones that will be followed by serenity; they are deaths, but ones that will be converted into eternal feasts. Thus far you have overcome the waves of the *Rhine* in a happy course, not to hold the harbor of *Cologne*, but so that through the poured-out waves of blood, you might lead new colonies to the gate of heaven. When you have been purpled by your own blood in the Virginity of the *White Ones* <note>Referring to the state of purity/martyrdom</note>, the *Spouse* will recognize you as worthy to be admitted, dressed in nuptial robes, to the solemn banquet of eternity. The *Supreme Emperor* will praise your faith, glorious warriors, if you are not content to have affirmed it with a Sacrament, but seal it with war, wounds, and death. Raise up your spirits, therefore; oppose fortitude to wrath, Constancy to fury, and the greatness of your breast to the</translation>

<keywords>Saint Ursula, Cologne, Virginity, Martyrdom, Faith, Constancy, Christian Virtue</keywords>

<header>OF THE ROMAN EMPIRE.</header>
<sig>B 3</sig>

Furthermore, Cicero called the Sun Phoebus and Apollo, the leader and prince of all other lights, the moderator, the center of all planets, the mind of the world, the light of life, and the god of wisdom. We are aware that these titles are, in a certain sense, appropriate for you, the Emperor. It is fitting that you, who are first and supreme in majesty, should act as the arbiter and moderator of other kings, and as the light of life and the deity of wisdom. Because it is fitting, we hope you will act with the highest wisdom. You will survey and illuminate all lands, all regions, and the Christian world, for you are Helius <note>Greek for Sun</note>, you are the Sun. Having now risen, you will clear away the mists of war wherever they exist, as we trust; and by consuming every harm of weaponry with your most auspicious heat, you will bring forth renewal, just as Phoebus once loved this Daphne, or the Laurel. And indeed, Helius Hadrian acted as Helius and the Sun, wandering through the Roman world, sailing the Ocean, the Rhine, the Danube, the Euxine <note>Black Sea</note>, and later far-distant rivers—the Nile, the Phasis, the Pactolus, and the Euphrates. He surveyed all the boundaries of the entire Empire and, having consumed the vapors of war rising on all sides, he rendered the world secure against every flood of encroaching barbarians through the effective and most powerful rays of his Majesty. You act as that same Helius Hadrian, the fourteenth from the divine Julius, you the fourteenth</translation>

<translation page="14">
<header>PLAUSUS</header>

and fourth of the august House from Rudolph I, **LEOPOLD**, and we, your most devoted subjects, pray that you may continue to act so that, through the eclipse of the Turkish Moon, you may happily penetrate to the Sun of the Persians, restore Jerusalem under still better auspices, and then, in the highest peace, submit your Imperial rods to Wisdom, listen to the philosophical Favorini, and cherish the Epicteti <note>referring to philosophers like Favorinus and Epictetus</note>. May the heavenly patrons grant this to you, most Sacred **LEOPOLD**, and add this: that, being most happy and the first in so many names and omens—Vladislaus, Rudolph, Charles, Alexander, Helius Hadrian, Julius, Augustus—you exhibit in your own person the many great honors of these Caesars and Kings, as well as those of your own august House, who filled the earth with clemency and the heavens with piety. Presenting the lamb alongside the lion, and linking gentleness with fortitude, after the fashion of your most Serene Uncle *LEOPOLD WILLIAM*, a man of absolute virtue in every respect, you are great not through another, but through yourself. You are the light of life, the Sun of the Empire, the Head of the World, the Ornament of the Globe, and Majesty in that Flower, and the Flower in that Majesty; intermediate between Wisdom and Justice, Clemency and Fortune, may you bring forth a welcome eternity.

->THE END.<-</translation>

# S I L V A.

*Luxuriousness, scorning to set a limit on delights,*
*Rages at its own ruin: Ambition plunders or buys the fasces <note>the rods and axes representing Roman magisterial authority</note>: Audacity, having poured itself into the steep descent, is carried away:*
*Crime stands with Law prostrate, and Envy is gloomy at successes,*
*And Anger swells with untamed surges.*
*Horrible Furies stand by, and with twisted snakes*
*They whip and burn the hearts with Stygian torches:*
*Neither in darkness nor in light is there rest: thus a conscious horror*
*Agitates the mind with a lash that never spares.*
*This also must be learned: what turn the reins of power*
*Should take, and by what supports authority is to be strengthened,*
*Whether one hand holds the scepter, consecrated and close to God,*
*Possessing such kings as your France once had,*
*Since the Seine began to venerate the long-haired Cauchi <note>an ancient Germanic tribe</note>:*
*Or whether the Senate displays the Fathers as masters of affairs,*
*Which is the custom for the city enclosed by the Adriatic waves,*
*And for our own Dutch <note>original: "Batavis"</note> (and may it remain so through the ages):*
*(O fatherland, O great ruler of the vast deep,*
*Recognize your citizen), or whether all obey all,*
*A system of government such as the Alps see within their walls.*
*Moreover, the wise paper of the ancients will teach you*
*What stirs up peace among peoples, which waves to break,*
*To which it is better to yield, what diseases time may heal,*
*And on the contrary, how evils are accustomed to swell from small causes.*
*Selected reading will give you these uses, written in whatever age in Latin*
*Or even in Greek annals.*
*But you, especially, should be mindful to leaf through your father’s papers.*
*He alone restored the interrupted honors and the long-*
*Lost praises to our own centuries.*
*Free simplicity shines forth in every part,*
*And faith uncorrupted by studies: industry, anxious for the truth,*
*Runs through the whole world and through a hundred years.*
*Rejoice, posterity. There is no witness more certain than he*
*Who teaches, himself unmoved by his own disasters while an exile.*
*The forces of the Greeks turned into mutual wounds,*
*And he who subdues the fierce Jugurtha with Marius conquering,*
*And he by whose student the land of the Antenoridae <note>the Venetians</note> boasts,*
*Or he who notes the obscene rocks of Capri, and more*
*Infamous Seneca than Nero who killed his mother.*
*Yet behold these books, where the weights of affairs contend</translation>

<translation page="10">

*And the brilliance of discourse (what barbaric times*
*See us now?) which envy has dared to sprinkle with degenerate poison:*
*Does anyone still endure to hang his life upon writings*
*And hope for a reward for such great labor?*
*Hoary Themis <note>goddess of divine law</note> will soon open her sanctuaries to you*
*Once you have traversed this path: you will see what decrees, founded by stern Lycurgus,*
*Made a city safe without walls,*
*What laws Solon softened, what the care of the Quirites <note>the Roman citizens</note> added*
*To the twelve tables, and what he scattered throughout the whole world,*
*What the school of Proculus objects to Sabinus,*
*In what ways France might amend Roman laws.*
*Join divine oracles to human arts:*
*Your father did this too, whose poem recounts the punishments*
*Of the heavenly fugitive <note>Lucifer</note> of the wicked kingdom,*
*Just as Prometheus, sighing on the Caucasian rock,*
*Moved the Cecropian <note>Athenian</note> theater with a pitiable sight.*
*By that poet, the citizen of Idumea <note>Job</note>, unconquered by evils,*
*To whom his house was plundered and in whose whole body there was no*
*Body, earned the related rewards of the palm:*
*And Jonah, coming from the vast maw of the sea-monster,*
*Healed the peoples by frightening Assyria.*
*Following that example, let the page release the frequent*
*Sacred hand for you: it lies open to the pious. But more often*
*Turn your eyes back from our years to the ancient ages,*
*When religion, rude and simple, had not yet made itself an art:*
*When thunderous Mars and the dire desire for the scepter*
*Did not yet have the title of piety:*
*When a brief rule dictated this whole thing by which a better life is prepared,*
*Known not only to masters,*
*But as the common good of the people: nor did learned*
*Disputes bring discord, but they contended by loving:*
*In all, the same ardor to defend the truth, so much so*
*By one's own death, and no use of another's blood.*
*When the age has now progressed through these cares,*
*It will not flow further in private. With the Senate rejoicing,*
*You will take up the purple robes. Pious laws and laws oppressed by evil*
*Morals will rise with you as judge:*
*And through degrees you will come to the height of honor,*
*Where father and great-grandfather, or, what stands more sublime,*
*Where your grandfather ascended, and Achilles second to none</translation>

XXXIX. Pleurisy that strikes a <term>cachectic</term> <gloss>wasted or diseased</gloss> body, or one that follows a chronic illness, is usually lethal.

XL. A relapse in pleurisy, for the most part, tends toward death.

<margin>Treatment.</margin>
XLI. The last thing we undertake to discuss in our present dissertation is the **TREATMENT** of pleurisy. This must be established according to a threefold indication—namely, the preventative, the curative, and the vital—so that the humors causing trouble by their motion may be drawn back and diverted (on account of the nearby heart, one should refrain here from using repellents and interceptors); those abundant in quantity must be diminished and evacuated; those excessive in quality must be altered; and the humor that has already flowed in must be dispersed, or if that is not possible, matured and concocted so that it may be rejected by coughing as soon as possible; and finally, so that the strength and vigor of the parts may be conserved. All and each of these things must be satisfied through remedies drawn from surgery, pharmacy, and diet.

<margin>SURGERY. Venesection.</margin>
XLII. <translation page="22">
Thus, after the clouds, Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> reveals the desired light:
    Thus, when evils are driven away, joys return, turned around.
Therefore, I congratulate you on these honors which you now enjoy,
    O Leonhart, loved by me in the place of a brother:
May they be happy for you, may they be the goal of your heavy labors,
    May they be ample hope for your own, may they be a medicine for your FATHER:
Who, bringing back the sacred oracles of the divine mind,
    Has a name of no light weight due to the merits of his intellect:
Where the swift Cassius, who flows through the green fields of Elysium,
    Wanders near the HEGIDMATIAM <note>likely a reference to the region around the Oder/Heide area near Legnica</note> soil.
By pressing on in his virtue, may you continue to multiply
    Your own exceptional honor with fitting praise.
If anything heavy remains besides, CONQUER BY ENDURING:
    He conquers twice who can bear his lot well.

# OF THE SAME ARGUMENT
->A poem, written<-
->by<-
### JOHANNES FRIDERICUS
->of Legnica, student<-

Whoever first dedicated his camp to the sacred Muses,
    He was truly a wise man (believe me).
Since he saw that exceptional honor is prepared
    In a similar way for both Mars <note>god of war</note> and the Pierides <note>the Muses</note>.
He who desires to enjoy the sought-after honor of praise
    Has endured many rough things, has sweated much, and has shivered.
</translation>

<translation page="23">
The lover of Mars is compelled to endure the rapid heat of summer,
    And to suffer the harsh cold of winter.
Neither the wandering battles of the swollen wind,
    Nor the ferocious madness of the South Wind will impede him.
The unfeigned lover of the sacred Muses
    Also undergoes many things, things scarcely to be endured by the few.
Both endure much, neither ever rests:
    The latter guards the doors of the Muse, but the former, those of the leader.
The latter besets heavy cities, the former the learned thresholds of the Wise:
    The latter moves the mind, but the former moves the body.
The latter considers for himself the fervent struggles of rigid Mars,
    But the former thinks it shameful to have deserted the Muses.
Nor does the labor and constancy of this man lack some gift,
    But the victor has his own rewards for his merits.
The victor has rewards, signs of a lively glory,
    Flowering garlands from the soft leaves of the laurel.
Truly, just as the laurel is never without leaf:
    So also does praise and honor remain for the victor, perennial.
Therefore, after various labors, sweet Leonhart,
    Behold, take the rewards that are given to you, victor.
See how Weariness, defeated, follows your triumphal chariots,
    And Labor, with downcast eyes.
See how much Glory promises you, she who goes before the chariot,
    And tosses her joyful head toward the stars.
Continue to follow the splendid footsteps of your famous Father,
    Of whose name the earth resounds in many places.
</translation>

<summary>This Latin elegiac sequence celebrates Leonhart Krentzheim's academic success by comparing the hardships of the scholar to those of the soldier, ultimately crowning him with the laurel of victory and urging him to emulate his father's reputation.</summary>
<keywords>Leonhart Krentzheim, academic achievement, Muses, Mars, laurel, victory, Latin elegy, Johannes Fridericus</keywords>

O God, bless and grant peace to our master Muhammad, and to his family and companions, all of them. A blessing and peace that secures for us Your satisfaction, and for Your presence, and by his creation, my performance. Suns have perfected themselves in the hearts of my station, and I have spoken while standing upon their feet. I followed his path, and it showed me the magnitude of my condition; my waist-wrapper has been watered. My grandfather, Sayyid Ahmad the Great, he who has no master, is the <term>aqtab</term> <gloss>poles/pinnacles of spiritual hierarchy</gloss> and the saints. My grandfather is my servant. My grandfather is the Messenger of God; I have sufficed them with my sleeping. My portion and my peace, or Zaydi, and an heir to the darkness of the heavy affliction has fallen, and likewise...

<column-break/>

And likewise Umm Zaydi and all my servants. And likewise, my Lord, the reckoning is with the <term>qutb</term> <gloss>spiritual pole</gloss> of our estimation. And regarding the story of my mother, the worst of what I have is an <term>izara</term> <gloss>loincloth/shroud</gloss>. He who possesses pride, the helper king comes to me, Sayyid Ahmad, the people of the lineage. And after my completion, I return if I am sufficient for my secret in every dead one. He said, "O dead one, have mercy through your power, the speech of my feet." So the Lord of men, God, is with them all; I am the master of the masters of the heights. The master of men, the <term>ghawth</term> <gloss>helper/arch-saint</gloss>, I have chosen him from my Lord to raise me up gently on this day, with all my floods. Do not break my covenant, for Ya'qub is for you, my Lord, gently on this day, for the intelligence of the <term>murid</term> <gloss>spiritual seeker</gloss> is his journey in my need. If a reprisal occurs regarding them, my year, the Lord has given me by them gentleness and companionship. And each of them is a support for my aim, vast and knowing on the earth entirely, that a sheikh came from them and raised my station.

O God, bless and grant peace to our master Muhammad, and to his family and companions all together, with a prayer and peace that enables us to attain Your pleasure. And for the Presence <note>referring to the Divine Presence</note>, and by his creation, my performance reached the suns in my heart's station. I spoke at the feet that have precedence for me, and I walked in his path, to let it be seen from the greatness of my state; my belt has been tightened. My grandfather, Sayyid Ahmad the Great <note>referring to Ahmad al-Rifa'i</note>, to whom the poles <term>aqtab</term> <gloss>the highest-ranking saints</gloss> and the saints <term>awliya</term> <gloss>friends of God</gloss> have no master. My grandfather serves me, my grandfather, the Messenger of God; I have sufficed through them with my remaining. A portion and my peace, or Zaydi, and the inheritor, the darkness of the obstacle occurred, and likewise.

<column-break/>

And likewise, Umm Zaydi, and all who serve me, and likewise, O master of my Lord, the reckoning. By the pole, that he narrated the predestination, and about the story of my mother, the evil of what is in me is a heavy burden. Possessor of pride, the Helper <term>al-ghawth</term> <gloss>the supreme intercessor/saint</gloss> comes to me, the master Ahmad of the people of high lineage. And after that, my perfection, I am an intermediary if my secret is sufficient in every deceased person; he said: "A deceased person, show mercy with your strength, the words of my feet." So the Lord of men, God, through them all, I am the master of the masters of the elevated. So the master of men, the Helper, I chose him from my Lord to nurture me, gently. On this day, all of them are overwhelming. Do not break my covenant, for Ya'qub is for you, my Lord, gently on this day, that his intelligence is in the hearts of the disciple <term>murid</term> <gloss>a student on the Sufi path</gloss>, his journey in my need, if retribution occurs from them, my year. My Lord gave me, through them, gentleness and companionship, and every one of them I entrust with my goal. Spacious and Knowing upon the earth, all of it, that a Sheikh came from them, he raises my station.

<translation page="13">
*Digest, On Penalties: No one suffers punishment for their thoughts:* Ulpian, the author of the law, a man of the highest talent, opposes his own authority in law to Justinian in *l. 1, § 9, Code On the Repeal of Escheats*, to Valerian in *l. 9, Code On Institutions and Substitutions*, to Diocletian in *l. 11, Code On Questions*, and as a friend to the Emperor Alexander in *l. 4, Code On Contracting Stipulations*. Indeed, what is more, the most Sacred Legislator Justinian himself, who made his own the responses of the Jurisconsults <note>the Roman legal scholars</note> reported in the Pandects through the elucidators of ancient jurisprudence—whom he praises in *§ 3 and following, Institutes, in the proem; l. 2, § 3, Code On the Elucidation of Ancient Law*—filled whatever was imperfect in their minds in *said l. 2, § 10, l. 1, § 7, Code of the same*. This was done regarding *said l. 18*, and therefore it is to be judged not so much based on Ulpian’s intent regarding the edict of what is prohibited by law, as rather based on the broader sense of the Emperor and the Canons that followed his sense in *c. 14, On Penance, dist. 1*. The very acute Bachovius rightly judges this against Cujacius in his notes to *Treutl., vol. 2, Disp. 32, th. 1, lit. G, at the word Attempt*.

->VII.<-

Proceed then: how does anyone suffer punishment for thought while preserving the majesty of the Law? The opinion of those who distinguish between a merely naked will and an attempt does not please me; the latter, while also naked, bears the appearance of a will clothed in some way by the excessive uncovering of itself through the act into which it erupts, thus exempting the former from legal punishment while subjecting the latter to it always and entirely. Both are clearly contrary to the laws, through which

<column-break/>

and attempts sometimes enjoy impunity, and a will that has not exited the mind is accustomed to being harshly punished. Therefore, more correctly and conveniently for the Law, we understand by a thought that is impatient of our Forum or of Civil punishment that which (to use the Imperial words from law 2, Code On Credit Matters) has God sufficiently as its avenger. Such is that internal <term>ἀταξία</term> <gloss>disorder/lack of order</gloss> of the mind, which the Church does not judge in chapter 34, Extra, On Simony. But it leaves it to be judged by God in chapter 20, cause 2, question 4. For the wish of a disobedient mind is not sufficient in the forum of the court for a penalty:

> How I would wish, if it were permitted. Let subjects hate, provided they fear; let them hate to sin; whether it is from the fear of punishment or the love of virtue matters little to the Republic, which values a good citizen without considering the title of a good man, except incidentally and presumptively.

It is the property of Divine law to annex the prohibition of concupiscence to the precept of external obedience, as if it were punishable by itself alone. Civil reason does not scrutinize the simulator and the hypocrite, nor does it presume an evil thought in a good action; but it entrusts its judgment to another Forum, where crimes are taxed in a manner greater than ours.</translation>

<translation page="14">
<note>A small symbol appears in the margin.</note> And this is the other way by which we reconcile the challenged law 18 with our opinion. Namely, the Civil Judge does not regard thoughts to be punished in the same way that God does. For the law does not order a penalty for this one on account of <term>ἀνομία</term> <gloss>lawlessness/sin</gloss> or viciousness alone without any regard for the harm that arises from it either to private persons or to the Republic. Rather, it is necessary that either present harm or at least the fear of it in more serious crimes intervenes, so that the thought might cease to have God alone as its avenger for having wished to do evil, and so that it might expect not only heavenly but also legitimate punishments.

<insert>anon 38</insert>
</translation>

<summary>The text discusses the legal interpretation of "thoughts" versus "acts," arguing that civil law only punishes internal thoughts when they result in public or private harm, whereas divine law addresses the internal state of the mind. It critiques previous legal scholars who attempted to distinguish between "naked will" and "attempts," asserting instead that the civil forum relies on the presence of harm to trigger legal consequences.</summary>
<keywords>legal philosophy, Justinian, civil law, thoughts, criminal intent, attempts, divine law, forum, harm</keywords>

<translation page="19">...reinforced with iron, costs twenty <term>English Shillings</term> <gloss>or one Pound Sterling</gloss>.

To these, other benefits can be added, which concern both increasing profits and preventing losses in ports and during voyages. But the honorable Mr. <term>Robert Fitzgerald</term> has already made mention of all these things quite aptly in his recently published booklet.

Finally, something must be said concerning the other, and indeed most highly estimable, benefit of this water: the preservation of the sailors' health.

Without a doubt, <term>Thames water</term> <gloss>the water of the River Thames</gloss>, when not confined in vessels for too long, is useful enough for drinking. And usually, though not always, it is the sailors' care to choose the most opportune time for drawing water (which is mid-ebb tide) and also the location, such that during greater tides, they sometimes go upstream beyond <term>London</term> Bridge, even as far as <term>Chelsea</term>, to draw water. Let us grant, furthermore, that this <term>Thames water</term>, even if it ferments on a longer voyage to the point of foul odor, cleanses itself of its own accord and returns to its pristine state, and does not putrefy in all casks at once and at the same time.

Nevertheless, who is so lacking in sense that they would prefer to drink water that is not safe from defects in every respect, rather than pure water from a source if it were available to them, or water equally laudable—indeed, much better—provided it be true what</translation>

<translation page="20">some report: that many <term>Fontana waters</term> <gloss>spring waters</gloss> ferment somewhat on longer voyages.

Certainly, nothing can be more pleasant for a ship's captain than an abundance of the best water, whether for diluting wine or for other uses, always at the ready. And as often as sailors contribute their share to prepare a cup of <term>oenoxycrat</term> <gloss>a mixture of wine and water</gloss>, they hold it as a rule that pure water is to be valued no less than that burning spirit which they commonly call <term>Brandy</term>.

The sailors themselves will perhaps abstain from <term>Thames water</term> as long as it is stirred in the highest degree of fermentation; although, when it has not yet fully cooled down, it is reasonable to believe that it tastes palatable enough to them. For since they live in thick and humid air, and have a tongue that is perpetually as if scorched from salted foods, it is not to be thought that they enjoy an exquisite sense of taste or smell. Therefore, although perfectly sweet water is not required to gratify the sailors' senses, I judge that they can rarely drink a liquid not entirely free from the motion of fermentation, even for a few days, without harm. Indeed, I have no doubt that they have often been endangered by burning fevers, which they call <term>calentures</term> <gloss>tropical fevers</gloss>, and others that have arisen from there, or at least have been exacerbated by them; especially in the vicinity of the <term>Equator</term>, where sailors are more prone to fevers and the water is excited into maximum fermentation. To promote which, <term>Thames water</term>, however simple it may appear, provides no meager fuel.</translation>

The first of these is that the citizens, who are under his rule, should be of a humble, servile, and abject spirit, for these will dare to attempt nothing great. The second is that they should not trust one another, but distrust each other through mutual suspicions and contentions; for on this account he also holds good men to be especially hateful, because they keep faith with one another and do not easily betray one another. The third is that they should be deprived of the ability to carry out affairs; for thus, lacking strength, they will not be capable of rising against the Tyrant. And to these points, enumerated from Aristotle, the ten institutes of the Tyrant, reviewed in <term>Bartolus</term>’ <gloss>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a famous jurist</gloss> treatise on Tyranny, are reduced without labor, and indeed are taken from them, as will appear from comparison.

13. Regarding the second mode, and the sophistical one of preserving tyranny, it looks in general to this: to feign that he is a King and to simulate royal rule, yet preserving power over those who are not only willing but also unwilling.
pages.12:
to be ruled. For just as a Kingdom is most destroyed if a King rules too tyrannically, so a Tyranny is most stabilized if it appears to conform to royal rule. Special sophisms and stratagems for this matter are: I. That the Tyrant appear to have the utmost care for the common good, and to show himself not as the master, but as the dispenser and administrator of the public treasury, taxes, and tributes. Hence (1.) he should not expend great costs on prostitutes, banquets, foreigners, bodyguards, artisans, buffoons, flatterers, horses, dogs, etc., lest the subjects become angry and turn to rage when they see money, extracted from them—burdened by labors and living sparingly and meagerly—so lavishly spent on trivial matters of no use. (2.) He should also render accounts of expenses and receipts. (3.) Nor should he fear that he will ever be destitute of wealth, so as to scrape together many riches for that reason: for since the judgment of the whole state is in his hands, it will be easy to acquire money at any time; indeed, it does not benefit a Tyrant at all to accumulate excessive wealth, since he must sometimes be away from home and involved in wars, where it will be to be feared that the guards and caretakers left at home, having stirred up sedition, might seize the Tyrant's property. (4.) When demanding tributes and services from the citizens, he should claim the utmost necessity, both for conserving the economy and for meeting military expenses. In sum, he should conduct himself like a good father of a family, thrifty and diligent, and as a guardian and steward of goods as if they were public and common, not as if they were his own.

14. II. The stratagem is: Not to be austere, morose, savage, and difficult, but to show forth royal gentleness and humanity in countenance, speech, and gestures, so that those who converse or associate with the Tyrant do not tremble and shudder, but rather respect and venerate him, using this moderation so that the Tyrant does not incur the contempt and vilification of his subjects. <translation page="42">
<header>Heroic Poem</header>

The magnanimous man, with great virtue he laid low the Men,
who were waging hostile wars against the Empire:
Above him approaches the hero most learned in speaking,
that Father of yours, FREDERICK, O CHARLES <note>referring to the addressees or figures in the poem's dedication</note>, excellent one,
whom RUDOLPH, not the least fame of the Austrian Kingdom,
sends as Legate to the shores of the Roman FATHER.

O therefore, since so many are related to you by blood,
all of them outstanding in war or in virtues;
if you wish to fly through the mouths of many men,
proceed to follow the examples of these, nor will it repent you to have willed it;
Since because the fates move things, nor does the judgment fail me,
most beautiful ROME will one day see you,
brought among the purple-clad Princes and the sacred Senate.

<note>A decorative initial 'O' features floral motifs.</note>

O excellent ornament of the whole world on its shores,
and at the same time a great hope of the Faith, is the Martial land
which the Swabians and Raetians inhabit; because this most famous land
brings forth so many heroes of powerful Virtue,
as there are stars shining in the star-bearing heaven,
and fish in the sea, and as many as the shores keep grains of sand,
so that it may bring back the just palm and bear away praise,
SWABIA, among the rest, a race unconquered in war:
For even if I should pass over the examples of many men
whom it has produced, let one present to me, from the thousands,
be the Father of OTTO, LODOVICUS, whose fame
flies in the world, because while the harsh wars of the Kingdom were raging
under Emperor CHARLES, than whom no other was more outstanding,
the leader willed to exchange his fortunes and his very life for honor,
and to compose peace through a just war.

<summary>The poem continues by praising the military and political legacy of the Swabian region and the virtuous deeds of historical figures like Lodovicus, encouraging the current noble subjects to emulate their ancestors.</summary>
<keywords>Frederick, Charles, Rudolph, Rome, Swabia, Lodovicus, Otto, nobility, military virtue</keywords>
</translation>

thousands of men bear witness that it has been revealed to them for the eternal honor of God; and they freely preach the Father in the light of Him, just as He is in the light, obtaining communion with the Father and the Son and with one another. For this reason, immortal thanks are owed and rendered to God, world without end.

### A Testimony consonant with the Scriptures; but most contrary to Persecution for the sake of Religion. Or, Counsel concerning the abrogation of laws that constrain the tender Conscience, the Prerogative of God.

Haman wished to root out the Jews because their religious worship seemed contrary to King Ahasuerus; he said to the King that it was not in his interest that they should live. But he was removed from the midst, for it seemed otherwise to the King, who permitted them life and liberty because he clearly saw that it redounded to his own interest.

Christ, when those who wished to call down fire from Heaven to destroy those who would not receive Christ were rebuked, said: You do not know of what Spirit you are. Have those, then, who from the days of the Apostles have been intent on killing men for the sake of religion, understood of what spirit they were? They have not indeed prayed for fire from Heaven to destroy others, but they have taken care to build the very pyres on Earth for that same purpose. Are not these, therefore, who perpetrate such things, deserving of greater rebuke and more blind in their souls than those who strove to call down fire from Heaven to burn those who would not receive Christ?

We read indeed that Christ, with a whip made of cords, cast the buyers and sellers out of the Temple of God; (a) but we never read that anyone was driven by Him with whips to enter it.

Christ also said: Let the tares and the wheat grow together until the harvest, which is the end of the world, lest the wheat be uprooted; and at the end of the world, Christ will send forth His angels, the reapers. (b) But the angels destined for this office are spirits, and not men, who now dare to arrogate such a thing to themselves.

Christ ordered Peter to put his sword back into its sheath, adding: all who have used the sword shall perish by the sword. (c) Did Peter or any of the Apostles afterwards use a drawn carnal sword or carnal weapons with which to defend the Church of Christ, religious worship, or the faith? On the contrary, Peter, by the command of Christ, sheathed his sword, and Christ healed the ear of the high priest's servant that had been cut off, which is a most manifest indication that the Gospel of Christ does not contain the nature of destroying, but of healing. If this had been the mind of the Apostle, why did he not submit himself to the religion of the Jews and of the Roman Emperor Caesar, and also to that of the Ephesian Diana? From rubbing, she demands eye-salve <note>original: "collyria"</note> after checking her <term>genesis</term> <gloss>horoscope</gloss>.
Though she may lie ill, no hour seems more suitable
For taking food, unless one that <term>Petosiris</term> <gloss>an Egyptian astrologer</gloss> has assigned.
If she is of the middle class, she will pace through both
Of the turning posts, and will draw lots, and will offer her
Forehead and hand to the prophet, who keeps asking with frequent smacking of lips.
To the wealthy, the <term>Phrygian augur</term> will give responses, and from there,
Hired, the one skilled in the stars and the world will give them.
And some elder, who performs public lightning-divinations.
It is the lot of the commoner in the circus, and on the embankment.
She who displays long gold on her bare neck,
Consults the <term>Phalas</term> <gloss>Phallic images</gloss> and the columns of the dolphins
Before the races, whether she should marry the seller, leaving the innkeeper,
Yet these women also undergo the danger of childbirth, and endure all
The labors of a nurse, when fortune presses.
But hardly any woman who has just given birth lies in a gilded bed.
So great are the arts of this woman, so great are the medicines she possesses,
Which makes women sterile, and arranges for humans to be killed
Inside the womb. Rejoice, unhappy woman, and you yourself

And irritate the womb with leaping children, you might
