the endowed daughter of the late Reinken Wittemeyer / widow of the late Johann Schlensecker / having left behind temporal goods after her death / to be divided among the nearest relatives <term>ex linea collaterali</term> <gloss>from the collateral line</gloss> <term>in stirpes</term> <gloss>by branch/lineage</gloss> / and therefore the Defendant is obligated / to hand over and restore to the Plaintiffs the hereditary shares due to them from both inheritances <term>cum fructibus perceptis</term> <gloss>with the fruits/profits already received</gloss> / just as we hereby recognize such a division in the aforementioned manner / and impose restitution upon the Defendant. (12.) <term>Bona adventitia</term> <gloss>acquired assets</gloss>, namely those that have come to children from elsewhere than from the ancestor to whom they are succeeding, are not brought into collation by children succeeding a father; but those succeeding a mother do not bring into collation <term>profectitia</term> <gloss>assets derived from the ancestor</gloss> specifically so-called, nor those <term>adventitia</term> <gloss>acquired assets</gloss> that did not come from the mother but from elsewhere, such as from the son’s own labor. Law 6, Code, on goods which children in power [possess], and the Doctors there. Struvius, *Exercitationes* XXXVII, thesis 32 and the following thesis 33, where he notes two precautions for the succeeding son: that if a son has acquired something from the property of an ancestor and his own workmanship, he is bound to bring this into collation in proportion to the property derived from the ancestor, and partly not to bring it into collation according to the proportion of the skill or labor added by the son, or, if it seems more beneficial to him, he may request a preference from the co-heir brothers in place of a salary; see also Coppen, decision 49. (13.) Neither legacies and trusts left by a father, nor a donation <term>mortis causa</term> <gloss>in contemplation of death</gloss> are subject to collation and division. Struvius, in the mentioned *Exercitationes*, thesis 34. (14.) Nor those things which the deceased owed to the heir, Law 20, paragraph 1, Digest, on the action for partition of an inheritance. (15.) Likewise, major fiefs, having an annexed dignity, such as Electorates, Duchies, Marquisates, Counties, and Baronies, are indivisible; Golden Bull of Charles V, Title 24; see Law of Fiefs 13, at the end, on the alienation of fiefs; Andreas Iserniensis on the use of fiefs, at the said chapter, number 7; Rosenthal on fiefs, chapter 2, conclusion 82. And although in some families they permit division by contrary custom: nevertheless, the division of such fiefs having an annexed royal dignity is rightly abrogated by the head of the family. (16.) Moreover, by Saxon and Minden law, neither sons are bound to bring into collation expeditionary items, nor daughters their <term>gerada</term> <gloss>paraphernalia/dowry items</gloss>, because the <term>gerada</term></translation>

<translation page="18">
<note>Floral and scrolled printer's ornaments flank the page number 18.</note>

and items of expedition are not transferred by hereditary right, as to an heir, but rather to the family by reason of the right of kinship and respectively agnation, as acquired gain. *Matthaeus Coler, page 1, decision 12, number 58. Crusius on article 7, Minden Statutory Law, Title on expeditionary and household items.*

### TH. XI.

<margin>To be removed.</margin>
Indeed, all the Doctors contend that bad medicines and poisons are clearly to be removed, according to Law 4, § 1, Digest, on the action for partition of an inheritance, with which I agree, unless an apothecary’s shop comes into this judgment and the estimation of this is at issue, for there, poisons are kept for a good use; see Law 236, on the Meaning of Words. But books of disapproved reading, perhaps magical or similar ones, are to be clearly burned, and indeed under penalty of confiscation of goods, so that they may not be possessed, read, or transcribed by anyone hereafter, according to the said Law 4, § 1, Digest, on the action for partition of an inheritance, and Law 6, Code, on Heretics and Manichaeans. Because he who knows, but can prevent, is not free from blame; argument of Law 50, Digest, on Rules of Law, and this tolerance or at least negligence is counted among the ways of participating in the sins of others, which are contained in these verses:

->Ordering, Counsel, Consent, flattery, recourse.<-
->Participating, silent, not obstructing, not manifesting.<-

Similarly, things which the deceased acquired from embezzlement or sacrilege, or which came to him by violence, robbery, or assault, are not to be divided according to the said Law 4, § 2, but are to be restored to the owner, if it is established who he is; argument of Law 31, § 1, Digest, on deposit.

### TH. XII.

<margin>And to be adjudicated.</margin>
Conversely, things which do not admit of division are neither to be divided nor removed in a judgment for the partition of an inheritance, but are to be adjudicated; such are incorporeal rights, such as jurisdiction, the right of patronage, as well as fishing and hunting, which are best adjudicated to be used at alternating times. *Struve, Exercitatio XV, thesis 8*, which alternation is called in German <term>Muthschierung</term> <gloss>rotation/alternation</gloss>, as if from *Mutung* <gloss>request/mutation</gloss> from changing. *Strykius in the precautions of contracts, section 3, chapter 4, § 11.* Also real servitudes, Law 25, § 9 and 10, on the action for partition of an inheritance.</translation>

Therefore, what they say—that the Human nature has Omnipresence in the Person of the Word, really communicated to itself—is either inexplicable or it means that the Human nature is personally united with the Word, which Word is indeed Omnipresent, so that it may be said in an orthodox manner: Christ is Omnipresent, and other things of that kind, using words that signify the Person itself. Otherwise, nothing would prevent them from also saying that the Human nature has it in the Person of the Word so that it is God.

VI.

If the communication of properties is real, then they speak of contradictory things, since they deny that all the properties of the Divine nature are communicated to the Human nature, lest they be forced to posit the eternity of the body of Christ.

I confirm the consequence thus: if properties are communicated Really, then all of them are, because the properties of the Deity are really indivisible and inseparable, for they are the very essence, which is most simple, as was said before. Item: because the <term>ὁ λόγος</term> <gloss>the Word</gloss> united his whole self really with the Human.

<sig>D. iij.</sig>

nor has the Body of Christ laid aside this property: from these words, *Handle me, and see*, he says. It is not spiritual, because a body cannot be more really present with a spiritual presence than a spirit can be really present with a bodily presence. Whoever denies this argument must necessarily deny the very nature of things.

V.

Nothing that is an eternal essence can really happen to anyone.
Omnipresence is an eternal essence.
Wherefore, it cannot really happen to anyone. Yet it would happen to the Body of Christ if it were communicated to it, so that it could be called Omnipresent. For this is not of the essence of the body of Christ, which they do not deny. They respond that Divine properties are not in the Human nature as in a Subject, because it does not subsist by itself, but that the human nature has them in the Person of the Word, really communicated to it. <translation page="124">
<meta>Continues from previous page, discussing the interpretation of biblical verses in a Kabbalistic context.</meta>
And after it, the intention of the verse is written: "To tell of the troubles," and this indicates the righteousness that has no perversion regarding the sin of the heavy-handed wicked, for in every place, the Name of Divinity implies judgment. And because the gate of the arrangement is short regarding the entire sin of one blemish, the kings and the judges were commanded, according to the holy Kabbalists, of blessed memory, [regarding] this verse. And they said: The Queen and the judges were commanded, according to the Kabbalah, to lead the people so that they might remove the end of the lips of the blemish, meaning the blemish at a flawed hour, in order to gain merit before the Place <note>a rabbinic term for God</note>. And there is a place of guidance in hearing the binding of the blemish, and through this, you will be exalted and draw upon yourself the flow of upper blessing, in which you will exist. And the one who causes the blemish [damages] the precious foundation, the foundation of the arrangement, from the holy flow that is influenced upon the <term>Atarah</term> <gloss>Crown/Diadem</gloss> <note>a reference to the Sefirah of Malkhut</note>... and the intention of the lower degree will rise correctly. And in this matter, it is the kindness of Abraham, which is the internal [aspect] of this verse, as I have written, and every holy gate and gate of judgment—for the most powerful deeds are not prevented, and it speaks of the judgment from every side, but rather that they should grasp the flow, a flow that will be for good, and fighting against everything. And all this is the kindness of Sarah, required for the building, in this [way] the face of the day is engraved upon the name of kindness, and it is awakened from the skin of the right for the building of the verse "the lips of mud," <note>a reference to Proverbs 10:10</note> as I have written, for in the cessation of flow and goodness, "Turn away, you," <note>alluding to the fear of Isaac, the attribute of judgment</note> God forbid. Therefore, he said and completed what the acts of kindness performed in the end, the wages of the workers of wickedness, instead of the measure, he answered with openings and will bless. Now, it is correct to the language of the Kabbalah, and after it is the verse of the intention of "lips of righteousness," and they gave a reason: He established the Kingdom in the leadership of wealth, regarding being the treasure of children, life, and sustenance, that they might also be in righteousness. [It is] also kindness, kindness to teach to its children, that the King and the half were from His kindness, and the leadership is holy kindness, and the holiness of mercy is correctly upon it, and the holiness of life. And because of this, it is a commandment: "lest [he] cease righteousness before Him," he will return. And all the power of life in it belongs to the foundation of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss>, and the entire stature of the matter with the kindness, for thus he coerced and invented and added all to benefit, kindness and blessing and goodness. And behold, behold, behold the power of strength, and the merchant for him is flow and mercy, the matter of the secret of the 18 living beings <note>referring to the numerical value of the word 'chai' meaning life</note>, and every gate and <term>Sefirah</term> <gloss>divine emanation</gloss>, kindness and righteousness, the life of the foundation of the arrangement, so that it may be in the building of the arrangement. And after them, the power and skin of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss> and secrets were written in that return, and the secrets of the hidden one, the Name in the mysteries, and it is called by the name of the verse, the seal: "Gate of Holiness, Righteousness, Selah," <note>liturgical term</note> and righteousness, Eternity, Selah, upon us, <unclear>Abai</unclear>. And this matter was explained in the voice of the horses of the King YHWH, for kindness, strength, the attribute of the day, [are] from the commandments, lest the walls and the states with the holy people above, and in this there was mercy upon their lips through the righteousness, kindness to awaken the end of our days, and the <term>Atarah</term> <gloss>Crown/Diadem</gloss> shall be on the head of the groom, and the seven days of the feast, blessings of righteousness, and the seven days of Tabernacles, righteousness to awaken the secret of the matter of distance. Therefore, hear their lips and the entire arrangement, for the arrangement draws the judgment and the end of the <term>Atarah</term> <gloss>Crown/Diadem</gloss>, and it shall be pleasantness.

<summary>This page discusses the Kabbalistic interpretation of biblical verses regarding judgment, kindness, and the divine flow through the Sefirot.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Sefirot, Kindness, Judgment, Atarah, Divine Flow</keywords>
</translation>

And after it is written the intention of the verse: "To recount the troubles," and this indicates the righteousness in which there is no distortion regarding the sin of those heavy with wickedness. For in every place, the name of Divinity hints at judgment. And because the gate of the arrangement for every transgression regarding one blemish was shortened, the kings and the judges were commanded according to the holy Kabbalists, of blessed memory, regarding this verse. They said that the king and the judges were commanded according to the <term>Kabbalah</term> <gloss>received tradition</gloss> to lead the people so that they might remove the end of the lips of the blemish—that is to say, the blemish at the time it is flawed—in order to attain merit before the Place <note>a rabbinic term for God</note>. And there is a place of leadership in hearing the binding of the blemish, and through this, you will be elevated and draw into yourself a flow of supreme blessing. Through this, you will be a cause of a blemish to the precious <term>Yesod</term> <gloss>Foundation</gloss>, which is within the secret of the arrangement, from the holy flow that is influenced upon the <term>Atarah</term> <gloss>Crown/Diadem</gloss> in the hour of the rock <note>a reference to the divine attribute of power</note>, and a correct intention will ascend to every lower level. And in this matter, it is the <term>Chessed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss> of Abraham, which is internal in this verse, and what I have written, and every holy gate and gate of judgment. For the strongest actions were not prevented, and it speaks of judgment from every side, except that they should grasp the flow—a flow that will be for good—and it fights against everything. All of this is the <term>Chessed</term> of Sarah, obligated to the building in this face of the day, engraved upon the name of <term>Chessed</term>. And it is awakened from the skin of the right to the building of the verse: "Life of the lips of filth" <note>a play on words referencing the reversal of positive speech</note>, which is what I have written. For in the cessation of flow and goodness, "Turn away, you fear of Isaac," God forbid. Therefore he said, and they completed what the <term>Chessadim</term> <gloss>acts of kindness</gloss> did at the end, the wages of the workers of wickedness instead of the measure. He answered the openings and blessed; here now is straight for the language of <term>kabbalah</term> <gloss>reception/tradition</gloss>. And after it is the verse of the intention of "lips of righteousness," and they provided a reason to settle the kingdom in the leadership of wealth, in order to be the virtue of children, life, and sustenance that will also be in integrity. Also <term>Chessed</term>, <term>Chessed</term> to teach her children that the King was the half of his <term>Chessed</term>, and the leadership is holy <term>Chessed</term>, and the holiness of mercy is upright upon it, and the holiness of living beings. And because of this, it is a commandment, lest a righteous one cease before him, he will return. And every power of life within him belongs to the <term>Sefirah</term> <gloss>divine emanation</gloss> of <term>Yesod</term>, and the whole stature of the matter with the <term>Chessed</term>—for thus he covered and invented and added all to benefit <term>Chessed</term> and blessing and goodness. And behold, behold, behold the power of <term>Gevurah</term> <gloss>Strength</gloss> and the merchant for him is a flow and mercy, the matter of the <term>Sefirah</term> of the 18 living beings, and every gate and <term>Sefirah</term> is <term>Chessed</term> and righteousness, the life of the foundation of the arrangement, so that it will be in the building of the arrangement. And after them are the power and the skin of the <term>Sefirot</term>, and secrets written in that turn, and the secrets of the Hidden Name in the mysteries. And it is called by the name of the verse of the seal: "The gate of the holy righteousness, Selah. Selah and righteousness, victory Selah upon us..." and this matter was explained in the voice of the horses, the King, the Lord. For <term>Chessed</term> and <term>Gevurah</term> are the measure of the day of the commandments, lest the walls and the states with the holy people above, and in this there was mercy upon her lips through the righteousness, <term>Chessed</term> to the end of our days. And the <term>Atarah</term> shall be upon the head of the groom, and the seven days of the feast are blessings of righteousness, and the seven days of Sukkot are righteousness to awaken the secret of the matter of distance. Therefore, hear her lips and the entire arrangement, for the arrangement draws in the judgment and the end of the <term>Atarah</term>, and it shall be pleasant.
</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the Kabbalistic interpretation of divine names and verses related to judgment, righteousness, and the flow of divine grace through the Sefirot.</summary>
<keywords>Sefirot, Kabbalah, Chessed, Gevurah, divine names, Yesod, Atarah, righteousness, judgment</keywords>

### TH. XI.

Once the wound is dressed, the patient should be placed in bed with the head slightly elevated, and he should rest until he complains of the pressure of the fluid. Then, he should be redressed with the body positioned in the same state in which it was at the time of the incision, so that the wounds of the parts correspond and the fluid may flow out. With all things removed, the lungs are to be pressed down with a pad, the humor evacuated, and finally, the wound is to be dressed again. Take care, however, not to evacuate it all, since with it, many spirits depart and the patient is weakened too much. While the wound is being dressed, do not allow air to enter as much as possible, for gangrene seizes the parts, as seen by C. Solingen in *Manual of Surgical Operations, Part 2, Chapter 1*, and for that reason, it may be altered without clear fire. While we draw out the fluid daily, it often happens that we cannot procure its exit by instrument or by finger, either because the lungs have by chance adhered to the pleura or because the fluid is thickened. In these cases, the lungs should be separated with the finger, provided they cohere to the pleura only with the help of small fibers and there is no fear of rupturing major vessels. The thickness of the fluid should be diluted with warm injections prepared from barley water and rose honey, taking care not to make them bitter with added aloe at the very beginning, for the patient rejects them with his mouth; nevertheless, they are very useful once the vessels are consolidated. The injections, once made, should be drawn out again each time. This should be done twice, thrice, or four times a day if the fluid has become watery and presses too much. The efflux of the humor should be promoted until nothing further flows except what the wound itself supplies, which sometimes does not occur before the second or third month. Then, the wound should be filled with flesh as quickly as possible, and to that end, instead of a cannula,

If a physician gathers from the signs that fluid is stagnating within the duplicature of the mediastinum, an incision in the shape of a cross or triangle should be made in the middle of the sternum—so that the mammary vessels are avoided—as far toward the ensiform cartilage as possible without injury to the diaphragm. A silver cannula should be driven in, which fits the opening accurately so that we may evacuate the fluid through it like a tap at our pleasure. Hildan., Surgical Observations, Century 1, Obs. 47*, regarding Petrus Kickup, a forty-year-old man with ascites, who was most completely cured when his umbilicus ruptured of its own accord. All agreed, ready to obey the words.
Immediately, swift rumor spreads through the great city,
That Augustus has established a massive amount of silver for building
The tower: there is no long delay, the Senate
Urges the craftsmen, skilled in the art of building, with sagacious minds,
To bring their spirits—accustomed to extraordinary arts—to the task from everywhere,
To erect the aerial tower with the wondrous joints of heavy stones:
When, after the birth of Christ the King,
Three hundred years had passed, with another sixteen added,
And the sun had moved through the winter orbits in addition.
Behold, the men, with immense ardor, now [work on] the tower, rejoicing
To have found a way to show their skills—hidden by sagacious mind—
To be seen by all in clear light,
Whatever their diligence can promise in their art,
What can be done by iron or the rigid axe,
As much as arts and strengths avail, they desire to provide all these things
With a ready heart and constant labor.
Soon one man, older and wiser than the rest,
Addresses his companions, and begins thus with a placid breast:
> Lift everything, he says: put aside your previous cares,
> O companion craftsmen, now turn your minds here:
> A sacred tower must be built, now there is need for strength,
> Now for strong hands, now for the sagacious art of Pallas <note>the goddess of wisdom and craftsmanship</note>,</translation>

<translation page="10">
Now, delay must be cast aside: he had spoken thus: and they
Set upon the work. One part fits the strength of the tower with countless
Ropes: another part pulls down the ancient
High masses: a part carries away the ruined stones:
A part brings material for the uses of the tower to be built:
A part extinguishes living lime with rainwater:
Here some cut stones, others cut massive columns
From the rocks, the future high decorations of the tower:
Here others begin to place stones in a certain order,
The foundations of the new mass, with wondrous skill of labor:
Others here decorate the vestibule with carved insignias:
Here others join stones to stones with mixed mortar, all
Burning to increase such great labors. Thus, the high tower rises little by little,
Like the constant labor of bees, when they rejoice
To fashion liquid honey and forge new
Wax with innate art: one part carries the noble
Burden from those arriving: one part wards off drones from the hives.
But when it had now come to the highest peaks of the tower,
Behold the new mass, the circuits are duly built in pairs
With squared stone, from where a high person can observe
All the people, the streets, and the houses,
From where the air rings with the wandering sounds of trumpet blasts.
Here also they shine with glowing yellow metal</translation>

(because the debtor can be sued immediately from this, which is a property of a pure obligation) and it is perpetuated. For nothing can be owed at a certain time, since time, which is nothing in itself, also neither constitutes an obligation by itself, nor takes away one that was legitimately born. However, because it is inequitable and contrary to good faith for someone to be bound beyond the law of the agreement, therefore, the plaintiff or the one seeking after the time annexed to the stipulation should be turned away by the exception of an agreed pact, or of evil intent <note>original: "exceptio pacti conventi, sive doli mali"</note> *law 56, paragraph 4, concerning Verbal Obligations; law 44, concerning Obligations and Actions.* For instance, if a day is set as a limit <term>ad quem</term> <gloss>to which</gloss>, that is, for the sake of ending an obligation, in this manner: "do you promise to give ten as long as I live?", he rightly sues for it to be given immediately. Otherwise, an heir suing is repelled by an exception, for it is clear that the stipulator acted so that his heir would not sue. Thus, also, his heir, to whom a praedial servitude was granted in such a way that he had the right of way as long as he lived, will be moved aside by the exception of an agreed pact *the said law, paragraph "he who thus", law 2, paragraph 4, concerning the exception of evil intent; add Oldendorp, chapter 36, on Exceptions.* Yet a promise made for individual years, with no time added as to "as long as the stipulator lives," and which passes to his heirs, the effect of the obligation transmits *law "if Stichus," paragraph 1, this title; law 13, in the Code concerning contracting and committing a stipulation;* for in this instance, the addition or mention of years intervenes for the sake not of delaying, but of multiplying, as our people say *law 118, paragraph 1, concerning Verbal Obligations.*

XV. We asserted in Thesis 11 that a pure stipulation is estimated from the promised object and from that which is intended in effect, not from the mere figure of speech or the external form of words, because even if the obligation is pure in its words, the object itself tacitly knots in delays <note>original: "inducias nectit"</note> *law 41, paragraph 1; law 73; law 137, paragraph 2; the said [law] on Verbal Obligations; law 3, paragraph 6, concerning that which concerns a certain place.* For example: "do you promise to give one hundred at Ephesus?" Although this stipulation seems to be made purely, the place, which the promisor uses to give the money at Ephesus, introduces a space of time. *Paragraph in the Institutes on this title; law "he who," paragraph "as often as," in the same [place].* But as often as the application
</translation>

<translation page="17">
of place or time involves something impossible, it is of no moment, as if someone stipulating at Rome should say: "do you promise to give at Carthage today?" Such a promise is impossible, as it is contradictory in itself. He who is at Rome today cannot give at Carthage unless he reaches Carthage within one day. From pre-arrangements, a stipulation made at Rome to be given at Carthage today can sometimes be rendered both useful and possible. For it could happen that both the stipulator and the promisor, before some time, each made the future stipulation known to their own steward for that day, and the promisor had commanded his steward to give, and the stipulator [had commanded] his own to receive; and if it were done in this way, the stipulation can be valid *law 141, paragraph 4, of this title;* thus, therefore, pre-arrangement into the future can induce the presence of future things. *Gloss to this law.*

XVI. Conditions that are annexed to stipulations are properly about future things, from which an uncertain obligation arises. Those that are referred to the present or past time do not suspend the obligation, but either break it immediately or do not delay it at all. Just as future things are uncertain, so present and past things are always certain. Nor do we look at the error or ignorance of men in these, since the ignorance of men cannot stand against the truth *law 37, concerning Credited Things; law 2, paragraph "he who," concerning purchase; law 6, paragraph 1, concerning the office of the prefect.* For in these stipulations, if [one says]: "do you promise to give if the King of the Persians is alive?" or tacitly, no condition appears regarding the effect, because the power of acting immediately falls to the stipulator, nor does he fall into the penalty of claiming more than is due *paragraph 33, Institutes, on Actions.*

XVII. Where, finally, all these things concur, we have that which has been sought until now, namely, a stipulation legitimately made to stand by the highest law. Meanwhile, it may happen that the defendant, led perhaps by repentance, may fulfill his promise
</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the legal constraints of time and place within stipulations, arguing that purely worded obligations may be subject to implicit temporal delays, and that conditions regarding present or past facts do not suspend the force of an obligation as future conditions do.</summary>
<keywords>stipulation, legal obligation, Roman law, inheritance, time constraints, conditions, evidence</keywords>

of place or time involves something impossible, it is of no moment, as if someone stipulating at Rome should say: "do you promise to give at Carthage today?" ze, whoever wanted to see this whole palace would consume an entire day. Among the others, there are four main halls where sometimes the King gives audience to his principals; one of them is completely covered below and above with metal, another is entirely of silver, and another entirely of gold, and all of them have their walls covered with pearls and most precious jewels. When his vassals bring him gold or other precious things, they place them in this hall and say, "This is for the honor and glory of our Santhoa Raia." These people of China, as the said Moor said, are white and go dressed like us, and they eat at tables like us, and they have the cross, but they do not know why they keep it. In China, musk is born from a beast that is similar to a cat, which eats a sweet wood as thick as a finger, and is called <term>Comaru</term>. Behind the coast of China are many peoples, such as those of <term>Chenchii</term>, where pearls and some cinnamon wood are found, and the peoples called <term>Lechii</term>, where the King of <term>Moin</term> is, who has 22 kings under him, and he is subject to the King of China. There is also found the great city called eastern <term>Cathaio</term>, and many other peoples on the said mainland, and among others, some of such beastly customs that as soon as they see their father and mother old and feeble, they kill them so that they do not labor anymore in this life, and all these peoples are Gentiles.

On February 11, 1522, they departed from the Island of <term>Timor</term>, plunging deep into the great sea which is called <term>Lantchidol</term>, and took their path between West and Northwest, leaving the North on their right, for fear that by going toward the mainland they would be seen by the Portuguese. They passed outside the Island of <term>Samotra</term>, called by the ancients <term>Taprobana</term> as we have said, leaving still on their right above the mainland <term>Pegu</term>, <term>Bengala</term>, <term>Calicut</term>, <term>Cananor</term>, and <term>Goa</term>, <term>Cambaia</term>, the Gulf of <term>Ormus</term>, and the whole Coast of Greater India. And to pass more safely the Cape of Good Hope, which is above Africa, they went toward the Antarctic pole about 42 degrees, and stayed above said Cape for 7 weeks, always tacking with their sails up, because winds from the West and Northwest were blowing against them, which did not let them pass, and they also had no little misfortune. The Cape of Good Hope is toward the Antarctic pole below the Equinoctial line by 34 and a half degrees, and 1600 leagues from the cape of <term>Malaccha</term>, and it is the greatest and most dangerous Cape to be seen on the sea in all the world. Some of our men, out of a lack of provisions and because they were ill, wanted to go to a port above Africa of the Portuguese called <term>Monzanbich</term>; the others said that they would rather die than not go straight to Spain. Yet finally, with the help of the Lord God, they passed said Cape not too far away, then they began to sail toward the Northwest for two

<translation page="110">
months continuously without ever touching any port, and in this time about 21 of them died of various causes, whom they threw into the sea, and it seemed that the Christians went to the bottom with their faces turned upward, and the Indians with their faces downward, and if God had not given them good weather they would all have died of hunger. Finally, pressed by necessity and finding themselves half-dead, they went to the Island of Cape Verde called <term>San Iacopo</term> belonging to the King of Portugal, where they immediately sent men ashore on a boat to ask for provisions, letting the Portuguese know with every kindness of their misfortunes and hardships, and of the news of their men who were found in the Indies. With such good words and caresses that they knew how to use, they obtained some measures of rice, but desiring to return for more rice, 13 men were detained who had been assured that they could disembark on land. The others who remained at sea, fearing they might also be taken by some trick, departed by setting sail, and on the 7th of September, with the help of God, they entered the port of <term>San Lucar</term> near <term>Sibilia</term> with only 18 men, most of them ill. Of the rest of the 59 who departed from the <term>Molucche</term>, some died of various illnesses, and some were even beheaded on the Island of <term>Timor</term> for their crimes. Arrived at this port of San Lucar, by the account kept from day to day, they had sailed fourteen thousand four hundred and sixty leagues, circling the whole world from the East to the West. On the 8th of September, they came to <term>Sibilia</term>, and they unloaded all their artillery for joy, and all in their shirts, and barefoot with a torch in hand, they went to give thanks in the main church to the Lord God who had brought them safe to that point.

After a few days, <term>Antonio Pigafetta</term> departed and went to the City of <term>Vagliadolit</term>, where the Majesty of the <term>Emperor</term> was. He could not present gold, or silver, or precious stones that were worthy of the greatness of such a prince, but he gave him a book written by his own hand, where all the things that happened from day to day on this voyage were noted. Having then departed from there, he went to <term>Lisbona</term> to the Most Serene <term>King of Portugal</term>, to whom he told all the news of his men that they had found both in the Islands of the <term>Molucche</term> and in other parts. After Spain, he came to France, where he presented some gifts of the things brought from this voyage to the Most Serene <term>Madame the Regent</term>, mother of the most powerful and most Christian <term>King of France</term>. Finally, having come to Italy, he similarly presented this book of his to the Most Reverend Grand Master of <term>Rhodi</term>, Messer <term>Philippo Villiers Lisleadam</term>.

THE END.

<summary>The voyage concludes with the arrival of the final 18 survivors in Spain, followed by Pigafetta's presentation of his travel journal to various European monarchs and the Grand Master of Rhodes.</summary>
<keywords>Antonio Pigafetta, Molucche, San Lucar, Sibilia, Emperor, King of Portugal, King of France, Philippo Villiers Lisleadam, circumnavigation</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="16">
They say, however, that even those things which their maritime power carries with it—not less than clemency and goodness—have taken up arms for the sake of ecclesiastical and Etruscan liberty, in order to restore to every people their own rights. Or, even if they accomplish their pious intention with great slaughter, they will perceive all the greater pleasure from their good deeds the less they have disturbed the state of Etruria in the process. For this reason, therefore, they seek your alliance, so that they may preserve your liberty without any harm and restore to you what has been lost, extending your borders. They see that you, joined to the Florentines, would suffer great losses from the war before any time for gain or self-perception arrives. For in the heat of wars, since the causes of individuals are not clearly discussed, it is often the case that what the method of victory suggests is considered, not what each one deserves. I say that the two earthly luminaries of the Christians seek nothing else from you than that you should share with them the fruit of victory without any detriment of war. For if you believe that the weight of such a great war was undertaken in the hope of your aid, you are greatly deceived, and you do not sufficiently understand the wisdom of the King and the Pope. They bore much so as not to see war in Italy; they tried in vain everything by which it was probable that the fury of the tyrant, Lorenzo de' Medici, would be moderated. They proceeded to cut away the incurable wound with the sword, lest the healthy part be infected, when they already clearly saw the outcome of the war and that Mars—almost always common to them—was with them. They could not be torn away from the embrace of peace, not by the hope of gains, which they always despised, nor by the vengeance of injuries, nor by the desire for glory, nor for any cause or reason whatsoever, and [they are men] who in spirit and strength were not only superior to Lorenzo, who was recently raised to tyranny by trade and the mockery of fortune, but [would] not even [be] inferior to the powers of the whole world. Yet they did not undertake the war before they were provoked by the most just and necessary complaints of allies and friends, and they looked forward to the end of the matter from afar, as if from a watchtower, having examined the strength of their own side and the enemy’s regarding the hope of victory. If there had been any doubt about the victory, they would surely have foreseen it by their own intelligence and by that prudence in affairs by which they overcome both those of the past and those of the present.
</translation>

<translation page="17">
They would never have sent themselves into a war of uncertain outcome, and those who were once younger, having never undertaken anything without the most weighty counsel, would now, being older, have attempted nothing inconsiderately. It is by no means possible to note rashness in the King, and much less in the Pope, whose age, whole life, profession, and dignity demonstrate wisdom on all sides. Therefore, first, two lights of the Christians were drawn to war: for the sake of the safety of allies and friends and for ecclesiastical and Etruscan liberty, just as [it was] previously [for] justice; and then [for] the wisdom by which they are clearly taught that nothing is to be compared to the enemy. Place before your eyes the forces of the Florentine tyrant. He does not abound in horses, nor in men, nor in arms, nor in supplies. He has no allies except those who are unhappy and already almost despairing of all good fortune. He has no civil concord, no money—which those most experienced in military affairs call the sinews of war—no leaders whose virtue has often changed the fortune of wars against everyone’s opinion; and finally, no thing suitable for resisting, let alone fit for winning. And on the contrary, the King and the Pope have so great an abundance of horses that all the wealth of the Florentines is not sufficient to feed them for a few days; [they have] as many provisions as all of Italy could not consume in many years; and furthermore, so many men that you would not consider any provision small. And of what kind of men? Indeed, the princes of Italy, whose nobility, whose cities they rule, and whose fame in feats of arms the Florentine tyrant could not even hear of without trembling. Regarding the abundance of arms, you would say that if you look at the army, none is left in the cities of the King and the Pope; and if you look at the storehouses, you would believe none has been taken away by soldiers. [There is] harmony between them, which must exist between a most wise father and a son endowed with the highest piety. Now, the number of mules laden with struck gold and silver, passing daily through the fields and towns of the Sienese, sufficiently declares or rather signifies it to be innumerable. They have as allies all who hold any strength, except for those whom they partly conquer.
</translation>

Or, even if they accomplish their pious intention with great slaughter, they will perceive all the greater pleasure from their good deeds the less they have disturbed the state of Etruria in the process. For this reason, therefore, they seek your alliance, so that they may preserve your liberty without any harm and restore to you what has been lost, extending your borders. They see that you, joined to the Florentines, would suffer great losses from the war before any time for gain or self-perception arrives. For in the heat of wars, since the causes of individuals are not clearly discussed, it is often the case that what the method of victory suggests is considered, not what each one deserves. I say that the two earthly luminaries of the Christians seek nothing else from you than that you should share with them the fruit of victory without any detriment of war. For if you believe that the weight of such a great war was undertaken in the hope of your aid, you are greatly deceived, and you do not sufficiently understand the wisdom of the King and the Pope. They bore much so as not to see war in Italy; they tried in vain everything by which it was probable that the fury of the tyrant, Lorenzo de' Medici, would be moderated. They proceeded to cut away the incurable wound with the sword, lest the healthy part be infected, when they already clearly saw the outcome of the war and that Mars—almost always common to them—was with them. They could not be torn away from the embrace of peace, not by the hope of gains, which they always despised, nor by the vengeance of injuries, nor by the desire for glory, nor for any cause or reason whatsoever, and [they are men] who in spirit and strength were not only superior to Lorenzo, who was recently raised to tyranny by trade and the mockery of fortune, but [would] not even [be] inferior to the powers of the whole world. Yet they did not undertake the war before they were provoked by the most just and necessary complaints of allies and friends, and they looked forward to the end of the matter from afar, as if from a watchtower, having examined the strength of their own side and the enemy’s regarding the hope of victory. If there had been any doubt about the victory, they would surely have foreseen it by their own intelligence and by that prudence in affairs by which they overcome both those of the past and those of the present.
pages.17: They would never have sent themselves into a war of uncertain outcome, and those who were once younger, having never undertaken anything without the most weighty counsel, would now, being older, have attempted nothing inconsiderately. It is by no means possible to note rashness in the King, and much less in the Pope, whose age, whole life, profession, and dignity demonstrate wisdom on all sides. Therefore, first, two lights of the Christians were drawn to war: for the sake of the safety of allies and friends and for ecclesiastical and Etruscan liberty, just as [it was] previously [for] justice; and then [for] the wisdom by which they are clearly taught that nothing is to be compared to the enemy. Place before your eyes the forces of the Florentine tyrant. He does not abound in horses, nor in men, nor in arms, nor in supplies. He has no allies except those who are unhappy and already almost despairing of all good fortune. He has no civil concord, no money—which those most experienced in military affairs call the sinews of war—no leaders whose virtue has often changed the fortune of wars against everyone’s opinion; and finally, no thing suitable for resisting, let alone fit for winning. And on the contrary, the King and the Pope have so great an abundance of horses that all the wealth of the Florentines is not sufficient to feed them for a few days; [they have] as many provisions as all of Italy could not consume in many years; and furthermore, so many men that you would not consider any provision small. And of what kind of men? Indeed, the princes of Italy, whose nobility, whose cities they rule, and whose fame in feats of arms the Florentine tyrant could not even hear of without trembling. Regarding the abundance of arms, you would say that if you look at the army, none is left in the cities of the King and the Pope; and if you look at the storehouses, you would believe none has been taken away by soldiers. [There is] harmony between them, which must exist between a most wise father and a son endowed with the highest piety. Now, the number of mules laden with struck gold and silver, passing daily through the fields and towns of the Sienese, sufficiently declares or rather signifies it to be innumerable. They have as allies all who hold any strength, except for those whom they partly conquer.

<translation page="191">
<header>Golden Text Oral Interpretations</header>
<sig>Volume 5</sig>

Six in the fourth position: Going involves obstruction; coming involves connection.

<note>The <term>Benyi</term> <gloss>Original Meaning</gloss> says: "Connecting to the nine in the third position." The *Cheng Commentary* says: "To go is to enter even deeper into the danger of the <term>Kan</term> <gloss>Water/Pitfall</gloss> trigram; this is 'going into obstruction'."</note>

<column-break/>

[This line] is correct because it compares itself with the three, to which it is close and intimate. The two and the initial [line] are of the same class, and those who are the same do not need to plan in order to act in unison. Furthermore, the four dwells in a high position and has the ambition of one who, while in a low position and experiencing danger, has nevertheless attained their correct place.

<note>
An examination of the text:
Master Kong's commentary takes the two as the master of the meaning. The meaning is that the Yin line obtains its position and is safe, hence it can stop. Thus, "coming" is returning. 
Master Wu says: "To 'come' and 'return' is to stop at what is correct."
The *Jishuo* <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> says: "Master Kong says 'coming' means to return to what is correct. 'Going' means to enter the danger. The nine in the third [position] is the master of the inner trigram, which is why [one] stops at it."
The *Cheng Commentary* says: "The nine in the third [line] is strong and correct, therefore it is the one to which [the others] come and return."
The *Cheng Commentary* also says: "If one advances, one enters the danger. If one returns, one is at peace. This is the rationale for the Yin [line] being able to stop because it sees the danger."
Basically, the reason for the "coming" and "returning" is that the soft line has no [other] place to respond to, so it returns to the nine in the third [line].
</note>

<summary>This page provides a detailed analysis of the fourth line of the Obstruction hexagram, interpreting the concepts of "going" versus "coming" through various scholarly commentaries such as those of Master Kong and Master Wu.</summary>
<keywords>Six in the fourth, Jian, Obstruction, Kan, Connection, Commentary, Scholarly Exegesis</keywords>
</translation>

<header>Golden Text Oral Interpretations</header>
<sig>Volume 5</sig>

Six in the fourth position: Going involves obstruction; coming involves connection.

<note>The <term>Benyi</term> <gloss>Original Meaning</gloss> says: "Connecting to the nine in the third position." The *Cheng Commentary* says: "To go is to enter even deeper into the danger of the <term>Kan</term> <gloss>Water/Pitfall</gloss> trigram; this is 'going into obstruction'."</note>

<column-break/>

[This line] is correct because it compares itself with the three, to which it is close and intimate. The two and the initial [line] are of the same class, and those who are the same do not need to plan in order to act in unison. Furthermore, the four dwells in a high position and has the ambition of one who, while in a low position and experiencing danger, has nevertheless attained their correct place.

<note>
An examination of the text:
Master Kong's commentary takes the two as the master of the meaning. The meaning is that the Yin line obtains its position and is safe, hence it can stop. Thus, "coming" is returning. 
Master Wu says: "To 'come' and 'return' is to stop at what is correct."
The *Jishuo* <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> says: "Master Kong says 'coming' means to return to what is correct. 'Going' means to enter the danger. The nine in the third [position] is the master of the inner trigram, which is why [one] stops at it."
The *Cheng Commentary* says: "The nine in the third [line] is strong and correct, therefore it is the one to which [the others] come and return."
The *Cheng Commentary* also says: "If one advances, one enters the danger. If one returns, one is at peace. This is the rationale for the Yin [line] being able to stop because it sees the danger."
Basically, the reason for the "coming" and "returning" is that the soft line has no [other] place to respond to, so it returns to the nine in the third [line].
</note>

<summary>This page provides a detailed analysis of the fourth line of the Obstruction hexagram, interpreting the concepts of "going" versus "coming" through various scholarly commentaries such as those of Master Kong and Master Wu.</summary>
<keywords>Six in the fourth, Jian, Obstruction, Kan, Connection, Commentary, Scholarly Exegesis</keywords>

<translation page="434">

### LIV.

This, however, seems to proceed only unless the object of another is bequeathed by reason of a right that the testator held in it, for in this case it seems sufficient that said right, such as it is, be guaranteed.

### LV.

However, we believe this opinion is more correctly refuted if that right or the object which the legacy consists of is held in common by the testator and the heir himself. For in this case, we do not doubt that the entire legacy must be provided.

### LVI.

If he was ignorant, then it must be distinguished again whether the legacy was for a stranger or for a connected person; in the former case, the legacy vanishes, in the latter, it is sustained.

### LVII.

Although in the former case, it is entirely fair that the actions which the testator perhaps had by reason of the object, and transmitted to the heir, should be ceded to the legatee. Since reason undoubtedly also suggests that the legatee ought to obtain at least that which would exist without expense to the heir.

### LVIII.

II. It must be distinguished whether an object is bequeathed generally, or whether a specific type belonging to the testator is bequeathed. In the former case, we again distinguish, so that if the object is of a determined nature, the legacy must be provided in full; if not, then only if an object of that kind is found among the testator's assets.

### LIX.

Although we do not deny that in the case where an object is so generally bequeathed, there is room for eviction only if it is not a case of an uncertain legacy from certain items, and all individual items that belonged to the testator have perished without the heir's fault or have ceased to be in the estate; for otherwise, we maintain that in this respect also, the obligation lives and endures up to the last individual item that remains.

</translation>

<translation page="14">

until the last individual item that remains, we maintain that the obligation lives and endures.

->LX.<-

In the latter case, when a specific type belonging to the testator is bequeathed, the heir remains safe from the reason of eviction. Since, in this case, eviction can only occur through the fault or imprudence of the legatee, or by the injustice of a judge, the damage arising from this will be wrongly imputed to the heir.

->LXI.<-

But neither does this assertion proceed simply. For if an encumbered object, although belonging to the testator, is bequeathed, the heir is without doubt bound to redeem it, unless it otherwise appears that such was contrary to the testator's will.

->LXII.<-

It does not matter in general whether the whole object or a part of it is evicted, because the author <note>original: "author" <gloss>the seller or provider</gloss></note> is also bound by reason of a part. However, one must diligently attend to whether the part is evicted as an undivided whole or as a divided portion. For in the former way, a recourse <note>original: "regressus" <gloss>the right to claim compensation</gloss></note> is competent according to the quantity of the evicted part; but in the latter, recourse will be granted according to the quality of the location. Likewise, whether it is truly a part or not, and if it is a part, whether it adheres to the object itself, or whether the object consists of it and is named for it, and other things which are accustomed to come into consideration by the <term>Doctors</term> <gloss>legal scholars</gloss> in this place, to whom we refer the reader.

->LXIII.<-

It follows regarding the persons who provide for eviction. These are the sellers, namely, the authors from whom the buyers or others have lawfully acquired the object, provided that they are of such a condition that they do not contract against the prohibition of the law, and thus their contracts are not null by the law itself. Which, however, we wish to be understood concerning that alienation at least, where the entire act is annulled, as we will show in the actual conflict of this disputation.

</translation>

<summary>These pages continue the legal analysis of legacies and eviction, examining how the rights of heirs, legatees, and testators interact when bequeathed property is disputed, encumbered, or partially evicted, before turning to the identity of those responsible for guaranteeing against eviction.</summary>

then because the destruction of the property must be imputed to the Lord, he will obtain liberation from the rent <term>Canon</term> <gloss>fixed annual payment</gloss> by reason of both law and equity, and he will be freed from the danger of forfeiture.

### XXIII.

If, however, the yield should be sterile, or some particular or slight damage should occur, by which the substance of the property is not entirely injured: in this case, just as the advantage belongs to the Emphyteuticary, so he will not doubt that this loss also must be ascribed to his own share.

### XXIV.

Furthermore, this also must not be overlooked: although according to the common axiom of law, every person is the governor and arbiter of his own property, yet he who has received another’s property in <term>emphyteusis</term> <gloss>long-term lease/tenure</gloss> cannot, without consulting the Lord, transfer his improvements or the Emphyteutic right to another.

### XXV.

But if no pact has intervened between them regarding this, then the direct Lord must be requested, and the declaration of his will must be awaited for two months from the notification. If he is prepared to provide such an amount as the Emphyteuta can actually receive from another, he must deservedly be preferred over a stranger.

### XXVI.

If, however, he has not declared his intention within the interval of two months from the day of the notification, then the Emphyteuta has the faculty to transfer his right to another suitable person, even without his consent. And the Lord,
</translation>

<translation page="16">
provided the new Emphyteuta pays the fiftieth part of the price or the valuation of the place in the name of the <term>laudemium</term> <gloss>fee paid to the lord upon transfer of tenure</gloss>, is bound to accept and invest him.

### XXVII.

### Juan 13
<meta>Combined Commentary by the Four Ministers of the Jin and Zhen eras</meta>

Participating in Heaven and doubling the Earth <note>a reference to the Xici Zhuan of the Book of Changes</note> to rely upon the numbers does not refer to the standard numbers of Heaven and Earth. To "rely upon" <term>yi</term> <gloss>to lean on, to approximate</gloss> means to model them. It is because the standard numbers of Heaven and Earth exist that these are produced.

The numbers of the <term>Yi</term> <gloss>Book of Changes</gloss> exhaust the beginnings and endings of Heaven and Earth. One might ask, do Heaven and Earth also have a beginning and an end? I reply: if there is waxing and waning, how could there be no beginning and ending? Although Heaven and Earth are vast, they are still formed objects and thus consist of two things.

The generative numbers of the <term>Yi</term> total 129,600, which as a whole is 4,320. Compared to the great numbers of waxing and waning, the calculation of the <term>chen</term> <gloss>a period of time/the twelve earthly branches as hours</gloss> over thirty years is exactly this number. A year of 360 days yields 4,320 <term>chen</term>; multiplying this by 30 gives the total number. In all cases, <term>Jia-Zi</term> <gloss>first of the sixty-year cycle</gloss> and <term>Jia-Wu</term> <gloss>thirty-first of the sixty-year cycle</gloss> serve as the heads of the <term>shi</term> <gloss>a thirty-year generational period</gloss>. This is how the numbers of the <term>Jingshi</term> <gloss>World Ordering</gloss> begin from the Sun's <term>Jia</term>, the Moon's <term>Zi</term>, the Star's <term>Jia</term>, and the <term>Chen</term> <gloss>branch</gloss> <term>Zi</term>.

<summary>This page explains the cosmological calculation method of the Yi, focusing on the derivation of the 129,600-year cycle and the thirty-year generation (shi) based on celestial and earthly numerical correspondences.</summary>
<keywords>Yi Jing, cosmology, waxing and waning, Jia-Zi, Jingshi</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="47">
<page-num>1063</page-num>
<meta>Huangji Jingshi Shu</meta>

It is further stated that this is how the Sun, Moon, Star, <term>Jia</term>, <term>Chen</term>, and <term>Zi</term> of the <term>Jingshi</term> <gloss>World Ordering</gloss> follow one another.

Ten, one hundred, one thousand, ten thousand, and one hundred million are odd, representing the numbers of Heaven. Twelve, one hundred twenty, twelve hundred, twelve thousand, and one hundred twenty thousand are even, representing the numbers of Earth.

The ten <term>Gan</term> <gloss>Heavenly Stems</gloss> are Heaven, and the twelve <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>Earthly Branches</gloss> are Earth. The pairing of stems and branches is the function of Heaven and Earth.

The <term>Gan</term> implies a trunk <note>implying the source or main axis</note>, which is Yang. The <term>Zhi</term> implies a branch, which is Yin. Because there are ten stems and twelve branches, there is Yin within the Yang numbers, and there is Yang within the Yin numbers.

The Yang number one, when extended, becomes ten, such as ten thousands. The Yin number two, when extended, becomes twelve, such as the twelve branches and the twelve months.

<summary>This page defines the numerical properties of Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches, explaining how their combination reflects the interplay of Yin and Yang and the extension of basic units into larger cycles.</summary>
<keywords>Heavenly Stems, Earthly Branches, Yin Yang, cosmology, numerical extension</keywords>
</translation>

# THEOPHRASTUS, ON ODORS

<note>A large, ornate, historiated drop-cap letter 'A' featuring floral and vine-like scrollwork.</note>

Odors, in their entirety, arise from a mixture, just as flavors do; for everything that is unmixed is odorless, just as it is flavorless. Thus, many things are odorless, such as water, air, and fire. Earth, however, possesses odor more than any other element; for this reason, it is the most mixed. Among odors, some are, as it were, unpleasant and watery, just as they are in the case of flavors; others possess certain specific forms. These forms seem to correspond to those of flavors, though they do not all have the same designations, as we stated previously. Nor are they distinguished by their species in the same way as flavors are; rather, they are classified by their nature, as either sweet-smelling or foul-smelling. The varieties of foul odors have not been named, even though they possess great differences. For, since there are odors of sweet and bitter things, others are called pungent and strong, and a sweet odor is soft and heavy. Some of these are common to both, as well as to foul odors. The universal odor that exists in all things that are decaying is putridity. For everything that is putrefying is foul-smelling, unless one calls sharpness a primitive state due to the similarity of decay. This kind of foulness exists in all things, even in plants. </translation>

However, to divide them simply, some are odors in themselves, while others are by coincidence. Some are odors of flavors or food by coincidence; others are like those of respiration, in themselves. <translation page="13">
And upon his family and his noble companions, and grant them abundant peace. O people, fear God, and approach Him, may God have mercy on you. Perform your prayer with calmness and tranquility, and adorn yourselves with dignity. Praise your Lord on this great day, and occupy yourselves with His remembrance in the early parts of your prayer. Magnify God for what He has guided you to, and draw near to God the Almighty on this great day with your sacrificial animals. Honor the rites of God, your Lord, and choose the best of your offerings. Seek forgiveness, for piety is in your hidden hearts. The attainment of God does not come from deeds unless they are sincere. For He, Glory be to Him, says: "Their meat will not reach God, nor will their blood, but what reaches Him is piety from you." Thus He has subjected them to you that you may glorify God for that to which He has guided you; and give good tidings to the doers of good. May God make us and you among those whose hearts are filled with His love, and who do not accept the world as a substitute for the Hereafter.

I seek refuge in God from Satan, the accursed. "And the day We will remove the mountains and you will see the earth prominent, and We will gather them and not leave behind, from among them, anyone. And they will be presented to your Lord in rows, 'You have certainly come to Us just as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would never make for you an appointment.'" May God bless me and you with the Great Qur'an. Indeed, He is the Generous, the Kind, the King, the Righteous, the Compassionate, the Merciful. Say what you wish in secret, for He knows the secrets of the hearts. God is Most Great, God is Most Great, God is Most Great, God is Most Great, God is Most Great. Praise be to God, a praise as He commanded. I bear witness that there is no god but God, alone with no partner, a compulsion to those who deny and disbelieve. And I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, the master of mankind. May God bless him and grant him peace as long as an eye sees and an ear hears. O people, I advise you, servants of God, and myself, to fear God, for God is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good. And know
</translation>
<translation page="16">
that God the Almighty has commanded you with a universal command, beginning with Himself as the Great One: "Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, ask [God to send] blessings upon him and ask [God to grant him] peace." So answer God, O servants of God, to what He has called you, and pray for the one through whom God has guided you. O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, the leader of the righteous, the radiance of the disbelievers, and the intercessor of the nation to the Almighty, the Compeller. And upon the righteous and chosen ones. O God, be pleased with the chosen Caliph, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and Umar al-Faruq, and Uthman of the Two Lights, and Ali the Chosen. And upon the two grandsons, the two masters, the two leaders, the two men of great character, al-Hasan and al-Husayn. And upon his two uncles, Hamza and al-Abbas, and the Emigrants and the Helpers. And upon his pure wives, the mothers of the believers. And upon the Followers and those who followed the Followers, with excellence, until the Day of Judgment.

And upon us with them, and along with them, by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful. Amen. O God, grant victory to whoever supports the religion of Muhammad, and forsake whoever forsakes the religion of Muhammad. O God, forgive the believing men and women, and the Muslim men and women, the living among them and the dead. Indeed, You are near, answering prayers and fulfilling needs, by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful. O God, protect, aid, and grant victory to the state of the doer of good and benevolence, the one who manages in this land and the Sacred Sanctuary, the one who holds fast to God, the One, the Eternal Refuge, Your servant, our master Kanjeng Murada bin Frawirada Raja, son of our master Kanjeng Arya Kusuma Ningsra. May God be to them, and to those after them, a helper and an assistant at every time and moment, and a guide to the path of guidance and certainty, and established upon the Sharia <gloss>Islamic Law</gloss> of the master of the messengers, and a supporter in the reform of worldly and religious affairs, O God of the worlds. O God, repel from us the affliction.

pages.16:
that God the Almighty has commanded you with a universal command, beginning with Himself as the Great One: "Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, ask [God to send] blessings upon him and ask [God to grant him] peace." O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, the leader of the righteous, the radiance of the disbelievers, and the intercessor of the nation to the Almighty, the Compeller. And upon the righteous and chosen ones. O God, be pleased with the chosen Caliph, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and Umar al-Faruq, and Uthman of the Two Lights, and Ali the Chosen. And upon the two grandsons, the two masters, the two leaders, the two men of great character, al-Hasan and al-Husayn. And upon his two uncles, Hamza and al-Abbas, and the Emigrants and the Helpers. And upon his pure wives, the mothers of the believers. And upon the Followers and those who followed the Followers, with excellence, until the Day of Judgment.

And upon us with them, and along with them, by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful. Amen. O God, grant victory to whoever supports the religion of Muhammad, and forsake whoever forsakes the religion of Muhammad. O God, forgive the believing men and women, and the Muslim men and women, the living among them and the dead. Indeed, You are near, answering prayers and fulfilling needs, by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful. and the like, to rescind it. In that place, the aforementioned Lord Richter adduces many responses in favor of this opinion in the stated decision, number 55 and following. He notes, namely, that this remedy has no place in a transaction that has been ratified and confirmed after an interval, nor in a judicial transaction or one confirmed judicially. Gail also adds this in book 2, observation 1, number 9.

## THES. XXIX.

Furthermore, this benefit is granted to the <term>datio in solutum</term> <gloss>giving in payment</gloss>, both voluntary and extrajudicial, which is similar to a sale and takes its place (Law "finis" <note>original: "lex finis"</note>, Digest, "For what causes one may go into possession"), as well as judicial and necessary, just as Lord Richter proves and confirms this same point with cited doctors and responses in the stated decision, number 49; Struve, in the stated Exercise 23, thesis 94. However, this remedy does not obtain in a gift, specifically when someone has given another a thing that he thought was worth ten, when it was actually worth 20 or more. In this case, the donor can reclaim or recover the whole thing given, so that he does not fall into a communion <note>original: "communio"</note>—which otherwise no one is forced to undertake (Law "si non sortem" 26, paragraph 4, Digest, On the claim of indebtment)—with the donee; but it is sufficient if he provides the sum that he intended to give. Donellus, on this Law 2, number 62 and following.

## THES. XXX.

Regarding the action to be duly assigned to this our remedy of Law 2—what it is and what kind arises from that law—the doctors maintain not a few dissenting opinions. We, however, do not believe it to be a <term>condictio ex lege</term> <gloss>claim arising from law</gloss> (as Arius Pinellus asserted in his hypothesis, leaning on that false one which we refuted briefly above in our thesis 4 at the beginning), nor an imploring of the judge's office, nor an extraordinary remedy or <term>restitutio in integrum</term> <gloss>restoration to original condition</gloss>. Rather, we believe a civil action arises from this our Law 2, descending from the contract itself, such that if the seller is injured, he acts from the sale; if the buyer, from the purchase; if the lessor, from the lease; if the lessee, from the hiring, and so on (argument of Law 41, beginning, Digest, On obligations and actions, joined with Law 11, paragraph 5, Digest, On actions of purchase, with Sichard on this law, number 9; Lord Struve, stated Exercise 23, thesis 92). I do not dare to assert, however, that there is any place here for an action with prescribed words, as Lord Struve does in the cited Exercise, thesis 92, so absolutely and simply. But rather, with the</translation>

<translation page="21">
requisite terms presupposed, whenever it obtains under this Law 2 in <term>innominate</term> <gloss>unnamed</gloss> contracts, I judge that a place must be granted to that action with prescribed words. From these things, it is clear that this action is personal and arises from the force of the contract itself, and therefore it can in no way have the force of a real action. Let this be joined to our thesis 20; the law "dolus" 10, Code, On good faith judgments, title, also contributes to this. And that it cannot be instituted in a summary process, but must be ventilated in an ordinary one, I assert is placed beyond all note of doubt; since this cause is ordinary and requires the most complete cognizance, as is noted from Carpzovius by Lord Richter, decision 99, number 177, where he also, in the following number 178, submits for that opinion a response given in the College of Jena: "It is the remedy of Law 2 that belongs to ordinary and not summary causes or an inquisition." He reports that it was pronounced in the same manner in the year 1645, in the month of August, in the same place. The pleading to be conceived in this action is alternative, according to what was set forth above in our thesis 22. How it should be conceived in this Law 2, Lord Arumaeus teaches in his Disputation 4, thesis 29 on this law, to whom I am forced to remit the benevolent reader for the sake of avoiding excessive prolixity.

## THES. XXXI.

In this action, since it is personal, I determine that the judge of the domicile must be approached, notwithstanding the various opinions of various people regarding this judgment. Just as in a real action the forum of the place where the thing is situated is the competent forum (final law, Code, Where an action in rem should be exercised, verse "sed in locis"), so too in a personal action the forum of the domicile is asserted to be the competent one, most rightly according to the law "haeres absens" 19, Digest, On judgments, and elsewhere.

## THES. XXXII.

This complaint of injury is not to be extended infinitely, but must be finished in a certain course of years, so that some end to lawsuits may be found (last law, Digest, For his own sake), and so that the buyer may not always be in uncertainty, and so that the ownership of things may not hang in the balance, against the principle of the Institutes, On usucapions. But how much time for acting is granted? It is disputed. Some have handed down that this action is lulled to sleep by the course and lapse of one year, others 2, others 3, others 4, others 5, others 8, others 10, others 20, others 30 years, as Ernest Cothmann widely deduces in his responses of law 53, number 68 and following; see also Pinellus on this law, part 2, chapter 1, number 26. However, this action by civil law can be brought up to 30 years (by Saxon law, up to 30 years, or a year and a day).
