<translation page="7">took the name of Caesar and ordered themselves to be called Czar, which they claimed held the same meaning among them as the name Caesar. *Orb. Polit. de Imper. Moscow. §. 7*. Here Hornius states two things that deserve notice above others: 1. That Basil was the first to assume this title for himself. 2. That it holds the same meaning among the Russians as the name Caesar. Regarding the former, there is no need to labor, since that assertion is supported by historical evidence and is therefore clear, except that I wonder why <term>the learned man</term> <note>original: "τὸν δᾶνα"</note> appears to think otherwise and names not Basil, but his successor, Ivan Basilides, that famous tyrant of Russia, as the one who first used that term. The latter, however, deserves to be examined somewhat more carefully and at greater length. For if Hornius wishes this to be understood absolutely, we rightly disagree, as we believe that the times must be distinguished above all else. For in its first imposition, the word Czar in the Russian language meant nothing more than "King," as those who have recorded Muscovite affairs, trustworthy witnesses like Baron Sigismund von Herberstein and Adam Olearius, assert. Indeed, when the former was sent as an ambassador to the Muscovite by the Emperor Maximilian, and upon his return was severely accused for having attributed the title of Czar to the Great Duke of Moscow, he argued at length in an apologetic document titled *A Defense against Unjust Accusations* (from which the celebrated Arnoldi cites some words on this matter in *Observations on Caron’s Description of Japan*, p. 34) that in the Russian language that name properly denotes nothing but "King." He did the same in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*: "If you unfold," he says, "all their histories and the Holy Scriptures, you will find King called 'Czar' everywhere, and Emperor called 'Kesfar'. p. 12." Here, indeed, he records that even King David is called a Czar by the Russians in the Holy Scriptures.

> "They call their Grand Prince," he says, "a Czar, and some want it to be derived from Caesar. The interpreters and the Germans living there call him an Emperor (*Keyser*), although the Russians also call King David a Czar."

*Travels to Persia*, fol. 149. From these it appears clearly enough that the word Czar, in its proper and genuine meaning, intends to indicate only *royal* dignity. Certainly, Hornius himself interprets Tzar not only as Emperor, but also as King. *Orb. Imperant. de Russia*, Can. 4. Nor is it improbable that Basil, by first assuming that term, did not intend a higher pinnacle of honor than *Royal*. For since his predecessor, Ivan Basilides, was the first to call himself Prince of all Russia, having acquired the name of "Great" for that reason—and was thus saluted according to Hornius as *VVelikiknesa* <note>original: "Velikiy Knyaz" or Grand Duke</note>—Basil, having expanded the borders of his principality once again, and having brought the principality of Smolensk and whatever remained of the Siberian dominion under his power, ought to be considered as not having been content with the title of Great Prince or Duke, and thus having aspired to nothing less than the Royal. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that the word Czar later took on another meaning and began to be used to designate the Majesty of an Emperor as well: which can be gathered even from the words of Olearius cited a little earlier. At what time and on what occasion this happened is not so easy to say. Baron von Herberstein speaks of this matter in the work cited: "Czar in the Ruthenian language signifies King. But since in the common Slavic language among the Poles, Bohemians, and all others, taken from a certain consonance from the last and truly heavy syllable, *Czar* is understood as Emperor or</translation>

<translation page="8">Caesar: Whence all who are not skilled in the Ruthenian idiom or letters, as well as the Bohemians, Poles, and Slavs subject to the Hungarian Kingdom, call a King by another name, namely *Kral*, others *Kyrall*, others *Koroll*: but they suppose that *Czar* is said only of a Caesar or Emperor: Whence it happened that the Ruthenian interpreters, hearing their Prince called this way by foreign nations, began themselves from then on to name him Emperor, and to consider the name *Czar* more worthy than that of King (though it signifies the same), etc." And thus he ascribes that change to the crudeness of the people. Cf. the excellent L. Mencken, *Observations on Hornius, Orb. Pol.*, l. c., p. 46. Yet no light suspicion arises that this new force of meaning was given to the word out of a certain pride of spirit, so that the Great Duke of the Russians might not appear inferior to the supreme Christian Prince, and this perhaps—if one may divine in a matter not yet sufficiently brought to light—happened in that time when that most famous tyrant, Ivan Basilides II, whom the Russians call Ivan Basilouviz, was in power. For he not only subdued the Tartar kingdoms of Kazan and Astrakhan, and, having made almost the entire Caspian Sea subject to his own law, extended his empire as far as Persia, and thus undoubtedly aspired to a name greater than Royal; but he was also the first to insert the eagle, the emblem of our Holy Empire, the double-headed eagle, into his own insignias. Thus Olearius, l. c.: "The Czar, like the Roman Emperor, carries a double eagle in the Imperial seal, and that with 2 crowns and wings cast down. This eagle the tyrant Ivan Basilowiz first introduced out of arrogance, in that he supposed himself to be sprung from the blood of the Roman Emperors." Nor did his successors hesitate from that time on to demand the title of Emperor, regarding which matter the celebrated Arnoldi is to be consulted in his *Annotations to the collectanea on the Kingdom of Siam*, appended to Schouten, p. 792. But whatever may be the case with this conjecture, which it would be rash to force upon others, I end, and I transmit this entire argument regarding the name of Caesar to the more learned, who have a richer apparatus of material and a greater power of wit and judgment, to be examined more closely. For it may suffice for me to have drawn the outlines, however much they are. Regarding C. Julius Caesar himself, from whose cognomen this treatise of ours has in some way been born, the first of the Roman Emperors, tomorrow, with God’s help, after the morning services, three of the alumni of our Gymnasium, youths of not contemptible progress, will recite orations written by them, of which the first, GEORGIUS ADAMUS Seidel of Lichtenberg in Vogtland, will recount the better virtues of Caesar: the second, JOHANNES PETRUS Meidhart of Brambach in Vogtland, will recount his flaws and vices: finally the last, JOHANNES JACOBUS Beyer, a local, placing himself as a judge of the previous orations, will signify what is to be approved in them and what is to be disapproved, and will thus finally settle the dispute regarding the murder of Caesar, asserting that with the blessed Boecler, his suffering ought to be considered just, but the action most unjust. That the Most Illustrious Count, with his noble offspring, might deign to illuminate this Act with their gracious and illustrious presence, and that the other leaders of the city, patrons, and supporters may not deny theirs, we strive as is fitting and right, promising in return to each the humblest service, respect, and readiness to serve with all our might. Here Hornius states two things that deserve notice above others: 1. That Basil was the first to assume this title for himself. 2. That it holds the same meaning among the Russians as the name Caesar. Regarding the former, there is no need to labor, since that assertion is supported by historical evidence and is therefore clear, except that I wonder why <term>the learned man</term> <note>original: "τὸν δᾶνα"</note> appears to think otherwise and names not Basil, but his successor, Ivan Basilides, that famous tyrant of Russia, as the one who first used that term. The latter, however, deserves to be examined somewhat more carefully and at greater length. For if Hornius wishes this to be understood absolutely, we rightly disagree, as we believe that the times must be distinguished above all else. For in its first imposition, the word Czar in the Russian language meant nothing more than "King," as those who have recorded Muscovite affairs, trustworthy witnesses like Baron Sigismund von Herberstein and Adam Olearius, assert. Indeed, when the former was sent as an ambassador to the Muscovite by the Emperor Maximilian, and upon his return was severely accused for having attributed the title of Czar to the Great Duke of Moscow, he argued at length in an apologetic document titled *A Defense against Unjust Accusations* (from which the celebrated Arnoldi cites some words on this matter in *Observations on Caron’s Description of Japan*, p. 34) that in the Russian language that name properly denotes nothing but "King." He did the same in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*: "If you unfold," he says, "all their histories and the Holy Scriptures, you will find King called 'Czar' everywhere, and Emperor called 'Kesfar'. p. 12." Here, indeed, he records that even King David is called a Czar by the Russians in the Holy Scriptures.

> "They call their Grand Prince," he says, "a Czar, and some want it to be derived from Caesar. The interpreters and the Germans living there call him an Emperor (*Keyser*), although the Russians also call King David a Czar."

*Travels to Persia*, fol. 149. From these it appears clearly enough that the word Czar, in its proper and genuine meaning, intends to indicate only *royal* dignity. Certainly, Hornius himself interprets Tzar not only as Emperor, but also as King. *Orb. Imperant. de Russia*, Can. 4. At what time and on what occasion this happened is not so easy to say. Baron von Herberstein speaks of this matter in the work cited: "Czar in the Ruthenian language signifies King. But since in the common Slavic language among the Poles, Bohemians, and all others, taken from a certain consonance from the last and truly heavy syllable, *Czar* is understood as Emperor or
pages.8: Caesar: Whence all who are not skilled in the Ruthenian idiom or letters, as well as the Bohemians, Poles, and Slavs subject to the Hungarian Kingdom, call a King by another name, namely *Kral*, others *Kyrall*, others *Koroll*: but they suppose that *Czar* is said only of a Caesar or Emperor: Whence it happened that the Ruthenian interpreters, hearing their Prince called this way by foreign nations, began themselves from then on to name him Emperor, and to consider the name *Czar* more worthy than that of King (though it signifies the same), etc." And thus he ascribes that change to the crudeness of the people. Cf. the excellent L. Mencken, *Observations on Hornius, Orb. Pol.*, l. c., p. 46. Yet no light suspicion arises that this new force of meaning was given to the word out of a certain pride of spirit, so that the Great Duke of the Russians might not appear inferior to the supreme Christian Prince, and this perhaps—if one may divine in a matter not yet sufficiently brought to light—happened in that time when that most famous tyrant, Ivan Basilides II, whom the Russians call Ivan Basilouviz, was in power. For he not only subdued the Tartar kingdoms of Kazan and Astrakhan, and, having made almost the entire Caspian Sea subject to his own law, extended his empire as far as Persia, and thus undoubtedly aspired to a name greater than Royal; but he was also the first to insert the eagle, the emblem of our Holy Empire, the double-headed eagle, into his own insignias. Nor did his successors hesitate from that time on to demand the title of Emperor, regarding which matter the celebrated Arnoldi is to be consulted in his *Annotations to the collectanea on the Kingdom of Siam*, appended to Schouten, p. 792. But whatever may be the case with this conjecture, which it would be rash to force upon others, I end, and I transmit this entire argument regarding the name of Caesar to the more learned, who have a richer apparatus of material and a greater power of wit and judgment, to be examined more closely. For it may suffice for me to have drawn the outlines, however much they are. Regarding C. Julius Caesar himself, from whose cognomen this treatise of ours has in some way been born, the first of the Roman Emperors, tomorrow, with God’s help, after the morning services, three of the alumni of our Gymnasium, youths of not contemptible progress, will recite orations written by them, of which the first, GEORGIUS ADAMUS Seidel of Lichtenberg in Vogtland, will recount the better virtues of Caesar: the second, JOHANNES PETRUS Meidhart of Brambach in Vogtland, will recount his flaws and vices: finally the last, JOHANNES JACOBUS Beyer, a local, placing himself as a judge of the previous orations, will signify what is to be approved in them and what is to be disapproved, and will thus finally settle the dispute regarding the murder of Caesar, asserting that with the blessed Boecler, his suffering ought to be considered just, but the action most unjust. That the Most Illustrious Count, with his noble offspring, might deign to illuminate this Act with their gracious and illustrious presence, and that the other leaders of the city, patrons, and supporters may not deny theirs, we strive as is fitting and right, promising in return to each the humblest service, respect, and readiness to serve with all our might. Given the 27th of November, in the year 1677.

There is no reason for us to labor over the first, since that assertion is supported by historical evidence, and thus it is in the open, except that I wonder that <term>tòn dâna</term> <gloss>the learned man</gloss> seems to think otherwise, naming not Basil, but his successor, Ivan Basilides, that famous tyrant of Russia, who had been the first to use that word. The latter, however, must be examined somewhat more carefully and at greater length. For if Hornius wishes that to be understood absolutely, we rightly disagree, as we believe that the times must be distinguished above all else. For at its first imposition, the word <term>Czar</term> in the Russian language did not signify anything other than King, according to those who have consigned Muscovite affairs to writing, witnesses worthy of belief, Sigismund Baron von Herberstein and Ad. Olearius. The former, indeed, when he was sent as an ambassador to the Muscovite by Emperor Maximilian, and upon his return was gravely accused because he had attributed the title of <term>Czar</term> to the Grand Duke of the Muscovites, argued at length in an apologetic text under the title: *Defense of the Unjustly Accused* (from which the celebrated Arnoldi cites some words on this matter in *Observ. ad Caronis descript. Japon.* p. 34), that by that name in the language of the Russians, nothing is properly meant but King. He did the same in *Comment. Rer. Moscov.*: “If you unfold,” he says, “all their histories and the Holy Scripture, everywhere you will find <term>Czar</term> by the name of King, and <term>Kesfar</term> <gloss>Emperor</gloss> by the name of Emperor.” p. 12. He recalls here that even King David is called <term>Czar</term> by the Russians in the Sacred Scriptures.

> Their Grand Duke, he says, they call a <term>Czar</term>, and some wish it to come from <term>Caesar</term>. The interpreters and the Germans living there call him an <term>Emperor</term> (*Keyser*), although the Russians also call King David a <term>Czar</term>.

*Itiner. Pers.* f. 149. From which it appears clearly enough that the word <term>Czar</term> in its proper and genuine meaning wishes to indicate only <term>Royal</term> dignity. Certainly, Hornius himself interprets <term>Tzar</term> not only as Emperor but also as King. *Orb. Imperant. de Russia*, Can. 4. Nor is it improbable that Basil, when he first assumed that word, did not intend a higher peak of honor than <term>Royal</term>. For since his predecessor, Ivan Basilides, was the first to call himself Prince of all Russia, having on that account obtained the name of "Great" (*Magni*), and was thus saluted according to Hornius as <term>VVelikiknesa</term> <gloss>Grand Prince</gloss>, Basilius, having again expanded the borders of the principality, and having brought the principality of Smolensk and whatever remained of the Siberian dominion under his power, not content with the title of Great Prince or Duke, should be considered to have aspired to a title superior to Ducal, and thus nothing less than Royal. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that the word <term>Czar</term> later took on another meaning and began to be usurped to designate the Majesty of an Emperor as well: which one may collect even from the words of Olearius cited a little earlier. At what time and on what occasion this happened is not so easy to say. The Baron von Herberstein speaks of the matter in the aforementioned place as follows: "<term>Czar</term> in the Ruthenian language signifies King. But since in the common Slavonic language among the Poles, Bohemians, and all others, taken from a certain consonance from the last and indeed deep syllable, <term>Czar</term> is understood as Emperor or
pages.8: <term>Caesar</term>: Whence all who are not skilled in the Ruthenian idiom or letters, likewise the Bohemians, Poles, and Slavs subject to the Hungarian Kingdom, call the King by another name, namely <term>Kral</term>, others <term>Kyrall</term>, others <term>Koroll</term>: but they think <term>Czar</term> is said only for Caesar or Emperor: Whence it happened that the Ruthenian interpreters, hearing their Prince called thus by foreign Nations, began themselves to name him Emperor thereafter, and to think that the name <term>Czar</term> is more worthy than that of King (though it signifies the same), etc. And thus he attributes that change to the crudity of the race. Cf. the Excellent L. Mencken, *Animadv. ad Horn. Orb. Pol.*, loc. cit., p. 46. Yet not a slight suspicion arises that from a certain arrogance of spirit, and so that the Grand Duke of the Russians might not seem inferior to the supreme Prince of Christians, this new meaning was given to the word, and that perhaps—if one is allowed to divine in a matter not yet brought to sufficient clarity—it happened in that time when that most famous Tyrant, Ivan Basilides II, whom the Russians call <term>Ivan Basilouviz</term> <gloss>Ivan son of Basil</gloss>, held power. For he not only subdued the Tartar kingdoms of Kazan and Astrakhan, and, having made almost the entire Caspian Sea his own, extended the empire as far as Persia, and thus undoubtedly aspired to a name greater than Royal; but he was also the first to insert the ensign of our Sacred Empire, the <term>double-headed eagle</term>, into his own emblems. Thus Olearius, loc. cit.: "The Czar, like the Roman Emperor, carries a double eagle in the Imperial seal, and that with 2 crowns and wings cast down." Such an eagle the tyrant Ivan Basilowiz first introduced out of arrogance, as he imagined himself to be descended from the blood of the Roman Emperors, nor did his successors hesitate from that time to demand the title of Emperor; on which matter see the celebrated Arnoldi in *Annotat. ad collectanea de Regno Siam*, added to Schouten, p. 792. But whatever may be the case with this conjecture, which it would be rash to want to force upon others, I finish, and I transmit this whole argument concerning the Name of Caesar to more learned men, who have a richer apparatus of facts and a greater force of talent and judgment, to be examined more closely. For it should suffice for me to have drawn the outlines in some fashion. As for C. Julius Caesar himself, from whose surname this treatise of whatever kind was born for us, the First of the Roman Emperors, tomorrow, with God's help, after the morning rites, three students of our Gymnasium, young men of no contemptible progress, will recite Orations written by themselves. The first of whom, GEORGIUS ADAMUS Seidel of Lichtenberg in Vogtland, will recount the major virtues of Caesar; the second, JOHANNES PETRUS Meidhart of Brambach in Vogtland, will enumerate his faults and vices; the last finally, JOHANNES JACOBUS Beyer, our local student, positioning himself as it were as an arbiter of the previous orations, will signify what is to be approved in them and what is to be disapproved, and will thus finally compose the dispute concerning the slaughter of Caesar, so that, with the Blessed Boecler, he will assert that the passion ought to be judged just, but the action most unjust. That the Most Illustrious Count, along with his Noble Offspring, might deign to illuminate this Act with their Gracious and Illustrious presence, and that the other leaders of the City, patrons, and supporters may not deny theirs to him, as is fitting and proper, we contend, promising in return for our part the most humble service, observance, and readiness to assist, given on the 5th day before the Kalends of December, in the year 1677.

To prepare for wars with a great heart, and in a prudent manner
to arrange the affairs of war; to be able to cautiously 
avoid frauds, engines, tricks,
and deceits which the host of enemies attempts,
is a matter of great labor and importance.
But it is considered to be of greater weight
to enter the fight with a stronger effort,
and with sharp force and martial virtue
to strike the enemies, and to advance with glowing
iron through his phalanxes and troops.
But he is thought to possess all these moments,
and is judged to deserve all the praise 
of fortitude, who destroys opposing forces
with a huge slaughter,
and, departing as victor, he rejoices and triumphs.
In an equal manner, it is a praiseworthy thing indeed,
and very beautiful, to be consumed by a burning
love for good and pleasant letters;
to handle the sciences by day and night.
But he is worthy of even greater praise
who not only sings to his own Muses
at home, but sometimes produces the powers
of his own genius, and sets forth theses in a public place,
and happily entrusts himself to the hazard
of disputation, and challenges the opposing side:
but he is able to be proud of a most beautiful thing
</translation>

<translation page="24">
who disputes, and brings back
from the disputation the name and fame
of a victor, with learned men applauding.
With this mind, dear Lerse, mount the chair,
and defend with a masculine heart and ready tongue,
defend against the attacks of the enemy and the hostile
missiles of objections, those things which your learned pen
wrote down, relying on the hope of victory; and the illustrious
palm with which Apollo will adorn your hair.

hence fitting rewards are to be hoped for by YOU for your labor:
